derivations.claim: Interleaving $(a_n,b_n)_{n\ge1}$ as $(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots)$ is a linear isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so [F7] gives the stated real Hilbert structure. The integral of $f^\dagger$ over $[-\pi,\pi]$ is $\pi^2-\pi^2=0$, so its constant Fourier coefficient vanishes and its real Fourier coefficient sequence lies in the stated mean-zero coefficient space. The real cosine and sine modes are orthonormal because they are the real and imaginary parts of the orthonormal character basis in [F1].

For every $n\ge1$, $t_n>0$ and $t_n\to0$ exponentially since $R>1$. The ratio of consecutive squared multipliers is $((n+1)/n)^2((n+2)/(n+1))^2R^{-2}$, which tends to $R^{-2}<1$; choose $\rho$ strictly between $R^{-2}$ and $1$, then the ratio is at most $\rho$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Thus $\sum_{n\ge1}2t_n^2<\infty$. The operator is injective because all its diagonal multipliers are positive. Its truncation to frequencies $n\le N$ is finite rank and the operator-norm error is $\sup_{n>N}t_n\to0$, so $T_R$ is compact and Hilbert–Schmidt.

The frequency multipliers satisfy $t_{n+1}/t_n=(n+2)/(nR)$, which can exceed $1$ for small $n$; thus the frequency order is not always the singular-value order. The multiset of modes has a nonincreasing enumeration: at every stage a remaining maximum exists because $t_n\to0$ and only finitely many modes lie above any fixed positive threshold, and the fixed tie rule selects one uniquely. Every mode is eventually listed because only finitely many modes have multiplier at least its positive multiplier. The operator is diagonal on the orthonormal cosine–sine basis, so the frequency eigenvalue is $\mu_n=t_n^2=n^2(n+1)^2R^{-2n-4}$ twice at each frequency, and the enumerated singular system has these values in nonincreasing order. Since $(n+1)^2\asymp n^2$, $\mu_n\asymp n^4e^{-2n\log R}$, an exponential spectrum with exponent $\vartheta=1$.

For every $\lambda\ge0$, $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ is nonnegative, $\alpha q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$, and $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$. If $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, then $\lambda+\widetilde\alpha<\lambda+\alpha$, so $q_\alpha(\lambda)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(\lambda)$. Thus it is an ordered filter with $C_q'=1$ by [F6]. Its trace variance is
$$
V(\alpha):=2\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\mu_n}{(\mu_n+\alpha)^2},\qquad \alpha>0.
$$
On every compact interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, each summand is continuous and is bounded above by $2\mu_n/a^2$. Since $\sum_n2\mu_n<\infty$ by step 1.2, the series converges uniformly there, so $V$ is continuous. Each summand strictly decreases as $\alpha$ increases, hence so does $V$. Also $V(\alpha)\le2\alpha^{-2}\sum_n\mu_n\to0$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. For every fixed $n$, $V(\alpha)\ge2\mu_n/(\mu_n+\alpha)^2\to2/\mu_n$ as $\alpha\downarrow0$; because $\mu_n\to0$, these lower bounds imply $V(\alpha)\to\infty$. Fix any $c>0$ and $\theta>1$. Continuity, strict decrease, and these endpoint limits give a unique $\alpha_m>0$ with $V(\alpha_m)=c\theta^m$ for every $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Thus $\alpha_m$ decreases to zero and the variances $v_m=\sigma^2V(\alpha_m)$ have the constant consecutive ratio $\theta$. The resulting infinite grid meets [F2], and the SOLIT rule truncates it at its finite $m_{\max}$.

The truth lies in $L^2$ because it is bounded, and its Fourier coefficients are coordinates in the model by [F1]. The positive diagonal multipliers give the injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator verified in step 1.2; the Tikhonov filter satisfies [F6] and its candidates satisfy [F2], and the positive-noise experiment and finite selector are [F3]–[F4]. The well-definedness and moment properties of its estimators follow from [F5]. This example asserts no rate for the resulting estimator.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The characters
$(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]): they are
orthonormal and their closed linear span is all of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact linear operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces (each with a countable dense subset), and assume $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, meaning that for its positive singular values $s_j$ the sum $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^2$ is finite. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

An ordered spectral filter is a family of functions $q_\alpha:[0,\lambda_1]\to[0,\infty)$ indexed by a set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\infty)$ with $0$ as an accumulation point, such that for constants $C_q'<\infty$ and $C_q''=1$,
$$
0\le\alpha q_\alpha(x)\le C_q',\qquad 0\le xq_\alpha(x)\le1,
$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$
\theta_1\le\frac{V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)}{V_{T,q}(\alpha_{m-1})}\le\theta_2\qquad(m\ge1).
$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$
the operator norm of the estimator-noise covariance in the singular basis. The bound $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ make each $u_m$ and $v_m$ finite. The finite candidate set ends at
$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces, let $S=T^*T$, and let $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ be a fixed positive singular system with $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Let $Z$ be a real isonormal Gaussian process on $Y$, meaning that $g\mapsto Z(g)$ is linear into $L^2$, is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. In the weak observation experiment $Y_x(g)=\langle Tx,g\rangle_Y+\sigma Z(g)$ with known noise standard deviation $\sigma>0$, use the ordered filter $q_\alpha$, the geometric-variance candidates $\alpha_0>\cdots>\alpha_{m_{\max}}$, and variances $v_m=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2$ from the preceding definition. For each candidate index $m$, the regularized estimator $\widehat x_m$ is the $L^2$ limit of its finite singular-coordinate sums; its $j$th coordinate is $\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$, where $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ and $\xi_j=Z(u_j)$.

Take as input the observed sequence $y=(y_j)_{j\ge1}$, where $y_j:=Y_x(u_j)$. For each candidate $m$ and each $N=1,2,\ldots$, compute
$$
\widehat x_{m,N}^{\mathrm{obs}}:=\sum_{j=1}^N s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)y_jv_j.
$$
If these partial sums converge in $X$, define $\widehat x_m(y)$ to be their limit; otherwise set $\widehat x_m(y)=0_X$. This specifies an $X$-valued output for every input sequence. The quantities $v_{m_1,m_2}$ and $z_{m_1,m_2}(x)$ are determined by the known operator, filter, noise level and Gaussian coordinate law.

For $0\le m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, set
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2
$$
and let $N_{m_1,m_2}$ be the norm of the centered estimator difference divided by $\sigma$. For $x>0$, define its upper quantile by
$$
z_{m_1,m_2}(x):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N_{m_1,m_2}>z)\le e^{-x}\}.
$$
Given fixed $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$, for $0\le m<m_{\max}$ put $x_m:=2(1+\gamma)\log(v_{m+1}/v_0)$, and for each pair $m_1<m_2$ put $\eta_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma z_{m_1,m_2}(x_{m_1})+\beta\sqrt{v_{m_1,m_2}}$. Accept an index $m_1$ exactly when $\|\widehat x_{m_1}(y)-\widehat x_{m_2}(y)\|_X\le\eta_{m_1,m_2}$ for every $m_2$ with $m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, and output the smallest accepted index $\widehat m$ and parameter $\widehat\alpha=\alpha_{\widehat m}$. For $m_1=m_{\max}$, accept without comparisons, including when $m_{\max}=0$. This rule uses only the observed sequence, the known operator and filter, the noise level, the fixed candidate grid, and $\beta,\gamma$; it does not use $x$ or its source index $\varphi$.

Assume Countable Choice and the positive-noise Gaussian sequence model with $\sigma>0$, a fixed complete positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ for an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator $T:X\to Y$, and a truth with coordinates $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ in $\ell^2$. Write $\lambda_j=s_j^2$ and let $\xi_j$ be the independent standard-normal noise coordinates. Let $q_\alpha$ be nonnegative and satisfy $0\le\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le1$, $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$, and $q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\le q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$ whenever $m_1<m_2$. For each candidate $m$, form the finite sums
$$
X_{m,N}:=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j\bigr)v_j.
$$
The conclusion below includes the existence of their limit $\widehat x_m$ in $L^2(\Omega;X)$. Put $f_m:=\mathbb E\widehat x_m$, $B_m:=\|f_m-x\|_X$, and $v_m:=\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-f_m\|_X^2$. Then $\widehat x_m$ is a measurable $X$-valued random element with finite second moment and
$$
\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|_X^2=B_m^2+v_m,\qquad v_m=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
If $m_1<m_2$, then $B_{m_2}\le B_{m_1}$, $\|f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}\|_X\le B_{m_1}$, and
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\mathbb E\| (\widehat x_{m_2}-f_{m_2})-(\widehat x_{m_1}-f_{m_1})\|_X^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2\le v_{m_2}.
$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact linear operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces (each with a countable dense subset), and assume $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, meaning that for its positive singular values $s_j$ the sum $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^2$ is finite. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

$$

$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$

$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$

$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.

derivations.claim: Interleaving the constant coordinate and cosine–sine pairs is a linear isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so [F7] gives the stated real Hilbert structure. The real Fourier modes are orthonormal by taking real and imaginary parts of the character basis in [F1]. On each positive frequency, $\partial_{xx}\cos(nx)=-n^2\cos(nx)$ and $\partial_{xx}\sin(nx)=-n^2\sin(nx)$, so solving $\partial_tu=\partial_{xx}u$ multiplies both coefficients by $e^{-n^2\bar t}$; the constant mode is unchanged. Therefore the operator in the Example is the periodic heat forward map in Fourier coordinates.

Every multiplier of $T_{\bar t}$ is positive, so $T_{\bar t}$ is injective. The positive-frequency multipliers tend to zero, so finite-frequency truncations converge in operator norm and $T_{\bar t}$ is compact. Moreover, $\sum_{n\ge1}2e^{-2n^2\bar t}<\infty$ by comparison with the geometric series $\sum_{n\ge1}2e^{-2n\bar t}$, so the operator is Hilbert–Schmidt. Squaring the multipliers gives the stated eigenvalues of $T_{\bar t}^*T_{\bar t}$.

For spectral cut-off, the inverse-eigenvalue contribution at frequency $n$ is $2e^{2n^2\bar t}$. Since $V_{n-1}\le(2n-1)e^{2(n-1)^2\bar t}$,
$$
\frac{V_n}{V_{n-1}}=1+\frac{2e^{2n^2\bar t}}{V_{n-1}}\ge1+\frac{2}{2n-1}e^{2(2n-1)\bar t}\longrightarrow\infty.
$$
Hence no finite $\theta_2$ bounds all consecutive ratios in this sequence, as claimed.

For every $\lambda\ge0$, $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ is nonnegative, $\alpha q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$, and $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$. If $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, then $\lambda+\widetilde\alpha<\lambda+\alpha$, so $q_\alpha(\lambda)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(\lambda)$. Thus it is an ordered filter with $C_q'=1$ by [F6]. Its variance is $V(\alpha)=1/(1+\alpha)^2+2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-2n^2\bar t}(e^{-2n^2\bar t}+\alpha)^{-2}$. On each compact interval $\alpha\ge a>0$, the summands are continuous and bounded by $2a^{-2}e^{-2n^2\bar t}$, a summable sequence, so $V$ is continuous there by uniform convergence. It is strictly decreasing. For $\alpha\ge1$, $V(\alpha)\le\alpha^{-2}(1+2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-2n^2\bar t})\to0$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. It tends to infinity as $\alpha\downarrow0$: for every $N$, its first $N$ positive-frequency terms tend to $2\sum_{n=1}^N e^{2n^2\bar t}$, and these partial sums are unbounded in $N$. The intermediate value theorem therefore selects recursively a decreasing sequence with any prescribed fixed ratio $\theta_1>1$ between consecutive variance values; its upper ratio is the same $\theta_1$. The estimator and each finite comparison are well-defined by [F3]–[F5].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then

   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor

2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable

derivations.claim: Put $Q_n=\sum_{j\le n}a_j\xi_j^2$, $v_n=\sum_{j\le n}a_j$, and $w_n=\sum_{j\le n}a_j^2$. On finite intervals integration by parts with $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$ gives $\int x^{2k}\phi(x)\,dx=[-x^{2k-1}\phi(x)]+(2k-1)\int x^{2k-2}\phi(x)\,dx$. The boundary terms vanish at infinity; the integrals converge since a polynomial times $e^{-x^2/2}$ is bounded by a constant times $e^{-x^2/4}$, whose integral is finite by [F3] and the given unit Gaussian integral. Starting from $\int\phi=1$ therefore gives $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^4=3$. Thus $\mathbb E Q_n=v_n$ and finite independence gives $\mathbb E Q_n^2=v_n^2+2w_n$. Also $u\le v$ and $w\le uv\le v^2$.

The measurable series $Q_n\uparrow Q$ satisfies $\mathbb E Q=v$ by [F1]; hence $Q<\infty$ almost surely, since [F2] gives $\mathbb P(Q\ge r)\le v/r$ for every $r>0$. Extending $N$ by zero on the null exceptional set does not change an integral. Applying [F1] also to $Q_n^2\uparrow Q^2$ proves $\mathbb E N^4=v^2+2w\le3v^2$.

Suppose $u>0$. For $0<s<(2u)^{-1}$ the scalar substitution $y=\sqrt{1-2sa_j}\,x$ in [F3], using the supplied unit density, gives $\mathbb E e^{s a_j\xi_j^2}=(1-2sa_j)^{-1/2}$. Finite factorization [F4] and the power-series inequality $-\log(1-z)-z\le z^2/[2(1-z)]$ for $0\le z<1$ therefore give $$\log\mathbb E e^{s(Q_n-v_n)}=\sum_{j\le n}\left[-sa_j-\tfrac12\log(1-2sa_j)\right]\le\frac{s^2w_n}{1-2us}.$$ If $w_n>0$, apply [F2] to this exponential and choose $s=\sqrt t/(\sqrt{w_n}+2u\sqrt t)$. Substitution gives $-s(2\sqrt{w_nt}+2ut)+s^2w_n/(1-2us)=-t$, so $\mathbb P\{Q_n>v_n+2\sqrt{w_nt}+2ut\}\le e^{-t}$. If $w_n=0$, then $Q_n=v_n=0$ almost surely and this inequality is immediate.

The deterministic levels $v_n+2\sqrt{w_nt}+2ut$ converge to $v+2\sqrt{wt}+2ut$. Whenever $Q$ strictly exceeds this final level, sufficiently large $n$ have $Q_n$ exceeding their corresponding levels. The probability of this eventual-event set is at most the lower limit of their probabilities, as follows directly by countable additivity applied to unions of intersections. Step 2.2 thus gives the first tail inequality. Since $w\le uv$ and $v+2\sqrt{uvt}+2ut\le(\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut})^2$, the second follows. If $u=0$, all weights vanish and both bounds hold directly.

The second tail bound makes the set defining $q(t)$ nonempty and implies $0\le q(t)\le\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut}$. This set is upward closed. Every $q(t)+1/n$ therefore belongs to it: by the definition of an infimum some member lies strictly below that number. The events $\{N>q(t)+1/n\}$ increase to $\{N>q(t)\}$, so countable additivity gives $\mathbb P(N>q(t))\le e^{-t}$. When $v=0$, step 2.1 gives $N=0$ almost surely and the quantile is zero. Finally, in a fixed orthonormal system the squared norm of the finite Gaussian sum is $Q_n$; finiteness of $Q$ gives norm convergence of that series and the asserted norm interpretation.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, where separable means having a countable dense subset, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\Theta\subseteq X$ be a nonempty parameter set, let $K:X\to H$ be a signal map, and let $\epsilon>0$. For $x\in\Theta$ and $g\in H$, define the observation functional

$$Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g).$$

The associated statistical inverse experiment has sample space $\mathbb R^H$ with the cylinder sigma-algebra generated by the evaluation maps $y\mapsto y(g)$, and its sampling law $P_x$ is the law of the random function $g\mapsto Y_x(g)$. Each sample is indexed by test functionals on $H$; it is not asserted to be a vector in $H$ or to have a continuous path. If $H=\{0\}$, linearity forces $Z(0)=0$ and the experiment is deterministic.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Fix a probe $\Phi\in H$. By [F1] and [F2], whose supplier hypotheses are recorded in [A1], its mean at parameter $x$ is $\langle x,K^*\Phi\rangle_X$ and its variance is finite, equal to $\epsilon^2\|\Phi\|_H^2$. If it is unbiased for every $x$, then $\langle x,K^*\Phi-h_\phi\rangle_X=0$ for every $x\in X$. Taking $x=K^*\Phi-h_\phi$ gives $K^*\Phi=h_\phi$, so $h_\phi\in R(K^*)$.

Conversely, if $h_\phi\in R(K^*)$, use [A1] to choose $\Phi\in H$ with $K^*\Phi=h_\phi$. Equations [F1] and [F2] then give $\mathbb E_xY_x(\Phi)=\langle x,h_\phi\rangle_X=\phi(x)$ for every $x$, and [F1] gives its finite variance $\epsilon^2\|\Phi\|_H^2$. Hence this probe is an exact one-probe estimator, proving both directions and the variance assertion.

It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\Theta\subseteq X$ be a nonempty parameter set, let $K:X\to H$ be a signal map, and let $\epsilon>0$. For $x\in\Theta$ and $g\in H$, define the observation functional

$$Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g).$$

The associated statistical inverse experiment has sample space $\mathbb R^H$ with the cylinder sigma-algebra generated by the evaluation maps $y\mapsto y(g)$, and its sampling law $P_x$ is the law of the random function $g\mapsto Y_x(g)$. Each sample is indexed by test functionals on $H$; it is not asserted to be a vector in $H$ or to have a continuous path. If $H=\{0\}$, linearity forces $Z(0)=0$ and the experiment is deterministic.

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

Let a proper Bayesian model be given, and let $J$ be its joint prior-predictive probability on $(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$, supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. More generally, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X:\Omega\to\Theta$ and $Y:\Omega\to\mathsf Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). A **posterior regular conditional distribution (posterior RCD)** is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, in the sense of [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. It is a kernel indexed by the sample point $\omega\in\Omega$. The canonical realization is $\Omega=\Theta\times\mathsf Y$ with $Q=J$ and coordinate maps $X(\theta,y)=\theta$, $Y(\theta,y)=y$.

A **data-indexed posterior kernel** is a probability kernel $\Pi_{\cdot}$ from $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ to $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) for which $\omega\mapsto\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ ([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). Equivalently, for every $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$Q(X\in A,\ Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,Q_Y(dy),$$
where $Q_Y$ is the data marginal (equal to $J_Y$). This kernel is indexed by data values, not sample points.

The definition asserts no existence of either conditional kernel. Values of a data-indexed version on a measurable $J_Y$-null set are not fixed by the conditional-law identities; replacing them there by a fixed probability preserves those identities. A dominated-density construction is a separate route: [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] requires a proper prior, a sigma-finite data measure, and a specified jointly measurable sampling density, and fills fibres whose marginal density is zero or infinite with the prior. It does not require the data space to be standard Borel.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_jX_{t_j}
$$
has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of Multivariate normal law, including singular covariance. Indeed, that definition says
exactly that every scalar projection of the vector is normal. This also covers
repeated times, zero coefficients, and singular covariance matrices; no
distinct-time convention is needed for this definition.

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint positive operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ is a
nonnegative real for every $x$. Then there is a compact self-adjoint positive
operator $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ with $S^{2}=T$, and it is unique: if
$R\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact and positive
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]) with $R^{2}=T$,
then $R=S$. The root acts by multiplication by $\sqrt\lambda$ on each positive
eigenspace $E_\lambda(T)=\ker(T-\lambda I)$, $\lambda>0$, and by zero on
$\ker T$; in particular $S$ is the operator denoted $\sqrt T$ or $T^{1/2}$.

Throughout, $H$ and $K$ are real or complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-hilbert-space]]), $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) of
operator norm $\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]), and $E$ is a **Hilbert basis**
of $H$, that is, a complete orthonormal subset of $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
The basis $E$ is **supplied as data**; the definitions below are stated
relative to it.

**The Hilbert–Schmidt square-sum.** The family $(\|Te\|^2)_{e\in E}$ consists of
nonnegative real numbers and is indexed by the arbitrary set $E$. Its sum is the
supremum of the finite subsums,

$$s_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2 \;:\; F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

in the finite-subset-supremum convention of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]; the empty finite
subset contributes the empty sum $0$, so the supremum is over a nonempty
set and exists in $[0,+\infty]$. No enumeration, ordering or countability of
$E$ is used or asserted, and no choice is performed: the supremum ranges over
the set of finite subsets of the fixed index set $E$. For finite $E$ the
supremum is the ordinary finite sum over $E$, because all terms are
nonnegative.

**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a basis.** The operator $T$ is
**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$** when $s_E(T)<+\infty$, that is, when the
finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$. In that case the
**Hilbert–Schmidt norm of $T$ relative to $E$** is the nonnegative square root

$$\|T\|_{HS,E}:=\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,+\infty).$$

When $s_E(T)=+\infty$, no Hilbert–Schmidt norm relative to $E$ is defined, and
$T$ is not Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**Degenerate and extreme cases.** The zero operator satisfies $s_E(0)=0$ for
every basis $E$, so it is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every basis with norm
$0$. If $H=\{0\}$ then the empty family is a Hilbert basis of $H$, the only
finite subset is empty, and $s_\varnothing(T)=0$ for the only linear operator
$T:\{0\}\to K$; that operator is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to the empty basis
with norm $0$. If $H$ is finite dimensional and $E$ is finite, $s_E(T)$ is an
ordinary finite sum of the squared norms $\|Te\|^2$, and $T$ is automatically
Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**The basis is part of the notation.** The symbol $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ keeps the
basis in the subscript on purpose. Until the next result is proved, the phrase
"$T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt" is never used without a specified Hilbert basis, and
nothing here asserts that a Hilbert basis of $H$ exists: the existence of $E$
is a hypothesis of the definition, and the question of whether the finiteness
of $s_E(T)$ and the value $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ depend on $E$ is taken up in
[[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]. In particular this
definition makes no basis-existence claim and no comparison with the operator
norm $\|T\|$; every such statement is proved later, where its own hypotheses
are displayed.

**Notation.** For a finite $F\subseteq E$ we write
$s_F(T):=\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2$ for the finite subsum, so that
$s_E(T)=\sup\{s_F(T):F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]), with Hilbert adjoint
$T^*\in\mathcal B(K,H)$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]],
[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]). Let $E$ be a Hilbert basis of $H$ and $F$ a
Hilbert basis of $K$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
let $s_E(T)=\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2$ and $s_F(T^*)=\sum_{f\in F}\|T^*f\|^2$ be the
finite-subset-supremum sums of
[[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]] and
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Then:

1. **(matrix-coefficient form)** the finite-subset supremum
   $$\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{e\in A}\sum_{f\in B}|\langle Te,f\rangle|^2 \;:\; A\subseteq E,\ B\subseteq F \text{ finite}\Bigr\}$$
   equals $s_E(T)$, and it also equals $s_F(T^*)$;
2. **(basis independence)** $s_E(T)=s_{E'}(T)$ for every Hilbert basis $E'$ of
   $H$, and $s_E(T)=s_F(T^*)$ for every Hilbert basis $F$ of $K$;
3. **(membership and norms)** $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$ if and
   only if it is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every other Hilbert basis of $H$,
   and then $\|T\|_{HS,E}=\|T\|_{HS,E'}=\|T^*\|_{HS,F}$ for all such bases
   $E,E'$ and every Hilbert basis $F$ of $K$; when the common defining sum is
   $+\infty$, none of these Hilbert–Schmidt norms is defined, and $T$ is
   Hilbert–Schmidt relative to none of the bases.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Let $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. If
$T:X\to Y$ is compact ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) and $A:W\to X$ and
$B:Y\to Z$ are bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), then
the composites $TA:W\to Y$ and $BT:X\to Z$ are compact.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex
Hilbert spaces and let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For
$\lambda>0$, define

$$B_\lambda:=A^*A+\lambda I_X.$$

Then $B_\lambda:X\to X$ is bijective and

$$\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le\frac1\lambda.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Assume AC. Let $(U_1,U_2)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal vector with mean $(m_1,m_2)$ and covariance
$$\begin{pmatrix}S&0\\0&T\end{pmatrix},$$
where $S$ and $T$ are allowed to be singular positive-semidefinite matrices. Then the random vectors $U_1$ and $U_2$ are independent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $E$ be a Hilbert basis of $H$
(supplied as data), with $s_E(T)=\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2$ the Hilbert–Schmidt
square-sum and $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ the Hilbert–Schmidt norm of
[[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]. Then:

1. if $S,T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$, then so is
   $aS+bT$ for all scalars $a,b$, and
   $$\|aS+bT\|_{HS,E}\le|a|\,\|S\|_{HS,E}+|b|\,\|T\|_{HS,E};$$
2. if $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$, then for every
   Hilbert basis $F$ of $K$ the adjoint $T^*$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $F$
   and
   $$\|T^*\|_{HS,F}=\|T\|_{HS,E};$$
3. if $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$ and
   $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$ are bounded with $E_0$ a
   Hilbert basis of $H_0$ and $F$ a supplied Hilbert basis of $K$, then
   $AT\in\mathcal B(H,L)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$ and
   $TB\in\mathcal B(H_0,K)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E_0$, with
   $$\|AT\|_{HS,E}\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_{HS,E},\qquad \|TB\|_{HS,E_0}\le\|T\|_{HS,E}\,\|B\|,$$
   and consequently
   $$\|ATB\|_{HS,E_0}\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_{HS,E}\,\|B\| .$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $E$ be a Hilbert
basis of $H$ and $G$ a Hilbert basis of $K$ (both supplied as data), and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then:

1. **(factorization of a trace-class operator)** if $T$ is trace class
   ([[def-trace-class-operator]]), then, with $|T|$, $U$ and the singular system
   of $T$ ([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]],
   [[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]), the operators
   $$B:=|T|^{1/2}\in\mathcal B(H),\qquad A:=U|T|^{1/2}\in\mathcal B(H,K)$$
   satisfy $T=AB$, are both Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$
   ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), and
   $$\|A\|_{HS,E}=\|B\|_{HS,E}=\|T\|_1^{1/2},$$
   so that $\|A\|_{HS,E}\|B\|_{HS,E}=\|T\|_1$: the trace norm is attained by this
   factorization;
2. **(products of Hilbert–Schmidt operators are trace class)** conversely, if
   there are a real or complex Hilbert space $H_0$ with a supplied Hilbert basis
   $E_0$, a Hilbert–Schmidt operator $B\in\mathcal B(H,H_0)$ relative to $E$ and a
   Hilbert–Schmidt operator $A\in\mathcal B(H_0,K)$ relative to $E_0$ with
   $T=AB$, then $T$ is trace class and
   $$\|T\|_1\le\|A\|_{HS,E_0}\|B\|_{HS,E};$$
   in particular $AB$ is compact and $\|T\|\le\|A\|_{HS,E_0}\|B\|_{HS,E}$.

The bases $E$, $E_0$, $G$ are supplied data; no existence of a Hilbert basis is
asserted or used, and the adjoint-stability of the Hilbert–Schmidt norm across
$G$ is the imported invariance theorem.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Set $S=C_0^{1/2}$. The positive trace-class operator $C_0$ is compact by [F4], so $S$ is compact and self-adjoint. Then $B=SK^*KS$ is compact, self-adjoint, and positive, because a composition containing a compact operator is compact. By [F5], applied to $KS$, $B+\epsilon^2I_X$ is bijective and $R$ is bounded. Its inverse is self-adjoint: writing $x=(B+\epsilon^2I)u$ and $z=(B+\epsilon^2I)v$ transfers symmetry of $B+\epsilon^2I$ to $R$. It is positive because $\langle Rz,z\rangle=\langle v,(B+\epsilon^2I)v\rangle\ge\epsilon^2\|v\|^2$ when $z=(B+\epsilon^2I)v$. The inverse identities give $BR=RB=I-\epsilon^2R$. For $z\in X$, put $v=Rz$, so $z=(B+\epsilon^2I)v$. Expanding this equation and using self-adjointness of $B$ gives $\|z\|^2-\epsilon^2\langle Rz,z\rangle=\|Bv\|^2+\epsilon^2\langle Bv,v\rangle\ge0$. Thus $0\le\epsilon^2R\le I_X$, so $BR=I-\epsilon^2R$ is positive and $I-BR=\epsilon^2R\ge0$. Define $D=SBR S$; then $D$ is positive, $C_{\rm post}=\epsilon^2SRS$ is positive, and $D+C_{\rm post}=S(BR+\epsilon^2R)S=C_0$. The products are trace class by [F8] because $S$ is Hilbert–Schmidt and the intervening operators are bounded. Consequently $0\le D\le C_0$ and $\operatorname{tr}D\le\operatorname{tr}C_0$.

For $g\in H$, write $Y_0(g)=Y(g)-\langle Km_0,g\rangle_H$. The signal and noise are independent, so covariance expansion gives $\mathbb E[Y_0(g)Y_0(k)]=\langle K C_0K^*g,k\rangle_H+\epsilon^2\langle g,k\rangle_H$. For $h\in X$, $Y_0(\Phi_h)=y(\Phi_h)-\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle_H$ when the observed field is $y$. Using $S K^*\Phi_h=BRSh$ and $\Phi_h=KSRSh$, the covariance identity yields $\mathbb E[Y_0(\Phi_h)Y_0(\Phi_k)]=\langle SBRSh,k\rangle_X=\langle Dh,k\rangle_X$. Likewise $\mathbb E[\langle U-m_0,h\rangle_XY_0(\Phi_k)]=\langle Dh,k\rangle_X$. These equalities follow by expanding the two covariance terms, using $BR=RB$ and $(B+\epsilon^2I)R=I$.

For the supplied finite or countable basis $(v_j)$ of $X$, [F8] and step 1.1 give $\mathbb E\sum_j|Y_0(\Phi_{v_j})|^2=\sum_j\langle Dv_j,v_j\rangle_X=\operatorname{tr}D\le\operatorname{tr}C_0<\infty$. Therefore the nonnegative sum is finite almost surely: if it were infinite on a set of positive probability, its expectation would exceed every finite bound. Parseval gives $\sum_j|\langle m_0,v_j\rangle_X|^2=\|m_0\|_X^2<\infty$, and $|a+b|^2\le2|a|^2+2|b|^2$ shows $\sum_j b_j(Y)^2<\infty$ on that probability-one set. Hence the first branch of the Statement's definition applies and $M_Y=m_0+\sum_jY_0(\Phi_{v_j})v_j$ there. The same argument includes finite and empty bases. The series converges in $X$ by [F7]. Its partial sums are measurable; their Cauchy set is a countable intersection and union of norm-comparison events, hence measurable, and completeness of $X$ gives a limit there. For each nonempty closed set $F\subseteq X$, distance to $F$ is continuous, so the distance of the limit to $F$ is the limit of the measurable distances of the partial sums; [F11] makes this limit measurable. Because each coordinate map $y\mapsto y(\Phi_{v_j})$ is measurable for the cylinder sigma-algebra, the convergence construction and the default value $m_0$ show that $y\mapsto M_y$ is measurable from $(\mathbb R^H,\mathcal C_H)$ to $X$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. For each fixed $h$, expand $h$ in the supplied basis. The corresponding finite linear combinations of $Y_0(\Phi_{v_j})$ converge in $L^2$ to $Y_0(\Phi_h)$, since [F7] makes the basis projections converge to $h$ and [step 2.1] bounds the squared error by $\|D\|$ times the squared projection error. The same finite combinations converge almost surely to the inner product of the coordinate-series limit with $h$. Uniqueness of limits in probability gives $\langle M_Y-m_0,h\rangle_X=Y_0(\Phi_h)$ almost surely for this fixed $h$. This proves the displayed posterior-mean formula, with an exceptional set allowed to depend on $h$.

For fixed $h\in X$ and $g\in H$, covariance expansion gives $\operatorname{Cov}(\langle U-m_0,h\rangle_X,Y_0(g))=\langle KC_0h,g\rangle_H$. The covariance of $Y_0(\Phi_h)$ with $Y_0(g)$ is $\langle KC_0K^*\Phi_h+\epsilon^2\Phi_h,g\rangle_H$. Since $C_0=S^2$, $SK^*KS=B$, and $(B+\epsilon^2I)R=I$, one has $KC_0K^*\Phi_h+\epsilon^2\Phi_h=KSB RSh+\epsilon^2KSRSh=KS(B+\epsilon^2I)RSh=KSS h=KC_0h$. By step 3.1, $\langle M_Y-m_0,h\rangle=Y_0(\Phi_h)$ almost surely, so the residual $W=U-M_Y$ has zero covariance with every observation $Y(g)$. Both $\langle U-m_0,h\rangle$ and $Y_0(\Phi_h)$ are centered, so the same identity shows $\mathbb E\langle W,h\rangle=0$ for each $h$; thus $W$ is centered. Its covariance is $C_0-D=C_{\rm post}$ by the two covariance identities in step 2.1 and the covariance of $U$.

For each fixed basis vector $v_j$, step 3.1 identifies $\langle M_Y-m_0,v_j\rangle$ almost surely with $Y_0(\Phi_{v_j})$. For any finite list of basis vectors, intersect the corresponding probability-one events; the associated coordinates of $W$ are then linear images of finite Gaussian projections of $U-m_0$ and $Z$. The same holds jointly with any finite list of observations. These two blocks are independent by [F12] and jointly Gaussian by [F3] and [F6]; step 4.1 makes their cross-covariance zero, so [F6] makes the residual-coordinate block independent of the observation block. The rational finite linear combinations of the supplied basis $(v_j)$ form a countable dense subset of $X$. For each center in this set, Parseval expresses the squared distance from $W$ as the limit of finite sums of squared basis-coordinate differences, so open balls with rational radii about these centers are measurable in the basis-coordinate sigma-algebra; they form a countable base, proving that these coordinates generate the Borel sigma-algebra of $W$. Finite basis-coordinate cylinder rectangles have the product of their marginal probabilities; since they form a generating pi-system for the joint Borel and basis-observation sigma-algebras, [F9] extends this identity and proves that $W$ is independent of $\mathcal G:=\sigma(Y(e_n):n)$. To compare with the full field sigma-algebra, write the supplied basis of $H$ as $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ if finite, allowing $m=0$, or as $(e_n)_{n\ge1}$ if countably infinite. For finite $m$ put $P_Ng=\sum_{1\le n\le\min(N,m)}\langle g,e_n\rangle_He_n$; for an infinite basis put $P_Ng=\sum_{1\le n\le N}\langle g,e_n\rangle_He_n$. In either case the empty sum is zero, $r_N:=g-P_Ng$ tends to zero, and in the finite or empty case $r_N=0$ after the basis is exhausted. The mean-square error of $D_N:=Y(g)-Y(P_Ng)$ is at most $(\|Km_0\|^2+\|K\|^2\|C_0\|+\epsilon^2)\|r_N\|^2$. Choose the least $N_k\ge k$ with $\|r_{N_k}\|\le2^{-k}$. For each positive integer $r$, Markov gives $\mathbb P(|D_{N_k}|\ge1/r)\le r^2(\|Km_0\|^2+\|K\|^2\|C_0\|+\epsilon^2)4^{-k}$, a summable bound; [F11] implies $|D_{N_k}|<1/r$ eventually almost surely. The countable intersection over $r$ still has probability one, so $D_{N_k}\to0$ and each field evaluation is measurable with respect to the completion $\overline{\mathcal G}^{\mathbb P}$. Thus $\sigma(Y(g):g\in H)\subseteq\overline{\mathcal G}^{\mathbb P}$. Independence of $W$ from $\mathcal G$ extends to its completion because every completed event differs by a null set from an event in $\mathcal G$; therefore $W$ is independent of the full field.

The map $y\mapsto M_y$ is measurable by step 3.1. Let $
u$ be the Borel law of the residual random element $W$, whose mean is zero and covariance is $C_{m post}$ by step 4.1. Define $\Pi_y(A)=\int_X\mathbf1_A(M_y+w)\,
u(dw)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(X)$. The map $(y,w)\mapsto M_y+w$ is measurable, and [F10] makes $y\mapsto\Pi_y(A)$ measurable; for each $y$, translation of $
u$ is a probability measure. Since $W$ is independent of the full data field by step 5.1 and $U=M_Y+W$, integrating first with respect to the fixed law $
u$ gives $\mathbb P(U\in A,Y\in C)=\int_C\Pi_y(A)\,P_Y(dy)$ for every Borel $A\subseteq X$ and $C\in\mathcal C_H$. This is the regular conditional distribution identity from [F2].

For every finite list $h_1,\ldots,h_q\in X$, step 3.1 gives almost surely, simultaneously for this finite list, $\langle W,h_a\rangle=\langle U-m_0,h_a\rangle-Y_0(\Phi_{h_a})$. The vector of these residual functionals is therefore a linear image of finite Gaussian projections of $U-m_0$ and $Z$, whose blocks are independent by [F12] and jointly Gaussian by [F3] and [F6]; hence it is jointly Gaussian. Step 4.1 gives that $W$ is centered with covariance $C_{\rm post}$, so $W$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element with that covariance. Translating by $M_y$ shows that every section $\Pi_y$ is Gaussian with mean $M_y$ and covariance $C_{\rm post}$, including the zero-dimensional and finite-dimensional cases. For fixed $h$, step 3.1 identifies the posterior mean with $\langle m_0,h\rangle+y(\Phi_h)-\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle$ almost surely, and the scalar marginal under a translated Gaussian is normal with variance $\langle C_{\rm post}h,h\rangle$. This proves all asserted posterior-law and feature-marginal formulas; the exceptional set remains feature-dependent.
