The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $0<\epsilon$, let $(s_j)_{j\ge1}$ be the positive singular values in the Gaussian sequence inverse model, and let a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger=(\theta^\dagger_j)_{j\ge1}$ belong to $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$. Let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\tau_j^2<\infty$, and let the prior be a Borel probability on $\ell^2$ whose coordinates are independent $N(0,\tau_j^2)$ variables, independent of the observation noise. Under the prior-predictive law the observations are $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$; under the fixed truth they are $Y_j=s_j\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. Define $v_j=(\tau_j^{-2}+s_j^2/\epsilon^2)^{-1}$ and $\lambda_j=\tau_j^2s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)$. For fixed-truth-almost every data sequence, a posterior version on $\ell^2$ is the restriction of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jY_j/s_j,v_j)$. Its expected posterior squared distance from the truth is
$$S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger):=\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}\!\left[\int_{\ell^2}\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid Y)\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\left[(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta^\dagger_j)^2+\frac{v_j^2s_j^2}{\epsilon^2}+v_j\right].$$
The identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$; under the stated trace condition its right side is finite. For every $R>0$, the expected posterior mass outside the radius-$R$ ball is at most $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)/R^2$. In particular, if $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$ for a constant $C$ and a positive $r_\epsilon\to0$, then $r_\epsilon$ is a posterior contraction rate in the sense of the preceding definition.

Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon\!\left[\Pi_\epsilon\!\left(\{\theta\in\ell^2:\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2>M_\epsilon r_\epsilon\}\mid Y\right)\right]\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\epsilon\downarrow0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal basis of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$,
that is, a complete orthonormal family
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
define the **Fourier coefficient map**

$$\Phi:H\to\ell^2(I,\mathbb F),\qquad \Phi(x):=(\langle x,e_i\rangle)_{i\in I}$$with values in the space of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Then $\Phi$ is a linear bijection satisfying$$\|\Phi(x)\|_2=\|x\|,\qquad \langle \Phi(x),\Phi(y)\rangle_{\ell^2}=\langle x,y\rangle \qquad\text{for all } x,y\in H .$$

In particular $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete, hence a Hilbert space, with
the inner product of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let
$T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of
finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space, let $Y$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), and let
$T_n:X\to Y$, $n\in\mathbb N$, be compact operators
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) with $\|T_n-T\|\to0$ for a bounded linear
operator $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-operator-norm]], [[def-metric-convergence]]). Then $T$ is compact.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
converges to $T$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-metric-convergence]]).  Here the displayed scalar series is, under the
library convention, the series of the sequence
$(\|u_{m+1}\|\,\|v_{m+1}\|)_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case
$$\|T\|_1=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|:\ R_m\to T\ \text{in operator norm}\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being over all such **nuclear representations** of $T$, with the
same zero-based shift understood in every displayed sum, and the
infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,
the singular-value series
$T=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ is a nuclear representation with
sum $\|T\|_1$.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let $\Gamma:H\to H$ be positive, self-adjoint and trace class. Then there is a Borel $H$-valued random element $G$ such that every $\langle G,h\rangle_H$ is a centered real normal random variable and
$$\mathbb E[\langle G,h\rangle_H\langle G,k\rangle_H]=\langle\Gamma h,k\rangle_H\qquad(h,k\in H).$$
This is the centered Gaussian law with covariance operator $\Gamma$; it includes finite-rank and zero covariance.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

It is positive and self-adjoint; its truncations $\Gamma_N$ have finite rank, and $\|\Gamma-\Gamma_N\|\le\sup_{j>N}\tau_j^2\le\sum_{j>N}\tau_j^2\to0$, so [F6] makes $\Gamma$ compact. For each finite coordinate vector, every linear projection is centered normal by [F7], hence it is jointly Gaussian by [F8]; its covariance matrix is diagonal with entries $\tau_j^2$. Repeatedly applying [F9] to the first coordinate and the remaining block proves that the coordinates are independent, and [F10] identifies their laws as $N(0,\tau_j^2)$. Put $d=1+2\alpha+2p$ and $J=\lceil\epsilon^{-2/d}\rceil$. Since $\epsilon^{-2/d}\ge1$, one has $\epsilon^{-2/d}\le J\le2\epsilon^{-2/d}$. Write $b_j=1-\lambda_j=\epsilon^2/(\epsilon^2+j^{-d})\le\min\{1,\epsilon^2j^d\}$. The ellipsoid condition gives $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le L^2\sup_j b_j^2j^{-2\beta}$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $0<\epsilon$, let $(s_j)_{j\ge1}$ be the positive singular values in the Gaussian sequence inverse model, and let a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger=(\theta^\dagger_j)_{j\ge1}$ belong to $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$. Let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\tau_j^2<\infty$, and let the prior be a Borel probability on $\ell^2$ whose coordinates are independent $N(0,\tau_j^2)$ variables, independent of the observation noise. Under the prior-predictive law the observations are $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$; under the fixed truth they are $Y_j=s_j\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. Define $v_j=(\tau_j^{-2}+s_j^2/\epsilon^2)^{-1}$ and $\lambda_j=\tau_j^2s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)$. For fixed-truth-almost every data sequence, a posterior version on $\ell^2$ is the restriction of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jY_j/s_j,v_j)$. Its expected posterior squared distance from the truth is
$$S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger):=\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}\!\left[\int_{\ell^2}\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid Y)\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\left[(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta^\dagger_j)^2+\frac{v_j^2s_j^2}{\epsilon^2}+v_j\right].$$
The identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$; under the stated trace condition its right side is finite. For every $R>0$, the expected posterior mass outside the radius-$R$ ball is at most $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)/R^2$. In particular, if $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$ for a constant $C$ and a positive $r_\epsilon\to0$, then $r_\epsilon$ is a posterior contraction rate in the sense of the preceding definition.

Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon\!\left[\Pi_\epsilon\!\left(\{\theta\in\ell^2:\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2>M_\epsilon r_\epsilon\}\mid Y\right)\right]\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\epsilon\downarrow0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal basis of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$,
that is, a complete orthonormal family
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let

By [F8] there is a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G$ in $H$ with covariance $\Gamma$. For each finite coordinate vector, every linear projection is centered normal by [F8], hence it is jointly Gaussian by [F9]; its covariance matrix is diagonal with entries $\tau_j^2$. Repeatedly applying [F10] to the first coordinate and the remaining block proves that the coordinates are independent, and [F11] identifies their laws as $N(0,\tau_j^2)$. Thus the law of $G$ is the stated prior on $\ell^2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $0<\epsilon$, let $(s_j)_{j\ge1}$ be the positive singular values in the Gaussian sequence inverse model, and let a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger=(\theta^\dagger_j)_{j\ge1}$ belong to $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$. Let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\tau_j^2<\infty$, and let the prior be a Borel probability on $\ell^2$ whose coordinates are independent $N(0,\tau_j^2)$ variables, independent of the observation noise. Under the prior-predictive law the observations are $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$; under the fixed truth they are $Y_j=s_j\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. Define $v_j=(\tau_j^{-2}+s_j^2/\epsilon^2)^{-1}$ and $\lambda_j=\tau_j^2s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)$. For fixed-truth-almost every data sequence, a posterior version on $\ell^2$ is the restriction of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jY_j/s_j,v_j)$. Its expected posterior squared distance from the truth is
$$S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger):=\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}\!\left[\int_{\ell^2}\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid Y)\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\left[(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta^\dagger_j)^2+\frac{v_j^2s_j^2}{\epsilon^2}+v_j\right].$$
The identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$; under the stated trace condition its right side is finite. For every $R>0$, the expected posterior mass outside the radius-$R$ ball is at most $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)/R^2$. In particular, if $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$ for a constant $C$ and a positive $r_\epsilon\to0$, then $r_\epsilon$ is a posterior contraction rate in the sense of the preceding definition.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon\!\left[\Pi_\epsilon\!\left(\{\theta\in\ell^2:\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2>M_\epsilon r_\epsilon\}\mid Y\right)\right]\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\epsilon\downarrow0.$$

derivations.claim: The prior $\delta_0=N(0,0)$ is a proper centered Gaussian law. Under its prior-predictive joint law, $\theta=0$ almost surely, so for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, $\mathbb P(\theta\in A,Y\in B)=\mathbf 1_A(0)\mathbb P_0^\epsilon(Y\in B)=\int_B\delta_0(A)\,\mathbb P_0^\epsilon(dy)$. Thus the constant kernel $y\mapsto\delta_0$ is a posterior version. The prior assigns zero mass to every ball centered at $e_1$ of radius less than $1$.

Under the fixed truth $e_1$, only the first data coordinate shifts. Relative to the prior-predictive data law, the one-coordinate normal density ratio is $L(y)=\exp\!\left(\frac{s_1y_1}{\epsilon^2}-\frac{s_1^2}{2\epsilon^2}\right)$, and it integrates to $1$ under the prior-predictive first-coordinate law. It is positive and finite for every $y$ by [F4]–[F6]. All remaining coordinates have identical independent laws. The two full product-Borel data laws therefore agree as finite measures on the generating cylinder $\pi$-system after weighting by $L$; [F5] extends the identity to all data events. Since $L>0$, the laws are equivalent, so the posterior version $\delta_0$ remains the same almost surely under the truth law.

For any candidate rate $r_\epsilon\to0$, take $M_\epsilon=r_\epsilon^{-1/2}$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon$. Then $M_\epsilon\to\infty$ and $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon=\sqrt{r_\epsilon}<1$ eventually. The posterior is concentrated at $0$, whose distance from $e_1$ is $1$, so its mass outside the radius-$M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ ball is exactly $1$ under the truth law. This violates [F7] and refutes the Statement. The example lies outside the positive-coordinate-variance hypotheses in [F2].

$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$\Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}.$$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2.$$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

The adaptive empirical-Bayes credible balls have nonvanishing frequentist
coverage uniformly over every truth in a hyperrectangle $\Theta_\beta(M)$.

**Explicit sparse-gap construction.**

Use [[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]], assume AC,
and fix $\beta>0$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and a finite
$A>\beta$. Run the procedure with the fixed cap $A_n=A$ and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Choose
$0<M\le(1984C^8)^{-1}$. Put $s=1+2\beta+2p$, $\rho_j=2^j$,
$n_1=2$, and
$$n_{j+1}=\left\lceil(2\rho_{j+1}^2)^s n_j\right\rceil,\qquad N_j=n_j^{1/s}.$$
Define the fixed nonnegative truth by
$$\theta_{0,i}^2=\begin{cases}0,&N_j/\rho_j<i\le N_j\text{ for some }j,\\0,&2N_j<i\le\rho_jN_j\text{ for some }j,\\Mi^{-1-2\beta},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$
Then $\theta_{0,1}=0$ and $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$. For every
deterministic nonnegative inflation sequence for which there exist
$K_L\in(0,\infty)$ and $j_0\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every $j\ge j_0$,
$$L_{n_j}\le K_L\sqrt M\,\rho_j^{(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)}$$
one has
$$P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_{n_j}(L_{n_j})\}\longrightarrow0.$$
The finitely many indices with $n_j<3$ are irrelevant. In particular,
for every $\beta>0$ this gives a counterexample for any fixed cap
$A>\beta$, including constant inflation factors.

Use the Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$,
$\rho\ge2$, and $\gamma\in(0,1)$. Assume that
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ and
$\theta_{0,1}=0$. Then there is a finite inflation constant $L>0$,
depending only on the fixed model and class parameters, such that
$$\inf_{\substack{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)\\ \theta_{0,1}=0}} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_n(L)\} \longrightarrow1.$$
This is conservative frequentist coverage tending to one, not exact
asymptotic coverage $1-\gamma$. The source also allows a sequence of caps
$A_n>0$ satisfying, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$A_n\le \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}.$$
In that case there is a constant $K_{\mathrm{infl}}>0$, depending only on the
fixed model and class parameters and not on $n$, such that the same coverage
conclusion holds for any deterministic inflation sequence satisfying
$$L_n\ge K_{\mathrm{infl}}(3\rho^{3(1+2p)})^{A_n}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge3$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$,
an inflation factor $L\ge0$, and a finite $A_n>0$. Let
$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}.$$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1,$$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}).$$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}.$$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$\ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right].$$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$\widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

derivations.claim: Every squared coordinate is either zero or $Mi^{-1-2\beta}$, so $\sup_i i^{1+2\beta}\theta_{0,i}^2\le M$ and $\sum_i\theta_{0,i}^2\le M\sum_i i^{-1-2\beta}<\infty$. Also $N_1=2^{1/s}\in(1,2)$ and $\rho_1=2$, hence $N_1/\rho_1<1\le N_1$ and the first zero gap contains $i=1$. Thus $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$ and $\theta_{0,1}=0$.

Fix any polished-tail parameters $L_0\ge1$, integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho_*\ge2$. The recursion gives $N_j/\rho_j\ge2\rho_jN_{j-1}>\rho_{j-1}N_{j-1}$, so every earlier gap ends below $N_j/\rho_j$. Also $N'_j=\lfloor2N_j\rfloor+1\le2N_j+1$; because $N_j\to\infty$ and $\rho_j\to\infty$, for all sufficiently large $j$ we have $N'_j\ge N_0$ and $\rho_*(2N_j+1)\le\rho_jN_j$, whence $\lfloor\rho_*N'_j\rfloor\le\rho_jN_j$. Since $N'_j>2N_j$, the block $[N'_j,\lfloor\rho_*N'_j\rfloor]$ lies in the current zero gap $(2N_j,\rho_jN_j]$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $i_j=\lfloor\rho_jN_j\rfloor+1\le\rho_jN_j+1<4\rho_jN_j\le N_{j+1}/\rho_{j+1}$, so $i_j$ is before the next first gap; applying the same separation at later indices puts all still later gaps farther right. Since $\rho_jN_j>2N_j+1\ge N'_j$ eventually, $i_j>N'_j$; earlier gaps end below $N_j/\rho_j<i_j$. Hence $i_j$ lies outside every zero gap and is in the tail from $N'_j$, with $\theta_{0,i_j}^2=Mi_j^{-1-2\beta}>0$. The block sum is zero while that tail is positive, violating [F2]. Thus $\theta_0$ is outside every fixed polished-tail class.

For a fixed $L\ge1$, take $L_{n_j}=L$ and $K_L=L/\sqrt M$. Since $(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)>0$ and $\rho_j\ge1$, we have $L_{n_j}=L\le K_L\sqrt M\,\rho_j^{(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)}$ for every $j$. Applying [F3] gives $P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_{n_j}(L)\}\to0$. By [F6] this is the frequentist coverage at the fixed truth; because $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$ by step 1.1, the infimum coverage over that hyperrectangle cannot have lower limit at least $1-\gamma$.

The positive coverage statement [F4] has the additional polished-tail hypothesis, which fails for $\theta_0$ by step 2.1. Thus the sparse-gap undercoverage does not contradict the polished-tail theorem; it refutes only the broader fixed-inflation claim over the full hyperrectangle.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]]. A compatible complete metric may be fixed for a construction; it is not additional data in the law. The empty space admits no such law, since its measure must be both zero and one.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The rationals embed densely in the reals), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $A$ be at most countable ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then
$B$ is at most countable.

The proof establishes the sharper statement about subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ from
which this follows: **a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is finite if it is
bounded above, and countably infinite if it is not.**

**No choice principle is used.** This is the point of the lemma rather than a
footnote to it. The enumeration of an unbounded $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is built
by always taking the *least* element of $S$ above the previous one, and the least
element of a nonempty set of naturals is canonical
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): it is determined by $S$, not selected from it.
Replacing "least" by "some" would turn the construction into an appeal to
dependent choice.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of at most countable sets
([[def-countable]]) indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. Then

$$U = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$$

is at most countable.

**The role of $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.** It is spent at exactly one step, step 3.1 below, where a surjection $\mathbb N\to A_n$ is selected simultaneously for each nonempty $A_n$. The individual countability hypotheses assert that these sets of surjections are nonempty; they specify no simultaneous selection.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ (Order on the reals). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric (Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear (Isometry, isometric embedding, and the subspace metric on a subset): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: If $H=\{0\}$, then it has only one Borel probability measure and the conclusion holds. Otherwise, let $\mathcal C$ be the family of all finite coordinate cylinder sets $\pi_F^{-1}(B)$, where $F\subseteq J$ is finite and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^F$ is Borel. Each cylinder is Borel by continuity in [F1]. The family contains $H$, and the intersection of two cylinders is the finite-coordinate cylinder obtained on the union of their index sets. Hence $\mathcal C$ is a pi-system.

Enumerate the basis if it is infinite, and in the finite case repeat the last partial sum after all basis vectors have appeared. For $x_0\in H$ and $r>0$, put $S_N(x)=\sum_{j\le N}|\langle x-x_0,e_j\rangle|^2$. By [F2], $\|x-x_0\|^2=\sup_N S_N(x)$, so $$B(x_0,r)=\bigcup_{\substack{q\in\mathbb Q\\0\le q<r^2}}\ \bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x:S_N(x)\le q\}.$$ Indeed, if $\|x-x_0\|^2<r^2$, choose a rational strictly between these two numbers; conversely, membership in one intersection gives $\|x-x_0\|^2\le q<r^2$. By [F1] and [F6], each $S_N$ is Borel, and $\{S_N\le q\}$ is a cylinder over a Borel subset of $\mathbb R^F$. Thus every open ball belongs to $\sigma(\mathcal C)$.

Let $D$ be the set of all finite rational linear combinations of basis vectors. If the basis is finite, $D$ is at most countable by [F3]. If it is countably infinite, enumerate it and write $D$ as the union over $N$ of the sets of rational linear combinations of the first $N$ vectors. Each of those sets is at most countable by [F3], so their union is at most countable by the Countable Choice clause of [F3]. The real span of the basis is dense by completeness. Each finite real linear combination is approximated by a rational one: approximate each of its finitely many coefficients by a rational and use the triangle inequality and $\|e_j\|=1$. Thus $D$ is dense in $H$. By definition, this makes $H$ separable. [[def-separable-space]] The balls $B(d,s)$ with $d\in D$ and positive rational $s$ form an at most countable family by [F3], and they are open by [F5]. They are a base: given $x\in U$ with $U$ open, choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$, then $d\in D$ with $\|d-x\|<r/3$, and a rational $s$ with $\|d-x\|<s<r-\|d-x\|$. The triangle inequality gives $x\in B(d,s)\subseteq B(x,r)\subseteq U$. By step 2.1 every such ball lies in $\sigma(\mathcal C)$, so every open set, as a union of a subfamily of this countable base, lies in $\sigma(\mathcal C)$.

Every coordinate map is continuous by [F1], so $\sigma(\mathcal C)\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$. Step 3.1 and the definition of the Borel sigma-algebra give the reverse inclusion. Thus $\sigma(\mathcal C)=\mathcal B(H)$.

The assumed equality of finite-coordinate measures makes $
u$ and $
u'$ agree on every cylinder in $\mathcal C$. They are probability measures, so they agree on $H$ as well. The pi-system $\mathcal C$ generates $\mathcal B(H)$ by step 4.1; [F4] therefore gives $
u=
u'$.
