Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) converges to a real
number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ be a real or complex normed space. Let $I$ be a nonempty directed preorder and $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ a net in $X$ ([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). For $x\in X$, write $x_i\rightharpoonup x$ and say the net **converges weakly to $x$** when it converges to $x$ in $\sigma(X,X^*)$ ([[def-weak-topology-on-a-normed-space]], [[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). Equivalently,

$$\forall f\in X^*\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists i_0\in I\ \forall i\ge i_0:\quad |f(x_i)-f(x)|<\varepsilon.$$

Indeed, topological convergence implies each of these eventual conditions because the inverse disk is a neighborhood. Conversely, a neighborhood contains a finite intersection of inverse scalar neighborhoods containing $x$. Coordinate convergence gives an eventual index for each of the finitely many conditions; directedness gives a common upper bound for them, after which the whole intersection contains the net. For the empty intersection use any index of the nonempty $I$. This proves the equivalence without a choice axiom.

A **weakly convergent sequence** is this definition with $I=\mathbb N$ in its usual order. A constant net converges weakly to its value, including in the zero space. The specified limit must be a point of $X$; without a separation hypothesis uniqueness is not part of the definition. Weak closure continues to mean topological closure, not merely the set of limits of sequences.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $D\subseteq X$ be nonempty, and let $F:D\to Y$ be a forward map. The domain $D$ is **weakly closed** when it is closed in the weak topology $\sigma(X,X^*)$, the coarsest topology making every bounded real-linear functional on $X$ continuous. The graph of $F$ is **sequentially weak-to-weak closed** when, for every sequence $(x_n)$ in $D$ and every $x\in X$ and $z\in Y$, the conditions $x_n\rightharpoonup x$ and $F(x_n)\rightharpoonup z$ imply $x\in D$ and $F(x)=z$; here weak convergence means convergence under every bounded real-linear functional on the corresponding Hilbert space. We call $F$ a **weakly closed forward map** when its domain is weakly closed and its graph is sequentially weak-to-weak closed. No linearity, norm continuity, Fréchet differentiability, or convexity is assumed; linear maps are allowed as special cases.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $D\subseteq X$ be a nonempty domain, and let $F:D\to Y$ be a forward map. For a regularization parameter $\alpha>0$, reference element $x_0\in X$, and datum $y\in Y$, the **nonlinear Tikhonov functional** is the map $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}:D\to[0,\infty)$ defined by

$$
J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x):=\frac12\|F(x)-y\|_Y^2+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x-x_0\|_X^2\qquad(x\in D).
$$

A **global minimizer** is a point $x_\alpha\in D$ such that $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x_\alpha)\le J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x)$ for every $x\in D$. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty open set in the norm topology. A **nonlinear forward model on Hilbert spaces** is a map $F:U\to Y$; no linearity is assumed, and linear maps are allowed as special cases. For $y\in Y$, its exact solution set is

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

A point $x^\dagger\in U$ generates the exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$. When $F$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x\in U$, write $F'(x):X\to Y$ for its unique bounded real-linear derivative.

Thus the graph has the required sequential weak-to-weak closure, and [F1, F5] identify this as an open-domain nonlinear forward map between real Hilbert spaces.
By [F4] and the given parameters, $J(t)=\frac12(t^2-1)^2+\frac12t^2$. Set $u=t^2\ge0$. Then $J(t)=\frac12(u-1)^2+\frac12u$.

Completing the square gives $J(t)=\frac12(u-\frac12)^2+\frac38$. This is at least $3/8$, with equality exactly when $u=1/2$, equivalently $t=1/\sqrt2$ or $t=-1/\sqrt2$. These two distinct points are therefore exactly the global minimizers.

The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

A **measure space** is a triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ in which $X$ is a set, $\mathcal A$ is a sigma-algebra on $X$, and $\mu$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measure]]). The members of $\mathcal A$ are the **measurable sets** of the space.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $X$ be a real or
complex Banach space. An $X$-valued **measurable simple function** is a function
$s:\Omega\to X$ having a representation

$$s=\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_j\mathbf 1_{A_j},$$

where $m\geq 0$, the sets $A_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint, and the
vectors $x_j\in X$ are distinct and nonzero. The value of $s$ off
$\bigcup_jA_j$ is $0$. The empty representation is therefore the zero
function.

The simple function is **integrable** when $\mu(A_j)<\infty$ for every nonzero
coefficient $x_j$. Its integral over $E\in\mathcal A$ is

$$\int_E s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mu(E\cap A_j)x_j.$$

In particular, $\int s\,d\mu$ means $\int_\Omega s\,d\mu$. Requiring finite
measure only for the nonzero level sets avoids the undefined product
$0\cdot\infty$. The next lemma proves that the displayed value does not depend
on the chosen disjoint representation.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

The integral of an integrable Banach-valued simple function is independent of
its disjoint measurable representation. It is linear, is unchanged when the
integrand is changed on a null set, and satisfies

$$\left\|\int_Es\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|s\|\,d\mu$$

for every measurable $E$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) converges to a real
number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ be a real or complex normed space. Let $I$ be a nonempty directed preorder and $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ a net in $X$ ([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). For $x\in X$, write $x_i\rightharpoonup x$ and say the net **converges weakly to $x$** when it converges to $x$ in $\sigma(X,X^*)$ ([[def-weak-topology-on-a-normed-space]], [[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). Equivalently,

$$\forall f\in X^*\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists i_0\in I\ \forall i\ge i_0:\quad |f(x_i)-f(x)|<\varepsilon.$$

Indeed, topological convergence implies each of these eventual conditions because the inverse disk is a neighborhood. Conversely, a neighborhood contains a finite intersection of inverse scalar neighborhoods containing $x$. Coordinate convergence gives an eventual index for each of the finitely many conditions; directedness gives a common upper bound for them, after which the whole intersection contains the net. For the empty intersection use any index of the nonempty $I$. This proves the equivalence without a choice axiom.

A **weakly convergent sequence** is this definition with $I=\mathbb N$ in its usual order. A constant net converges weakly to its value, including in the zero space. The specified limit must be a point of $X$; without a separation hypothesis uniqueness is not part of the definition. Weak closure continues to mean topological closure, not merely the set of limits of sequences.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty open set in the norm topology. A **nonlinear forward model on Hilbert spaces** is a map $F:U\to Y$; no linearity is assumed, and linear maps are allowed as special cases. For $y\in Y$, its exact solution set is

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

A point $x^\dagger\in U$ generates the exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$. When $F$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x\in U$, write $F'(x):X\to Y$ for its unique bounded real-linear derivative.

Assume the ultrafilter lemma, dependent choice, and the real Hahn–Banach dominated-extension principle. Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $D\subseteq X$ be nonempty and weakly closed, and let $F:D\to Y$ be a map such that for every sequence $(x_n)$ in $D$ and every $x\in X,z\in Y$, $x_n\rightharpoonup x$ and $F(x_n)\rightharpoonup z$ imply $x\in D$ and $F(x)=z$. Here $D$ is closed in the coarsest topology making every bounded real-linear functional continuous, and weak convergence means convergence under every such functional. For any $\alpha>0$, $x_0\in X$, and $y\in Y$, the nonlinear Tikhonov functional

$$
J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x)=\frac12\|F(x)-y\|_Y^2+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x-x_0\|_X^2\qquad(x\in D)
$$

attains a global minimum on $D$; that is, there exists $x_\alpha\in D$ such that $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x_\alpha)\le J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x)$ for every $x\in D$. No exact solution of $F(x)=y$ is required.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $D\subseteq X$ be a nonempty domain, and let $F:D\to Y$ be a forward map. For a regularization parameter $\alpha>0$, reference element $x_0\in X$, and datum $y\in Y$, the **nonlinear Tikhonov functional** is the map $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}:D\to[0,\infty)$ defined by

$$
J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x):=\frac12\|F(x)-y\|_Y^2+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x-x_0\|_X^2\qquad(x\in D).
$$

A **global minimizer** is a point $x_\alpha\in D$ such that $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x_\alpha)\le J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x)$ for every $x\in D$. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

In ZF, the Axiom of Dependent Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice:
every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-choice-function]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $D\subseteq X$ be nonempty, and let $F:D\to Y$ be a forward map. The domain $D$ is **weakly closed** when it is closed in the weak topology $\sigma(X,X^*)$, the coarsest topology making every bounded real-linear functional on $X$ continuous. The graph of $F$ is **sequentially weak-to-weak closed** when, for every sequence $(x_n)$ in $D$ and every $x\in X$ and $z\in Y$, the conditions $x_n\rightharpoonup x$ and $F(x_n)\rightharpoonup z$ imply $x\in D$ and $F(x)=z$; here weak convergence means convergence under every bounded real-linear functional on the corresponding Hilbert space. We call $F$ a **weakly closed forward map** when its domain is weakly closed and its graph is sequentially weak-to-weak closed. No linearity, norm continuity, Fréchet differentiability, or convexity is assumed; linear maps are allowed as special cases.

derivations.claim: The assignment $\mu(A)=|A|/2$ is a measure: it is zero on $\varnothing$, and any disjoint sequence of subsets of the two-point set has at most two nonempty members, so cardinalities, hence measures, add over the union. For $s\notin\{0,1\}$, the two singleton level sets of $g_s$ have distinct nonzero coefficients $s,s^2$ and measure $1/2$ each. For $s=0$, use the empty representation of the zero function; for $s=1$, use $g_1=\mathbf1_\Omega$. In all cases [F2] gives an integrable simple function with integral $\frac12s+\frac12s^2$, and the constant approximating sequence in [F3] gives the same Bochner integral. Since $F(1)=1$, $F(-1)=0$, and $F(0)=0$, it fails additivity and is nonlinear.

The domain $D=\mathbb R$ is the entire weak topology space and is therefore weakly closed. If $s_n\rightharpoonup s$, [F5] applied to the identity functional gives $s_n\to s$ in the usual real topology. The factorization $F(s_n)-F(s)=\frac12(s_n-s)(1+s_n+s)$ shows $F(s_n)\to F(s)$, because convergence of $s_n$ makes the second factor bounded. If also $F(s_n)\rightharpoonup z$, [F5] gives $F(s_n)\to z$; uniqueness of real limits yields $z=F(s)$. Thus the graph is sequentially weak-to-weak closed.

The domain $U=\mathbb R$ is norm-open and nonempty, so [F6] confirms that this is also a forward map in the batch-25 open-domain convention. The graph and domain conditions just verified satisfy [F10]; with the real-Hilbert structure [F4] and axioms [A1]–[A3], they meet the hypotheses of [F7]. The DC-to-countable-choice consequence [F9] is the selection strength used in that theorem's proof. By [F8] this is the stated functional, so for every $\alpha>0$, $x_0,y\in\mathbb R$ it attains a global minimum.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: The supremum defining $R^*(\xi)$ includes the term at $z=x$, so $R^*(\xi)\ge\langle\xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}-R(x)$. Adding $R(x)$ gives the Fenchel–Young inequality.
If $\xi\in\partial R(x)$, [F1] gives $\langle\xi,z\rangle_{X^*,X}-R(z)\le\langle\xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}-R(x)$ for all $z$; taking the supremum and then using the term $z=x$ proves equality.

Conversely, if equality holds, every term in the supremum satisfies $\langle\xi,z\rangle_{X^*,X}-R(z)\le R^*(\xi)=\langle\xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}-R(x)$. Rearrangement gives [F1], hence $\xi\in\partial R(x)$.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, the **Bregman distance** generated by $\xi^\dagger$ from the reference point $x^\dagger$ to $x$ is

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}.$$

The subgradient inequality makes this quantity nonnegative, and $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x^\dagger,x^\dagger)=0$. The definition fixes the orientation: the first argument is the comparison point and the second is the reference point carrying the chosen subgradient.

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, let $F:D(F)\subseteq X\to Y$, let $x^\dagger\in D(F)$ with exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$, and let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex with $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$. Fix $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$, an exponent $1\le p<\infty$, a continuous nondecreasing concave function $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, a coefficient $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0\ge R(x^\dagger)$. The **variational source condition** with these data holds on the named regularizer sublevel $L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}$ when

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad(x\in L_{R_0}).$$

The condition is an assumption on the selected subgradient and the stated sublevel; it makes no assertion that a subgradient exists at every point or that a regularized minimizer exists.

Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing, concave, and satisfy $\psi(0)=0$. Extend $g=-\psi$ to $\mathbb R$ by $g(s)=+\infty$ for $s<0$, and define $H(q):=g^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$ for $q>0$, assuming the displayed suprema below are finite. For $c_1,c_2,C_3,\alpha>0$ and $d,r,e\ge0$, if

$$c_1r+c_2\alpha e\le d+\alpha\psi(C_3r),$$

then

$$e\le\frac1{c_2}\left(\frac d\alpha+H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{C_3\alpha}\right)\right),\qquad r\le\frac2{c_1}\left(d+\alpha H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{2C_3\alpha}\right)\right).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty open set in the norm topology. A **nonlinear forward model on Hilbert spaces** is a map $F:U\to Y$; no linearity is assumed, and linear maps are allowed as special cases. For $y\in Y$, its exact solution set is

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

A point $x^\dagger\in U$ generates the exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$. When $F$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x\in U$, write $F'(x):X\to Y$ for its unique bounded real-linear derivative.

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty open set, let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map, let $y\in Y$, and let $x_0\in X$. A point $x^\dagger\in U$ is an **$x_0$-minimum-norm solution** of $F(x)=y$ on $U$ if $F(x^\dagger)=y$ and

$$\|x^\dagger-x_0\|\le\|x-x_0\|\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ with }F(x)=y.$$

This definition asserts no existence or uniqueness; it describes the minimizing property of a supplied exact solution. The minimum is global over the exact solution set on $U$, with distance measured from the specified reference point $x_0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $D\subseteq X$ be a nonempty domain, and let $F:D\to Y$ be a forward map. For a regularization parameter $\alpha>0$, reference element $x_0\in X$, and datum $y\in Y$, the **nonlinear Tikhonov functional** is the map $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}:D\to[0,\infty)$ defined by

$$
J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x):=\frac12\|F(x)-y\|_Y^2+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x-x_0\|_X^2\qquad(x\in D).
$$

A **global minimizer** is a point $x_\alpha\in D$ such that $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x_\alpha)\le J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x)$ for every $x\in D$. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Comparing the approximate-minimum inequality with the exact solution gives $J_\alpha^\delta(x_\delta)\le\delta^p/p+\alpha R(x^\dagger)+\varepsilon_\delta$. Since the data term is nonnegative, $R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger)\le\delta^p/(p\alpha)+\varepsilon_\delta/\alpha=O(\rho_\delta)$ by [A1] and [A3]. As $\rho_\delta\to0$ and $R_0>R(x^\dagger)$, $x_\delta\in L_{R_0}$ for sufficiently small $\delta$.

By [F5]–[F7] the special case uses the open-domain Hilbert map, the stipulated global $x_0$-minimum-norm exact solution, and the existing quadratic nonlinear Tikhonov functional. Under [A6], define $\xi^\dagger(h):=\langle x^\dagger-x_0,h\rangle_X$. By [F10] this is a bounded real-linear functional; expansion using [F9] gives $R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}=\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2\ge0$, so [F1] gives $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$ and [F2] gives $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)=\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2$. Taking $\psi(s)=(\beta_2+1)\sqrt{s}$, the stated Hilbert source inequality implies the VSC with $p=2$.

By [F8], $T_\delta^{1/p}\le r_\delta+\delta$. For $p=1$, $(u+v)^p=u^p+v^p$; for $p>1$, $t\mapsto t^p$ is continuous at zero and has nonnegative second derivative $p(p-1)t^{p-2}$ on $(0,\infty)$, hence is convex on $[0,\infty)$, and its defining convexity inequality at the midpoint gives $(u+v)^p\le2^{p-1}(u^p+v^p)$. Taking $u=r_\delta$, $v=\delta$ yields $T_\delta\le2^{p-1}(r_\delta^p+\delta^p)$ and thus $r_\delta^p/p\ge c_pT_\delta-\delta^p/p$. Substituting into the comparison inequality from 1.1 gives $c_pT_\delta+\alpha(R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger))\le2\delta^p/p+\varepsilon_\delta$.

For $B:=\beta_2+1>0$, the conjugate is $H(q)=\sup_{u\ge0}(Bu-qu^2)=B^2/(4q)$, by completing the square. With $p=2$, $c_p=1/4$, so $\alpha H(c_p/\alpha)=B^2\alpha^2\asymp\delta^2$ and $\rho_\delta=H(c_p/\alpha)=B^2\alpha\asymp\delta$ when $\alpha\asymp\delta$. The scale comparability in [A3] also holds because $H(c_p/(2\alpha))=2H(c_p/\alpha)$.

By [F2] and [F3], $R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger)=D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)+\langle\xi^\dagger,x_\delta-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\ge(1-\beta)D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)-\psi(T_\delta)$. Combining this with the objective comparison in step 2.1 gives $c_pT_\delta+\alpha(1-\beta)D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)\le d_\delta+\alpha\psi(T_\delta)$, where $d_\delta:=2\delta^p/p+\varepsilon_\delta$.

Apply [F4] with $c_1=c_p$, $c_2=1-\beta$, $C_3=1$, $r=T_\delta$, $e=D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)$, and $d=d_\delta$. It follows that $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)\le\frac1{1-\beta}\left(\frac{d_\delta}{\alpha}+\rho_\delta\right)$ and $T_\delta\le\frac2{c_p}\left(d_\delta+\alpha H(c_p/(2\alpha))\right)$.

From [A1] and [A3], $d_\delta=O(\delta^p)$, $d_\delta/\alpha=O(\rho_\delta)$, and $d_\delta+\alpha H(c_p/(2\alpha))=O(\delta^p)$. Thus $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)=O(\rho_\delta)$ and $T_\delta=O(\delta^p)$. The triangle inequality gives $r_\delta\le T_\delta^{1/p}+\delta$, so the noisy-data residual is $O(\delta)$.

For the penalty rate, [F2]–[F3] give $R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger)\ge-\psi(T_\delta)$, while step 1.1 supplies its upper bound. If [A4] holds for a fixed $C_0$ bounding $T_\delta/\delta^p$, then $|R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger)|=O(\rho_\delta)$. If [A5] also holds, the Bregman bound in step 5.1 gives $\|x_\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^s=O(\rho_\delta)$.

Applying the Bregman bound from step 5.1 and the exact Bregman identity from step 1.2 gives $\|x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2=O(\delta)$ and $\|F(x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta)$, hence the asserted $O(\sqrt\delta)$ solution error and $O(\delta)$ residual.

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, $D(F)\subseteq X$, and $F:D(F)\to Y$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, let $x^\dagger\in D(F)\cap\operatorname{dom}R$, set $y=F(x^\dagger)$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. Fix $1\le p<\infty$, $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0>R(x^\dagger)$. Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, and assume the variational source inequality

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad\left(x\in L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}\right),$$

where $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}$. Extend $-\psi$ by $+\infty$ on negative arguments and write $H(q):=(-\psi)^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$; assume $H(q)$ is finite for sufficiently large $q$ and $H(q)\to0$ as $q\to\infty$. For sufficiently small noise levels $\delta>0$ and data $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, define $J_\alpha^\delta(x):=p^{-1}\|F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha R(x)$. Suppose $\alpha=\alpha(\delta)>0$ tends to zero, $0\le\varepsilon_\delta\le C_\varepsilon\delta^p$, and $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in D(F)$ is an $\varepsilon_\delta$-minimizer, meaning $J_\alpha^\delta(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})\le\inf_{z\in D(F)}J_\alpha^\delta(z)+\varepsilon_\delta$. Set $c_p:=2^{1-p}/p$ and $\rho_\delta:=H(c_p/\alpha(\delta))$. Assume that for constants $c_-,c_+,C_H>0$ independent of $\delta$,

$$c_-\delta^p\le\alpha(\delta)\rho_\delta\le c_+\delta^p,\qquad H(c_p/(2\alpha(\delta)))\le C_H\rho_\delta$$

for all sufficiently small $\delta$. Then for all sufficiently small $\delta$, $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in L_{R_0}$ and

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon},x^\dagger)=O(\rho_\delta),\qquad \|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta).$$

If, in addition, $\psi(C_0\delta^p)=O(\rho_\delta)$ for a fixed $C_0$ such that $T_\delta:=\|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\le C_0\delta^p$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$, then $|R(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-R(x^\dagger)|=O(\rho_\delta)$. If also $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)\ge c_R\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^s$ on $L_{R_0}$ for constants $c_R,s>0$, then $\|x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}-x^\dagger\|_X^s=O(\rho_\delta)$.

In the Hilbert special case, set $p=2$ and suppose $X,Y$ are real Hilbert spaces, $F:U\to Y$ has the real open-domain interface of a nonlinear forward map, $x^\dagger$ is an $x_0$-minimum-norm exact solution, $R(x)=\frac12\|x-x_0\|_X^2$, and the source inequality on a regularizer sublevel contained in $U$ is

$$\langle x^\dagger-x_0,x^\dagger-x\rangle_X\le\beta_1\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2+\beta_2\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y$$

with $0\le\beta_1<1$ and $\beta_2\ge0$. For exact global minimizers of the nonlinear Tikhonov functional with $\alpha(\delta)\asymp\delta$, the theorem gives $\|x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X=O(\sqrt\delta)$ and $\|F(x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta)$. The assertion is conditional on such a global minimizer being supplied; it does not assert existence or cover local numerical minima.

Extend $g=-\psi$ to $\mathbb R$ by $g(s)=+\infty$ for $s<0$, and define $H(q):=g^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$ for $q>0$, assuming the displayed suprema below are finite. For $c_1,c_2,C_3,\alpha>0$ and $d,r,e\ge0$, if

derivations.claim: For $q>0$, the function $s\mapsto As^\mu-qs$ has derivative $A\mu s^{\mu-1}-q$, which decreases from $+\infty$ to $-q$ and vanishes only at $s_q=(A\mu/q)^{1/(1-\mu)}$. The function is increasing before $s_q$ and decreasing after it, with value $0$ at $s=0$ and limit $-\infty$ as $s\to\infty$, so this point is its global maximizer. Substitution gives $H(q)=(1-\mu)A^{1/(1-\mu)}\mu^{\mu/(1-\mu)}q^{-\mu/(1-\mu)}$.

With $q=c_p/\alpha$ this gives $H(c_p/\alpha)=C_{p,A,\mu}\alpha^{\mu/(1-\mu)}$, so the chosen $\alpha$ yields $H(c_p/\alpha)\asymp\delta^{p\mu}$ and $\alpha H(c_p/\alpha)\asymp\delta^p$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at every point with a derivative map $F':U\to\mathcal B(X,Y)$ that is continuous in operator norm. This is the real-Hilbert forward-map convention. Assume Countable Choice, so every bounded derivative $F'(x)$ has the Hilbert adjoint $F'(x)^*:Y\to X$ characterized by $\langle F'(x)u,v\rangle_Y=\langle u,F'(x)^*v\rangle_X$.

An **admissible local instance** consists of an initial point $x_0\in U$, a radius $r>0$, an exact solution $x^\dagger\in\overline B_r(x_0):=\{x\in X:\|x-x_0\|_X\le r\}$ with exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$, a noise level $\delta\ge0$, noisy datum $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, a constant $0\le\eta<1/2$, a discrepancy parameter $\tau>2(1+\eta)/(1-2\eta)$, and a finite update budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. The closed outer ball $\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$ is contained in $U$; $\|F'(x)\|\le1$ for every $x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$; and the uniform two-point tangential-cone inequality

$$
\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)-F'(x)(x-\widetilde x)\|_Y\le\eta\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)\|_Y
$$

holds for every $x,\widetilde x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$. This is the uniform family of the one-basepoint local tangential-cone inequality; the shared constant and pair domain are part of the admissibility hypothesis. The exact solution and the bounds are analysis data and need not be available to the computational loop.

**Inputs:** $F$, $x_0$, $y^\delta$, $\delta$, $\tau$, and $M$ from an admissible local instance.

**Output:** Either `stopped` with an index $k$, iterate $x_k^\delta$, and residual $\|y^\delta-F(x_k^\delta)\|_Y$, or `budget_exhausted` with the last iterate and its residual.

**Procedure:** Set $x_0^\delta:=x_0$. For $k=0,1,\ldots,M$, compute $r_k^\delta:=\|y^\delta-F(x_k^\delta)\|_Y$. If $r_k^\delta\le\tau\delta$, return `stopped` with $(k,x_k^\delta,r_k^\delta)$. If $k=M$, return `budget_exhausted` with $(k,x_k^\delta,r_k^\delta)$. Otherwise set

$$
x_{k+1}^\delta:=x_k^\delta+F'(x_k^\delta)^*(y^\delta-F(x_k^\delta))
$$

and continue at the next index. Each update is evaluated at a current point in $U$, where the derivative and its Hilbert adjoint are defined.

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at $x\in U$. For $\delta>0$ such that the closed ball

$$\overline B_\delta(x):=\{x+h:h\in X,\ \|h\|_X\le\delta\}$$

is contained in $U$, the **local tangential cone condition at $x$ on radius $\delta$ with constant $\eta$** holds if $0\le\eta<1$ and

$$\|F(x+h)-F(x)-F'(x)h\|_Y\le\eta\,\|F(x+h)-F(x)\|_Y\qquad(\|h\|_X\le\delta).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field (The real numbers) and
a **sequence of reals** is a function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
(Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences), written $(a_k)$; recall that $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$.

**Partial sums.** Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals. Its **sequence of partial
sums** is

$$s_n \;:=\; \sum_{k < n} a_k \qquad (n \in \mathbb{N}),$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. In particular $s_0 = 0$, the empty sum, and
$s_{n+1} = s_n + a_n$ for every $n$, those being exactly the two recursion clauses
that define the finite sum. Note that $s_n$ is the sum of the $n$ terms
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$, so the index $n$ counts terms rather than naming the last
one.

**Convergence, the sum, divergence.** The **series** of $(a_k)$, written
$\sum a_k$, **converges** when the sequence $(s_n)$ of partial sums converges
(Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals), and then the **sum of the series** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;:=\; \lim_{n} s_n .$$

The series **diverges** when $(s_n)$ does not converge. A convergent sequence of
reals has exactly one limit (A sequence has at most one limit), so the displayed symbol names
a single real number and nothing further has to be checked for it to be
well defined.

**Series with a general starting index.** Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a$ be a
function on $\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : k \ge m \,\}$, which we call a **family from
$m$** and write $(a_k)_{k \ge m}$. The series

$$\sum_{k \ge m} a_k$$

is by definition the series of the sequence $b_j := a_{j + m}$,
$j \in \mathbb{N}$, which is a genuine sequence of reals; it converges exactly
when that series converges, and its sum is then written
$\sum_{k = m}^{\infty} a_k$. Its partial sums are

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k \;=\; \sum_{j < n-m} a_{m+j} \qquad (n \ge m),$$

in the notation of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion, the value at $n = m$ being the empty sum
$0$. A sequence on $\mathbb{N}$ is the case $m = 0$, and the two readings of
$\sum a_k$ agree there, since $b_j = a_j$.

**This clause is not a convenience.** Sequences in this library are functions on
$\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ (Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences), while many of the
classical series are built from expressions that are undefined at the index $0$:
$1/k$, $1/k^{p}$ and $|a_k|^{1/k}$ all require $k \ge 1$. Writing such a series as
$\sum_{k \ge 1} a_k$ names an honest object, whereas writing it as a sequence on
$\mathbb{N}$ would require a value at an index where the defining expression has
none. Every statement on this page says which starting index it uses.

**Tail series.** For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the **$N$-th tail series** of
$\sum a_k$ is $\sum_{k \ge N} a_k$, that is the series of the $N$-th tail
$a^{(N)}$ of Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences, whose terms are $a^{(N)}_j = a_{j+N}$. The
$0$-th tail series is the series itself.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing (Nondecreasing, increasing, nonincreasing, decreasing, monotone, and eventually monotone sequences) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   (Divergence to $+\infty$ and to $-\infty$) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) converges to a real
number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

Every complete ordered field $F$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
(Ordered field). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty open set in the norm topology. A **nonlinear forward model on Hilbert spaces** is a map $F:U\to Y$; no linearity is assumed, and linear maps are allowed as special cases. For $y\in Y$, its exact solution set is

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

A point $x^\dagger\in U$ generates the exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$. When $F$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x\in U$, write $F'(x):X\to Y$ for its unique bounded real-linear derivative.

On this page the scalar field is the field $\mathbb R$ of real numbers: $X$, $Y$
and $Z$ always denote real Banach spaces ([[def-banach-space]]) and $U
\subseteq X$ always denotes an open subset of $X$, in the metric topology of the
norm ([[def-metric-topology]]).

Let $f : U \to Y$ be a map and let $x \in U$. For a bounded linear operator
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) write

$$r(h) := f(x+h) - f(x) - Th \qquad (h \in X,\ x+h \in U).$$

Then $f$ is **Fréchet differentiable at $x$** when there is
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ with

$$\lim_{\substack{h \to 0 \\ h \ne 0}} \frac{\|f(x+h)-f(x)-Th\|}{\|h\|} = 0 ,$$

the limit being taken over those $h$ with $x + h \in U$. Such an operator $T$ is
a **Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$**, written $T = Df(x)$, and $\|T\|$ is its
operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). When $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at
every point of $U$, $f$ is **differentiable on $U$** and the **derivative** is
the map $Df : U \to \mathcal B(X,Y)$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$.

derivations.claim: Fix a current point $u$ and any exact solution $z$ in the outer ball, and set $e=u-z$, $R=F(u)-y^\delta$, and $w=F(u)-F(z)-F'(u)e$. The uniform TCC gives $\|w\|_Y\le\eta\|F(u)-F(z)\|_Y$. Since $y=F(z)$, $y^\delta-F(u)+F'(u)e=y^\delta-y-w$, so by the noise bound and the triangle inequality, $\|y^\delta-F(u)+F'(u)e\|_Y\le\delta+\eta\|F(u)-y\|_Y\le(1+\eta)\delta+\eta\|R\|_Y$.

The update has $e^+=e+A^*(y^\delta-F(u))$. Expanding its squared norm and using the adjoint identity yields $\|e^+\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2=2\langle y^\delta-F(u),Ae\rangle_Y+\|A^*(y^\delta-F(u))\|_X^2$. Since [F13] makes $A$ a bounded operator, [F11] gives $\|A^*(y^\delta-F(u))\|_X\le\|A^*\|\,\|R\|_Y=\|A\|\,\|R\|_Y\le\|R\|_Y$.

Write $Ae=-(y^\delta-F(u))+(y^\delta-F(u)+Ae)$. By [F5] and step 1.2, $\|e^+\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2\le-\|R\|_Y^2+2\|R\|_Y\,\|y^\delta-F(u)+Ae\|_Y$. Substituting step 1.1 gives the stated one-step estimate $\|e^+\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2\le\|R\|_Y\bigl(2(1+\eta)\delta-(1-2\eta)\|R\|_Y\bigr)$.

If $\delta>0$ and $\|R\|_Y>\tau\delta$, then $2(1+\eta)\delta-(1-2\eta)\|R\|_Y<0$ by the strict lower bound on $\tau$, so the squared error decreases. For exact data $\delta=0$, the same bound is $-(1-2\eta)\|R\|_Y^2\le0$ for every residual, including zero.

Put $c_\tau:=1-2\eta-2(1+\eta)/\tau$, which is positive by the strict hypothesis on $\tau$. For each $n<N(\delta,y^\delta)$, the residual is greater than $\tau\delta$; step 2.1 then gives $\|x_{n+1}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2-\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le-c_\tau(R_n^\delta)^2$.

For exact data, step 2.1 gives $\|x_{n+1}-x^\dagger\|_X^2-\|x_n-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le-(1-2\eta)\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y^2$ for every $n$. Summing the first $K$ inequalities telescopes and yields $(1-2\eta)\sum_{n<K}\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y^2\le d_0^2-\|x_K-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le d_0^2$.

The initial point satisfies $\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X=d_0\le r$. At every update before the noisy stop, or at every exact-data update, step 3.1 keeps $\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X\le d_0$; consequently $\|x_n^\delta-x_0\|_X\le\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X+d_0\le2r$. Induction therefore keeps every iterate needed by the recurrence in the declared outer ball and proves Fejér decrease relative to $x^\dagger$.

Suppose $\delta>0$ and the discrepancy test never succeeds. Summing step 3.2 over the first $K$ updates telescopes, while every residual exceeds $\tau\delta$, so $K\tau^2\delta^2<\sum_{n<K}(R_n^\delta)^2\le d_0^2/c_\tau$ for every natural $K$. The Archimedean property in [F9] supplies a natural $K>d_0^2/(c_\tau\tau^2\delta^2)$, contradicting this bound. Hence the first stopping index is finite.

The partial sums of the nonnegative residual-square series are bounded by step 3.3. By [F8] the series converges, its tails tend to zero, and its terms tend to zero; thus $\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y\to0$ and the claimed infinite-series bound holds.

Let $e_j:=x_j-x^\dagger$, $a_j:=\|e_j\|_X^2$, and $\rho_j:=\|F(x_j)-y\|_Y$. The sequence $a_j$ is nonincreasing by step 3.1. Hence $\Delta_j:=a_j-a_{j+1}\ge0$, and the partial sums satisfy $\sum_{j<K}\Delta_j=a_0-a_K\le a_0$. Applying [F8] again shows that the tail sums $D_n:=\sum_{j\ge n}\Delta_j$ tend to zero.

If $d_0>0$, the same telescoping through the finite first index gives $N(\delta,y^\delta)\tau^2\delta^2<d_0^2/c_\tau$, hence $N(\delta,y^\delta)<C\delta^{-2}$. If $d_0=0$, then $x_0=x^\dagger$ and the initial residual is at most $\delta<\tau\delta$, so $N=0$ and the same bound holds for the stated positive $C$. By [F1], a budget reaching $N$ returns the first stop, while a shorter budget returns `budget_exhausted`.

Fix $m\ge n$ and choose $k\in\{n,\ldots,m\}$ minimizing the finite set of residuals $\rho_j$; [F10] supplies a least index among minimizers. For $n\le j<m$, put $A_j=F'(x_j)$, $w_j=F(x_j)-y-A_je_j$, and $v_{j,k}=F(x_j)-F(x_k)-A_j(x_j-x_k)$. The uniform TCC gives $\|w_j\|_Y\le\eta\rho_j$ and $\|v_{j,k}\|_Y\le\eta\|F(x_j)-F(x_k)\|_Y\le\eta(\rho_j+\rho_k)\le2\eta\rho_j$. Since $A_je_k=\bigl(F(x_j)-y-w_j\bigr)+\bigl(F(x_k)-F(x_j)+v_{j,k}\bigr)=F(x_k)-y-w_j+v_{j,k}$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle y-F(x_j),A_je_k\rangle_Y|\le\rho_j(\rho_k+\|w_j\|_Y+\|v_{j,k}\|_Y)\le(1+3\eta)\rho_j^2$.

For any fixed finite number of executed updates, the noisy iterates converge to the exact iterates as $\delta\to0$ along data sequences whose discrepancy stop occurs no earlier. Indeed, the update map $(x,z)\mapsto x+F'(x)^*(z-F(x))$ is continuous: $F$ is continuous by Fréchet differentiability, $F'$ is continuous by hypothesis, and [F3] together with [F11] gives operator-norm continuity of the adjoint action. Induction from the common initial point proves the fixed-index assertion.

The exact update gives $e_{j+1}-e_j=A_j^*(y-F(x_j))$. Summing this identity and using [F3] shows $\langle e_k-e_m,e_k\rangle_X\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j=k}^{m-1}\rho_j^2\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2$, and likewise $\langle e_k-e_n,e_k\rangle_X\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j=n}^{k-1}\rho_j^2\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2$.

Real inner-product expansion gives $\|e_m-e_k\|_X^2=2\langle e_k-e_m,e_k\rangle_X+a_m-a_k\le2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2$, since $a_m\le a_k$. It also gives $\|e_k-e_n\|_X^2=2\langle e_k-e_n,e_k\rangle_X+a_n-a_k\le2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2+D_n$, because $a_n-a_k=\sum_{j=n}^{k-1}\Delta_j\le D_n$.

By the triangle inequality, $\|e_m-e_n\|_X\le\sqrt{2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2}+\sqrt{2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2+D_n}$, which tends to zero uniformly in $m\ge n$ by steps 4.3 and 4.4. Thus $(e_n)$ is Cauchy. Completeness of $X$ gives $x_n\to\bar x$. By Fréchet differentiability at $\bar x$, $F(x_n)-F(\bar x)=F'(\bar x)(x_n-\bar x)+o(\|x_n-\bar x\|_X)$, so boundedness of $F'(\bar x)$ implies $F(x_n)\to F(\bar x)$; step 4.3 gives $F(\bar x)=y$. step 4.1 and the triangle inequality give $\|x_n-x_0\|_X\le2r$, so passage to the limit gives $\bar x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$.

Suppose the uniform noisy-data conclusion fails. Then some $\varepsilon>0$ and, for every $j$, a positive $\delta_j<1/j$ and admissible datum $y_j$ can be selected so that the stopped iterate is at least $\varepsilon/2$ from $\bar x$; [A1] supplies this countable selection from the nonempty bad-data sets. Let $N_j=N(\delta_j,y_j)$. Passing to a subsequence, either $N_j$ is a fixed integer or $N_j\to\infty$: a bounded sequence of natural indices has a value occurring infinitely often, and an unbounded one has an increasing subsequence chosen recursively by least indices.

In the fixed-index case, write $N_j=N$. Step 5.3 gives $x_N^{\delta_j}\to x_N$. Fréchet differentiability at $x_N$ and boundedness of $F'(x_N)$ imply $F(x_N^{\delta_j})\to F(x_N)$. The discrepancy test and noise bound give $\|F(x_N^{\delta_j})-y\|_Y\le\tau\delta_j+\delta_j$, so $F(x_N)=y$. The exact update at $x_N$ is then zero, so $x_n=x_N$ for every $n\ge N$ and therefore $x_N=\bar x$. Step 5.3 now gives $x_N^{\delta_j}\to\bar x$, contradicting the selected distance lower bound.

In the case $N_j\to\infty$, choose $L$ with $\|x_L-\bar x\|_X<\varepsilon/4$ by step 8.1. For all sufficiently large $j$, $N_j\ge L$ and step 5.3 gives $\|x_L^{\delta_j}-x_L\|_X<\varepsilon/4$. Each noisy iterate before its stop stays in the outer ball by step 4.1, and $\bar x$ lies there by step 8.1; applying the one-step estimate of step 2.1 with the exact solution $\bar x$ makes the noisy iterates Fejér monotone relative to $\bar x$ up to $N_j$. Hence $\|x_{N_j}^{\delta_j}-\bar x\|_X\le\|x_L^{\delta_j}-\bar x\|_X<\varepsilon/2$, again contradicting the selected lower bound.
Both subsequence cases contradict the failure assumption in step 9.1. Therefore the supremum over all data satisfying $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$ tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$.

citations.quote:
Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at every point with a derivative map $F':U\to\mathcal B(X,Y)$ that is continuous in operator norm. This is the real-Hilbert forward-map convention. Assume Countable Choice, so every bounded derivative $F'(x)$ has the Hilbert adjoint $F'(x)^*:Y\to X$ characterized by $\langle F'(x)u,v\rangle_Y=\langle u,F'(x)^*v\rangle_X$.

An **admissible local instance** consists of an initial point $x_0\in U$, a radius $r>0$, an exact solution $x^\dagger\in\overline B_r(x_0):=\{x\in X:\|x-x_0\|_X\le r\}$ with exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$, a noise level $\delta\ge0$, noisy datum $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, a constant $0\le\eta<1/2$, a discrepancy parameter $\tau>2(1+\eta)/(1-2\eta)$, and a finite update budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. The closed outer ball $\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$ is contained in $U$; $\|F'(x)\|\le1$ for every $x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$; and the uniform two-point tangential-cone inequality

$$
\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)-F'(x)(x-\widetilde x)\|_Y\le\eta\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)\|_Y
$$

holds for every $x,\widetilde x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$. This is the uniform family of the one-basepoint local tangential-cone inequality; the shared constant and pair domain are part of the admissibility hypothesis. The exact solution and the bounds are analysis data and need not be available to the computational loop.

**Inputs:** $F$, $x_0$, $y^\delta$, $\delta$, $\tau$, and $M$ from an admissible local instance.

**Output:** Either `stopped` with an index $k$, iterate $x_k^\delta$, and residual $\|y^\delta-F(x_k^\delta)\|_Y$, or `budget_exhausted` with the last iterate and its residual.

**Procedure:** Set $x_0^\delta:=x_0$. For $k=0,1,\ldots,M$, compute $r_k^\delta:=\|y^\delta-F(x_k^\delta)\|_Y$. If $r_k^\delta\le\tau\delta$, return `stopped` with $(k,x_k^\delta,r_k^\delta)$. If $k=M$, return `budget_exhausted` with $(k,x_k^\delta,r_k^\delta)$. Otherwise set

$$
x_{k+1}^\delta:=x_k^\delta+F'(x_k^\delta)^*(y^\delta-F(x_k^\delta))
$$

and continue at the next index. Each update is evaluated at a current point in $U$, where the derivative and its Hilbert adjoint are defined.

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at $x\in U$. For $\delta>0$ such that the closed ball

$$\overline B_\delta(x):=\{x+h:h\in X,\ \|h\|_X\le\delta\}$$

is contained in $U$, the **local tangential cone condition at $x$ on radius $\delta$ with constant $\eta$** holds if $0\le\eta<1$ and

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex
Hilbert spaces and let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For
$\lambda>0$, define

$$B_\lambda:=A^*A+\lambda I_X.$$

Then $B_\lambda:X\to X$ is bijective and

$$\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le\frac1\lambda.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $\alpha>0$ and write $B_\alpha:=T^*T+\alpha I_X$. By [F2], $B_\alpha$ is bijective, so $h_\alpha:=B_\alpha^{-1}T^*r$ is defined and satisfies $T^*(Th_\alpha-r)+\alpha h_\alpha=0$.

For any $h\in X$, set $d:=h-h_\alpha$. Expanding with [F4] gives $\Phi_\alpha(h)-\Phi_\alpha(h_\alpha)=\langle Th_\alpha-r,Td\rangle_Y+\alpha\langle h_\alpha,d\rangle_X+\frac12\|Td\|_Y^2+\frac\alpha2\|d\|_X^2.$ The first two terms sum to $\langle T^*(Th_\alpha-r)+\alpha h_\alpha,d\rangle_X=0$ by [F1] and step 1.1. The remaining terms are nonnegative, and because $\alpha>0$ their sum vanishes only when $d=0$. Thus $h_\alpha$ is the unique global minimizer and $\Phi_\alpha(h_\alpha)\le\Phi_\alpha(0)$, so $\|h_\alpha\|_X\le\|r\|_Y/\sqrt\alpha$.

Define $f(\alpha):=\|Th_\alpha-r\|_Y$. For $\alpha,\beta>0$, the inverse identity $B_\alpha^{-1}-B_\beta^{-1}=(\beta-\alpha)B_\alpha^{-1}B_\beta^{-1}$ and [F2] give $h_\alpha-h_\beta=(\beta-\alpha)B_\alpha^{-1}h_\beta$. Therefore, when $\alpha,\beta$ lie near a fixed $\alpha_0>0$, $\|h_\alpha-h_\beta\|_X\le|\beta-\alpha|\frac{\|r\|_Y}{\alpha\sqrt\beta},$ which tends to zero with $|\beta-\alpha|$. Thus $h_\alpha$ and $f(\alpha)$ are continuous on $(0,\infty)$, using [F6] for continuity of the norm.

By step 2.1 and [F3], $\|Th_\alpha\|_Y\le\|T\|\|r\|_Y/\sqrt\alpha\to0$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. The reverse triangle inequality from [F6] gives $|f(\alpha)-\|r\|_Y|\le\|Th_\alpha\|_Y$, so $f(\alpha)\to\|r\|_Y>\sigma\|r\|_Y$.

Comparing the minimizer with the fixed vector $v$ gives $f(\alpha)^2+\alpha\|h_\alpha\|_X^2\le\|Tv-r\|_Y^2+\alpha\|v\|_X^2.$ Because $\|Tv-r\|_Y\le(\sigma/\gamma)\|r\|_Y<\sigma\|r\|_Y$, there is a strict squared-norm gap below $\sigma^2\|r\|_Y^2$. Also $v\ne0$, since $v=0$ would contradict the range bound and $r\ne0$. Choose $a>0$ small enough that $\|Tv-r\|_Y^2+a\|v\|_X^2<\sigma^2\|r\|_Y^2$. The minimizer comparison in this step gives $f(a)^2\le\|Tv-r\|_Y^2+a\|v\|_X^2<\sigma^2\|r\|_Y^2$, so $f(a)<\sigma\|r\|_Y$.

By step 3.2, choose $b>a$ with $f(b)>\sigma\|r\|_Y$. Continuity from step 3.1 and [F5] give $\alpha\in[a,b]$ such that $f(\alpha)=\sigma\|r\|_Y$. Since $a>0$, this is an admissible positive parameter and proves the forcing claim.
