Extend $\partial_1\phi_1$ by zero outside $B$. It is integrable because it is bounded and supported in a finite-measure disk [F5]. Fubini [F4] expresses its integral as the integral over $y\in(-1,1)$ of the slice integrals over $[-a(y),a(y)]$, where $a(y)=\sqrt{1-y^2}$. Each slice integrand is continuous, so [F6] identifies its Lebesgue integral with its Riemann integral, and [F7] evaluates that integral as $\phi_1(a(y),y)-\phi_1(-a(y),y)$. In the right graph $x=a(y)$, [F8] gives $d\mathcal H^1=dy/a(y)$ and $
u_1=a(y)$; in the left graph $x=-a(y)$, it gives $d\mathcal H^1=dy/a(y)$ and $
u_1=-a(y)$. Thus the slice difference equals $\int_{\partial B}\phi_1
u_1\,d\mathcal H^1$. The same argument with the coordinates exchanged gives the second component, hence $\int_B\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=\int_{\partial B}\phi\cdot
u\,d\mathcal H^1$.

By the distributional derivative convention [F1], step 1.1 yields $D\chi_B=-\nu\mathcal H^1|_{\partial B}$. The circle has finite arclength, so this is a finite vector Radon measure and $\chi_B\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$.

The parametrization $\theta\mapsto(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ has speed one on $[0,2\pi]$, so $\mathcal H^1(\partial B)=2\pi$. For every admissible test field, step 1.1 gives $$\int_B\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=\int_{\partial B}\phi\cdot\nu\,d\mathcal H^1\le2\pi.$$ Choose a smooth radial cutoff $q$ supported in $(1/2,3/2)$, with $0\le q\le1$ and $q(1)=1$, and set $\phi(x)=q(|x|)x/|x|$ on that annulus and zero outside. By [F3] this is smooth, compactly supported and has norm at most one; on $\partial B$ it equals $\nu$. Its flux is $2\pi$. The supremum in [F2] is therefore exactly $2\pi$, proving the asserted total variation and perimeter.

derivations.claim: The intervals are disjoint and have Lebesgue measure $2^{-(k+1)}$ by [F4], so $\|u_N\|_1=\sum_{k=1}^N2^{-(k+1)}<1/2$. Integration by parts on each interval, justified by [F5] and [F6], shows that $Du_N$ is an atomic signed measure: its jump at $1/2$ has magnitude $1$, its $N-1$ interior jumps at $2^{-2},\ldots,2^{-N}$ have magnitude $2$, and its jump at $2^{-(N+1)}$ has magnitude $1$. These are all jumps in $(0,1)$, so $u_N\in BV((0,1))$ and $TV(u_N;(0,1))=1+2(N-1)+1=2N$.

The sequence converges in $L^1$ to $u=(-1)^k$ on each $I_k$ and $u=0$ on $(1/2,1)$, since $|u_N-u|\le1$ and its support lies in $(0,2^{-(N+1)})$, whose measure tends to zero by [F4]. For each $M$, choose disjoint small intervals around $x_j=2^{-j}$, $1\le j\le M$, avoiding every other dyadic jump, and smooth bumps equal to one at these points, with signs chosen opposite to the jumps of $u$. Their sum is a compactly supported smooth test function $\phi_M$ with $|\phi_M|\le1$. Every bounded real linear functional $L$ on $C_0(X;\mathbb R)$ can be written $L=L^+-L^-$, where $L^+$ and $L^-$ are bounded positive linear functionals and $\|L^\pm\|\le\|L\|$.

For an outer measure $\mu^*$ on $X$, the Carathéodory measurable subsets form a sigma-algebra, and the restriction of the outer measure to it is a complete measure.

derivations.claim: First let $P$ be bounded and positive. For relatively open $G\subseteq U$ put $p(G)=\sup\{P(f):f\in C_c(U),\ 0\le f\le1,\ \operatorname{supp}f\subseteq G\}$. Then $0\le p(G)\le\|P\|$, $p(\varnothing)=0$, and $p$ is monotone. If a compact $K$ is covered by open sets $G_j$, finitely many suffice, and there are continuous nonnegative compactly supported functions $b_1,\ldots,b_N$, each supported in one of these sets, whose sum is positive on $K$. Indeed cover $K$ by finitely many balls with doubled closures compactly contained in the relevant $G_j$ and use distance cutoffs on these balls. On a neighborhood of $K$ normalize the $b_i$ by their sum. Thus any $f$ supported on $K$ with $0\le f\le1$ decomposes into finitely many $f_i\ge0$ with $\sum f_i=f$ and each $f_i\le1$ compactly supported in its assigned $G_j$; combine terms assigned to the same $j$. Consequently $p(\bigcup_jG_j)\le\sum_jp(G_j)$. For pairwise disjoint opens, adding finitely many admissible functions gives the reverse inequality for every finite partial sum, so $p$ is countably additive on disjoint open unions. These compact partitions use only finite choices.

Define $\mu^*(A)=\inf\{p(G):A\subseteq G\subseteq U,\ G\text{ open}\}$. For a sequence $(A_j)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [A1] selects open $G_j\supseteq A_j$ with $p(G_j)<\mu^*(A_j)+\varepsilon2^{-j}$; step 1.1 proves countable subadditivity. Zero and monotonicity are immediate, so $\mu^*$ is an outer measure, and $\mu^*(G)=p(G)$ for open $G$. If $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0$, they have disjoint open neighborhoods $V,W$ in $U$. Every open $G\supseteq A\cup B$ satisfies $p(G)\ge p(G\cap V)+p(G\cap W)\ge\mu^*(A)+\mu^*(B)$, by step 1.1. Taking the infimum and using subadditivity proves the metric condition. By [F2], restriction to Borel sets is a finite measure $\mu$ with $\mu(U)\le\|P\|$.

For an admissible $f$ in the definition of $p(G)$, let $K=\operatorname{supp}f$. Every open $V\supseteq K$ admits $f$, hence $\mu(K)=\inf_{V\supseteq K}p(V)\ge P(f)$. Taking the supremum over $f$ proves $\mu(G)=\sup_{K\subseteq G\text{ compact}}\mu(K)$. Outer regularity on every Borel set is the definition of $\mu^*$. Finiteness gives compact inner regularity on every Borel set as well: given Borel $A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose compact $H\subseteq U$ with $\mu(U\setminus H)<\varepsilon$ and open $V\supseteq U\setminus A$ with $\mu(V\setminus(U\setminus A))<\varepsilon$. Then $H\setminus V\subseteq A$ is compact and misses at most $2\varepsilon$ of $\mu(A)$. Thus $\mu$ is finite Radon, including regularity on all Borel sets.

If $0\le g\in C_c(U)$ and $g\le\mathbf1_K$ for compact $K$, the argument in step 3.1 gives $P(g)\le\mu(K)$. If instead $g\ge\mathbf1_K$, then for $0<\eta<1$, the open set $G_\eta=\{g>1-\eta\}$ contains $K$ and every admissible $f$ for $p(G_\eta)$ satisfies $f\le g/(1-\eta)$ on all of $U$. Positivity yields $\mu(K)\le p(G_\eta)\le P(g)/(1-\eta)$. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ gives $\mu(K)\le P(g)$.

Fix $0\le f\in C_c(U)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, take $N$ with $N\varepsilon\ge\|f\|_\infty$, and put $f_j=\min(\varepsilon,(f-(j-1)\varepsilon)_+)$, $K_0=\operatorname{supp}f$, $K_j=\{f\ge j\varepsilon\}$ for $1\le j\le N$. The sum of the $f_j$ is $f$, and $\varepsilon\mathbf1_{K_j}\le f_j\le\varepsilon\mathbf1_{K_{j-1}}$. Step 4.1 gives the same lower and upper bounds $\varepsilon\mu(K_j)$ and $\varepsilon\mu(K_{j-1})$ for $P(f_j)$ as for $\int f_j\,d\mu$. Summing and telescoping gives $|P(f)-\int f\,d\mu|\le\varepsilon\mu(K_0)$. Hence equality holds for $f\ge0$, then for every real $f\in C_c(U)$ by positive and negative parts. Uniform density [F3], boundedness of $P$, and finiteness of $\mu$ extend the identity to $C_0(U)$.

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure
$\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.

derivations.claim: For $\delta>0$, tile $\mathbb R^n$ by the half-open cubes $Q=\delta(z+[0,1)^n)$, $z\in\mathbb Z^n$, and let $A_\delta v$ equal $\delta^{-n}\int_Qv$ on $Q$. The triangle inequality, followed by [F1] and the substitution $y=x+h$ using [F2], gives $\|v-A_\delta v\|_1\le\delta^{-n}\sum_Q\int_Q\int_Q|v(x)-v(y)|\,dy\,dx\le\delta^{-n}\int_{[-\delta,\delta]^n}\|v(\cdot+h)-v\|_1\,dh$. Thus, writing $\omega(r)=\sup_{k,|h|\le r}\|v_k(\cdot+h)-v_k\|_1$, one has $\sup_k\|v_k-A_\delta v_k\|_1\le2^n\omega(\sqrt n\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$.

For each $m\ge1$, only finitely many cubes of side $2^{-m}$ meet a fixed ball containing the common supports; all other cell averages vanish. Enumerate all these cells at all levels by first increasing $m$ and then lexicographic order of their integer coordinates. Each cell-average coefficient $a_j(k)$ is a bounded real sequence, with bound $M$ divided by that cell's volume. Set $S_0=\mathbb N$ and initialize $k_0=0$. Recursively, at stage $m\ge1$, partition the bounded ranges of the first $m$ coefficients into finitely many half-open dyadic bins of width $2^{-m}$, adding an endpoint bin if necessary. Among the finitely many vector bins containing infinitely many indices in $S_{m-1}$, take the lexicographically first; let $S_m$ be exactly that infinite set of indices. The finite pigeonhole principle guarantees existence and the specified order makes the rule unique. Then let $k_m$ be the least member of $S_m$ larger than $k_{m-1}$; such a member exists because $S_m$ is infinite. This deterministic successor rule and initial pair $(S_0,k_0)$ define the sequence recursively by [F3], with no dependent-choice instance. For fixed $j$ and $m\ge j$, all selected indices $k_q$ with $q\ge m$ lie in $S_m$, so their $j$th coefficients differ by at most $2^{-m}$. Consequently every coefficient converges and, at each fixed cell level $\ell$, $(A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_m})_m$ is Cauchy in $L^1$, being a finite weighted sum of these coefficients.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a cell level $\ell$ for which $2^n\omega(\sqrt n2^{-\ell})<\varepsilon/3$, using step 1.1. For sufficiently large $a,b$, step 1.2 gives $\|A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_a}-A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_b}\|_1<\varepsilon/3$. The two approximation errors from step 1.1 then show $\|v_{k_a}-v_{k_b}\|_1<\varepsilon$. Thus the subsequence is Cauchy.

For completeness at exactly the stated axiom strength, choose representatives of this countable sequence by [A1]. Select a further subsequence $g_j$ with $\|g_{j+1}-g_j\|_1<2^{-j}$, always choosing the least sufficiently late index, which exists by the Cauchy property. By [F1], $\sum_j|g_{j+1}-g_j|$ is integrable and finite almost everywhere. Hence $g_j$ has a measurable almost-everywhere limit $g$; moreover $|g|\le|g_1|+\sum_j|g_{j+1}-g_j|$, so $g\in L^1$, and $\|g-g_j\|_1\le\sum_{i\ge j}2^{-i}\to0$. The original Cauchy subsequence also converges to this $L^1$ class by the triangle inequality. This proves the assertion using only [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For each integer $n\ge1$ there is a finite $c_n\in[1,n^{n/2}]$ such that

$$\mathcal H^n(B)=c_n\lambda_n(B)\quad(B\text{ Borel}),\qquad \mathcal H^n(A)=c_n\lambda_n^*(A)\quad(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $f:D\subseteq X\to Y$ satisfies $d_Y(f(x),f(y))=c\,d_X(x,y)$ for a finite constant $c>0$, then for every $A\subseteq D$ and finite $s\ge0$,

$$\mathcal H^s(f(A))=c^s\mathcal H^s(A).$$

This includes isometries and Euclidean translations and dilations. The Hausdorff outer value of a subset of a metric subspace equals its value computed in the ambient metric space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $f:D\subseteq X\to Y$ be an $L$-Lipschitz map between metric spaces and $A\subseteq D$. For finite $s\ge0$ and $L>0$,

Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same

derivations.claim: We first need the integral identity for Lipschitz interval functions without invoking the stronger published general absolutely continuous FTC. If $b$ is $L$-Lipschitz on $[a,d]$, extend it constantly past the endpoints. Its difference quotients are bounded by $L$ and converge to $b'$ almost everywhere by [F1]. For any $a\le s<t\le d$, dominated convergence gives $$\int_s^t b'(r)\,dr=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac1\epsilon\left(\int_t^{t+\epsilon}b(r)\,dr-\int_s^{s+\epsilon}b(r)\,dr\right)=b(t)-b(s).$$ Coordinate difference quotients of $h$ are measurable; [F1] and [F2] show their limits $g_i$ exist almost everywhere, with $|g_i|\le L$. Define them to be zero on the exceptional sets. Applying the preceding identity and one-dimensional integration by parts on each line, then [F2], gives $\int h\partial_i\eta=-\int g_i\eta$ for smooth compactly supported $\eta$. The same line identities hold for every coordinate line of $h$, outside the appropriate line-null exceptional set of derivatives.

For a cube $C$ of side $2r$ and a Lipschitz $w$, join $x$ to $y$ by the $m$ coordinate segments replacing their coordinates in order. Step 1.1 bounds $|w(x)-w(y)|$ by the sum of the line integrals of $|\partial_iw|$. Integrate in $x,y\in C$. For coordinate $i$, the unused coordinates contribute $(2r)^{m-1}$, while the measure of endpoint pairs whose interval contains a fixed coordinate value is at most $(2r)^2$. Thus, after division by $|C|$, the triangle inequality yields $$\int_C|w-w_C|\le 2r\sum_{i=1}^m\int_C|\partial_iw|,$$ where $w_C$ is its mean. Outside a null set, $g=(g_i)$ has strong Lebesgue points: apply [F3] to its coordinates and to $|g-q|$ for every rational vector $q$, then approximate $g(x)$ by such $q$. The countable union of the exceptional null sets is null under Countable Choice. Ball differentiation also gives cube differentiation by the fixed volume comparison. At such a point $x$, set $p=g(x)$ and $w(y)=h(y)-h(x)-p\cdot(y-x)$. The displayed inequality gives $\int_{C(x,r)}|w-w_C|=o(r^{m+1})$. As $w(x)=0$ and $w$ has a fixed Lipschitz bound, a mean with $|w_C|\ge\epsilon r$ would give $|w-w_C|\ge\epsilon r/2$ on a cube of side proportional to $r$ centered at $x$, contradicting this estimate. Thus $w_C=o(r)$. If $|w(y)|\ge\epsilon r$ at some $y$ in the half cube, the Lipschitz bound gives the same contradiction on a cube of side proportional to $r$ centered at $y$. Hence $\sup_{C(x,r/2)}|w|=o(r)$, proving differentiability with derivative $p$. Difference quotients then give $|p|\le L$. Countably many rational boxes cover $Q$, so the assertion is global.

We prove the area identity first for bounded Borel base sets within one $L$-Lipschitz box. On the differentiability set, for any $0<\epsilon<1/4$, form countably many Borel pieces on each of which $Dh$ lies within $\epsilon$ of a fixed rational vector $p$, the differentiability remainder is at most $\epsilon|z-y|$ whenever $|z-y|<1/k$, and the points lie in one cube of diameter less than $1/k$. Such pieces cover the differentiability set: the remainder condition follows from differentiability, can be tested on countably many rational $z$ by continuity, and is measurable; use increasing integers $k$ and a rational-vector enumeration. Subtract earlier pieces to make them disjoint. For two points $y,z$ of a single piece $E$, set $A_pv=(v,p\cdot v)$. Then $|F(z)-F(y)-A_p(z-y)|\le2\epsilon|z-y|\le2\epsilon|A_p(z-y)|$. Consequently $F\circ A_p^{-1}:A_p(E)\to F(E)$ is at most $(1+2\epsilon)$-Lipschitz, and its inverse is at most $(1-2\epsilon)^{-1}$-Lipschitz. The sets $F(E)$ are Borel because $F$ is a homeomorphism from $Q$ onto its graph.

Choose an orthonormal coordinate system on the range plane of $A_p$. Its square coordinate matrix has determinant of absolute value $J_p=\sqrt{\det(A_p^TA_p)}=\sqrt{1+|p|^2}$. Thus [F4] gives $\sigma_m(A_p(E))=J_p|E|$. Apply [F4] to the two maps in step 3.1 to obtain $$(1-2\epsilon)^mJ_p|E|\le\sigma_m(F(E))\le(1+2\epsilon)^mJ_p|E|.$$ The function $p\mapsto\sqrt{1+|p|^2}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, so $|J_p-\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}|\le\epsilon$ on $E$. The excluded base-null set has graph image of zero $\sigma_m$ by [F4], since $F$ is Lipschitz. Sum the displayed inequalities over the disjoint pieces, using $|p|\le L+\epsilon$. The difference between $\sigma_m(F(B))$ and $\int_B\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ is bounded by $C_{m,L}\epsilon|B|$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves equality. Exhaustion and countable localization extend it to arbitrary Borel $B\subseteq Q$; indicator functions, simple functions and monotone convergence prove the asserted integral formula.

For a compactly supported smooth scalar $b$ in the chart, vertical integration gives $\int_G\partial_zb=-\int_Qb(y,h(y))\,dy$. For a horizontal coordinate put $B_i(y)=\int_{h(y)}^\infty b(y,z)\,dz$. This is Lipschitz and compactly supported in $Q$; step 2.1 and ordinary differentiation of the smooth integral give $\partial_iB_i=\int_{h(y)}^\infty\partial_i b\,dz-b(y,h(y))g_i$ almost everywhere. Its weak derivative integrates to zero by step 1.1 and [F2]. Apply these identities to the components of $\phi$ and sum. Step 4.1 converts the resulting flux into the unit-normal formula. The graph measure is a graph pushforward of the locally bounded measurable density $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}\,dy$; compact and open approximation in the base show it is locally Radon on the graph with its relative topology. The density is between $1$ and $\sqrt{1+L^2}$ on every local box, which also proves the null-set assertion.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. If two finite signed Radon measures on $\Omega$ have the same integrals against every function in $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, then the measures are equal.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: Fix $a>0$ with $C_{2a}$ inside the larger chart. On every compact subset of $G$, mollify $u$ using a nonnegative unit-mass bump, writing $u_\epsilon=u*\rho_\epsilon$ where the convolution ball stays in $G$. The distributional derivative identity and [F2] give $\partial_z u_\epsilon=(D_zu)*\rho_\epsilon$ there. For $0<s<t<a$, ordinary line integration gives $$\int_B|u_\epsilon(y,h(y)+t)-u_\epsilon(y,h(y)+s)|\,dy\le\int_{\{y\in B,\ s<z-h(y)<t\}}|\partial_z u_\epsilon|\,dx.$$ For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of this last strip lies in $C_{2a}$: its lower height is positive since $s>0$, its upper height is below $2a$, and its lateral projection lies in $B'$. The convolution bound and [F2] make the right side at most $|D_zu|(C_{2a})$, since each kernel integrates to at most one.

On each compact-height collar $y\in B$, $1/j<z-h(y)<a-1/j$, [F1] gives $L^1$ convergence of $u_\epsilon$ to $u$. Choose a sequence $\epsilon_\ell\downarrow0$ whose $L^1$ errors on the first $\ell$ such collars are below $2^{-\ell}$, always using the least sufficiently large dyadic exponent. By [F2], for a full-measure set of heights the slice functions converge in $L^1(B)$. Applying step 1.1 at two such heights proves $$\|u_t-u_s\|_{L^1(B)}\le |D_zu|(C_{2a}),\qquad u_t(y)=u(y,h(y)+t),\quad 0<s,t<a.$$ Repeat this construction for a countable sequence of smaller $a$ tending to zero and intersect the full-measure height sets. The collars $C_{2a}$ decrease to the empty set inside $G$, so finiteness of $|D_zu|$ implies their measures tend to zero. Thus $u_t$ is Cauchy in $L^1(B)$ as $t\downarrow0$ outside one null set.

Choose one height from each interval $(2^{-j-1}a,2^{-j}a)$ outside that null set by Countable Choice. The corresponding Cauchy sequence has an $L^1$ limit: choose measurable representatives, then a subsequence whose successive $L^1$ differences are below $2^{-j}$; [F2] makes the sum of the absolute differences integrable and gives its almost-everywhere and $L^1$ limit. The Cauchy estimate in step 2.1 makes this limit independent of heights and gives the asserted convergence along all good heights. This also proves uniqueness and linearity. Averaging the bound $\|\tau u\|_1\le\|u_t\|_1+|D_zu|(C_{2a})$ over $0<t<a$ using [F2] gives $\|\tau u\|_1\le a^{-1}\|u\|_{L^1(C_a)}+|D_zu|(C_{2a})$. Since $|D_zu|\le|Du|$, this is the stated bound. Traces obtained on nested base boxes coincide by the same slice convergence.

The distributional identity extends from smooth to compactly supported Lipschitz vector fields $\psi$ inside $G$. Indeed mollification converges uniformly to $\psi$, while its derivatives are uniformly bounded and converge almost everywhere to the weak derivatives, by [F3] and Lebesgue differentiation: if $g$ is a bounded weak derivative at a strong Lebesgue point $x$, then $|g*\rho_\epsilon(x)-g(x)|\le C\epsilon^{-n}\int_{B(x,\epsilon)}|g(y)-g(x)|\,dy\to0$. Consequently $\int\psi_\epsilon\cdot dDu\to\int\psi\cdot dDu$ by uniform convergence and finiteness, and $\int u\operatorname{div}\psi_\epsilon\to\int u\operatorname{div}\psi$ by dominated convergence. Set $r=z-h(y)$ and let $\theta$ be the continuous function zero on $(-\infty,0]$, linear from zero to one on $[0,1]$, and one on $[1,\infty)$. For fixed $\epsilon>0$ use $\psi=\phi\theta((r-\epsilon)/\epsilon)$, whose support is a compact subset of $G$. Its almost-everywhere gradient uses the ordinary chain rule from [F3], and its transition term is $$\epsilon^{-1}\int_\epsilon^{2\epsilon}\int u_t(y)\phi(y,h(y)+t)\cdot(-Dh(y),1)\,dy\,dt.$$ By step 3.1, the uniform bound on $Dh$, and uniform continuity of $\phi$, this converges to $\int\tau u\,\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(-Dh,1)\,dy$. The other terms converge to $\int_Gu\operatorname{div}\phi$ and $-\int_G\phi\cdot dDu$, since the cutoff tends pointwise to one in $G$. Rearrangement proves the Green formula.

These formulas also show independence of the direction of a valid graph chart. On an overlap, [F3] applied to $u=1$ first identifies the outward vector surface measures by [F4]. Their variations are their scalar graph measures: for a unit measurable density $n$ against a finite positive measure $\mu$, variation is at most $\mu$ by the triangle inequality, and is at least $(1-\eta)\mu$ by partitioning the unit sphere into finitely many Borel sets of diameter below $\eta$ and projecting each vector integral onto a representative direction. Let $\eta\downarrow0$. Thus the outward normals agree almost everywhere. Subtract the two Green formulas for general $u$; [F4] makes $(\tau_1u-\tau_2u)n\mu$ zero, and the same variation argument gives $\tau_1u=\tau_2u$ almost everywhere. Reflection gives the subgraph formulas. In dimension one, omit the base integral: the convolution and line estimate in steps 1.1–2.1 make $u(t)$ Cauchy through almost every $t$ approaching an endpoint, and step 4.1 gives the endpoint boundary term. All arguments and bounds remain valid, with scalar absolute value and counting measure.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $u\in BV(\Omega)$ there is a sequence $u_k\in C^\infty(\Omega)$ such that $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$ and $\int_\Omega |\nabla u_k|\,dx\to TV(u;\Omega)$. When $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$, the approximating functions may be chosen compactly supported.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)\cap L^1(\Omega)$ satisfy $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx<\infty$. For $t>0$ set $E_t^+:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>t\}$ and for $t<0$ set $E_t^-:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)<t\}$. Then the level sets have finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ for almost every applicable $t$, and
$$\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\Omega)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\Omega)\,dt.$$

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure
$\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$.

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: For any real $f\in L^1(\Omega)$, define its extended test variation $V(f)$ as the supremum of $\int f\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields with $|\varphi|\le1$. It is a lower semicontinuous extended nonnegative function on $L^1$: each test integral is a continuous linear functional and $\{f:V(f)>a\}$ is the union of its open superlevel sets. By [F2], $V(f)<\infty$ is equivalent to $f\in BV$, in which case $V(f)=TV(f;\Omega)$. For $t>0$ the indicator $\chi_{\{f>t\}}$ lies in $L^1$, since its norm is at most $\|f\|_1/t$, and it is right continuous as an $L^1$-valued function of $t$: if $t_j\downarrow t>0$, its indicators increase to $\chi_{\{f>t\}}$ and their errors tend to zero by monotone convergence. Dyadic right-step approximations therefore make this map Borel measurable. For $t<0$, $t\mapsto\chi_{\{f<t\}}$ is similarly left continuous and Borel. Composition with the lower semicontinuous $V$ shows that both extended level-variation functions are measurable.

By [F1], take smooth strict approximants $u_j$ with $\|u_j-u\|_1<2^{-j}$ and $\int|\nabla u_j|\to TV(u;\Omega)$, passing to a subsequence by least indices if needed. For real numbers $a,b$, the total length of the positive and negative levels at which their signed superlevel or sublevel indicators differ is $|a-b|$. Hence [F3] gives $$\int_0^\infty\|\chi_{\{u_j>t\}}-\chi_{\{u>t\}}\|_1\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0\|\chi_{\{u_j<t\}}-\chi_{\{u<t\}}\|_1\,dt=\|u_j-u\|_1.$$ Sum over $j$ and apply [F3]: for almost every applicable nonzero level, the indicator errors are summable, and in particular the level indicators converge in $L^1$. The lower semicontinuity from step 1.1 gives $V(\chi_{E_t^\pm})\le\liminf_jV(\chi_{\{u_j\gtrless t\}})$ at those levels. Fatou and the smooth coarea identity [F1] consequently give $$\int_0^\infty V(\chi_{E_t^+})\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0V(\chi_{E_t^-})\,dt\le\liminf_j\int_\Omega|\nabla u_j|\,dx=TV(u;\Omega).$$ The integral is finite, so its integrands are finite almost everywhere; [F2] then proves the stated almost-everywhere finite-perimeter assertion.

For any admissible smooth test field $\varphi$, signed layer cake gives $u(x)=\int_0^\infty\chi_{E_t^+}(x)\,dt-\int_{-\infty}^0\chi_{E_t^-}(x)\,dt$ almost everywhere. The absolute integral against $\operatorname{div}\varphi$ is bounded by $\|\operatorname{div}\varphi\|_\infty\|u\|_1$, so iterated integration is valid. Each level test integral in absolute value is at most its extended variation, using also $-\varphi$ in step 1.1. Therefore $\int u\operatorname{div}\varphi$ is at most the sum of the two perimeter integrals. Take the supremum over $\varphi$ and apply [F2] to $u$ to obtain the reverse of the inequality in step 2.1. Equality follows. Changing the representative of $u$ changes each level set only by a spatial null set, so all conclusions concern the given $L^1$ class.

Assume Countable Choice. In a Lipschitz graph chart let $G$ be the side $z>h(y)$, and let $u\in BV(G)$ locally, with finite $L^1$ norm and variation on each smaller bounded graph collar under consideration. On every smaller base box $B$ there is a unique local $L^1(B)$ trace $\tau u$ such that
$$u(y,h(y)+t)\longrightarrow\tau u(y)\quad\text{in }L^1(B)\text{ as }t\downarrow0\text{ through almost every }t.$$
The trace is linear and satisfies a bound $\|\tau u\|_{L^1(B)}\le C(a^{-1}\|u\|_{L^1(C_{2a})}+|Du|(C_{2a}))$, where $C_{2a}$ is a fixed larger graph collar with positive margins at the chart sides and $a>0$ is sufficiently small. For every smooth vector field $\phi$ compactly supported away from those sides,
$$\int_Gu\operatorname{div}\phi=-\int_G\phi\cdot dDu+\int \tau u(y)\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(Dh(y),-1)\,dy.$$
The corresponding assertions hold for the subgraph with the normal reversed. For an interval endpoint in dimension one, the same assertions mean the one-sided scalar limit, the usual endpoint sign, and counting measure on the boundary.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $h:Q\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Then $h$ is differentiable almost everywhere, its partial derivatives are measurable and are its weak derivatives. On every open region where $h$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $|Dh|\le L$ almost everywhere. Let $H^m$ denote the repository's unnormalised Hausdorff measure, put $c_m=H^m((0,1]^m)$, and write $\sigma_m=c_m^{-1}H^m$ also on Euclidean spaces containing $m$-dimensional subsets. The graph map $F(y)=(y,h(y))$ satisfies, for every nonnegative Borel $a$,
$$\int_{F(Q)}a(x)\,d\sigma_m(x)=\int_Qa(F(y))\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}\,dy.$$
For the epigraph $G=\{(y,z):y\in Q,\ z>h(y)\}$, a smooth vector field compactly supported away from the chart sides satisfies
$$\int_G\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=\int_Q\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(Dh(y),-1)\,dy.$$
Thus its outward normal is $(Dh,-1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ almost everywhere. The sign reverses for a subgraph. The graph surface measure is locally finite and Radon on $F(Q)$ with its relative topology, and its null sets coincide with graph images of Lebesgue-null subsets of the base.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. If two finite signed Radon measures on $\Omega$ have the same integrals against every function in $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, then the measures are equal.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its BV space and boundary $L^1$ space are both the zero space, the zero trace is unique, and every formula and estimate holds with both sides zero. Assume henceforth $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. By [F5], $\partial\Omega$ is compact; choose finitely many smaller graph charts with positive margins inside the original charts that still cover it. Each smaller graph base is bounded and its Lipschitz constant finite, so [F2] gives finite Radon surface measure on that patch and $\mathcal H^{n-1}(\partial\Omega)<\infty$. In each chart [F1] defines a local trace and bounds its surface $L^1$ norm, using [F2], by a chart constant times $\|u\|_1+|Du|(\Omega)$. On overlaps these local traces agree by [F1]. Consequently they define one class $Tu\in L^1(\partial\Omega,\mathcal H^{n-1})$ with $\|Tu\|_1\le C(\|u\|_1+TV(u;\Omega))$. Linearity follows locally from [F1], hence globally.

Construct a finite smooth partition equal to one on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, subordinate to the boundary charts and the interior open set $\Omega$: by [F5] this compact set is covered by finitely many balls with doubled closures in those open sets; take the bumps in [F3], and divide them by their positive sum near $\overline\Omega$. Multiply by one further smooth cutoff supported where the sum is positive and equal to one near $\overline\Omega$. First take $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^n)$ and apply the local Green identity [F1] to each chart-supported field $\eta_j\phi$. For the interior-supported field the defining distributional identity applies. Sum the identities. Since $\sum_j\eta_j=1$ and $\sum_j\nabla\eta_j=0$ near $\overline\Omega$, the interior and boundary sums are exactly $$\int_\Omega u\operatorname{div}\phi=-\int_\Omega\phi\cdot dDu+\int_{\partial\Omega}Tu\,\phi\cdot\nu\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}.$$ For an arbitrary $\phi\in C_c^1$, use [F7] to approximate $\phi$ and its first derivatives uniformly by compactly supported smooth fields; finite variation and $Tu\in L^1$ pass every term to the limit.

Extend each coordinate of $Du$ by zero from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb R^n$. It is a finite signed Radon measure: compact inner approximation can be performed inside $\Omega$, and outer approximation in the ambient space follows by applying that inner approximation to the complement and using finiteness. For each coordinate $i$, the boundary density $f_i:=Tu\,
u_i$ is integrable because $Tu\in L^1$ and $|
u_i|\le1$. By [F6], $f_i\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\partial\Omega}$ is a finite signed Radon measure; this verifies the required weighted-measure regularity, not just its finiteness. Thus their difference $\mu=i_\#Du-Tu\,
u\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\partial\Omega}$ is a finite Radon vector measure by [F4]. The formula in step 2.1 says exactly that $D\widetilde u=\mu$, so $\widetilde u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$.

The two summands defining $\mu$ in step 3.1 are supported on the disjoint Borel sets $\Omega$ and $\partial\Omega$. The partition definition of variation therefore gives the sum of their variations. For a unit measurable vector density $

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by Lipschitz graph neighborhoods with $\Omega$ on one side of each graph. For every $v\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ and $h\in\mathbb R^n$, $$\|v(\cdot+h)-v\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)}\le |h|TV(v;\mathbb R^n).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(v_k)$ be a sequence in real $L^1(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\sup_k\|v_k\|_1<\infty$, all zero almost everywhere outside one bounded set. If $\lim_{r\downarrow0}\sup_{k,\ |h|\le r}\|v_k(\cdot+h)-v_k\|_1=0$, then a subsequence converges in $L^1(\mathbb R^n)$. This assertion does not require Dependent Choice.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Every $u\in X$ is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz. Define its extended distributional total variation by
$$TV_2(u;\Omega):=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\ \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2),\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}|\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$
where $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ denotes smooth compactly supported vector fields, $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm, and $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\partial_1\varphi_1+\partial_2\varphi_2$. This definition treats $L^2$ functions as almost-everywhere classes and does not require $u\in L^1(\Omega)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.
For every open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the space $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $C_0(\Omega)$ in the uniform norm.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, every bounded real linear functional on $C_0(U;\mathbb R)$ is integration against a unique finite signed Radon measure. No Dependent Choice assumption is required.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$

derivations.claim: Every $L^2$ function is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz, so its distributional derivatives are defined. For $i=1,2$, set $L_i(\psi):=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\psi\,dx$ on $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. If $\psi\ne0$, the vector field $\varphi=\psi e_i/\|\psi\|_\infty$ and its negative are admissible in [F1]; hence $|L_i(\psi)|\le M\|\psi\|_\infty$. The same bound is immediate for $\psi=0$. By [F3], $L_i$ extends uniquely to a bounded real linear functional on $C_0(\Omega)$.

Countable Choice and [F4] represent each extension by a finite signed Radon measure $\mu_i$. Formula [F2] identifies $\mu_i$ with $D_i u$, so $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ has finite vector Radon variation by [F5]. For every continuous compactly supported $g$ with $\|g\|_\infty\le1$, approximate uniformly by a smooth compactly supported $h$ with $\|h-g\|_\infty<\varepsilon$, and replace $h$ by $h/\max\{1,\|h\|_\infty\}$. The replacement has norm at most one and differs from $g$ by at most $2\varepsilon$. Since $\sum_i|\mu_i|(\Omega)<\infty$, its integral against $\mu$ approaches that of $g$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Thus the supremum over smooth unit fields equals the continuous-field supremum in [F5]. By [F2], $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi=-\int\varphi\cdot d\mu$; symmetry of the unit test class removes this minus sign. Consequently $|Du|(\Omega)=M=TV_2(u;\Omega)$, proving the assertion.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Every $u\in X$ is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz. Define its extended distributional total variation by
$$TV_2(u;\Omega):=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\ \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2),\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}|\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$
where $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ denotes smooth compactly supported vector fields, $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm, and $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\partial_1\varphi_1+\partial_2\varphi_2$. This definition treats $L^2$ functions as almost-everywhere classes and does not require $u\in L^1(\Omega)$.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: The zero function has $TV_2(0;\Omega)=0$, so the functional is proper; its defining test class is symmetric under $\varphi\mapsto-\varphi$, hence its supremum is nonnegative. For $\lambda>0$, linearity of every test integral gives $TV_2(\lambda u;\Omega)=\lambda TV_2(u;\Omega)$, and the equality also holds for $\lambda=0$. For $\theta\in[0,1]$, every admissible field gives $\int(\theta u+(1-\theta)v)\operatorname{div}\varphi\le\theta TV_2(u;\Omega)+(1-\theta)TV_2(v;\Omega)$; taking the supremum proves convexity, with the extended-real cases automatic.

By [F3], every fixed test integral is a continuous linear functional on $L^2$. For each real $a$, the sublevel set $\{u:TV_2(u;\Omega)\le a\}$ is the intersection, over all admissible $\varphi$, of the closed half-spaces $\{u:\int u\operatorname{div}\varphi\le a\}$; hence it is closed and $TV_2$ is lower semicontinuous. If $u\in BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega)$, [F1] and [F2] give $TV_2(u;\Omega)=TV(u;\Omega)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $u\in BV(\Omega)$ there is a sequence $u_k\in C^\infty(\Omega)$ such that $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$ and $\int_\Omega |\nabla u_k|\,dx\to TV(u;\Omega)$. When $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$, the approximating functions may be chosen compactly supported.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)\cap L^1(\Omega)$ satisfy $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx<\infty$. For $t>0$ set $E_t^+:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>t\}$ and for $t<0$ set $E_t^-:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)<t\}$. Then the level sets have finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ for almost every applicable $t$, and
$$\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\Omega)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\Omega)\,dt.$$

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For a compact smooth planar region $D$ oriented by $dx\wedge dy$ and smooth $P,Q$ on a neighborhood, general Stokes gives
$$\int_{\partial D}(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=\int_D(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\,dy,$$
$$\int_{\partial D}(P\,dy-Q\,dx)=\int_D(P_x+Q_y)\,dx\,dy.$$
When $D$ also has the supplied finite elementary Green decomposition required by the classical results, these are exactly their circulation and outward-flux formulas. Outer boundary curves run counterclockwise and holes clockwise.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $X$ be a nonempty
compact connected one-dimensional topological manifold without boundary
([[def-compact-space]], [[def-connected-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Then $X$ is homeomorphic to the circle
$S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$
([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). If in addition $X$ carries a
smooth structure making it a smooth one-manifold without boundary, then $X$ is
diffeomorphic to this circle
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]).

The empty manifold is excluded by the hypothesis: it is compact and connected
under the conventions of this library, but it is not homeomorphic to a circle.
The hypothesis "without boundary" is likewise essential: the closed interval
$[0,1]$ is compact and connected but has boundary points and is not a circle.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For all
$f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$,

$$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)} ,$$where both sums are taken in the finite-subset-supremum/finite-subset-net sense of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. The bilinear series is absolutely convergent,$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\bigl|\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}\bigr|\le \Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat f(k)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} \Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat g(k)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

and the value is also the limit of the canonical symmetric partial sums
$\sum_{|k|\le N}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$.

derivations.claim: First suppose $G\subset\mathbb R^2$ is a bounded open set with compact smooth boundary $\Gamma$. The boundary is a compact smooth one-dimensional manifold without boundary. Connected coordinate arcs cover $\Gamma$; compactness gives a finite subcover, so $\Gamma$ has finitely many connected components. By [F5] each component is a smooth embedded circle. Parametrize component $i$ by an orientation-compatible unit-speed smooth periodic curve $\gamma_i:[0,L_i]\to\mathbb R^2$, where $L_i$ is its length. The divergence formula in [F3] gives $D\chi_G=-\nu\,\mathcal H^1|_\Gamma$ with $\nu$ the outward normal, and [F4] therefore gives $P(G;\mathbb R^2)=\mathcal H^1(\Gamma)=\sum_iL_i$. Applying Stokes in [F3] to $\omega=(x\,dy-y\,dx)/2$, whose exterior derivative is $dx\wedge dy$, gives $$|G|=\frac12\sum_i\int_0^{L_i}(\gamma_{i,1}\gamma'_{i,2}-\gamma_{i,2}\gamma'_{i,1})\,ds.$$ For each $i$, translating $\gamma_i$ by its arclength mean $\bar\gamma_i=L_i^{-1}\int_0^{L_i}\gamma_i(s)\,ds$ does not change this integral, since each coordinate derivative integrates to zero over a period. Write $z_i=\gamma_i-\bar\gamma_i$.

Now let $E$ be as in the Statement and put $u=\chi_E$. By [F1], choose $u_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ with $e_j:=\|u_j-\chi_E\|_1\to0$ and $a_j:=\int|\nabla u_j|\to P(E;\mathbb R^2)$. If $|E|=0$, the result is immediate. If some $e_j=0$, continuity forces $u_j$ to take only the values $0$ and $1$ everywhere; connectedness of $\mathbb R^2$ and compact support then force $u_j=0$, contradicting $|E|>0$. Thus $e_j>0$. Let $\tau_j=\sqrt{e_j}$ and discard finitely many terms so $0<\tau_j<\min\{1/2,|E|/2\}$. For every $t\in I_j:=[\tau_j,1-\tau_j]$, a point where $\chi_E$ and $\chi_{\{u_j>t\}}$ differ contributes at least $\tau_j$ to $|u_j-\chi_E|$; hence $|\{u_j>t\}\mathbin\triangle E|\le e_j/\tau_j=\tau_j$.

For a smooth $L$-periodic scalar function $z$ of mean zero, set $v(\theta)=z(L\theta/(2\pi))$. Its zeroth Fourier coefficient vanishes. Integration by parts gives $\widehat{v'}(k)=ik\widehat v(k)$ for every integer $k$. Parseval [F6] and $k^2\ge1$ for $k\ne0$ imply $\int_0^{2\pi}|v|^2\,d\theta\le\int_0^{2\pi}|v'|^2\,d\theta$. Changing variables yields $$\int_0^L|z(s)|^2\,ds\le\left(\frac L{2\pi}\right)^2\int_0^L|z'(s)|^2\,ds.$$ Apply this to both coordinates of $z_i$ and add. Since $|z'_i|=|\gamma'_i|=1$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $$\left|\frac12\int_0^{L_i}(z_{i,1}z'_{i,2}-z_{i,2}z'_{i,1})\,ds\right|\le\frac12\|z_i\|_{L^2}\|z'_i\|_{L^2}\le\frac{L_i^2}{4\pi}.$$ Summing over the finitely many boundary components and using $\sum_iL_i^2\le(\sum_iL_i)^2$ proves $4\pi|G|\le P(G;\mathbb R^2)^2$.

By [F2], the measurable level-perimeter function has integral at most $a_j$ on $I_j$, whose length is $1-2\tau_j$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, the set of $t\in I_j$ with $P(\{u_j>t\};\mathbb R^2)\le a_j/(1-2\tau_j)+\varepsilon$ has positive measure; otherwise its integral over $I_j$ would exceed $a_j$. The critical values of $u_j$ form a null set by [F2], so choose such a regular value $t_j$ and take $\varepsilon=1/j$. Since $t_j>0$ and $u_j$ is compactly supported, $G_j:=\{u_j>t_j\}$ is bounded and its closure is a compact smooth domain with boundary $\{u_j=t_j\}$. Thus step 2.1 applies to $G_j$, and $$|G_j\mathbin\triangle E|\le\tau_j,\qquad P(G_j;\mathbb R^2)\le\frac{a_j}{1-2\tau_j}+\frac1j.$$ The right side has limit $P(E;\mathbb R^2)$, while $|G_j|\to|E|$.

Step 2.1 gives $4\pi|G_j|\le P(G_j;\mathbb R^2)^2$ for every selected $j$. Taking upper limits, the convergence $|G_j|\to|E|$ and the perimeter upper bound from step 3.1 give $4\pi|E|\le P(E;\mathbb R^2)^2$. This proves the claimed inequality for every finite-measure finite-perimeter set.

Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $B(0,1)$, $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset B(0,2)$, and let $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ for integers $R\ge1$. This proves existence of a family with $\sup_R R\|\nabla\chi_R\|_\infty<\infty$. Now fix any family satisfying all four conditions in the statement, write $C=\sup_R R\|\nabla\chi_R\|_\infty$, and put $v_R=\chi_Ru$. Then $v_R\in L^2$ has compact support, hence is in $L^1$, and $v_R\to u$ in $L^2$ because $\chi_R=1$ on $B(0,R)$ and $u\in L^2$.

For every scalar $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, local integrability of $u$ and the definition of distributional derivative give $$-\int \chi_Ru\,\partial_i\psi=-\int u\,\partial_i(\chi_R\psi)+\int u\psi\,\partial_i\chi_R=\int\chi_R\psi\,dD_i u+\int u\psi\,\partial_i\chi_R.$$ Thus $D v_R=\chi_RDu+u\nabla\chi_R\,dx$. The variation of the first term is at most $|Du|(\mathbb R^2)$, and the second has variation at most $$\frac CR\int_{B(0,2R)\setminus B(0,R)}|u|\,dx\le C'\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus B(0,R))},$$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the annulus area bound $|B(0,2R)\setminus B(0,R)|^{1/2}\le C''R$. This error tends to zero. Since $v_R\in L^1$ and its derivative is a finite vector Radon measure, $v_R\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$, and [F1] yields $\limsup_R TV(v_R;\mathbb R^2)\le |Du|(\mathbb R^2)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$. The estimate applies to the arbitrary controlled family fixed in step 1.1 and proves the statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Set $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ for a measure space $(\Sigma,\mu)$, using the real integral inner products; under Countable Choice these are real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $A^*:Y\to X$ be its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$. Define $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ as follows. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

Identify each $q\in X$ with the continuous linear functional $h\mapsto\langle q,h\rangle_X$ by the real Hilbert-space Riesz representation. For exact data $f=Au^\dagger$, a **minimum-TV exact solution** is a point $u^\dagger\in X$ satisfying $Au^\dagger=f$ and $R(u^\dagger)\le R(u)$ for every $u\in X$ with $Au=f$. A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, the **Bregman distance** generated by $\xi^\dagger$ from the reference point $x^\dagger$ to $x$ is

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}.$$

The subgradient inequality makes this quantity nonnegative, and $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x^\dagger,x^\dagger)=0$. The definition fixes the orientation: the first argument is the comparison point and the second is the reference point carrying the chosen subgradient.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, and define its Fenchel conjugate $R^*:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ by $R^*(\xi):=\sup_{z\in X}(\langle\xi,z\rangle_{X^*,X}-R(z))$. For every $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$ and $\xi\in X^*$, the Fenchel–Young inequality and its equality characterization are

$$R(x)+R^*(\xi)\ge\langle\xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X},\qquad R(x)+R^*(\xi)=\langle\xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \xi\in\partial R(x).$$

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, let $F:D(F)\subseteq X\to Y$, let $x^\dagger\in D(F)$ with exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$, and let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex with $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$. Fix $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$, an exponent $1\le p<\infty$, a continuous nondecreasing concave function $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, a coefficient $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0\ge R(x^\dagger)$. The **variational source condition** with these data holds on the named regularizer sublevel $L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}$ when

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad(x\in L_{R_0}).$$

The condition is an assumption on the selected subgradient and the stated sublevel; it makes no assertion that a subgradient exists at every point or that a regularized minimizer exists.

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, $D(F)\subseteq X$, and $F:D(F)\to Y$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, let $x^\dagger\in D(F)\cap\operatorname{dom}R$, set $y=F(x^\dagger)$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. Fix $1\le p<\infty$, $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0>R(x^\dagger)$. Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, and assume the variational source inequality

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad\left(x\in L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}\right),$$

where $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}$. Extend $-\psi$ by $+\infty$ on negative arguments and write $H(q):=(-\psi)^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$; assume $H(q)$ is finite for sufficiently large $q$ and $H(q)\to0$ as $q\to\infty$. For sufficiently small noise levels $\delta>0$ and data $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, define $J_\alpha^\delta(x):=p^{-1}\|F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha R(x)$. Suppose $\alpha=\alpha(\delta)>0$ tends to zero, $0\le\varepsilon_\delta\le C_\varepsilon\delta^p$, and $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in D(F)$ is an $\varepsilon_\delta$-minimizer, meaning $J_\alpha^\delta(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})\le\inf_{z\in D(F)}J_\alpha^\delta(z)+\varepsilon_\delta$. Set $c_p:=2^{1-p}/p$ and $\rho_\delta:=H(c_p/\alpha(\delta))$. Assume that for constants $c_-,c_+,C_H>0$ independent of $\delta$,

$$c_-\delta^p\le\alpha(\delta)\rho_\delta\le c_+\delta^p,\qquad H(c_p/(2\alpha(\delta)))\le C_H\rho_\delta$$

for all sufficiently small $\delta$. Then for all sufficiently small $\delta$, $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in L_{R_0}$ and

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon},x^\dagger)=O(\rho_\delta),\qquad \|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta).$$

If, in addition, $\psi(C_0\delta^p)=O(\rho_\delta)$ for a fixed $C_0$ such that $T_\delta:=\|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\le C_0\delta^p$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$, then $|R(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-R(x^\dagger)|=O(\rho_\delta)$. If also $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)\ge c_R\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^s$ on $L_{R_0}$ for constants $c_R,s>0$, then $\|x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}-x^\dagger\|_X^s=O(\rho_\delta)$.

In the Hilbert special case, set $p=2$ and suppose $X,Y$ are real Hilbert spaces, $F:U\to Y$ has the real open-domain interface of a nonlinear forward map, $x^\dagger$ is an $x_0$-minimum-norm exact solution, $R(x)=\frac12\|x-x_0\|_X^2$, and the source inequality on a regularizer sublevel contained in $U$ is

$$\langle x^\dagger-x_0,x^\dagger-x\rangle_X\le\beta_1\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2+\beta_2\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y$$

with $0\le\beta_1<1$ and $\beta_2\ge0$. For exact global minimizers of the nonlinear Tikhonov functional with $\alpha(\delta)\asymp\delta$, the theorem gives $\|x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X=O(\sqrt\delta)$ and $\|F(x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta)$. The assertion is conditional on such a global minimizer being supplied; it does not assert existence or cover local numerical minima.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: Put $q^\dagger=A^*p^\dagger$. Applying [F2] at $u^\dagger$ with $z=0$ and $z=2u^\dagger$, and using $R(0)=0$ and $R(2u^\dagger)=2R(u^\dagger)$, gives $\langle q^\dagger,u^\dagger\rangle_X=R(u^\dagger)$. For arbitrary $z\in X$, [F2] then yields $R(z)\ge\langle q^\dagger,z\rangle_X$, so $q^\dagger\in\partial R(0)$ and $p^\dagger\in K$. Every $p\in K$ satisfies $\langle f,p\rangle_Y=\langle u^\dagger,A^*p\rangle_X\le R(u^\dagger)$; equality holds for $p^\dagger$. Thus $P_0$ is nonempty, closed, and convex.

The set $K$ is nonempty because $0\in\partial R(0)$, convex by the subgradient inequality, and closed because $\partial R(0)=\{q:R(z)\ge\langle q,z\rangle_X\text{ for all }z\}$ is an intersection of closed half-spaces and $A^*$ is continuous. For any nonempty closed convex subset $C$ of a Hilbert space, let $d=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$ and use Countable Choice to select $c_n\in C$ with $\|x-c_n\|^2\le d^2+1/n$. The midpoint belongs to $C$, so the parallelogram identity gives $\|c_n-c_m\|^2\le2/n+2/m$; thus $(c_n)$ is Cauchy. Completeness and closedness yield a nearest point, and strict convexity of squared norm makes it unique. Applying this to $K$ and $P_0$ defines their projections.

Completing the square gives $D_{\alpha,w}(p)=\frac{\|f+w\|_Y^2}{2\alpha}-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|p-(f+w)/\alpha\|_Y^2$. Hence its unique maximizer on $K$ is $p_{\alpha,w}=\operatorname{Proj}_K((f+w)/\alpha)$.

Let $u_{\alpha,w}$ be a supplied global minimizer and put $p=(f+w-Au_{\alpha,w})/\alpha$. For any $h\in X$ and $t>0$, objective minimality and expansion of the square give $[R(u_{\alpha,w}+th)-R(u_{\alpha,w})]/t\ge\langle A^*p,h\rangle_X-t\|Ah\|_Y^2/(2\alpha)$. As $t\downarrow0$, the lower limit of these secants is at least $\langle A^*p,h\rangle_X$; convexity makes the unit secant at least every smaller positive secant, so $R(u_{\alpha,w}+h)-R(u_{\alpha,w})\ge\langle A^*p,h\rangle_X$. This for every $h$ proves $A^*p\in\partial R(u_{\alpha,w})$. Applying [F2] with $z=0$ and $z=2u_{\alpha,w}$ gives $\langle A^*p,u_{\alpha,w}\rangle_X=R(u_{\alpha,w})$, and then [F2] for arbitrary $z$ gives $A^*p\in\partial R(0)$, so $p\in K$. By [F4] at $0$, $R^*(A^*q)=0$ for every $q\in K$; Fenchel–Young in [F4] therefore gives $\langle A^*q,u_{\alpha,w}\rangle_X\le R(u_{\alpha,w})$. Thus $D_{\alpha,w}(q)\le R(u_{\alpha,w})+\alpha\langle p,q\rangle_Y-\alpha\|q\|_Y^2/2=D_{\alpha,w}(p)-\alpha\|q-p\|_Y^2/2$. Hence $p=p_{\alpha,w}$. Finally $Au_{\alpha,w}=f+w-\alpha p$, so $\frac12\|Au_{\alpha,w}-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u_{\alpha,w})=\alpha D_{\alpha,w}(p)$, establishing the normalized value identity in the Statement.

If $P_Kx=p$ and $P_Ky=q$, minimizing squared distance along the segment from $p$ to any $z\in K$ gives $\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0$. Apply this with $z=q$, and the corresponding inequality for $P_Ky$ with $z=p$. Adding yields $\|p-q\|_Y^2\le\langle x-y,p-q\rangle_Y\le\|x-y\|_Y\|p-q\|_Y$ by [F7], so $\|p-q\|_Y\le\|x-y\|_Y$. Taking $x=(f+w)/\alpha$ and $y=f/\alpha$ proves the first noise-stability bound; applying $A^*$ proves the second.

Write $p_n=p_{\alpha_n,0}$. Maximality against $p_0\in P_0$ and the support bound $\langle f,p_n\rangle_Y\le R(u^\dagger)$ give $\|p_n\|_Y\le\|p_0\|_Y$ and $\langle f,p_n\rangle_Y\to R(u^\dagger)$. The closed span of any subsequence is separable; Gram–Schmidt on rational finite linear combinations of its terms gives a finite or countable orthonormal family with dense span. Repeated use of [F8] and [A1] selects a further subsequence whose coordinates all converge. For each finite initial segment, expanding the nonnegative squared norm after orthogonal projection shows that the sum of squared limiting coordinates is at most $\|p_0\|_Y^2$; hence the coordinates define a vector $p$ in that closed span. Approximation by finite linear combinations proves weak convergence there, and [F9] represents each functional $x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_Y$ restricted to the span, so convergence is weak in $Y$. The limit lies in $K$: by [F2], $K=\bigcap_{z\in X}\{q:\langle q,Az\rangle_Y\le R(z)\}$, an intersection of weakly closed half-spaces. It also attains $\langle f,p\rangle_Y=R(u^\dagger)$, so $p\in P_0$. Weak lower semicontinuity of the norm and the bound force $\|p\|_Y=\|p_0\|_Y$, hence uniqueness gives $p=p_0$. Every subsequence therefore has a further subsequence weakly converging to $p_0$; testing against any fixed $y\in Y$ shows that every scalar subsequence has a further subsequence converging to $\langle p_0,y\rangle_Y$, so $\langle p_n,y\rangle_Y\to\langle p_0,y\rangle_Y$. Thus $p_n\rightharpoonup p_0$. Weak lower semicontinuity and the uniform upper bound then give $\|p_n\|_Y\to\|p_0\|_Y$. The norm identity [F10] yields strong convergence, and boundedness of $A^*$ yields strong convergence of $A^*p_n$.

For $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$, [F1] and [F7] give $-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X=\langle p^\dagger,f-Au\rangle_Y\le\|p^\dagger\|_Y\|Au-f\|_Y$. Therefore the VSC [F5] holds with $\beta=0$, $p=2$, and $\psi(s)=C\sqrt{s}$, $C=1+\|p^\dagger\|_Y$, on every regularizer sublevel; [F3] identifies its Bregman term with the distance in the Statement. Its conjugate is $H(q)=C^2/(4q)$ for $q>0$. For an exact minimizer with $\|w\|_Y\le\delta$, comparison to $u^\dagger$ gives $R(u_{\alpha,w})\le R(u^\dagger)+\delta^2/(2\alpha)$; if $\alpha\asymp\delta$, this is below any fixed $R_0>R(u^\dagger)$ for small $\delta$. With $c_p=1/4$, $\rho_\delta=H(c_p/\alpha)=C^2\alpha\asymp\delta$ and $H(c_p/(2\alpha))=2\rho_\delta$, so all parameter-coupling hypotheses in [F6] hold and the stated rates follow.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. If $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ and $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$, there exist smooth cutoffs $\chi_k$ with $0\le\chi_k\le1$, $\chi_k=1$ on $B(0,k)$, support in $B(0,2k)$, and $\sup_{k\ge1}k\|\nabla\chi_k\|_\infty<\infty$. For every family satisfying these four conditions, $v_k:=\chi_ku$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1(\mathbb R^2)$, has support in $B(0,2k)$, converges to $u$ in $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$, and
$$\limsup_{k\to\infty}TV(v_k;\mathbb R^2)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $u\in BV(\Omega)$, and for $t>0$ set $E_t^+:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>t\}$ while for $t<0$ set $E_t^-:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)<t\}$. Then for almost every applicable $t$ these sets have finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$, and $$TV(u;\Omega)=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\Omega)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\Omega)\,dt.$$

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. Assume Countable Choice. For every nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, there is a finite constant $C_\Omega>0$ such that every $u\in BV(\Omega)$ satisfies
