Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

For a smooth manifold $M^n$, with boundary allowed, the **density bundle** is $DM=\coprod_{p\in M}D(T_pM)$. In coordinates $x$, let $|dx|=|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ be the density taking value one on the coordinate frame. On overlaps,
$$|dy|=|\det D_x y|\,|dx|.$$
A smooth density is a section with smooth real coefficient in these frames. Its support is the closure of its nonzero locus. The absolute determinants are positive smooth transition functions and satisfy the cocycle identities by the chain rule. A countable atlas and [[thm-vector-bundle-construction-from-a-smooth-cocycle]] therefore give a smooth line bundle. For boundary charts the same gluing proof uses half-space product charts; smoothness of transitions follows from their local extensions, and Hausdorffness and second countability follow as for the supplied cocycle construction. The fibers are lines by [[prop-one-densities-form-a-one-dimensional-vector-space]]. When $n=0$ the empty frame trivializes $DM=M\times\mathbb R$.

Here $0\in\mathbb N$, $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$, and $c_\alpha=D^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$. [[thm-power-series-define-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables]] therefore gives a holomorphic sum on the complex $s$-polydisc and the displayed derivative formula. Restriction to the real slice recovers $f$.

$$|f^{(n)}(a)|\le\frac{n!M}{r^n}.$$

The positive-phase hypothesis and compactness of $\operatorname{supp}a\setminus B_r(0)$ give $\operatorname{Im}(\Phi-\Phi_0)\ge d>0$ there. Since $a$ is bounded and $\chi_N$ is bounded by one, the absolute value of that contribution after multiplication by $e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}$ is at most $\|a\|_\infty |U|e^{-\lambda d}$, uniformly in $N$. Thus only the integral over the fixed local ball affects the power series; the complement contributes $O(e^{-d\lambda})$.

Put $\phi=-i(\Phi-\Phi_0)$, so $\operatorname{Re}\phi=\operatorname{Im}(\Phi-\Phi_0)$ and $\phi''(0)=H$. Apply [F1] to obtain a holomorphic Morse coordinate $w=\Psi(x)$ with $\phi(x)=\tfrac12 w\cdot w$. The transformed real ball is a local contour $\Gamma$ through $0$. The transformed amplitude $ b(w)=a(\Psi^{-1}(w))\det D\Psi^{-1}(w) $ is holomorphic in a fixed polydisc and has coefficients bounded by $M R^{-|\alpha|}$ for some $M,R>0$ by [F3]–[F5].

Taylor's formula gives $\operatorname{Re}(\phi(tv))=\tfrac12t^2v^T(\operatorname{Re}H)v+o(t^2)$; comparing with $\operatorname{Re}\phi(tv)\ge ct^2|v|^2$ and dividing by $t^2/2$ as $t\to0$ yields $v^T(\operatorname{Re}H)v\ge2c|v|^2$. In particular, the real projection on $A\mathbb R^n$ is injective, hence bijective by dimension, and $A\mathbb R^n=\{u+iKu:u\in\mathbb R^n\}$ for a real linear map $K$. For nonzero $u$, applying the strict inequality to $v=A^{-1}(u+iKu)$ gives $|Ku|<|u|$; compactness of the unit sphere gives $\|K\|<1$. The real inverse theorem [F6] makes the nonlinear contour $\Gamma$ a graph $u+i(Ku+r(u))$, with $r(u)=O(|u|^2)$. For sufficiently small $r_0$, the homotopy graphs $u+i(Ku+t r(u))$ remain in the holomorphic chart and satisfy $\operatorname{Re}(w\cdot w)\ge c_0|u|^2$ for $|u|\le r_0$, because the linear margin $|u|^2-|Ku|^2\ge(1-\|K\|^2)|u|^2$ dominates the $O(|u|^3)$ error. The homotopy $u+i tKu$, $0\le t\le1$, also has $\operatorname{Re}(w\cdot w)=|u|^2-t^2|Ku|^2\ge(1-\|K\|^2)|u|^2$. On the fixed outer boundary these bounds, together with boundedness of the transformed amplitude and Jacobian, make the integrals $O(e^{-c_1\lambda})$. [F7] and the contour statement in [F1] therefore deform $\Gamma$ to the real Gaussian contour, with only that exponential boundary term.

Truncate the Taylor series after total degrees below $2N$. On a smaller ball $|w|\le r_0<R$, the Cauchy bound [F5] and a geometric-series estimate give $ \left|b(w)-\sum_{|\alpha|<2N}b_\alpha w^\alpha\right| \le C_2^{N+1}|w|^{2N}. $ Integrating this remainder against $e^{-\lambda|w|^2/2}$ and using $z=\sqrt{\lambda}\,w$ bounds it by $ C_3^{N+1}\lambda^{-N-n/2}\int_{\mathbb R^n}|z|^{2N}e^{-|z|^2/2}\,dz \le C_4^{N+1}N!\lambda^{-N-n/2}. $ For the last inequality, convexity gives $(\sum_{j=1}^n z_j^2)^N\le n^{N-1}\sum_{j=1}^n|z_j|^{2N}$. Fubini factors each summand into one-dimensional Gaussian moments; integration by parts gives $M_N=(2N-1)M_{N-1}$ with $M_0=\sqrt{2\pi}$, since the polynomial times Gaussian boundary term tends to zero. Cauchy's coefficient bound and the at most exponential count of degree-$k$ multi-indices give $D_N:=\sum_{k<2N}\sum_{|\alpha|=k}|b_\alpha|r_0^{k-2N}\le C_5^{N+1}$, since $r_0,R$ are fixed positive constants and the sum has $2N$ terms after grouping degrees. An analytic double fibration is a diagram of real-analytic manifolds and real-analytic submersions
$$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X
$$
such that $Z$ is embedded in $G\times X$, both projections are submersions, and
$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$
Write $C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}$ for the incidence cotangent relation. Assume $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

derivations.claim: The relation is a smooth conic submanifold in local incidence coordinates: the conormal equations are smooth constant-rank linear equations in the covector variables, and the zero section is removed. Thus projection onto its first cotangent factor is a well-defined smooth map.

Global injectivity means that every data covector has at most one object covector paired with it; at a specified point $c$, the corresponding fiber condition is exactly $\pi_L^{-1}(\pi_L(c))=\{c\}$. Injectivity of the differential means that every tangent vector to $C_Z$ mapped to zero is itself zero. Both conditions are invariant under coordinate changes because [F2] makes $C_Z$ coordinate independent and cotangent coordinate changes are diffeomorphisms. This proves the two clauses in the definition.

For a smooth manifold $M^n$, with boundary allowed, the **density bundle** is $DM=\coprod_{p\in M}D(T_pM)$. In coordinates $x$, let $|dx|=|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ be the density taking value one on the coordinate frame. On overlaps,

derivations.claim: Since $F$ is a submersion, its differential has rank $k$. The tangent space of its zero level is $T_{(g,x)}Z=\ker DF(g,x)$. In finite-dimensional linear algebra, the annihilator of the kernel of a rank-$k$ linear map is the image of its transpose: inclusion follows from $\tau^TDFv=0$ for $v\in\ker DF$, and both spaces have dimension $k$. Hence every conormal is uniquely $DF^T\tau=(D_gF^T\tau,D_xF^T\tau)$.

By [F1], the incidence functional is integration of a test function against a smooth density on $Z$. Complete $F$ to submersion coordinates $(s,t)$ with $t=F(g,x)$, using [F3]. In these coordinates its action is $\int_{t=0}\Phi(s,0)c(s)|ds|$ for a smooth coefficient $c$. Rewriting the ambient density as $|dg\,dx|$ and applying the ordinary change-of-variables rule gives $b(g,x)\delta(F(g,x))|dg\,dx|$ for a smooth $b$; the Jacobian factor is nonzero because the coordinate map is a diffeomorphism.

The cotangent relation uses the conormal $(\eta,-\xi)$ by [F1]. Substituting the formula from step 1.1 gives $\eta=D_gF^T\tau$ and $-\xi=D_xF^T\tau$, so $\xi=-D_xF^T\tau$. Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,R)$ and let $0<r<R$. Suppose $M\ge0$ and

$$|f(\zeta)|\le M\qquad\text{whenever }|\zeta-a|=r.$$

Then, for every $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$|f^{(n)}(a)|\le\frac{n!M}{r^n}.$$

Let $\phi$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^n$, with $d\phi(0)=0$ and complex Hessian $H=\phi''(0)$ invertible. There is a local biholomorphic coordinate map $w=\Psi(z)$ with $\Psi(0)=0$ such that
$$
\phi(z)=\phi(0)+\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^n w_j^2.
$$
Its linear part satisfies $(\det D\Psi(0))^2=\det H$. For a continuous parameter family of invertible Hessians $H(p)$, near any fixed parameter $p_0$ the determinant remains in a disc avoiding $0$; choosing one square root at $p_0$ therefore fixes a continuous branch on that neighborhood. If $\operatorname{Re}H$ is positive definite, then
$$
\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\lambda x^THx/2}\,dx =(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2},\qquad \lambda>0,
$$
with the integral interpreted as an absolutely convergent improper integral and the branch analytically continued from real positive-definite matrices. Finally, deforming a holomorphic contour preserves the integral of a holomorphic top-degree form when the contours are homologous through a region of holomorphy and the swept boundary integrals tend to zero.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded open set, let $\Phi$ be holomorphic on a complex neighborhood of $\overline U$, and let $a\in C_c^\infty(U)$ have a holomorphic extension near $0$. Assume $0\in\operatorname{supp}a$, $\Phi(0)=\Phi_0$, $d\Phi(0)=0$, and $d\Phi(x)\ne0$ at every $x\in\operatorname{supp}a\setminus\{0\}$. Let $H=-i\Phi''(0)$ be complex symmetric with positive-definite real part. Assume there are $r,c_0,d_0>0$ such that
$$
\operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge c_0|x|^2 \quad(|x|\le r),\qquad \operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge d_0 \quad(x\in\operatorname{supp}a,\ |x|\ge r).
$$
Let $\chi_N$ be the finite-order cutoff sequence equal to one on a fixed neighborhood of $0$, with $0\le\chi_N\le1$, and supported where these phase hypotheses hold. For every integer $N\ge1$ and every $\lambda\ge1$, put $I_N(\lambda)=\int e^{i\lambda\Phi(x)}a(x)\chi_N(x)\,dx$. There are coefficients $c_j$ determined by the full Taylor series of the phase and amplitude at $0$ and constants $C,\delta>0$, independent of $N,\lambda$, such that
$$
I_N(\lambda)=e^{i\lambda\Phi_0}(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\lambda^{-j}\right)+E_N(\lambda),
$$
$$
|c_j|\le C^{j+1}j!,\qquad |e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)|\le C^{N+1}N!\lambda^{-N-n/2}+Ce^{-\delta\lambda}.
$$
The square-root branch is fixed by the preceding holomorphic Morse/Gaussian-contour lemma, and $c_0=a(0)$. Taking $N=\lfloor\epsilon\lambda\rfloor$ for sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $\lambda$ makes the normalized remainder $e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)=O(e^{-\delta_2\lambda})$ for some $\delta_2>0$. The expansion includes every coefficient through the stated truncation order; it is not only a leading-term estimate.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $K\subset U$ be compact. There are constants $A,C>0$ and functions $\chi_N\in C_c^\infty(U)$ for each integer $N\ge1$ such that $0\le\chi_N\le1$, $\chi_N=1$ on a fixed neighborhood of $K$, and
$$
|\partial^\alpha\chi_N(x)|\le C(AN)^{|\alpha|} \qquad (x\in\mathbb R^n,\ |\alpha|\le N).
$$
These are smooth compact cutoffs; no compactly supported analytic function is asserted.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ be
holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)\ne0$, then there are
open neighbourhoods $U_0\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $V_0$ of $F(a)$ such that
$F|_{U_0}:U_0\to V_0$ is biholomorphic.

If $G:V_0\to U_0$ denotes the inverse, then

$$DG(w)=DF(G(w))^{-1}\qquad(w\in V_0).$$

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Every compactly supported distribution $v\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ has a
unique extension $\widetilde v\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.  Restricting
$\widetilde v$ to $\mathcal D$ recovers $v$.  No choice axiom is required.

derivations.claim: We retain the formal inverse algebra needed to identify the external operator construction [F9]. For a formal holomorphic symbol $p=\sum_{j\ge0}h^jp_j(x,\xi)$, with $|p_j|\le C^{j+1}j!$ on a fixed polydisc, define $ p\#q=\sum_{j,k,\gamma}\frac{h^{j+k+|\gamma|}}{i^{|\gamma|}\gamma!} (\partial_\xi^\gamma p_j)(\partial_x^\gamma q_k). $ There are finitely many terms in each degree. Associativity follows directly by applying the product rule to the two triple products: splitting a multi-index $\gamma=\mu+\nu$ contributes $\gamma!/(\mu!\nu!)$, which cancels its denominator and leaves identical terms. The map $p\mapsto P=p(x,\xi+hD_x)$, with $D_x=\partial_x/i$, respects this product; expansion by the product rule gives the displayed formula.

The actual contour realization is [F8], with $\rho=-\operatorname{Im}S$ and $h=\lambda^{-1}$. In fixed-offset coordinates $y=x+w$, its oriented volume and prefactor give the explicit formula
$$
A_hv(x)=\left(\frac{R}{\pi h}\right)^n\int_{|w|\le r}\exp\left(\frac{-iw\cdot S_x(x)-R|w|^2}{h}\right)p\bigl(x,x+w,S_x(x)-iR\overline w;h\bigr)v(x+w;h)\,dL(w).
$$
Here $dL$ is Euclidean $2n$-dimensional measure, the phase-space cycle and its orientation are exactly those of [F8], and $R,r$ are fixed within the common holomorphy neighborhood. The Gaussian bound and amplitude-$1$ identity are the specified operator theorem [F8]; equivalently, for amplitude $1$ the holomorphic factor $e^{-iw\cdot S_x(x)/h}v(x+w;h)$ has constant Taylor coefficient $v(x;h)$ and all positive-degree holomorphic monomials have zero angular integral. The remaining Gaussian tail is exponentially small in the weighted germ. For this pluriharmonic weight the fixed-offset formula is holomorphic in $x$; it also specifies precisely the previously implicit cycle and measure. The fixed-derivative real-localization bounds used later are [F10], rather than an assertion obtained solely from this formal identity.

Here are estimates for this formal algebra that also control its inverse. Use nested complex $x$ neighborhoods $\Omega_t$, $0<t<t_0<1$, whose boundary separation is at least $t-s$, and keep $\xi$ in a smaller fixed polydisc. Write $P=\sum h^kP_k$, where $P_k$ has differential order at most $k$. Cauchy's inequality, first in the fixed $\xi$ polydisc and then in $x$, gives $ \|P_k\|_{t,s}\le C^{k+1} k^k(t-s)^{-k},\qquad 0<s<t<t_0. $ Indeed a term with $j+|\gamma|=k$ costs at most $C^{k+1}j!\gamma!(t-s)^{-|\gamma|}$; $j!\gamma!\le k!\le k^k$, $t-s<1$, and the number of terms is at most exponential in $k$. For $k=0$ use $0^0=1$. Let $f_k(P)$ be the least admissible constant in $\|P_k\|_{t,s}\le f_k(P)k^k(t-s)^{-k}$. If $R=PQ$, choose the intermediate radius with $r-s=j(t-s)/(j+k)$ for the term $P_jQ_k$. Then $ f_\ell(PQ)\le\sum_{j+k=\ell}f_j(P)f_k(Q). $ The endpoint cases use the same estimate without an intermediate loss. Consequently $\|P\|_\rho=\sum\rho^kf_k(P)$ is submultiplicative whenever finite. Conversely $p_k=P_k1$, evaluated with a fixed radius loss, satisfies $|p_k|\le C^{k+1}k^k\le (eC)^{k+1}k!$; the last inequality follows by integrating $\log t$ from $1$ to $k$. These estimates are on one fixed smaller neighborhood, independent of $k$.

If $p_0\ne0$, shrink so $1/p_0$ is bounded holomorphic. The formal product $p\#(1/p_0)=1-r$ has $r_0=0$ and finite $\|r\|_\rho$ for small $\rho$ by step 2.1; decreasing $\rho$ makes this norm less than $1/2$. Thus $ q=(1/p_0)\#\sum_{\ell\ge0}r^{\#\ell} $ has finite norm, because in each degree its defining sum is finite and the geometric norm sum is at most $2$. It follows that $q_j$ have factorial bounds on a fixed smaller neighborhood. This gives a right inverse. The identical construction on the other side gives a left inverse; associativity shows they agree. Truncating at $j<\epsilon/h$ realizes these symbols. A term with index $j$ has modulus at most $C(Chj)^j$; for $j\le\epsilon/h$ and $C\epsilon<1/2$ it is at most $C2^{-j}$. Two admissible truncations therefore differ by $O(e^{-c/h})$, also in every fixed derivative by [F1].

The actual composition and inverse statements invoked here are the external results [F9]–[F10]. The following calculation identifies their specialization and symbol; it is not an independent reconstruction of that analytic contour calculus. Products of these kernels are actual iterated contour integrals. All weights needed here are of this form, with $S$ the packet phase and its holomorphic critical value; thus the saddle phases used for contour comparison are holomorphic. Their composed contour is good: if the inner integration has loss $c|y-y(z)|^2$ and the outer one loss $c|z-z(x)|^2$, their sum controls the square distance from the combined critical point, since the critical-point maps have bounded derivatives. The holomorphic Morse coordinates [F2] identify this contour and the contour obtained by doing the integrations in the other order with graphs over a common negative-definite real subspace. Such graphs have slope less than one after a linear scaling; their straight interpolation has the same positive quadratic margin on a smaller ball. Stokes therefore changes the order and reduces the composition, with exponentially small boundary errors. Taylor expansion in $y-x$, followed by integration by parts in $\theta$, gives the full symbol $ p_{\mathrm{red}}(x,\xi;h)\sim\sum_\gamma\frac{h^{|\gamma|}}{i^{|\gamma|}\gamma!} \partial_\xi^\gamma\partial_y^\gamma p(x,y,\xi;h)|_{y=x}. $ For a product this is exactly the $\#$ formula in step 1.1. To estimate rather than just manipulate this expansion, apply [F3] on the good contour after its quadratic normalization. Cauchy bounds for the analytic amplitudes give $C^{N+1}N!h^N$ for the remainder after total degree $N$; each of the finitely many symbol indices contributes the convolution estimates in step 2.1. Taking $N=\lfloor\epsilon/h\rfloor$ makes this $O(e^{-c/h})$. The actual operator consequences are supplied by [F9]–[F10]: a zero reduced symbol acts by an exponentially small operator, and the inverse symbol of step 3.1 gives an actual two-sided inverse modulo such errors. Fixed-contour local remainders and symbols are holomorphic in $x$ by the fixed-offset representation in step 1.2, so Cauchy on a further smaller neighborhood controls their fixed derivatives. Errors involving smooth spatial cutoffs or moving outer boundaries are instead differentiated by the chain rule under the fixed-parameter boundary integrals. Each of their fixed $m$ derivatives costs at most $C_m h^{-M_m}$, or an additional fixed power of $N$ for a finite-order localizer with $N$ proportional to $h^{-1}$. The boundary has a fixed positive phase margin, so these polynomial losses are absorbed by reducing that margin. No Cauchy estimate is applied to a merely smooth cutoff error.

The same calculation permits a nonstandard holomorphic phase $S(x,y,\theta)$ with $S(x,x,\theta)=0$ and invertible mixed derivative $S_{x\theta}$ at the diagonal. Indeed $ S(x,y,\theta)=(x-y)\cdot\Theta(x,y,\theta),\qquad \Theta=\int_0^1 S_x(y+t(x-y),y,\theta)\,dt. $ By [F5], $\theta\mapsto\Theta$ is a local biholomorphism. The change of variable, including its holomorphic Jacobian, gives the standard kernel of step 1.2. A good contour for one kernel is good for the other because the exponent is identical. Ellipticity is preserved by the nonzero Jacobian. Hence the composition and inverse theorems [F9], with the symbol identification above, hold for these phases too.

For the given positive phase form the kernel $ A(x,y;h)=h^{-3n/2}\int e^{i(\phi(x,q,p)-\phi^*(y,q,p))/h}a(x,q,p;h)\,dq\,dp. $ Locally this is a kernel of the type just constructed. To see this, first integrate in $q$ by analytic stationary phase. At $x=y=q$ the $q$ derivative vanishes, and the imaginary part of its Hessian is positive definite because $\operatorname{Im}\phi(x,q,p)+\operatorname{Im}\phi(y,q,p)\ge c(|x-q|^2+|y-q|^2)$. Its critical value $S(x,y,p)$ is zero at $x=y$, and $S_x(x,x,p)=-p$. Thus $S_{xp}=-I$ there. The resulting kernel has prefactor $h^{-n}$ and a classical analytic amplitude whose leading term is a nonzero Gaussian determinant times $a_0(x,x,p)$. It is elliptic. The actual elliptic inverse theorem [F9], with the phase and symbol identified in steps 1.2, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1, gives an analytic operator $B$ with $AB=BA=I$ modulo exponential errors on the appropriate holomorphic germs.

Real realization, nested-domain composition, and all fixed-derivative localization bounds are the external input [F10]. We identify its hypotheses here, preserving the local contour and cutoff calculations. Restrict $(q,p)$ to $W$ and insert a fixed smooth spatial cutoff equal to one near $x=y=q$. Away from this diagonal, positivity supplies $\operatorname{Im}(\phi(x,\alpha)-\phi^*(y,\alpha))\ge d>0$ on the cutoff transition. When the kernel acts on a holomorphic packet $v_\beta(y)=t(y,\beta;h)e^{i\psi(y,\beta)/h}$, the total phase has its unique nearby critical point at $y=q=x$, $p=p_\beta$ when $x=q_\beta$. In a small neighborhood it satisfies the stronger contour estimate $ \operatorname{Im}S_{\mathrm{total}}\ge c\bigl(|x-q|^2+|y-q|^2+|p-p_\beta|^2\bigr) $ after deforming $y$ by $y\mapsto y+i\delta\overline{\partial_y S_{\mathrm{total}}}$ near the diagonal. Here Taylor's formula gives an added $\delta|\partial_y S_{\mathrm{total}}|^2+O(\delta^2|\partial_y S_{\mathrm{total}}|^2)$; $\partial_y S_{\mathrm{total}}=p-p_\beta+O(|x-q|+|y-q|)$, so sufficiently small $\delta$ proves the estimate. For complex $x$ nearby continue the critical point by [F5] and use the quadratic coordinates to deform a further $O(|x-q_\beta|)$, leaving the outer boundary fixed. The good-contour estimates of step 4.1 then apply uniformly. On the spatial cutoff transition the original positive margin persists; on $\partial W$, for $\beta\in W_0$, the displayed estimate supplies a fixed margin. Every swept boundary integral is consequently $O(e^{-c/h})$. For a fixed number of derivatives, its smoothly parameterized compact boundary, cutoff and phase contribute only fixed powers of $h^{-1}$ and, for finite-order localizers, of $N$. Those powers are absorbed into a smaller exponential margin. Holomorphic fixed-domain contour remainders separately have the Cauchy derivative bounds of step 4.1. If finite-order localization is needed in an integration by parts, [F4] with $N=\lfloor\epsilon/h\rfloor$ gives a factor at most $(ChN)^N$ on the nonstationary part; choose $C\epsilon<1/2$. This verifies the real realization of the compositions and of the identity on each such packet.

The packet-action lemma, Theorem 5.3 and Proposition 6.2 in [F10] supply the actual realization of this step. Applying $B$ to $v_\beta$ gives $e^{i\psi(y,\beta)/h}b(y,\beta;h)$ modulo exponential errors, where $b$ is a classical analytic amplitude bounded by a fixed power of $h^{-1}$. This follows from the same composition calculation, treating $\beta$ as a parameter and taking the weight $\rho=-\operatorname{Im}\psi$ in step 1.2; the combined critical point is the diagonal, and steps 4.1 and 7.1 give the factorial remainder on smaller fixed neighborhoods. Therefore $ABv_\beta=v_\beta+R_\beta$, and its realized real-variable expression is the representation in the statement with $ K(\beta,\alpha;h)=h^{-3n/2}\int e^{i(\psi(y,\beta)-\phi^*(y,\alpha))/h}b(y,\beta;h)\,dy. $ The imaginary part of this exponent is at least $c(|y-q_\beta|^2+|y-q_\alpha|^2)$ for real parameters, so the compact integral is bounded by a power of $h^{-1}$, uniformly in $\alpha\in W$, $\beta\in W_0$. Errors and cutoff transitions retain the derivative bounds of step 7.1. Pairing the representation with $u$ is legitimate by [F7]; its finite-order seminorm bound makes $\langle u,R_\beta\rangle$ exponential. The integral of a uniformly exponentially small source transform times the polynomially bounded $K$ is exponential too. Interchange the two elliptic packet families to obtain the reverse implication.

Finally use the reference phase $ \phi_G(y,q,p)=(q-y)\cdot p+\frac{i|p|}{2}|q-y|^2. $ It is holomorphic on a complex neighborhood of any nonzero real $p_0$, choosing the branch of $\sqrt{p\cdot p}$ positive there. Its packet with parameter $\lambda$ is exactly the unit-direction Gaussian packet with frequency parameter $\lambda|p|$ and direction $p/|p|$. On a fixed small parameter neighborhood $|p|$ is bounded above and below by positive constants, so the exponential criteria agree; bounded frequencies are absorbed into the constant. All amplitude and inverse constructions above involve finite sums or a uniquely determined formal recursion and its finite truncation. No choice axiom is used.

citations.quote:
An analytic double fibration is a diagram of real-analytic manifolds and real-analytic submersions
$$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X
$$
such that $Z$ is embedded in $G\times X$, both projections are submersions, and
$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$
Write $C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}$ for the incidence cotangent relation. Assume $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $K\subset U$ be compact. There are constants $A,C>0$ and functions $\chi_N\in C_c^\infty(U)$ for each integer $N\ge1$ such that $0\le\chi_N\le1$, $\chi_N=1$ on a fixed neighborhood of $K$, and
$$
|\partial^\alpha\chi_N(x)|\le C(AN)^{|\alpha|} \qquad (x\in\mathbb R^n,\ |\alpha|\le N).
$$
These are smooth compact cutoffs; no compactly supported analytic function is asserted.

Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,R)$ and let $0<r<R$. Suppose $M\ge0$ and

$$|f(\zeta)|\le M\qquad\text{whenever }|\zeta-a|=r.$$

Then, for every $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$|f^{(n)}(a)|\le\frac{n!M}{r^n}.$$

Let $f$ be a real analytic map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, $f$ has a real analytic local inverse near $f(a)$. Let $P(x,y)$ be real analytic near $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^k$, $k\ge1$, with $P(a,b)=0$ and $D_yP(a,b)$ invertible. On sufficiently small neighborhoods its zero set is exactly the graph of a unique real analytic $y=g(x)$ with $g(a)=b$.

derivations.claim: If $K=\varnothing$, then $u=0$ and the conclusion is immediate; assume $K\ne\varnothing$. Fix a relatively compact data chart $V_0$ about $z_0$ and a compact object neighborhood $K_2$ with $K\subset\operatorname{int}K_2$. By [F1], the incidence portion over $\overline V_0$ and $K_2$ is compact. The portion of $C_Z$ over it with unit data covector is compact as well. Indeed, at each incidence point the projection of its conormal fiber $(\eta,-\xi)\mapsto\eta$ is injective: if $\eta=0$, then $-\xi$ annihilates the image of $d\pi_X$, which is all of $T_xX$ by [F1], so $\xi=0$. On the compact incidence portion these injective linear maps have a uniform lower bound in fixed local metrics. Thus $|\eta|=1$ bounds $\xi$, and closedness of the normalized relation gives compactness. Write $\omega_0=\zeta_0/|\zeta_0|$ in the data chart. If no product neighborhood of $(z_0,\omega_0,K)$ were disjoint from the normalized relation, there would be relation points with data bases tending to $z_0$, unit data covectors tending to $\omega_0$, and object bases tending to $K$. Compactness would give a limiting relation point over $(z_0,\omega_0)$ and some $x\in K$, contradicting the hypothesis after rescaling by $|\zeta_0|$. Hence there are neighborhoods $V\Subset V_0$, $\Gamma\subset S^{\dim G-1}$ of $\omega_0$, and an open neighborhood $O$ of $K$, with $\overline O\subset\operatorname{int}K_2$, such that no relation point lies over $(q,\omega,x)$ for $q\in V$, $\omega\in\Gamma$, and $x\in O$. Choose a compact neighborhood $K_1$ with $K\subset\operatorname{int}K_1\subset K_1\subset O$. The incidence portion over $\overline V$ and $K_1$ is compact by [F1]. Use [F5] to cover it by finitely many analytic fiber charts for the projection to $X$, written $(t,x)\mapsto(z(t,x),x)$. In these coordinates the transpose data packet has integrals of the form $ \int e^{i\lambda\Psi(t,x;q,\omega)}b(t,x)\chi(z(t,x))\,dt,\qquad \Psi=(q-z(t,x))\cdot\omega+\frac i2|q-z(t,x)|^2, $ where $b$ is analytic and $\chi$ is a data cutoff. At incidence points $z(t,x)=q$, $\partial_t\Psi=-D_tz^T\omega$. If this vanished in every fiber direction, then $\omega$ would annihilate the vertical tangent of $\pi_X$ and extend to a nonzero conormal $(\omega,-\xi)$ of $Z$; the submersion hypotheses ensure both components are nonzero. This would be a relation point over $(q,\omega,x)$, excluded by the neighborhoods just chosen.

On the compact incidence portion over $\overline V$ and $K_1$, the no-relation property from step 1.1 gives a positive lower bound for $\max_j|\partial_{t_j}\Psi|$ when $z=q$ and $(q,\omega)$ ranges over smaller compactly contained neighborhoods of $(z_0,\omega_0)$. By continuity, shrink the data chart, direction neighborhood and fiber charts so this lower bound persists whenever $|z-q|$ is sufficiently small. A finite refinement therefore gives the uniform alternative on each piece, for $x$ in a neighborhood of $K$ and $(q,\omega)$ near the supplied data point: either $|z-q|\ge d>0$, or one fiber coordinate satisfies $|\partial_{t_j}\Psi|\ge d>0$. The first pieces have Gaussian exponential decay in every fixed object derivative. For the second pieces shrink the analytic neighborhoods so $1/\partial_{t_j}\Psi$ is holomorphic and has uniform factorial derivative bounds by [F4]. The data cutoff can be chosen equal to one on the central data neighborhood. Its transition contributes only pieces of the first type, so it is never differentiated to an order growing with $\lambda$ in the second estimate.

For integration by parts choose finite-order localizers in the finitely many refined fiber charts. They can form an exact partition near the incidence compact without reciprocal derivatives: if $\chi_{j,N}$ are the cutoffs in [F3], take $\rho_{j,N}=\chi_{j,N}\prod_{\ell<j}(1-\chi_{\ell,N})$. At every point of the compact at least one $\chi_{j,N}$ is identically one on a fixed neighborhood. Hence $\sum_j\rho_{j,N}=1$ there. There are a fixed finite number of factors; the product rule gives $|\partial^\alpha\rho_{j,N}|\le C(CN)^{|\alpha|}$ for $|\alpha|\le N$. Extend the construction to a fixed slightly larger compact in the incidence charts, so all object derivatives through any fixed order $m$ preserve the exact partition identity near $K$. Use the sequence indexed by $N+m$.

On a nonstationary piece use $L=(i\lambda\partial_{t_j}\Psi)^{-1}\partial_{t_j}$, so $Le^{i\lambda\Psi}=e^{i\lambda\Psi}$. Let $u$ be a distribution, not necessarily compactly supported, or a distributional density (a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions), on a real-analytic $n$-manifold $X$. Let $x_0$ lie in an analytic coordinate chart and let $\xi_0\in T^*_{x_0}X\setminus\{0\}$ have coordinate components in that chart. For $\chi\in C_c^\infty$ supported in the chart and equal to $1$ near $x_0$, define the Gaussian FBI packet
$$
\mathcal F_\chi u(x,\lambda\omega) =\left\langle u(y),\chi(y) \exp\!\left(i\lambda(x-y)\cdot\omega-\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|x-y|^2\right)\right\rangle, \quad \lambda\ge1,\quad |\omega|=1.
$$
When $u$ is a scalar distribution, the pairing is with the displayed function times coordinate density $|dy|$; when $u$ is a distributional density, the pairing is with the displayed scalar function. In both cases $\lambda\omega$ is the cotangent frequency. The covector $(x_0,\xi_0)$ is analytically regular for $u$ in this chart if there are such a cutoff $\chi$, a neighborhood $U$ of $x_0$, an open neighborhood $\Gamma$ of $\xi_0/|\xi_0|$ in the unit sphere, and constants $c,C>0$ such that
$$
|\mathcal F_\chi u(x,\lambda\omega)|\le C e^{-c\lambda} \quad(x\in U,\ \omega\in\Gamma,\ \lambda\ge1).
$$
The analytic wavefront set $\operatorname{WF}_A(u)$ is the set of nonzero cotangent vectors for which this exponential estimate fails. This is a chart-local definition. The separate local FBI-invariance claim needed for a geometric interpretation is stated by the companion lemma.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $K\subset U$ be compact. There are constants $A,C>0$ and functions $\chi_N\in C_c^\infty(U)$ for each integer $N\ge1$ such that $0\le\chi_N\le1$, $\chi_N=1$ on a fixed neighborhood of $K$, and
$$
|\partial^\alpha\chi_N(x)|\le C(AN)^{|\alpha|} \qquad (x\in\mathbb R^n,\ |\alpha|\le N).
$$
These are smooth compact cutoffs; no compactly supported analytic function is asserted.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

Every compactly supported distribution $v\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ has a
unique extension $\widetilde v\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.  Restricting
$\widetilde v$ to $\mathcal D$ recovers $v$.  No choice axiom is required.

Give $C^\infty(\Omega)$ the topology generated by $q_{K,m}(f)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $m\ge0$. A compactly supported distribution $u$ has a unique continuous complex-linear extension to this space, given by
$$\widetilde u(f)=u(\chi f),$$
where $\chi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is any cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}u$. The result is independent of $\chi$. The extension vanishes on every smooth function zero near the support. No Hahn–Banach or choice axiom is needed.

Work near $(q_0,p_0)\in\mathbb R^n\times(\mathbb R^n\setminus0)$. A normalized positive analytic packet phase is a holomorphic function $\phi(y,q,p)$ on a fixed complex neighborhood of the indicated real variables, such that, for real arguments,
$$
\phi(q,q,p)=0,\qquad \partial_y\phi(q,q,p)=-p,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\phi(y,q,p)\ge c|y-q|^2
$$
for some $c>0$. A classical analytic amplitude is realized on each smaller complex neighborhood by
$$
a(y,q,p;\lambda)=\sum_{j<\epsilon\lambda}a_j(y,q,p)\lambda^{-j},\qquad \sup|a_j|\le C^{j+1}j!,
$$
with sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$. Changing $\epsilon$ to a smaller positive number changes the realization by an exponentially small function on a smaller neighborhood. An elliptic amplitude has $a_0(q_0,q_0,p_0)\ne0$.

For a distribution $u$ localized to a sufficiently small fixed compact neighborhood of $q_0$, the uniform exponential decay of
$$
\langle u(y),a(y,q,p;\lambda)e^{i\lambda\phi(y,q,p)}\rangle
$$
for $(q,p)$ in a neighborhood of $(q_0,p_0)$ is independent of the normalized positive phase and elliptic classical analytic amplitude. Smooth fixed cutoffs equal to one near the packet centers are understood. This criterion agrees with the Gaussian criterion with unit directions and arbitrary $\lambda\ge1$.

More precisely, after shrinking the parameter neighborhood $W$, every other such packet $v_\beta$ with $\beta$ in a smaller $W_0\Subset W$ has a representation
$$
v_\beta(y;\lambda)=\int_W a(y,\alpha;\lambda)e^{i\lambda\phi(y,\alpha)}K(\beta,\alpha;\lambda)\,d\alpha+R_\beta(y;\lambda),
$$
where $|K|\le C\lambda^L$ and $\|R_\beta\|_{C^m}\le C_m e^{-c_m\lambda}$ on the fixed localization compact, for every fixed $m$. There is a representation in the reverse direction as well. All estimates are uniform on the stated smaller neighborhoods. Thus the inverse is an actual local operator modulo exponentially small errors, rather than just a formal inverse series.

derivations.claim: Fix one real-analytic chart and two smooth cutoffs $\chi,\widetilde\chi$ that both equal one on a neighborhood of the base point. Choose a smaller center neighborhood $U_0$ and a compact support neighborhood so that $|x-y|\ge d>0$ whenever $x\in U_0$ and $y\in\operatorname{supp}(\chi-\widetilde\chi)$. By continuity in the fixed-support topology [F3], in either distributional type the pairing is bounded by $C_0$ times the maximum of finitely many derivatives of its test object; a coordinate density factor, when present, has bounded derivatives on the compact chart support. Those derivatives of $(\chi-\widetilde\chi)e^{i\lambda(x-y)\cdot\omega-\lambda|x-y|^2/2}$ are bounded by $C_1(1+\lambda)^m e^{-\lambda d^2/2}$ uniformly for $x\in U_0$, directions near $\omega_0$, and $\lambda\ge1$. Since a polynomial times $e^{-\lambda d^2/2}$ is bounded by $C_2e^{-c\lambda}$ for any fixed $0<c<d^2/2$, replacing one fixed-chart cutoff by the other changes the FBI packet by an exponentially small term.

Let $\kappa$ be an analytic chart change. After shrinking to nested compact neighborhoods, $|\kappa(q)-\kappa(y)|\ge c|q-y|$ and $D\kappa(q)$ is invertible uniformly. The pulled-back packet has phase $ \phi(y,q,\omega)=\omega\cdot(\kappa(q)-\kappa(y))+\frac{i}{2}|\kappa(q)-\kappa(y)|^2. $ It is holomorphic after complexification, vanishes at $y=q$, and has derivative $-D\kappa(q)^T\omega$ there. First [F6] allows $\omega$ to range over a bounded open ball about its nonzero reference direction: its reference phase $(q-y)\cdot\omega+i|\omega||q-y|^2/2$ is exactly the unit-direction packet with parameter $\lambda|\omega|$, and [F6] equates this phase to the Gaussian of width $\lambda$ on that open ball. Apply the same reference criterion in the new chart before pulling its packets back. We may therefore reparameterize the open frequency ball by $p=D\kappa(q)^T\omega$; this is an analytic local diffeomorphism of open frequency parameters and is precisely the cotangent rule. The phase is now normalized and positive in the sense of [F6]. The Jacobian amplitude for scalar distributions is analytic and nonzero: the sign of the real determinant is constant on the smaller connected chart, so its absolute value has an analytic continuation. For distributional densities the amplitude is $1$.

Thus the exponential-decay criterion is independent of the fixed-chart cutoff. The finite-order sequence [F2] supplies the uniform localizers required when a distribution is restricted to a smaller chart; it avoids any use of compactly supported analytic bumps. For a distributional density $V$ in the fixed chart, define the scalar distribution $u_V$ by $\langle u_V,\varphi|dy|\rangle=\langle V,\varphi\rangle$. Continuity follows from [F3], and the vanishing-open sets of $u_V$ and $V$ agree because $|dy|$ is nowhere zero, so their supports agree. The packet pairings agree by definition. Hence [F4]–[F5] give the local Euclidean tempered and smooth-function realizations for either distributional type. This proves the cutoff and localization clauses without a choice axiom.

Apply [F6] to the standard and pulled-back packets on the smaller neighborhoods. It supplies actual transition representations in both directions, with polynomially bounded transition kernels and errors exponentially small in every fixed derivative; the finite distributional order from [F3] therefore preserves their exponential size after pairing. The known exponential estimate on the source parameter neighborhood transfers to the target one. Swapping the two families gives the converse. Step 1.1 removes all fixed cutoff choices, and step 2.1 covers both distributional conventions. This proves every invariance clause in the statement, with the exact cotangent transformation from step 1.2.

An analytic double fibration is a diagram of real-analytic manifolds and real-analytic submersions
$$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X
$$
such that $Z$ is embedded in $G\times X$, both projections are submersions, and
$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$
Write $C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}$ for the incidence cotangent relation. Assume $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

For an analytic double fibration with incidence cotangent relation $C_Z\subset(T^*G\setminus0)\times(T^*X\setminus0)$, let
$$
\pi_L:C_Z\longrightarrow T^*G\setminus0,\qquad \pi_L(g,\eta;x,\xi)=(g,\eta).
$$
The double fibration satisfies the global Bolker condition if $\pi_L$ is an injective immersion. The Bolker condition holds at a specified point $c=(g,\eta;x,\xi)\in C_Z$ if the full fiber over its data covector is the singleton $\pi_L^{-1}(g,\eta)=\{c\}$ and $d\pi_L|_c$ is injective. Thus the pointwise condition has both a fiber-uniqueness clause, which excludes every other relation point over the same data covector even outside a chosen chart, and a local differential-rank clause.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded incidence submanifold of codimension $k>0$, and let $(g_0,x_0)\in Z$. Choose coordinates near this point and a submersion $F:G\times X\to\mathbb R^k$ with $Z=\{F=0\}$. Write $F=(F_1,\ldots,F_k)$. For every $\tau\in\mathbb R^k\setminus\{0\}$, the conormal covector at $(g,x)\in Z$ is
$$
(g,x;D_gF(g,x)^T\tau,\ D_xF(g,x)^T\tau).
$$
Consequently the incidence kernel has local delta representation $b(g,x)\delta(F(g,x))|dg\,dx|$, with a smooth density coefficient $b$, and its cotangent relation consists exactly of
$$
(g,D_gF^T\tau;\ x,-D_xF^T\tau),\qquad (g,x)\in Z,\quad \tau\ne0.
$$
No general Fourier-integral-operator composition calculus is used.

derivations.claim: A tangent vector to $Z$ at $(g,x(g,s))$ has the form $ (\dot g,D_gx\,\dot g+D_sx\,\dot s). $ A pair $(\eta,-\xi)$ annihilates every such tangent vector exactly when $(D_sx)^T\xi=0$ and $\eta=(D_gx)^T\xi$. This follows by setting $\dot g=0$ and then varying $\dot g$ arbitrarily. Thus all conormal pairs, except the zero pair, are parameterized by $(g,s,\xi)\in E_g$. The rank condition on $D_sx$ makes this conormal parameterization smooth.

Under this parameterization, the left projection sends $(g,s,\xi)$ to $(g,(D_gx)^T\xi)$, as stated. Because the first component is retained, two points in this chart portion have the same left image exactly when their $g$ coordinates agree and their values under $L_g$ agree. This proves the chart-portion injectivity criterion; it says nothing about a second preimage outside this chart.

A tangent vector in the kernel of the differential of the left projection has $\dot g=0$. Differentiating the defining equation $(D_sx)^T\xi=0$ along $(\dot s,\dot\xi)$ gives $ (D_sx)^T\dot\xi+(D_s^2x[\dot s, \cdot])^T\xi=0. $ Differentiating its output $(D_gx)^T\xi$ gives the second displayed equation in the statement. Therefore the differential is injective exactly when the simultaneous system has only the zero solution. This is the asserted rank test, and by [F2] it is precisely the local immersion clause of Bolker.

If $\Omega$ is a bounded complex domain and $f$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and holomorphic on $\Omega$, then $|f|$ attains its maximum on $\partial\Omega$.

Equivalently, there is $\zeta\in\partial\Omega$ such that
$$|f(z)|\le|f(\zeta)|\qquad(z\in\overline\Omega).$$

Give $C^\infty(\Omega)$ the topology generated by $q_{K,m}(f)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $m\ge0$. A compactly supported distribution $u$ has a unique continuous complex-linear extension to this space, given by

Locality in [[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]] shows that $u|_Z=0$, since these sets cover $Z$ and all its restrictions are zero. Thus $Z$ is the largest vanishing open set. The **support** is the relatively closed set $\operatorname{supp}u=\Omega\setminus Z$.

In particular $\operatorname{supp}u=\varnothing$ if and only if $u=0$: emptiness gives $Z=\Omega$ and vanishing there, while the zero distribution vanishes everywhere. If a test $\varphi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$, its compact support is contained in $Z$, so $u(\varphi)=0$ by restriction. Consequently two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$ have equal pairings with $u$, by applying this fact to their difference.

**Compactly supported** means that $\operatorname{supp}u$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Relative closedness in an arbitrary open domain is not by itself compactness or closedness in the ambient Euclidean space. On the empty domain support is empty. The union and locality argument require no selection of vanishing neighborhoods and no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Multiply $u$ by a compact smooth cutoff equal to one near $0$ and supported where the one-sided hypothesis holds. It remains supported in $y_n\ge0$, and the wavefront hypothesis is unchanged by exponential Gaussian tail estimates. Denote this compact distribution again by $u$ and put $ U(z,\lambda)=\langle u(y),e^{-\lambda(z-y)^2/2}\rangle,\qquad z\in\mathbb C^n. $ This is entire by [F3]. A finite distributional derivative order gives the following bound on every fixed bounded complex set: $ |U(z,\lambda)|\le C\lambda^M e^{\lambda\Phi(z)},\qquad \Phi(z)=\frac{|\operatorname{Im}z|^2-(\operatorname{Re}z_n)_-^2}{2}, $ where $s_-:=\max(-s,0)$. To justify the sharp half-space bound for a distribution, insert a smooth factor $\vartheta(\lambda y_n)$ that is one for $\lambda y_n>-1/2$ and zero for $\lambda y_n<-1$. It equals one on a neighborhood of the support, so does not change the pairing. Its derivatives of each fixed order cost only a power of $\lambda$. On its support, $y_n\ge-1/\lambda$, and $\operatorname{Re}(z-y)^2=|\operatorname{Re}z-y|^2-|\operatorname{Im}z|^2$ gives the bound with $(s+1/\lambda)_-^2$ in place of $s_-^2$. Their difference is $O(1/\lambda)$ uniformly for bounded $s$, so it changes the exponential by a bounded factor. Gaussian derivatives contribute another fixed power of $\lambda$. This proves the displayed bound using the ordinary fixed-support distributional seminorm, without assuming an estimate on the exact support set.

We record the elementary quantitative continuation used in the left half-plane. If a holomorphic $g$ is bounded by $1$ on a disk of radius $R$ and by $e^{-d\lambda}$ on the concentric disk of radius $r<R$, then on the disk of radius $r<\rho<R$, $ |g|\le \exp\!\left(-d\lambda\frac{\log(R/\rho)}{\log(R/r)}\right). $ For the annulus compare $\log|g|$ with the harmonic function that is $-d\lambda$ on the inner circle and $0$ on the outer circle. This comparison follows from [F2]: near any hypothetical positive interior maximum of their difference, subtract a local harmonic conjugate and apply the maximum modulus principle; a small strict harmonic perturbation excludes a non-strict maximum, then let that perturbation decrease to zero. Zeros of $g$ cannot be positive maxima. Chaining finitely many overlapping disks contained in the connected left half-plane propagates a strictly positive exponent from the initial disk to any chosen compact subset there. To make the finite chain explicit, cover a polygonal path from the initial disk to the compact set by equal small disks whose doubled disks lie in the half-plane, take successive center distances less than one quarter of the radius, and iterate the displayed estimate. The exponent is multiplied by finitely many positive radius ratios.

Write $z=(z',s+it)$. The identity $ e^{-\lambda|p|^2/2}U(x-ip,\lambda) =\langle u,e^{i\lambda(x-y)\cdot p-\lambda|x-y|^2/2}\rangle $ and [F1] imply that absence of either normal gives $ |U(z,\lambda)|\le C e^{\lambda(|\operatorname{Im}z|^2/2-c)} $ in a fixed complex neighborhood of $(0,\mp i)$ for some $c>0$. The use of [F1] here is only to let $p$ range over an open ball about $\pm e_n$, rather than the unit sphere. Fix a small neighborhood of $z'=0$ and treat $z'$ as a parameter. For each such $z'$ the holomorphic function of one variable $ G(z_n,\lambda)=e^{-\lambda|\operatorname{Im}z'|^2/2}e^{\lambda z_n^2/2}U(z',z_n,\lambda) $ satisfies $|G|\le C\lambda^M e^{\lambda s_+^2/2}$ on bounded rectangles. On one small disk lying in $s<0$ near $\mp i$ it satisfies $|G|\le C e^{-c_1\lambda}$: in this regularity estimate the additional exponent is $s^2/2$, which is less than $c/2$ after shrinking that disk. Constants are uniform in $z'$.

Divide $G$ by its uniform polynomial bound $C\lambda^M$. In the left half-plane this quotient has modulus at most $1$. Step 1.2 gives $r,b,d>0$ such that on the segment $s=-r$, $|t|\le b$, it is at most $e^{-d\lambda}$, after decreasing $d$ and taking $\lambda$ large. The same construction works whether the initial disk is near $i$ or $-i$; both lie in the same connected left half-plane neighborhood joined by a bounded path to this segment. All paths, rectangles and constants can be fixed uniformly for the chosen $z'$ parameters.

Extend to the rectangle $-r\le s\le a$, $|t|\le b$, where $a>0$ will be small. For $k=\pi/(2b)$ define $ w(s,t)=\frac{\sinh(k(a-s))}{\sinh(k(a+r))}\cos(kt). $ This is harmonic, nonnegative in the rectangle, zero on the top, bottom and right sides, and between zero and one on its left side. For $H=G/(C\lambda^M)$, the global bound in step 2.1 and the left-side improvement give, by [F2] with a harmonic conjugate of $w$, $ \log|H(s+it)|\le\lambda\bigl(a^2/2-dw(s,t)\bigr). $ On the left the proposed upper bound is at least $-d\lambda$, and on the other three sides it is $\lambda a^2/2$, so all boundary inequalities hold. At $(s,t)=(0,0)$, $ w(0,0)=\frac{\sinh(ka)}{\sinh(k(a+r))}\ge c_2a $ for sufficiently small $a$, with fixed $c_2>0$. Choose $a$ so $a^2/2<dc_2a/2$. Continuity then gives a fixed disk about $z_n=0$ on which $|H|\le e^{-d_2\lambda}$ for some $d_2>0$. This is the needed strict improvement across the boundary.

For real $z=x$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $0$, the exponential factors defining $G$ give $|U(x,\lambda)|\le C\lambda^M e^{-d_2\lambda}$. On this real neighborhood the normalized Gaussian convolutions $(\lambda/(2\pi))^{n/2}U(x,\lambda)$ converge distributionally to $u$. For completeness, after pairing with a compact test $\vartheta$, Fubini for a compact distribution and a rapidly decreasing Gaussian writes the pairing as $\langle u,\rho_\lambda*\vartheta\rangle$, where $\rho_\lambda$ has mass one. Every fixed derivative of $\rho_\lambda*\vartheta-\vartheta$ tends uniformly to zero on the support compact: split the integral into $|y|<\delta$, where uniform continuity controls the translated derivative, and $|y|\ge\delta$, where the Gaussian tail tends to zero; the same argument bounds the derivatives outside the test support. Thus [F3] proves the asserted distributional convergence. The exponential bound makes its limit zero for tests in the smaller neighborhood, so $u=0$ there. Reflecting $x_n$ interchanges the half-spaces and interchanges the two normal orientations. Both claims follow without a reality assumption on $u$.
