The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this
definition. Let $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2$. A **bounded $C^k$ domain** in
$\mathbb R^n$ is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with
the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

In dimension $n=1$, the bounded sets satisfying this local one-sided condition
are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

This definition asserts no extension theorem, no trace operator, and no
uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
and the exact one-sided graph convention that later local statements use.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold with boundary admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\gamma>0$. There is a constant $C_P>0$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|
abla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv,
abla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $n=\dim M\geq0$ and let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. If $n=0$, define every $H^k(M)$ to be the space of scalar-valued functions on the finite set $M$ with the counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm. For $n\geq1$ and an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. If $\partial M=\varnothing$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\{0\}$. If $n=1$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\mathbb K^{\partial M}$ with its counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm, where $\mathbb K$ is the scalar field. For $n\geq2$, define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. For real scalars, define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous linear dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. For complex scalars, define it as the continuous conjugate-linear dual: its pairing with $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in $h$, using the Riemannian boundary density. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Choose boundary normal coordinates $(y,x_n)$ near $x_0$, with $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ and inward unit normal $\partial_{x_n}$. The induced metric on the boundary is smooth. Choose a smooth hypersurface $S$ in $\partial\Omega$ through $x_0$, orthogonal there to $\xi_0$ (if $n=2$, take $S=\{x_0\}$). The boundary geodesics starting normally from $S$ give, by smooth dependence of the geodesic ODE and the inverse function theorem, coordinates $(s,z)$ near $x_0$; define $\phi(s,z)=s$. Gauss' lemma gives $|d\phi|_{g_{\partial\Omega}}=1$ and $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$. Shrink the patch so these coordinates and $\chi$ are supported inside it.

In boundary normal coordinates, $g^{nn}=1$ and $g^{n\alpha}=0$ at the boundary. Set $\Phi|_{x_n=0}=\phi$ and $\partial_n\Phi|_{x_n=0}=i$. Then $g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi=0$ at $x_n=0$ because $|d\phi|=1$. Differentiate this eikonal equation successively in $x_n$. At each order the newest unknown normal jet $\partial_n^{j+1}\Phi|_{x_n=0}$ occurs linearly with coefficient $2i g^{nn}=2i\ne0$; all other terms use already assigned jets and derivatives of $g$. Solve recursively for every normal jet. Realize the resulting jet sequence by the following local Borel construction: if $c_j(y)$ is the prescribed $j$th normal derivative, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\theta$ equal to one near zero and supported in $(-1,1)$, and set $$\Phi(y,x_n)=\sum_{j\geq0}\frac{c_j(y)}{j!}x_n^j\theta(x_n/\varepsilon_j).$$ For all sufficiently large $j$, choose $\varepsilon_j<2^{-j}$ so that every derivative of order at most $j/2$ of the $j$th summand has sup norm at most $2^{-j}$; this is possible because those derivatives are bounded by constants times $\varepsilon_j^{j-m}$ with $m\leq j/2$. Choose any positive $\varepsilon_j$ for the finitely many smaller $j$. For each fixed derivative order, the tail then converges uniformly, so $\Phi$ is smooth and has the prescribed jets. In particular, the eikonal expression vanishes to infinite order at the boundary. Since $\partial_n\operatorname{Im}\Phi=1$ there, shrinking the collar gives $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$.

For $P_\gamma=\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla)$, direct differentiation gives $$P_\gamma(e^{i\lambda\Phi}b)=e^{i\lambda\Phi}\big[-\lambda^2p_\gamma b+i\lambda L_\gamma b+P_\gamma b\big],$$ where $p_\gamma=\gamma g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi$ and $L_\gamma b=2\gamma g^{ij}(\partial_i\Phi)(\partial_jb)+\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla\Phi)b$. The phase is common to both conductivities and $p_\gamma=\gamma p_1$ vanishes to infinite order on the boundary by step 2.1. Prescribe $b_{0,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=\chi$ and $b_{-j,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ for $j\geq1$. In boundary normal coordinates the coefficient of the new normal derivative in $L_\gamma b$ is $2i\gamma$, which is nonzero. Therefore the normal derivatives of $b_{0,\gamma}$ can be chosen successively so that $L_\gamma b_{0,\gamma}=0$ to infinite order at the boundary; after choosing $b_{0,\gamma},\ldots,b_{-(j-1),\gamma}$, the same recursion chooses all jets of $b_{-j,\gamma}$ so that $iL_\gamma b_{-j,\gamma}+P_\gamma b_{-(j-1),\gamma}=0$ to infinite order. Realize each sequence by the Borel series in step 2.1 and multiply by a fixed collar cutoff equal to one near the boundary support. Repeat for $\widetilde\gamma$.

Let $b_{\lambda,\gamma}=\sum_{j=0}^K\lambda^{-j}b_{-j,\gamma}$, with the same construction for $\widetilde\gamma$. The order-$\lambda^2$ eikonal term and the order-$\lambda,\ldots,\lambda^{1-K}$ transport terms in step 3.1 vanish to infinite order at $x_n=0$. Thus each remaining coefficient is $O(x_n^R)$ for every prescribed integer $R$. On the collar, $|e^{i\lambda\Phi}|\leq e^{-\lambda x_n/2}$. For every fixed $a,R$, direct integration gives $$\|\lambda^a x_n^R e^{-\lambda x_n/2}\|_{L^2(0,\delta)}=O(\lambda^{a-R-1/2}).$$ Choose $R$ and then $K$ large enough to make every residual term $O(\lambda^{-N})$. Derivatives of the collar cutoff are supported where $x_n\geq c>0$ and hence contribute $O(e^{-c\lambda})$. The same Gaussian integration shows $\|v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{L^2}=O(\lambda^{-1})$ and bounds its gradient norm above. Thus the $H^1$ norms are bounded above and the residual bounds hold for the arbitrary prescribed $N$.

Let $r_\lambda=u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Its weak equation is $P_\gamma r_\lambda=-P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}$. Test with $r_\lambda$, use $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, and use the Poincare inequality in [F3]: $$\gamma_*\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2^2\leq\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|r_\lambda\|_2 \leq C_P\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2.$$ If the last gradient norm is zero then $r_\lambda=0$ by [F3]; otherwise divide by it. This proves $\|r_\lambda\|_{H^1}=O(\lambda^{-N})$. The same argument applies to $\widetilde\gamma$.

In the collar, write $J(y,x_n)dS(y)dx_n$ for Euclidean volume in boundary normal coordinates, with $J(y,0)=1$. Since $\Phi=\phi+ix_n+O(x_n^2)$, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi=x_n+O(x_n^2)$ and $g(d\Phi,\overline{d\Phi})=2+O(x_n)$. The boundary values of both leading amplitudes are $\chi$, and lower amplitudes vanish there. Differentiating $v_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ therefore gives $$\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}} =2\lambda e^{-2\lambda x_n}|\chi(y)|^2+e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(1)+ e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(\lambda x_n),$$ uniformly for $0\leq x_n\leq\lambda^{-1/2}$. On this shrinking collar $\lambda x_n^2\leq1$, so after $t=\lambda x_n$ the phase remainder factor is uniformly bounded; boundedness of $F,J,\chi$ gives an integrable majorant $C t^ke^{-t}$ for the rescaled leading term. For each fixed $t$, the rescaled leading term tends to $2t^ke^{-2t}F(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2$. Each displayed remainder has an additional factor $\lambda^{-1}$ after scaling and is dominated by $C\lambda^{-1}(t^k+t^{k+1}+t^{k+2})e^{-t}$, including the phase error $e^{O(t^2/\lambda)}-1=O(t^2/\lambda)$; its integral tends to zero. On the rest of the fixed collar, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$ gives exponential decay $e^{-\lambda x_n}\leq e^{-\sqrt{\lambda}}$; every polynomial prefactor is therefore negligible. The cutoff region away from the collar is also exponentially small. Thus the limit for approximate beams is $$2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,$$ whose constant is strictly positive.

Taking equal conductivities, $F=1$, and $k=0$ in step 5.2 gives $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\int_\Omega|\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}|^2dx=c_0\int_{\partial\Omega}|\chi|^2dS>0$. Together with the upper bound in step 4.1 this proves the asserted two-sided $H^1$ norm bound.

The exact corrections satisfy $H^1$ errors $O(\lambda^{-N})$ by step 5.1, while both approximate beams have uniformly bounded $H^1$ norms by step 4.1. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the change in the weighted product integral, after multiplication by $\lambda^k$, by $C\lambda^k\lambda^{-N}$ because $0\leq\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k\leq C$ on the bounded domain. Choose $N>k$. The error tends to zero, so the same limit holds for the exact solutions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is
compactly embedded in $L^p(\Omega)$: the inclusion is bounded, and every
sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging in
$L^p(\Omega)$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is needed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded
$C^{k+2}$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$k\ge0$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega)$, $b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ and all
coefficient derivatives bounded, and let $f\in H^k(\Omega)$. If
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^{k+2}(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big),$$
with $C$ depending only on $n,k,\Omega$ and the coefficient bounds. The
derivative gain is exactly two orders; the boundary regularity required at
order $k$ is $C^{k+2}$, the coefficient regularity one order above the data
order, and the companion page records the sharp two-derivative example. For
$k=0$ the theorem is
[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$ and $\theta=1-1/p$, with
$W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$ as in
[[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]. Then the trace
operator $T$ of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] satisfies
$$\|Tu\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)} \qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)),$$
and it is onto: $T(W^{1,p}(\Omega))=W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$. For $p>1$
the range is a strict subset of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$, and the trace is not a
compact operator into $W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1\le p<\infty$, and let $T$ be the trace operator of
[[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]].

(i) If $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$, then
$T(\eta u)=(\eta|_{\partial\Omega})\,Tu$ in $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ for every
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and
$\|T(\eta u)\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C_\eta\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

(ii) If $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain and
$\partial\Omega\cap\partial\Omega'$ is relatively open in $\partial\Omega$,
then $(Tu)|_{\partial\Omega\cap\partial\Omega'}=T_{\Omega'}(u|_{\Omega'})$
a.e. for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, where $T_{\Omega'}$ is the trace
operator relative to $\Omega'$; in particular the trace is local and
compatible with restrictions to subdomains.

(iii) If a boundary chart $\Phi$ flattens a neighbourhood of a boundary point,
then for $u$ supported in a compact ambient patch inside that chart the transported trace
equals $T_+$ of the zero-extended flattened function after reflecting $t\mapsto-t$ and the corresponding boundary $L^p$ norms
agree up to the chart Jacobian.

In dimension one, endpoint evaluation is bounded on $H^1$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy--Schwarz. Any endpoint data have a smooth collar lift. Its kernel is $H_0^1$: for a zero-endpoint function, $|u(t)|^2\leq t\int_0^t|u'(r)|^2dr$ makes the derivative error of a cutoff on $[0,2\delta]$ tend to zero in $L^2$ as $\delta	o0$; cut off at both endpoints and mollify. Thus the trace, lift and kernel conclusions of [F5], [F9] and [F10] hold also in this dimension, without invoking their higher-dimensional Euclidean suppliers. There is a constant $C_P$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|
abla w\|_{L^2(M)}$ for $w\in H_0^1(M)$. Otherwise choose $w_j\in H_0^1(M)$ with $\|w_j\|_{L^2}=1$ and $\|
abla w_j\|_{L^2}	o0$. A finite chart partition and [F2] give an $L^2$-convergent subsequence. On compact $M$, the fixed finite chartwise $H^1$ norm is equivalent to $\|\cdot\|_{L^2}+\|
abla_g\cdot\|_{L^2}$ by bounded metric coefficients, so this subsequence is Cauchy in $H^1$ and converges to some $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with $\|w\|_{L^2}=1$ and weak gradient zero. Local convolution shows that a function with zero weak gradient is constant on each connected coordinate ball; overlapping balls and connectedness make $w$ constant on $M^\circ$. Its trace is zero because $w\in H_0^1(M)$, while [F9] makes the trace of a nonzero constant equal that same nonzero boundary value. This contradiction proves the inequality.

Compactness of $M$ and positivity of $\gamma$ give $\gamma_*:=\min_M\gamma>0$. Thus $a_\gamma(w,z)=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)\,dV_g$ is bounded on $H_0^1(M)$ and $a_\gamma(w,w)\geq c\|w\|_{H^1(M)}^2$ by step 1.1 and $\gamma_*$. By [F3], for any bounded conjugate-linear functional $G$ on $H_0^1(M)$ there is a unique $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with $a_\gamma(w,z)=G(z)$ for all $z$.

Flatten each boundary chart, apply the local half-space trace lift, and patch the finitely many chart lifts with a smooth partition. The resulting $Ef\in H^1(M)$ has trace $f$ and norm bounded by $C\|f\|_{H^{1/2}(\partial M)}$ by [F5]. For $h\in L^2(M)$ take $G(z)=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g-a_\gamma(Ef,z)$ in step 2.1 and set $v=Ef+w$. Then $v$ has trace $f$ and satisfies the weak equation. If $v_1,v_2$ are two such solutions, their difference has zero global trace, hence lies in $H_0^1(M)$ by [F10]. Its energy is zero; since $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, its gradient vanishes, and step 1.1 gives $v_1=v_2$.

Suppose $h$ and $f$ are smooth. By [F8], extend $f$ smoothly from the boundary into a collar and multiply by a cutoff to obtain a smooth extension $Ef$ on $M$. Then $w=v-Ef$ has zero trace, so $w\in H_0^1(M)$ by [F10], and solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gw)=h-\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gEf)$, whose right-hand side is smooth. For dimension one, the coordinate equation $(a w')'=H$ with smooth $a>0$ and smooth $H$ first gives $a w'\in H^1$ and then, by iteration, $w\in H^m$ for every $m$; the one-dimensional fundamental theorem gives smoothness up to the endpoints. For dimension at least two, in each boundary chart, flatten the boundary and write the principal matrix as $|g|^{1/2}\gamma g^{ij}$; it is smooth and uniformly elliptic because $g$ is positive definite and $\gamma$ has a positive minimum. For the base case, localize $w$ by a cutoff; its equation has an $L^2$ right-hand side since $w\in H^1$, so [F6] gives local $H^2$ regularity. If $w\in H^{m+1}$, each cutoff commutator contains derivatives of $w$ of order at most $m+1$ with smooth bounded coefficients, hence lies in $H^m$; the localized right-hand side is therefore in $H^m$, and [F6] gives $H^{m+2}$ regularity. Induction over $m$ and a finite chart cover give $w\in H^m(M)$ for every integer $m$. By [F7], $w$ and hence $v=Ef+w$ are smooth up to the boundary.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

derivations.claim: Embed the segment in a collar extension across $\partial M_0$ and cover it by finitely many coordinate neighborhoods. On an embedded subsegment, parallel transport an orthonormal normal frame and set $F(t,y)=\exp_{\gamma(t)}(\sum_\alpha y_\alpha E_\alpha(t))$. The inverse function theorem gives local Fermi coordinates with $g_{jk}(t,0)=\delta_{jk}$ and $\partial_i g_{jk}(t,0)=0$. This construction is along an interval and uses no orientation of $M_0$.

In one such chart, seek $v_s=e^{is\Theta}a$, $s=\tau+i\lambda$, with $\Theta(t,0)=t$ and $\operatorname{Im}\Theta(t,y)\geq c|y|^2$. Expand $\Theta$ into homogeneous transverse Taylor polynomials. The quadratic polynomial is $\frac12H(t)y\cdot y$; substituting into $g(d\Theta,d\Theta)=1$ gives the matrix Riccati equation $H'+H^2=F(t)$, where $F$ is determined by the second transverse Taylor coefficient of the inverse metric. An initial complex symmetric $H(t_0)$ with positive-definite imaginary part yields a smooth solution with positive imaginary part on a short subsegment. Each higher homogeneous phase term then solves a linear first-order ODE along $t$, because its newest coefficient occurs linearly in the eikonal equation.

Write $m=\dim M_0$, so the transverse dimension is $m-1$. Substituting $a=\tau^{(m-1)/4}\sum_{j=0}^N s^{-j}a_{-j}$ into $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)e^{is\Theta}a$ cancels successive powers of $s$ by linear transport ODEs for the transverse Taylor coefficients of each $a_{-j}$. The leading coefficient solves $a_0(t,0)=c_0\exp(-\frac12\int_{t_0}^t\operatorname{tr}H(r)\,dr)$. A finite Taylor realization to the order required for the fixed $K$ and a transverse cutoff produce a smooth local beam; Gaussian integration gives bounded $L^2$ norm and a residual that tends to zero faster than any prescribed power after increasing the Taylor order.

On an oriented transversal of dimension at least two, apply [F3] to complete the finite overlap matching and eliminate all distinct-branch cross terms. This gives the stated global family and limit; steps 1.1--2.1 describe its local ingredients, without claiming a new proof of the imported global estimates.

For a nonorientable transversal let $\pi:\widetilde M_0\to M_0$ be its orientation double cover, with deck involution $\sigma$, and lift $\gamma$ to $\widetilde\gamma$. Let $w_s$ be the oriented beam from [F3] along that lift. Define the descended function by $\pi^*v_s=w_s+\sigma^*w_s$. The residual and norm bounds follow by a finite sum and the covering integral formula. The two lifted segments have no common tangent branch: equality of position and velocity at different times would make the geodesic periodic, contrary to its nontangential boundary exit; opposite velocities at a repeated point would force a zero midpoint velocity by geodesic uniqueness. There are only finitely many crossing branches, by compactness and local uniqueness. The distinct-branch estimate in [F3], applied to these two lifts, therefore gives a zero mixed-term limit. For every continuous $\psi$ the covering formula is $$\int_{M_0}|v_s|^2\psi\,dV=\int_{\widetilde M_0}|w_s|^2(\psi\circ\pi)\,dV+\operatorname{Re}\int_{\widetilde M_0}w_s\overline{\sigma^*w_s}(\psi\circ\pi)\,dV.$$ The first term has precisely the required ray limit and the second tends to zero. In particular there is no extra factor two in the normalization. The same argument works if the cover is disconnected.

If the transversal has dimension one, the component containing the segment is an interval with arclength coordinate $t$ beginning at its incoming endpoint. Set $v_s=e^{ist}$ on this component and zero on all other components. The residual is zero and the asserted integral formula is exact. In dimension zero the given unit-speed segment cannot exist. This covers the dimensions not needed in the CTA application as well.

citations.quote: A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. The coordinate $x_1$ on $\mathbb R$ is the distinguished Euclidean coordinate; $M_0$ is the transversal manifold. All Laplacians use $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$. Neither $M$ nor $M_0$ is assumed orientable. A positive smooth conformal factor is not included in this definition; claims using a conformally related metric must state and prove the required conformal transformation separately.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $n=\dim M\geq0$ and let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. If $n=0$, define every $H^k(M)$ to be the space of scalar-valued functions on the finite set $M$ with the counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm. For $n\geq1$ and an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. If $\partial M=\varnothing$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\{0\}$. If $n=1$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\mathbb K^{\partial M}$ with its counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm, where $\mathbb K$ is the scalar field. For $n\geq2$, define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. For real scalars, define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous linear dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. For complex scalars, define it as the continuous conjugate-linear dual: its pairing with $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in $h$, using the Riemannian boundary density. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a complex normed space, let $M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, and
let $f_0:M \to \mathbb{C}$ be a bounded complex linear functional. Then there
exists a bounded complex linear functional $F:X \to \mathbb{C}$ such that
$F|_M=f_0$ and $\|F\|=\|f_0\|$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Put $s=\varphi$ and first set $q=0$. For a real smooth weight $\psi$, direct differentiation gives $$P_{\psi,h,0}=e^{\psi/h}(-h^2\Delta_g)e^{-\psi/h} =-h^2\Delta_g-|
abla_g\psi|^2+2h
abla_g\psi\cdot
abla_g+h\Delta_g\psi.$$ For $\psi=s$, $|
abla s|=1$ and $\Delta s=0$, so $P_{s,h,0}=A+C$ with $A=-h^2\Delta_g-1$ self-adjoint and $C=2h\partial_s$ skew-adjoint on compactly supported functions.

Convexify by $\psi=f(s)=s+\frac{h}{2\varepsilon}s^2$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is fixed small and then $h/\varepsilon$ is small. Since $M$ is compact, choose $h$ so $f'=1+hs/\varepsilon>1/2$ on $M$. The conjugated operator is $P_{\psi,h,0}=A_\varepsilon+C_\varepsilon$ with $$A_\varepsilon=-h^2\Delta_g-(f')^2,\qquad C_\varepsilon=2hf'\partial_s+hf'',\qquad f''=h/\varepsilon.$$ Here $A_\varepsilon$ is self-adjoint and $C_\varepsilon$ is skew-adjoint. Product independence of $s$ makes $-\Delta_g=-\partial_s^2-\Delta_{g_0}$, with $\Delta_{g_0}$ commuting with $C_\varepsilon$. Direct differentiation in the $s$ coordinate therefore gives the exact commutator $$[A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon]=4h(f')^2f''-4h^3f''\partial_s^2.$$ For compactly supported $w$, integration by parts yields $$\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2^2 =\|A_\varepsilon w\|_2^2+\|C_\varepsilon w\|_2^2+ 4h f''\|(f')w\|_2^2+4h^3f''\|\partial_sw\|_2^2 \geq c h^2\varepsilon^{-1}\|w\|_2^2.$$ The same identity implies $\|A_\varepsilon w\|_2\leq\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2$. Since $\|h\nabla w\|_2^2=\langle A_\varepsilon w,w\rangle+\|f'w\|_2^2$, the $L^2$ bound just obtained gives $\|w\|_2+\|h\nabla w\|_2\leq C_\varepsilon h^{-1}\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2$.

The convexified and unconvexified weights are related by multiplication with $m=e^{s^2/(2\varepsilon)}$: $P_{\psi,h,0}(mw)=mP_{s,h,0}w$. On compact $M$, $m$ and $m^{-1}$ are bounded, so step 2.1 yields $\|w\|_2\leq C h^{-1}\|P_{s,h,0}w\|_2$. Adding the potential changes the conjugated operator by $h^2q$. Its norm on $w$ is at most $h^2\|q\|_\infty\|w\|_2$, which is absorbed in the preceding estimate for sufficiently small $h$. Replacing $s$ by either sign of $x_1$ proves the a priori estimate in the statement.

Let $P=P_{\varphi,h,q}$ and apply the a priori estimate also to $P^*=P_{-\varphi,h,q}$, which has the same real potential and the opposite allowed sign. On $E=P^*(C_c^\infty(M^\circ))\subset L^2(M)$ define the complex-linear functional $\ell(P^*w)=\int_M\bar Fw\,dV_g$. The estimate makes this well-defined: $P^*w=0$ implies $w=0$. It also gives $|\ell(P^*w)|\leq\|F\|_2\|w\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_2\|P^*w\|_2$. By [A1] extend $\ell$ to $L^2(M)$ with the same bound; by [A2] there is $R\in L^2(M)$ with $\ell(z)=\int_Mz\bar R\,dV_g$ and $\|R\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_2$. Taking complex conjugates gives $\int_MR\overline{P^*w}\,dV_g=\int_MF\bar w\,dV_g$ for every test $w$, which is precisely $PR=F$ distributionally on $M^\circ$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $n=\dim M\geq0$ and let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. If $n=0$, define every $H^k(M)$ to be the space of scalar-valued functions on the finite set $M$ with the counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm. For $n\geq1$ and an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. If $\partial M=\varnothing$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\{0\}$. If $n=1$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\mathbb K^{\partial M}$ with its counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm, where $\mathbb K$ is the scalar field. For $n\geq2$, define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. For real scalars, define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous linear dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. For complex scalars, define it as the continuous conjugate-linear dual: its pairing with $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in $h$, using the Riemannian boundary density. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is
compactly embedded in $L^p(\Omega)$: the inclusion is bounded, and every
sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging in
$L^p(\Omega)$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a Banach space
over a fixed field $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $K:X\to X$ be a compact operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) and put $A:=I-K$. Then:

1. $A$ is injective if and only if it is surjective, and in that case $A$ is
   boundedly invertible;
2. for every $y\in X$ the equation $Ax=y$ has a solution if and only if
   $\varphi(y)=0$ for every $\varphi\in\ker A^*$, the transpose
   $A^*=I-K^*$ acting on $X^*$
   ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]);
3. $\ker A$ and the cokernel $X/\operatorname{ran}A$
   ([[def-quotient-vector-space-coset-notation]]) are finite dimensional with
   equal dimensions over $F$ ([[def-dimension]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
The right inverse is not unique and no canonical choice is claimed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded
$C^{k+2}$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$k\ge0$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega)$, $b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ and all
coefficient derivatives bounded, and let $f\in H^k(\Omega)$. If
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^{k+2}(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big),$$
with $C$ depending only on $n,k,\Omega$ and the coefficient bounds. The
derivative gain is exactly two orders; the boundary regularity required at
order $k$ is $C^{k+2}$, the coefficient regularity one order above the data
order, and the companion page records the sharp two-derivative example. For
$k=0$ the theorem is
[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$ and $\theta=1-1/p$, with
$W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$ as in
[[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]. Then the trace
operator $T$ of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] satisfies
$$\|Tu\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)} \qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)),$$
and it is onto: $T(W^{1,p}(\Omega))=W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$. For $p>1$
the range is a strict subset of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$, and the trace is not a
compact operator into $W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1\le p<\infty$, and let $T$ be the trace operator of
[[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]].

(i) If $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$, then
$T(\eta u)=(\eta|_{\partial\Omega})\,Tu$ in $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ for every
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and
$\|T(\eta u)\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C_\eta\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

(ii) If $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain and
$\partial\Omega\cap\partial\Omega'$ is relatively open in $\partial\Omega$,
then $(Tu)|_{\partial\Omega\cap\partial\Omega'}=T_{\Omega'}(u|_{\Omega'})$
a.e. for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, where $T_{\Omega'}$ is the trace
operator relative to $\Omega'$; in particular the trace is local and
compatible with restrictions to subdomains.

(iii) If a boundary chart $\Phi$ flattens a neighbourhood of a boundary point,
then for $u$ supported in a compact ambient patch inside that chart the transported trace
equals $T_+$ of the zero-extended flattened function after reflecting $t\mapsto-t$ and the corresponding boundary $L^p$ norms
agree up to the chart Jacobian.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $k\ge0$,
let $a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega)$, $b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ with
bounds $|D^\ell a^{ij}|\le M_\ell$ for $|\ell|\le k+1$ and
$|D^\ell b^i|,|D^\ell c|\le M_\ell$ for $|\ell|\le k$ almost everywhere, let
$f\in H^k_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ be a local weak
solution of $Lu=f$ on $\Omega$
([[def-local-weak-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]). Fix open sets
$\Omega_{-1},\Omega_0,\Omega_1,\dots,\Omega_{k+1}$ with
$\overline{\Omega_{-1}}\Subset\Omega$, $\overline{\Omega_0}\Subset\Omega_{-1}$
and $\overline{\Omega_{j+1}}\Subset\Omega_j$ for $0\le j\le k$. Then for every
$0\le j\le k$ one has $u\in H^{j+2}(\Omega_j)$, and there is a constant $C_j$
depending only on $n,\theta,k$, the principal-coefficient bounds through
order $j+1$, the lower-order coefficient bounds through order $j$, and the sets
$\Omega_{-1},\dots,\Omega_j$ with
$$\|u\|_{H^{j+2}(\Omega_j)}\le C_j\big(\|f\|_{H^j(\Omega_{-1})}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega_{-1})}\big).$$
The induction step is: each weak derivative $D^\alpha u$ of order $|\alpha|=j$
solves on $\Omega_{j-1}$ the iterated differentiated equation of
[[lem-weak-equation-for-a-first-derivative-includes-coefficient-commutators]]
with datum in $L^2(\Omega_{j-1})$ built from $D^jf$, principal coefficient
derivatives through order $j+1$, and derivatives of $u$ of order at most
$j+1$, so the interior $H^2$ theorem applied on
$\Omega_j\Subset\Omega_{j-1}$ recovers two further derivatives; the loss of
domain is absorbed into the fixed chain. The scaffold wrote $\Omega=\Omega_0$
and concluded $u\in H^{j+2}(\Omega_0)$ at $j=0$, which would be a global
$H^2(\Omega)$ claim and is false for an arbitrary local weak solution; the
outer set $\Omega_{-1}\Subset\Omega$ is the localisation needed for the
interior estimates, and all constants below depend on it.

derivations.claim: Choose a real constant $Q>1+\|q\|_{L^\infty(M)}$ and let $A=-\Delta_g+Q$ on $H_0^1(M)$, with form $a(w,z)=\int_M(g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)+Qw\bar z)\,dV_g$. The form is bounded and coercive in the chartwise $H^1$ norm, so [F2] gives a bounded inverse $A_D^{-1}:(H_0^1(M))^*\to H_0^1(M)$.

Multiplication by $Q-q$ maps $H_0^1(M)$ boundedly to $L^2(M)$, and the inclusion $H_0^1(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is compact: localize with the finite atlas and partition, apply [F3] on each bounded chart piece (using zero extension at a boundary face), then extract a finite diagonal subsequence and sum the localized limits. Hence $K:=A_D^{-1}(Q-q)$ is compact on $H_0^1(M)$.

For $w\in H_0^1(M)$, $(I-K)w=0$ is equivalent, after applying $A$, to $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$. The latter has only the zero solution by hypothesis, so $I-K$ is injective. By [F4], $I-K$ is boundedly invertible. This gives a unique weak zero-trace solution for every bounded functional on $H_0^1(M)$, in particular for every $F\in L^2(M)$ after subtracting any fixed boundary lift.

For $n=1$, the bounded endpoint trace, smooth finite-dimensional lift and zero-trace kernel follow from the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy--Schwarz; specifically, $|u(t)|^2\leq t\int_0^t|u'(r)|^2dr$ permits cutoff approximation at a zero endpoint, followed by interior mollification. For $n=0$ the boundary is empty, the trace space is zero and $H_0^1=H^1$. For $n\geq2$, a finite collection of flattened boundary charts, the collar neighborhood, and [F5] give a bounded extension $E:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^1(M)$ with trace $f$. Set $u=Ef+w$ and solve for $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with weak right-hand-side functional $z\mapsto\int_MF\bar z\,dV_g-a_q(Ef,z)$ by step 3.1. This proves existence for the stated data. The difference of any two solutions has zero global trace, so [F7] puts it in $H_0^1(M)$; the assumed trivial kernel then proves uniqueness.

First take zero boundary data and $F\in L^2$. For $n\geq2$, in each boundary chart the collar flattens the boundary and the pulled-back coefficients are smooth and uniformly elliptic; localize $u$ by a cutoff, whose trace remains zero and hence lies in $H_0^1$ locally by [F7], and apply the $m=0$ case of [F6]. In interior charts apply [F8]. A finite cover gives $u\in H^2(M)$ and the estimate with the additional $L^2$ term. If $f$ is smooth, extend it smoothly in a boundary collar by keeping its chart representative constant in the normal variable near the boundary and multiplying by a cutoff; a finite partition patches these extensions to a smooth $Ef$. Then $w=u-Ef$ has zero trace and, by [F7], lies in $H_0^1(M)$; the same local estimates apply to $w$. For $n=1$, in a coordinate the weak equation has form $-\partial_x(a\partial_xu)+b\partial_xu+cu=F$ with smooth $a>0$; it gives $\partial_x(a\partial_xu)\in L^2$, hence $u\in H^2$ with the corresponding estimate. For $n=0$, the equation is pointwise and the trivial-kernel hypothesis gives the estimate.

Fix $k\geq1$ and suppose inductively that $u\in H^{k+1}(M)$ and $F\in H^k(M)$. If $n\geq2$, in a boundary chart a cutoff localization has zero trace on the physical boundary and hence belongs locally to $H_0^1$ by [F7]; its equation has right-hand side $\chi F+[L,\chi]u\in H^k$, since the commutator is first order with smooth coefficients. Apply [F6] at order $k$ to these boundary-localized equations; in interior charts apply [F8]. This gives $u\in H^{k+2}(M)$ with a bound by $C_k(\|F\|_{H^k}+\|u\|_{H^{k+1}}+\|u\|_{L^2})$. If $n=1$, the coordinate equation in step 5.1 gives $\partial_x(a\partial_xu)=b\partial_xu+cu-F$; under the induction hypothesis the right-hand side belongs to $H^k$, so $a\partial_xu\in H^{k+1}$ and $u\in H^{k+2}$ with the analogous estimate. If $n=0$, all Sobolev orders coincide and the pointwise inverse gives it. For zero trace, the bounded inverse in step 3.1 controls $\|u\|_{H^1}$ by $\|F\|_{L^2}$; the induction hypothesis then absorbs the lower-order term and yields $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k\|F\|_{H^k}$. For smooth nonzero $f$, apply the same induction to $u-Ef$. No differentiation of normal boundary values is used.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $n=\dim M\geq0$ and let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. If $n=0$, define every $H^k(M)$ to be the space of scalar-valued functions on the finite set $M$ with the counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm. For $n\geq1$ and an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. If $\partial M=\varnothing$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\{0\}$. If $n=1$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\mathbb K^{\partial M}$ with its counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm, where $\mathbb K$ is the scalar field. For $n\geq2$, define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. For real scalars, define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous linear dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. For complex scalars, define it as the continuous conjugate-linear dual: its pairing with $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in $h$, using the Riemannian boundary density. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\gamma>0$. There is a constant $C_P>0$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|
abla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv,
abla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. For every $F\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique weak solution $u\in H^1(M)$ of $(-\Delta_g+q)u=F$ with trace $f$. If $f=0$, $F\in H^m(M)$ and $m\geq0$ is an integer, then $u\in H^{m+2}(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^{m+2}}\leq C_m\|F\|_{H^m}$. If $F$ and $f$ are smooth, this solution belongs to $H^m(M)$ for every integer $m\geq0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$, $Y$, $Z$ be real
Banach spaces, let $U \subseteq X \times Y$ be open for the product metric, let
$F : U \to Z$ be of class $C^k$ with $k \ge 1$
([[def-c-k-map-between-banach-spaces]]), and let $(a,b) \in U$ with
$F(a,b) = 0$. Let $D_XF(a,b) := DF(a,b)\circ i_X$ and
$D_YF(a,b) := DF(a,b)\circ i_Y$ be the partial derivatives, where
$i_X(x) := (x,0)$ and $i_Y(y) := (0,y)$. If $D_YF(a,b) : Y \to Z$ is a bounded
linear isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $A \subseteq X$ of $a$
and $B \subseteq Y$ of $b$ and a unique map $g : A \to B$ of class $C^k$ such
that

$$\{\,(x,y) \in A \times B : F(x,y) = 0\,\} = \{\,(x,g(x)) : x \in A\,\},$$

and along the graph $Dg$ satisfies
$$Dg(x) = -\,D_YF\bigl(x,g(x)\bigr)^{-1}\,D_XF\bigl(x,g(x)\bigr) \qquad (x \in A).$$
In particular $g(a) = b$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

derivations.claim: For $q=0$, the Dirichlet kernel of $-\Delta_g$ is trivial: if $w\in H_0^1(M)$ is weakly harmonic, testing with $w$ gives $\int_M|\nabla w|^2dV_g=0$, and the zero-trace Poincare inequality in [F2] gives $w=0$. Thus [F3] supplies the zero-boundary inverse $G=(-\Delta_g)^{-1}:H^{s-2}(M)\to X_s$, where $X_s=\{w\in H^s(M):w\in H_0^1(M)\}$. The high-order estimate in [F3], together with its bounded $H^1$ inverse, makes $G$ bounded.

Regard the complex Sobolev spaces as real Banach spaces, since the parameters are real. For $n\geq2$, [F4] and localization to the fixed finite atlas make $H^s(M)$ a Banach algebra. If $n=1$, then $s\geq3$; the one-dimensional estimate $H^1\hookrightarrow L^\infty$ and the Leibniz rule give the same algebra bound in each chart, hence on $M$. Thus $(\epsilon,w)\mapsto q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3$ is a continuous polynomial from $\mathbb R^m\times X_s$ into $H^{s-2}(M)$, where $f_\epsilon=\sum_j\epsilon_jh_j$ and $Ef_\epsilon$ is the smooth collar extension from [F7]. Define $$\mathcal F(\epsilon,w)=w-G\big[\Delta_g(Ef_\epsilon)-q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3\big]\in X_s.$$ It is $C^3$ (indeed polynomial plus bounded linear maps) and $\mathcal F(0,0)=0$.

At $(0,0)$, the derivative $D_w\mathcal F(0,0)$ is the identity on $X_s$, because the derivative of $u\mapsto q u^3$ at $u=0$ vanishes. By [F6], there is a neighborhood of $\epsilon=0$ and a unique $C^3$ map $w(\epsilon)\in X_s$ near zero such that $\mathcal F(\epsilon,w(\epsilon))=0$. The fixed-point equation is exactly $-\Delta_g(Ef_\epsilon+w)+q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3=0$ with boundary trace $f_\epsilon$, so $u_\epsilon=Ef_\epsilon+w(\epsilon)$ gives the unique small solution.

For $n\geq2$, [F5] gives $H^s(M)\hookrightarrow C^2(\overline M)$; for $n=1$, $s\geq3$ gives the same embedding by the one-dimensional Sobolev estimate. By [F8], $u\mapsto\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u|_{\partial M}$ is bounded from $C^1(\overline M)$ to $C^0(\partial M)$. Composing it with the $C^3$ parameter map proves the asserted $C^3$ dependence of $N_{q;h_1,\ldots,h_m}$.

A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\varphi=\sigma x_1$ for $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$. For $0<h\leq h_0$ define

For a smooth real function $f$, its **Riemannian gradient** is $\operatorname{grad}_g f=(df)^\sharp$.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let

**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;

$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$

in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed

By [F1] and $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$, $$g(d\Phi,d\Phi)=1+i^2|d\psi|_{g_0}^2=0.$$ Direct conjugation gives $$(-\Delta_g+q)(e^{-\tau\Phi}a) =e^{-\tau\Phi}\left[-\tau^2g(d\Phi,d\Phi)a+ \tau\left(2g(\nabla_g\Phi,\nabla_ga)+(\Delta_g\Phi)a\right) +(-\Delta_g+q)a\right].$$ The $\tau^2$ term vanishes by the eikonal equality, and the coefficient of $\tau$ is exactly the transport equation in the statement. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For complex boundary data, the duality pairing is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in its boundary test.

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. abla_gv,
abla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

derivations.claim: Write $a_{\gamma_j}(v,w)=\int_M\gamma_jg(\nabla v,\nabla\bar w)\,dV_g$. By [F1], $\langle\Lambda_{\gamma_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{\gamma_1}(u_1,u_2)$, since $u_2$ is an extension of $f_2$. Let $\widetilde u_1$ solve the $\gamma_2$ equation with boundary value $f_1$, which exists by [F2]. Then $\langle\Lambda_{\gamma_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{\gamma_2}(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $\gamma_2$ weak equation, Hermitian symmetry gives $a_{\gamma_2}(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_{\gamma_2}(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$. Hence $a_{\gamma_2}(\widetilde u_1,u_2)=a_{\gamma_2}(u_1,u_2)$. Subtracting the two equalities gives the conductivity identity.

Write $a_{q_j}(v,w)=\int_M(g(\nabla v,\nabla\bar w)+q_jv\bar w)\,dV_g$. By [F1], $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{q_1}(u_1,u_2)$ because $u_2$ extends $f_2$. Let $\widetilde u_1$ be the $q_2$ solution with boundary value $f_1$, which exists by [F3]. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{q_2}(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, real-valuedness of $q_2$ gives $a_{q_2}(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_{q_2}(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$. Thus $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{q_2}(u_1,u_2)$.
Subtract the identities in step 1.2. The gradient terms cancel and the remaining volume term is $\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g$, which proves the Schrödinger identity.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain of dimension $n\geq1$ with smooth nonempty boundary, assume every connected component of $M$ meets the boundary, and let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$. Fix an integer $s>n/2+2$ and a finite family $h_1,\ldots,h_m\in C^\infty(\partial M,\mathbb C)$. For $\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_m)\in\mathbb R^m$ sufficiently near zero, the equation
$$-\Delta_g u+q u^3=0\quad\text{in }M^\circ,\qquad u|_{\partial M}=\sum_{j=1}^m\epsilon_jh_j$$
has a unique solution in a fixed small $H^s(M)$ ball. The parameter map $\epsilon\mapsto u_\epsilon$ is $C^3$ into $H^s(M)$, and the corresponding nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann data $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_\epsilon|_{\partial M}$ is $C^3$ into $C^0(\partial M)$. For each such finite family, write $N_{q;h_1,\ldots,h_m}(\epsilon)=\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_\epsilon|_{\partial M}$ for this parameterized data map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. For every $F\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique weak solution $u\in H^1(M)$ of $(-\Delta_g+q)u=F$ with trace $f$. If $f=0$, $F\in H^m(M)$ and $m\geq0$ is an integer, then $u\in H^{m+2}(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^{m+2}}\leq C_m\|F\|_{H^m}$. If $F$ and $f$ are smooth, this solution belongs to $H^m(M)$ for every integer $m\geq0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For complex boundary data, the duality pairing is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in its boundary test.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, under the boundary-density identification of the conjugate-linear dual, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data, under the boundary-density identification of the conjugate-linear dual, this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $p'=p/(p-1)$,
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, $v\in W^{1,p'}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let
$T$ be the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] with
$\nu$ the outward normal of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Then for
every $i=1,\dots,n$,
$$\int_\Omega u\,\partial_iv\,dx=-\int_\Omega(\partial_iu)v\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega}(Tu)(Tv)\,\nu_i\,dS,$$
and all three integrals are finite. If $u,v\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, the
boundary term is the classical $\int_{\partial\Omega}uv\,\nu_i\,dS$ of the
divergence theorem
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] applied to the
field $uv\,e_i$; if in addition $Tu=\partial_\nu w$ on $\partial\Omega$ for a specified $w\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, the boundary term is $\int_{\partial\Omega}(\partial_\nu w)(Tv)\nu_i\,dS$. The normal derivative of [[def-classical-normal-derivative]] is defined on the boundary, and this extra identity is an assumption, not an interior substitution.

derivations.claim: Differentiate $-\Delta_g u_\epsilon+q u_\epsilon^3=0$ once in $\epsilon_j$ at $\epsilon=0$. Since $u_0=0$, the derivative $v_j=\partial_{\epsilon_j}u_\epsilon|_0$ solves $-\Delta_gv_j=0$ with trace $h_j$. Differentiating twice in distinct parameters gives $-\Delta_g(\partial_{\epsilon_i}\partial_{\epsilon_j}u_\epsilon|_0)=0$ with zero trace, so this second derivative vanishes by [F2].

The third mixed derivative of $u_\epsilon^3$ at zero has exactly the six permutations of $v_1v_2v_3$, hence equals $6v_1v_2v_3$; all other chain-rule terms contain $u_0$ or one of the vanishing second derivatives from step 1.1. Differentiating the equation gives $-\Delta_gw_{123}+6qv_1v_2v_3=0$, with zero boundary trace. By [F1], the third derivative of the nonlinear DN data is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}w_{123}|_{\partial M}$.

Since $v_4$ is harmonic and $w_{123}$ has zero trace, chartwise Green's formula and a finite partition of unity give $$\int_{\partial M}(\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}w_{123})\overline{h_4}\,dS_g =\int_M(\Delta_gw_{123})\overline{v_4}\,dV_g.$$ Indeed, the second Green identity has boundary term $w_{123}\partial_{\nu}\overline{v_4}$ equal to zero, and interior term $w_{123}\Delta_g\overline{v_4}=0$. In each boundary chart, write $\Delta_g w=|g|^{-1/2}\partial_i(|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}\partial_jw)$ and apply [F5] to the coordinate components; summing with the finite partition leaves the displayed Riemannian boundary integral by [F4].
The equation in step 2.1 gives $\Delta_gw_{123}=6qv_1v_2v_3$. Substituting this into step 3.1 and using the definition of the third DN derivative proves the displayed identity.
