Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth two-dimensional Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. For $x\in\partial M$, let $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}(x)$ be the outward unit normal. The boundary is **strictly convex** if
$$
g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0
$$
for every $x\in\partial M$ and every nonzero $w\in T_x\partial M$. A **Jacobi field** along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth vector field $J$ along $\gamma$ satisfying
$$
D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0,
$$
where $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if, on every unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$, a Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$ must be identically zero. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple surface** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

The unit tangent bundle is $SM=\{(x,v):x\in M,\ v\in T_xM,\ g_x(v,v)=1\}$. Write $\nu_{\mathrm{in}}=-\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$$
\partial_+SM=\{(x,v)\in SM:x\in\partial M,\ g_x(v,\nu_{\mathrm{in}})>0\}
$$
for inward-pointing unit boundary vectors. For $(x,v)\in\partial_+SM$, let $\gamma_{x,v}$ be the unit-speed geodesic with $\gamma_{x,v}(0)=x$ and $\dot\gamma_{x,v}(0)=v$, and let $\tau_+(x,v)$ be its first positive exit time from $M$. For $f\in C^\infty(M)$, its scalar **geodesic X-ray transform** is the function on $\partial_+SM$ defined by
$$
I_0f(x,v)=\int_0^{\tau_+(x,v)} f(\gamma_{x,v}(t))\,dt.
$$
The geodesic equation is interpreted up to first boundary exit; local smooth extensions of the metric are used only to solve the coordinate ODE at boundary initial data.

Their distinct tangent lines make the segments transverse at $p$. If they met again at a distinct point $z$, the two different subsegments from $p$ to $z$ would violate the unique-geodesic conclusion of [F5]. Thus the only intersection is $p$.

Put $T=c\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}Q(x_1,p)\,dx_1$, which is finite because $M$ is compact and $Q$ is bounded. If $Q=0$, four constant harmonic functions give the assertion. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ are strictly positive and $u_j$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma_j\nabla_gu_j)=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$
If instead $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ have trivial Dirichlet kernels for $-\Delta_g+q_j$ and $u_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u_j=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For complex boundary data, the duality pairing is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in its boundary test.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, under the boundary-density identification of the conjugate-linear dual, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data, under the boundary-density identification of the conjugate-linear dual, this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\geq3$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded smooth domain contained in a ball $B(0,R)$, and let $q\in L^\infty(\Omega,\mathbb C)$. There are constants $C>0$ and $\tau_0\geq1$, depending only on $n$, $R$, and $\|q\|_{L^\infty}$, such that for every $\zeta\in\mathbb C^n$ satisfying $\zeta\cdot\zeta=0$ and $|\zeta|\geq\tau_0$, there is $r_\zeta\in H^1(\Omega,\mathbb C)$ for which
$$u_\zeta(x)=e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta(x))$$
solves $(-\Delta+q)u_\zeta=0$ distributionally in $\Omega$, and
$$\|r_\zeta\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq C|\zeta|^{-1}\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad \|\nabla r_\zeta\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq C\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
The dot product in the null-phase condition is complex bilinear, and $|\zeta|=(\sum_{j=1}^n|\zeta_j|^2)^{1/2}$.
Assume AC. Finite complex Borel measures $\mu,\nu$ on $\mathbb R^n$ with $\widehat\mu=\widehat\nu$ are equal. Here finite means finite total variation, and $n\ge1$.

derivations.claim: Set $Q=q_1-q_2$. For exact $H^1$ solutions $u_j$ let $f_j=\operatorname{tr}u_j\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ and define the Hermitian weak forms $a_j(v,w)=\int_\Omega(\nabla v\cdot\nabla\overline w+q_jv\overline w)\,dx$. By the weak DN definition, $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_1(u_1,u_2)$. Let $\widetilde u_1\in H^1(\Omega)$ be the $q_2$ solution with trace $f_1$, which exists by nonresonant weak solvability. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_2(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, $a_2(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$, where the conjugation uses real-valuedness of $q_2$. Subtracting the two weak pairings gives $\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle=\int_\Omega Q u_1\overline{u_2}\,dx$. The maps agree on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, so this integral vanishes. This establishes the weak-trace extension of [F1] used here.

Fix $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. Since $n\geq3$, choose orthonormal $\omega_1,\omega_2\in\mathbb R^n$ perpendicular to $\xi$; when $\xi=0$, choose any orthonormal pair. For $\tau\geq1$, set $\sigma_\tau=(\tau^2+|\xi|^2/4)^{1/2}$ and $$\zeta_1=\tau\omega_1+i\sigma_\tau\omega_2+\xi/2,\qquad \zeta_2=-\tau\omega_1-i\sigma_\tau\omega_2+\xi/2.$$ The orthogonality gives $\zeta_j\cdot\zeta_j=\tau^2-\sigma_\tau^2+|\xi|^2/4=0$, $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=\xi$, and $|\zeta_j|\to\infty$. Apply [F2] directly to $q_1$ with phase $\zeta_1$ and to $q_2$ with phase $-\overline{\zeta_2}$, which is also null. This gives $$u_1=e^{i\zeta_1\cdot x}(1+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{-i\overline{\zeta_2}\cdot x}(1+r_2),\qquad \|r_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=O(\tau^{-1}).$$ Substitute in step 1.1. Since $Q\in L^2(\Omega)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)$, $$\left|\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\big(r_1+\overline{r_2}+r_1\overline{r_2}\big)\,dx\right| \leq \|Q\|_2(\|r_1\|_2+\|r_2\|_2)+\|Q\|_\infty\|r_1\|_2\|r_2\|_2=O(\tau^{-1}).$$ Taking $\tau\to\infty$ proves $\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\,dx=0$ for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$.

Define the finite complex Borel measure $\mu(E)=\int_{E\cap\Omega}Q(x)\,dx$ on $\mathbb R^n$. It has finite total variation because $\Omega$ is bounded and $Q$ is bounded. The identity in step 2.1 gives $\widehat\mu(\eta)=0$ for every $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$ (take $\xi=-2\pi\eta$). By [F3], $\mu=0$. Hence $\int_E\operatorname{Re}Q\,dx=\int_E\operatorname{Im}Q\,dx=0$ for every Borel $E$; applying this to the sets $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\geq1/m\}$, $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\leq-1/m\}$, and their imaginary-part analogues shows $Q=0$ almost everywhere. Continuity of $Q$ gives $Q=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

derivations.claim: Fix $x_0\in\partial\Omega$ and a sufficiently small patch. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported in the patch and equal to one near $x_0$, and use [F3] to construct approximate beams for $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ with the same boundary trace. Let $u_{\lambda,j}$ be their exact conductivity solutions. Equality of the DN maps and [F2] give $$\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_{\lambda,1}\cdot\overline{\nabla u_{\lambda,2}}\,dx=0.$$ Replacing each exact solution by its approximate beam changes this integral by $O(\lambda^{-N})$: the coefficient is bounded, the beam $H^1$ norms are uniformly bounded, and each exact correction is $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$ by [F3].

Set $k=0$ in [F3] and let $\lambda\to\infty$ in step 1.1. Since $c_0>0$, $$\int_{\partial\Omega}(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)|\chi|^2\,dS=0.$$ If $\gamma_1-\gamma_2$ were positive or negative at any boundary point, continuity would give a patch on which it has that strict sign; choosing $\chi$ supported in that patch and equal to one near the point would make this integral nonzero. Thus $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$ on $\partial\Omega$.

Fix an integer $k\geq1$ and suppose inductively that $\partial_{x_n}^j(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)=0$ on a boundary patch for every $j<k$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder in the inward normal coordinate gives $$\gamma_1(y,x_n)-\gamma_2(y,x_n)=x_n^kF_k(y,x_n),\qquad F_k(y,0)=\frac{\partial_{x_n}^k(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)(y,0)}{k!},$$ for a smooth $F_k$. Apply [F2] to the exact beams from [F3], replace them by their approximate beams, and multiply the resulting integral identity by $\lambda^k$. The replacement error is $O(\lambda^{k-N})$, since the weight $x_n^k$ is bounded and the corrections are $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$. Choose $N>k$ and apply the weighted limit in [F3]; then $$c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F_k(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2\,dS(y)=0.$$ Since $c_k>0$, the same localized sign argument as in step 2.1 gives $F_k(y,0)=0$ throughout the patch. Therefore the $k$th inward normal derivatives agree there.

Step 2.1 is the base case for the induction. Step 3.1 proves each subsequent order on a patch that may be chosen around any prescribed boundary point. Thus every boundary point has a neighborhood on which the order-$k$ normal derivative difference is zero for every integer $k\geq0$, proving the full boundary-jet assertion.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary and with every connected component meeting the boundary, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and fix smooth boundary directions $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$. For $\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon_3)$ near zero, let $u_\epsilon$ be the unique small solution of $-\Delta_g u+qu^3=0$ with boundary value $\epsilon_1h_1+\epsilon_2h_2+\epsilon_3h_3$, and set $\mathcal N(\epsilon)=\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_\epsilon|_{\partial M}$. Let $v_j$ be the harmonic solution with boundary value $h_j$. If
$$w_{123}=\left.\partial_{\epsilon_1}\partial_{\epsilon_2}\partial_{\epsilon_3}u_\epsilon\right|_{\epsilon=0},$$
where $u_\epsilon$ has boundary value $\epsilon_1h_1+\epsilon_2h_2+\epsilon_3h_3$, then
$$-\Delta_gw_{123}+6qv_1v_2v_3=0,\qquad w_{123}|_{\partial M}=0,$$
and
$$\int_{\partial M}\left.\partial_{\epsilon_1}\partial_{\epsilon_2}\partial_{\epsilon_3}\mathcal N(\epsilon)\right|_{\epsilon=0}\overline{h_4}\,dS_g =6\int_Mq\,v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$ be a three-dimensional transversally anisotropic product domain with compact connected simple surface transversal $(M_0,g_0)$. For every $p\in M_0^\circ$ choose two nontangential unit-speed geodesic segments $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ meeting transversely at $p$ and nowhere else. For every $\xi\in\mathbb R$ and every $Q\in C^\infty(\overline M)$, there are four exact harmonic solutions $u_{\tau,1}^+,u_{\tau,1}^-,u_{\tau,2}^+,u_{\tau,2}^-\in H^1(M)$, with no prescribed boundary values, such that
$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_MQ(x_1,x')u_{\tau,1}^+u_{\tau,1}^-u_{\tau,2}^+u_{\tau,2}^-\,dV_g =c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}Q(x_1,p)\,dx_1,$$
where $I_p=\{x_1\in\mathbb R:(x_1,p)\in M^\circ\}$ and $c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)=|\sin\angle(\dot\gamma_1(p),\dot\gamma_2(p))|^{-1}>0$.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

derivations.claim: Fix four smooth boundary directions $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$. Equality of the finite-parameter DN maps for $q_1$ and $q_2$ implies equality of their mixed third derivatives at the origin. Applying [F2] to each coefficient and subtracting gives $$\int_M(q_1-q_2)v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g=0$$ for every four harmonic functions $v_j$ arising from smooth boundary data.

The identity in step 1.1 holds also for complex smooth harmonic functions: write their boundary values as real and imaginary parts and expand the separately linear or conjugate-linear expression. Since the Laplacian has real coefficients, conjugation preserves harmonicity; replacing the fourth function by its conjugate therefore gives $\int_M Qw_1w_2w_3w_4\,dV=0$ for every four smooth complex harmonic functions, where $Q=q_1-q_2$.

Fix $p\in M_0^\circ$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R$. Choose the transverse boundary-to-boundary geodesic segments through $p$ supplied by [F3] (their existence is established in that supplier's proof). Apply [F3] with $Q=q_1-q_2$. Its witnesses are smooth by [F5], so their product integral is zero for every $\tau$ by step 2.1. Taking their stated limit gives $$c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}(q_1-q_2)(x_1,p)\,dx_1=0,$$ where $c>0$ is the crossing normalization. The coefficient transform therefore vanishes for every $\xi$ and every $p$.

For each $p$, extend $x_1\mapsto(q_1-q_2)(x_1,p)$ by zero outside $I_p$. It is a compactly supported $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function. By step 3.1, [F4] makes this section zero almost everywhere; its smoothness in the interior of $M$ then makes $q_1-q_2=0$ on $M^\circ$, and continuity gives equality on $\overline M$. Thus the theorem follows.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For complex boundary data, the duality pairing is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in its boundary test.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, under the boundary-density identification of the conjugate-linear dual, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data, under the boundary-density identification of the conjugate-linear dual, this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ are strictly positive and $u_j$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma_j\nabla_gu_j)=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$
If instead $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ have trivial Dirichlet kernels for $-\Delta_g+q_j$ and $u_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u_j=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For complex boundary data, the duality pairing is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in its boundary test.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, under the boundary-density identification of the conjugate-linear dual, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data, under the boundary-density identification of the conjugate-linear dual, this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. A geodesic segment in $M_0$ satisfies the geodesic equation for the Levi-Civita connection of $g_0$ on $(0,L)$ and extends smoothly to its endpoints, where derivatives are interpreted one-sided. A nontangential maximal geodesic segment is a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$, with $L>0$, whose initial velocity points strictly inward at $\partial M_0$, whose terminal velocity points strictly outward at $\partial M_0$, and whose points for $0<t<L$ lie in $M_0^\circ$. For $f\in C_c^\infty(M_0^\circ,\mathbb R)$ define its geodesic ray transform by $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=\int_0^L f(\gamma(t))\,dt$. The unweighted scalar ray transform is called injective on compactly supported smooth functions if $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=0$ for every such segment implies $f=0$. For complex-valued $f$, injectivity means injectivity of its real and imaginary parts separately.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\psi\in C^\infty$ be real on a neighborhood of the transversal projection of $M$, with $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$. Suppose $a\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb C)$ satisfies
$$2\partial_{x_1}a+2i\,g_0(\nabla_{g_0}\psi,\nabla_{g_0}a)+i(\Delta_{g_0}\psi)a=0.$$
Then, for all sufficiently large $\tau$, there is an exact solution
$$u_\tau=e^{-\tau(x_1+i\psi)}a+e^{-\tau x_1}r_\tau,\qquad (-\Delta_g+q)u_\tau=0\ \text{in }M^\circ,$$
with $r_\tau\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_\tau\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_{L^2(M)}$. No boundary value is prescribed for $r_\tau$.

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary and let $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$ be a unit-speed nontangential geodesic segment. For every real $\lambda$ and every $K>0$, there is a family $v_{\tau+i\lambda}\in C^\infty(M_0)$, $\tau\geq1$, such that
$$\|(-\Delta_{g_0}-(\tau+i\lambda)^2)v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(\tau^{-K}),\qquad \|v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(1),$$
and for every $\psi\in C(M_0)$,
$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_{M_0}|v_{\tau+i\lambda}|^2\psi\,dV_{g_0} =\int_0^L e^{-2\lambda t}\psi(\gamma(t))\,dt.$$
The statement permits transversal manifolds without an orientability assumption and makes no boundary condition assertion for the quasimodes.

derivations.claim: For exact $H^1$ solutions $u_j$ let $f_j=\operatorname{tr}u_j\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ and define $a_j(v,w)=\int_M(g(\nabla_gv,\nabla_g\overline w)+q_jv\overline w)\,dV_g$. By the weak DN definition, $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_1(u_1,u_2)$. Let $\widetilde u_1\in H^1(M)$ be the $q_2$ solution with trace $f_1$, which exists by nonresonant weak solvability. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_2(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, $a_2(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$, where the conjugation uses real-valuedness of $q_2$. Subtracting the weak pairings and using equality of the DN maps on all $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ gives $\int_M Q(x_1,x')u_1(x_1,x')\overline{u_2(x_1,x')}\,dV_g=0$, where $Q=q_1-q_2$. This derives the needed weak-trace extension of [F2]. Because $q_j\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ and $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$, extension of $Q$ by zero gives a smooth compactly supported function on $\mathbb R\times M_0$.

Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, put $s=\tau+i\lambda$, and choose the beam $v_s$ of [F6] with residual $O(\tau^{-K})$. Use the signed real-weight solver [F5] to obtain exact solutions $$u_1=e^{-s x_1}(v_s+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{s x_1}(v_s+r_2)$$ for the respective potentials, with $r_j\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_j\|_2=O(\tau^{-1})$. Indeed the conjugated residual is $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)v_s+q_jv_s$, of bounded $L^2$ norm on a fixed product cylinder; multiplication by $e^{\pm i\lambda x_1}$ is bounded there. Correcting with the real-weight solver gives precisely this bound. Their product in step 1.1 is $e^{-2i\lambda x_1}(v_s+r_1)(\overline{v_s}+\overline{r_2})$. Every error integral tends to zero by Cauchy--Schwarz, the boundedness of $Q$, $\|v_s\|_2=O(1)$, and $\|r_j\|_2=o(1)$. Integrating first in $x_1$ gives the smooth compactly supported transversal test function $\widehat Q_\lambda$ below. Applying [F6] proves the attenuated ray identity for every $\lambda$ and every nontangential $\gamma$. This argument works on the base manifold; it does not assume injectivity of a ray transform on its orientation cover.

Step 2.1 supplies $$\int_{\gamma}\widehat Q_\lambda(\gamma(t))e^{-2\lambda t}\,dt=0 \quad\text{for every real }\lambda\text{ and every nontangential geodesic }\gamma,$$ where $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2i\lambda x_1}Q(x_1,x')\,dx_1$. At $\lambda=0$, [F3] gives $\widehat Q_0=0$. Assume inductively that $\partial_\lambda^j\widehat Q_0=0$ for every $j<k$. Differentiate the ray identity $k$ times at $\lambda=0$. Differentiation under the finite geodesic integral is valid because $Q$ is smooth with compact $x_1$ support. Leibniz' rule leaves the unweighted ray integral of $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0$; all other terms contain lower derivatives and vanish by the induction hypothesis. Thus [F3], applied to real and imaginary parts, gives $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0=0$. Induction proves that every Taylor coefficient of $\lambda\mapsto\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ vanishes for each fixed $x'$.

For each fixed $x'$, compact $x_1$ support makes $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ entire in $\lambda$, so its zero Taylor series implies it vanishes for all real $\lambda$. This is the Fourier transform of the $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function $Q(\cdot,x')$ at every frequency $2\lambda$; [F4] gives $Q(\cdot,x')=0$ almost everywhere. Smoothness of $Q$ then yields $Q=0$ on $M$.

$$

$$
D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0,
$$
where $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if, on every unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$, a Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$ must be identically zero. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple surface** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

The unit tangent bundle is $SM=\{(x,v):x\in M,\ v\in T_xM,\ g_x(v,v)=1\}$. Write $\nu_{\mathrm{in}}=-\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ and

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $n=\dim M\geq0$ and let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. If $n=0$, define every $H^k(M)$ to be the space of scalar-valued functions on the finite set $M$ with the counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm. For $n\geq1$ and an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. If $\partial M=\varnothing$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\{0\}$. If $n=1$, set $H^{1/2}(\partial M)=\mathbb K^{\partial M}$ with its counting-measure $\ell^2$ norm, where $\mathbb K$ is the scalar field. For $n\geq2$, define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. For real scalars, define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous linear dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. For complex scalars, define it as the continuous conjugate-linear dual: its pairing with $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in $h$, using the Riemannian boundary density. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the boundary
conventions of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded $C^1$ domain, let
$0<s<1$, $1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix a
finite family of boundary charts: for each $j$ let $W_j\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
be open and $\Phi_j:W_j\to\Phi_j(W_j)\subseteq B_j\times\mathbb R$ a
flattening chart as in
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], so that
$\Phi_j(\Omega\cap W_j)=\Phi_j(W_j)\cap\{t<0\}$ and the boundary corresponds
to the graph $\{t=0\}$; write $\Psi_j:=\pi\circ\Phi_j|_{\partial\Omega\cap W_j}$
for the induced parametrisation of $\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ by an open subset
$V_j:=\Psi_j(\partial\Omega\cap W_j)\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and assume the
$\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ cover $\partial\Omega$. Fix a subordinate finite
ambient partition: nonnegative $\chi_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$\operatorname{supp}\chi_j\subseteq W_j$ and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a
neighbourhood of $\partial\Omega$
([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]).
Finally let $\partial\Omega$ carry the chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], which fixes the
meaning of almost-everywhere equality and of $L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

For a Borel function $g:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb K$ put
$$\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}:=\sum_j\bigl\|(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}\bigr\|_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})},$$
where the chart representation $(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}$ is read in graph
coordinates and extended by zero off $V_j$, and the norm on the right is that
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. The **fractional
Sobolev space of the boundary** is
$$W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):=\{g\in L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}<\infty\}.$$
The right-hand side is a finite sum of finite norms of compactly supported
chart representations, so $W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is exactly the
set of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ classes whose chart representations all lie in
the Euclidean space of
[[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]; that the resulting
space and the topology of the norm do not depend on the choices of atlas and
partition, up to equivalence of norms, is proved in
[[lem-fractional-boundary-norm-is-independent-of-atlas]] and is not assumed
here.

Three conventions belong to the definition. First, membership is a property of
the $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ class: $g$ is an almost-everywhere class with respect
to the surface measure, and the chart representations are classes in
$W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$; representative independence for the Euclidean
factor is established together with the well-definedness lemma on this page
and is not presupposed here. Second, the norm is a finite sum
over a finite atlas, and each $\chi_jg$ is supported in the interior of the
chart, so the localisations are compactly supported and no boundary behaviour
of $\Psi_j^{-1}$ outside $V_j$ enters. Third, on this page the exponent used
is the trace exponent $s=\theta=1-1/p$ for $1<p<\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded
$C^1$ domain, $0<s<1$ and $1\le p<\infty$.

(i) If $\Psi:V\to V'$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open subsets of
$\mathbb R^{d}$, $d\ge1$, which is bi-Lipschitz and whose derivatives in both directions are bounded,
then for every measurable $u:V'\to\mathbb K$,
$$\|u\circ\Psi\|_{W^{s,p}(V)}\le C(\Psi,s,p)\,\|u\|_{W^{s,p}(V')}$$
and symmetrically with $\Psi^{-1}$; in particular the Slobodeckij norm
$\|\cdot\|_{W^{s,p}}$ of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]
is preserved up to equivalence by such coordinate changes. Here the norm on an open set uses the same double integral restricted to that set, with its $L^p$ term. Bounded derivatives alone on arbitrary open sets do not imply the bi-Lipschitz hypothesis.

(ii) Consequently two finite boundary chart families with subordinate
partitions, as in
[[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]], define
equivalent norms on $\partial\Omega$: the sum norms differ by multiplicative
constants depending only on the two atlases, the dimension and $s,p$, so
$W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)$ is well defined as a set and its topology is
atlas-independent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open
and let $\Phi:U\to V$ be a $C^k$ diffeomorphism with inverse
$\Psi:=\Phi^{-1}:V\to U$. Fix open sets $U_0\subset\subset U$ and
$V_0\subset\subset V$ with $\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, and suppose that on
$\overline{U_0}$ the derivatives of $\Phi$ through order $k$ are bounded and
that on $\overline{V_0}$ the derivatives of $\Psi$ through order $k$ are
bounded; in the situation of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] these are exactly the compact
patches on which the flattening chart and its inverse have bounded derivatives
through order $k$. Then:

1. for every $u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K)$ the composition
$u\circ\Phi$ belongs to $W^{k,p}(U_0;\mathbb K)$, and for every
$1\le|\alpha|\le k$ its weak derivatives satisfy, almost everywhere on
$U_0$,
$$D^\alpha(u\circ\Phi)=\sum_{1\le|\beta|\le|\alpha|}\bigl((D^\beta u)\circ\Phi\bigr)\,P_{\alpha\beta}\bigl(D\Phi,\dots,D^k\Phi\bigr),$$
where $P_{\alpha\beta}$ is a universal polynomial with integer coefficients,
whose values on $\overline{U_0}$ are bounded by a constant depending only on
$n,k$ and the stated bounds for $\Phi$;

2. there is a constant $C$, depending only on $n$, $k$, $p$ and the two sets of
chart bounds, with
$$\|u\circ\Phi\|_{W^{k,p}(U_0)}\le C\,\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(V_0)}\qquad\text{for all }u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K).$$
If in addition $\Psi(V_0)\subseteq U_0$ (equivalently, under the stated
$\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, $\Phi(U_0)=V_0$), the same assertion holds for
composition with $\Psi$ from $W^{k,p}(U_0)$ to $W^{k,p}(V_0)$.

For $k=1$ only the first derivatives of $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ enter, so bounded
$C^1$ chart and inverse data suffice; no $C^1$-only claim is made for $k>1$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then the set of restrictions
to $\Omega$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ is dense in
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|\varphi|_\Omega-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The exponent range is $1\le p<\infty$; the result asserts no density in the
$W^{k,\infty}$ norm, and it does not hold on arbitrary open sets, as the
companion examples page shows.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$,
$H=\mathbb R^d\times(0,\infty)$, and let $T_+$ be the half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]]. Write
$|Du|^p:=\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}|D_ju|^p$ for the sum of the $p$-th powers of the
weak first derivatives, and $[\cdot]_{\theta,p}$ for the Slobodeckij seminorm
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. Then for every
$u\in W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)$ with $g=T_+u$,
$$[g]_{\theta,p}^p\le C(d,p)\int_H|Du|^p\,dx=C(d,p)\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\|D_ju\|_{L^p(H)}^p\le C(d,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(H)}^p;$$
equivalently $T_+:W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)\to W^{\theta,p}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K)$
is a bounded operator.

The homogeneous estimate is scale invariant: for $r>0$ and
$u_r(x',t):=u(rx',rt)$ one has $g_{u_r}(x')=g(rx')$ and
$$[g_{u_r}]_{\theta,p}^p=r^{-d+p\theta}[g]_{\theta,p}^p,\qquad \int_H|Du_r|^p\,dx=r^{-d+p\theta}\int_H|Du|^p\,dx,$$
because $p\theta=p-1$; so both sides of the homogeneous estimate scale with
the same exponent $r^{-d+p\theta}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
The right inverse is not unique and no canonical choice is claimed.

derivations.claim: On the common smooth core, the identity between the fixed-atlas and Euclidean $W^{1,2}$ norms is bounded in both directions. Indeed, each fixed chart representative is obtained by multiplying by a fixed smooth cutoff and composing with a smooth flattening chart, so [F3] bounds the finite fixed-atlas sum by the Euclidean norm. Conversely, the finite partition of unity writes $u$ as the sum of its localized chart pieces; pull each piece back and use [F3] to bound the Euclidean $W^{1,2}$ norm by the fixed-atlas sum. The constants are finite because the atlas and partition are finite. By the density and completeness in [F3], the identity extends to bounded inverse maps on the completions. Since the two norms are equivalent on $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, their closures give the same zero-boundary subspace.

For $u\in H^1_{\rm fix}$, take its localized boundary-chart representatives in the fixed-atlas definition. Apply [F4] to each representative (reflecting $t<0$ to $t>0$ when required), and sum the finitely many resulting local traces. The fixed-atlas norm [F1] gives a bounded map $T:H^1_{\rm fix}\to H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$. For smooth $u$ this sum is the classical boundary restriction because the partition equals one near the boundary and the half-space traces agree with classical restriction. As an $L^2$-valued map, this trace agrees with the Euclidean trace [F5]: the maps are bounded into $L^2$ by [F2] and [F5], and the Euclidean and fixed $H^1$ norms are equivalent by step 1.1, so equality on the dense smooth core extends to all of $H^1$.

If $Tu=0$ in $H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$, it is zero as an $L^2$ class by [F2]; the $L^2$ trace agreement of step 2.1 and [F6] imply $u\in H^1_{0,\rm E}$. Step 1.1 identifies this with $H^1_{0,\rm fix}$. Conversely, if $u\in H^1_{0,\rm fix}$, approximate it in the fixed $H^1$ norm by interior compactly supported smooth functions. Each has zero classical trace, so continuity of $T$ gives $Tu=0$. Therefore $\ker T=H^1_{0,\rm fix}$.

By [F7] and the boundary-norm equivalence [F2], the Euclidean $L^2$ trace has a bounded right inverse $R:H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}(\partial\Omega)\to H^1_{\rm E}(\Omega)$. The norm equivalence of step 1.1 makes $R$ bounded into $H^1_{\rm fix}$ as well. For every boundary class $f$, the Euclidean trace of $Rf$ is $f$; by step 2.1 the fixed trace agrees with it in $L^2$, hence as an $H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$ class. So $T$ is onto. The kernel identity of step 3.1 induces a bounded bijection $\bar T:H^1_{\rm fix}/H^1_{0,\rm fix}\to H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$. For any representative $u+v$ with $v\in H^1_{0,\rm fix}$, step 2.1 gives $\|Tu\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|u+v\|_{H^1_{\rm fix}}$; taking the infimum shows $\bar T$ is bounded. Also $\|\bar T^{-1}f\|\le\|Rf\|_{H^1_{\rm fix}}\le C_R\|f\|_{H^{1/2}}$, so its inverse is bounded. Composing with the quotient identity isomorphism of step 1.1 proves the asserted Euclidean quotient identification.

definition_review.source_exact:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary. Write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Define the boundary trace-data space $\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ with quotient norm; the trace-quotient lemma identifies this quotient with the fixed-atlas $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data convention of the scalar conductivity map. Let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite, so some $0<c\le C<\infty$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le \xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, a weak solution with boundary datum $f$ is a class $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and

$$\int_\Omega \gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

The weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is the bilinear-form candidate $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega\to\mathbb R$ given, whenever the weak solution exists, by

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

where $V_h\in H^1(\Omega)$ is any representative of $h$. all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$

$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$

$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.

axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

statement.

The space $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is a closed linear subspace of the complete space $H^1(\Omega)$ by [F1] and [F3]. Since $\Omega$ is bounded, it lies in a slab $a<x\cdot e<b$ for some unit vector $e$ and finite $a<b$; applying [F2] with $p=2$ gives $\|v\|_{L^2}\le C(2)(b-a)\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Thus $\|v\|_H:=\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$ is a norm equivalent to the inherited $H^1$ norm, and $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is a real Hilbert space for $(v,w)_H=\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot
abla w\,dx$.

Fix any representative $U\in H^1(\Omega)$ of $f$; the existence argument below is independent of which representative is fixed. On $H_0^1(\Omega)$ define $a_\gamma(z,v)=\int_\Omega\gamma
abla z\cdot
abla v\,dx$ and $F_U(v)=-\int_\Omega\gamma
abla U\cdot
abla v\,dx$. By [F6], $a_\gamma$ is bounded by $C\|z\|_H\|v\|_H$, coercive by $c\|z\|_H^2$, and $F_U$ is bounded by $C\|
abla U\|_{L^2}\|v\|_H$. Countable Choice follows from [F5], so [F4] gives a unique $z\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ with $a_\gamma(z,v)=F_U(v)$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Then $u_{\gamma,f}:=U+z$ has quotient class $f$ and satisfies the stated weak equation.

If $u_1,u_2$ are two weak solutions with boundary class $f$, then $w=u_1-u_2\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $\int_\Omega\gamma
abla w\cdot
abla v\,dx=0$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Taking $v=w$ and using [F6] gives $c\|
abla w\|_{L^2}^2\le0$, so $\|w\|_H=0$ and hence $w=0$ by the norm property in step 1.1.

Let $h\in\mathcal B_\Omega$ and let $V,V'$ be any two representatives of $h$. Their difference lies in $H_0^1(\Omega)$ by [F1], so the weak equation for $u_{\gamma,f}$ gives $\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla(V-V')\,dx=0$. Therefore the energy pairing is independent of the representative of $h$.

The weak solution minimizes the quadratic energy in its boundary class: if $W$ is any representative of $f$, then $W-u_{\gamma,f}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, and expanding the square with the weak equation gives $\int_\Omega\gamma|
abla W|^2\,dx=\int_\Omega\gamma|
abla u_{\gamma,f}|^2\,dx+\int_\Omega\gamma|
abla(W-u_{\gamma,f})|^2\,dx$. Using [F6] and taking the infimum over representatives yields $\|
abla u_{\gamma,f}\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{C/c}\,\|f\|_{\mathcal B_\Omega}$. The same infimum argument gives representatives $V$ of $h$ with $\|V\|_{H^1}\le\|h\|_{\mathcal B_\Omega}+\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Cauchy–Schwarz and the upper bound in [F6] now give $|\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,hangle|\le C\sqrt{C/c}\,\|f\|_{\mathcal B_\Omega}(\|h\|_{\mathcal B_\Omega}+\varepsilon)$; letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves boundedness. [F1, F6, step 2.1, step 3.2, algebra] To prove bilinearity, for $f_1,f_2\in\mathcal B_\Omega$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, the function $a u_{\gamma,f_1}+b u_{\gamma,f_2}$ has boundary class $af_1+bf_2$ and satisfies the weak equation by linearity of the quotient map and of the integral. Uniqueness from step 3.1 therefore gives $u_{\gamma,af_1+bf_2}=a u_{\gamma,f_1}+b u_{\gamma,f_2}$. For $h_1,h_2\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, representatives $V_{h_1},V_{h_2}$ give $aV_{h_1}+bV_{h_2}$ as a representative of $ah_1+bh_2$; representative independence from step 3.2 and linearity of the integral show that the energy pairing is linear in its second argument as well. Thus the energy form is bilinear, and the bound just proved makes it a bounded bilinear form on $\mathcal B_\Omega	imes\mathcal B_\Omega$.

[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

For smooth $F:M\to N$ and a Riemannian metric $h$ on $N$, its **pullback tensor** is $(F^*h)_p(v,w)=h_{F(p)}(dF_pv,dF_pw)$.

This is [[def-pullback-of-a-covariant-tensor-field]] for the tensor in [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]. It is always symmetric and positive semidefinite; the name does not assert positive definiteness. Smoothness and the precise immersion criterion are established next.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, hence Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected domain with smooth boundary, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite. Let $F:\overline\Omega\to\overline\Omega$ be a diffeomorphism smooth through the boundary, with smooth inverse and $F|_{\partial\Omega}=\operatorname{id}$. For $x=F(y)$, put $J_F(y)=|\det DF(y)|$ and define

$$ (F_*\gamma)(x)=\frac{DF(y)\,\gamma(y)\,DF(y)^T}{J_F(y)},\qquad y=F^{-1}(x). $$

Then $F_*\gamma$ is a smooth uniformly positive-definite matrix conductivity and its weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map equals that of $\gamma$. Explicitly, for every pair of boundary trace-data classes $f,h\in\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$,

$$\langle\Lambda_{F_*\gamma}f,h\rangle=\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle,$$

where each map is the weak energy form $\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx$, $u_{\gamma,f}$ is the unique weak solution with boundary class $f$, and $V_h$ is any $H^1$ representative of $h$.

The same gauge invariance has a Riemannian form. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold with boundary, $g$ a smooth Riemannian metric, $\Gamma\subseteq\partial M$ relatively open, and $\Phi:M\to M$ a smooth diffeomorphism with $\Phi|_\Gamma=\operatorname{id}$. Define $(\Phi^*g)_p(v,w):=g_{\Phi(p)}(D\Phi_pv,D\Phi_pw)$. The cotangent inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_g$ is induced by $g^{-1}$, and in coordinates $dV_g=\sqrt{\det(g_{ij})}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$. A smooth function $u$ is $g$-harmonic when $\int_M\langle du,d\psi\rangle_g\,dV_g=0$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$. Then $u\circ\Phi$ is $\Phi^*g$-harmonic; for any two smooth $g$-harmonic functions $u,v$,

$$\int_M\langle d(u\circ\Phi),d(v\circ\Phi)\rangle_{\Phi^*g}\,dV_{\Phi^*g}=\int_M\langle du,dv\rangle_g\,dV_g.$$

If the boundary traces of $u,v$ are supported in $\Gamma$, then composition by $\Phi$ leaves both traces fixed, so the local energy measurement of every such smooth harmonic pair is unchanged. In particular, if for each $f\in C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$ the Dirichlet solutions for $g$ and $\Phi^*g$ with trace $f$ are unique and smooth, then the corresponding local energy DN maps agree.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary. Write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Define the boundary trace-data space $\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ with quotient norm; the trace-quotient lemma identifies this quotient with the fixed-atlas $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data convention of the scalar conductivity map. Let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite, so some $0<c\le C<\infty$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le \xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, a weak solution with boundary datum $f$ is a class $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and

$$\int_\Omega \gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

The weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is the bilinear-form candidate $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega\to\mathbb R$ given, whenever the weak solution exists, by

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

where $V_h\in H^1(\Omega)$ is any representative of $h$. The local anisotropic conductivity well-posedness lemma proves existence and uniqueness for every boundary class, independence of the representative $V_h$, and boundedness on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$; it therefore makes this candidate a bounded bilinear map. The map is the boundary energy form for the equation $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u)=0$. Under the trace-quotient isomorphism and the local boundedness result, this form gives the usual weak map into the dual $H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ with the scalar convention.

derivations.claim: Write $R_\varepsilon(r)=r(1+\varepsilon(1-r^2))$ for $0\le r\le1$. Then $R_\varepsilon(0)=0$, $R_\varepsilon(1)=1$, and $R_\varepsilon'(r)=1+\varepsilon-3\varepsilon r^2\ge1-2\varepsilon>0$. Thus $R_\varepsilon$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $[0,1]$ to itself; $F_\varepsilon$ preserves each radial ray, is bijective on the ball, and fixes the boundary pointwise.

At the origin $DF_\varepsilon(0)=(1+\varepsilon)I_n$ and $J_{F_\varepsilon}(0)=(1+\varepsilon)^n>0$. At $r>0$ the radial derivative is $R_\varepsilon'(r)>0$ and each tangential eigenvalue is $R_\varepsilon(r)/r=1+\varepsilon(1-r^2)>0$. By continuity, $R_\varepsilon'$ stays positive on $[0,1+\delta]$ for some $\delta>0$. The same radial formula extends $F_\varepsilon$ to a smooth diffeomorphism from the ball of radius $1+\delta$ onto its image, which contains a neighborhood of $\overline{B^n}$; its inverse is smooth there. Thus the inverse is smooth through the boundary and the differential is nonsingular on the closed ball.

Since $F_\varepsilon(0)=0$, the pushforward formula in [F1] gives $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon(0)=DF_\varepsilon(0)DF_\varepsilon(0)^T/J_{F_\varepsilon}(0)=(1+\varepsilon)^{2-n}I_n$. Because $n\ge3$ and $\varepsilon>0$, this differs from $I_n$, so the pushed-forward conductivity is nontrivial.

The hypotheses of [F1] hold for $\gamma=I_n$ and $F_\varepsilon$, so $\Lambda_{\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon}=\Lambda_{I_n}$. The example therefore exhibits a distinct smooth anisotropic conductivity with exactly the same boundary energy map, caused by the stated boundary-fixing change of variables.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set, let $M:=|D|$, let $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. Here $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ are equivalence classes modulo null functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and $L^\infty$ means essentially bounded with respect to Lebesgue measure ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]). We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
For each $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the essential-supremum result gives $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|qv\|_{L^1(D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|v\|_2$. Thus, for $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume-potential integral is absolutely convergent: $\overline D$ is closed, so its complement contains a ball about $x$ disjoint from $D$.

If $M=0$, define $L^2(D)=\{0\}$ and $K_k=0$; all solution and far-field statements on that space are the zero-space statements. The substantive operator results below assume $0<M<\infty$.

This is a stipulated integral-equation model with the sign convention $(-\Delta-k^2)(u-f)=q u$ when the corresponding distributional Helmholtz equation is used. In the acoustic notation of Scherzer–Mindrinos, their equation $u=u_i-k^2\Phi*((1-n)u)$ corresponds to $q=k^2(n-1)$. No existence or uniqueness for all contrasts is asserted by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ have finite Lebesgue measure. For every product-measurable kernel $a\in L^2(D\times D;\mathbb C)$, the formula $T_av(x)=\int_Da(x,y)v(y)dy$ defines a representative-independent complex-linear map $L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\|T_a\|\le\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D)}$. Consequently, under [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$,
$$\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\|G_k(\cdot-\cdot)q(\cdot)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\,\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$
For $|D|=0$ the operator is zero.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. If $\rho:=\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}<1$, then for every $f\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ the equation $u=f+K_ku$ has a unique solution. For each integer $m\ge0$, define the Born partial sum $u_m:=\sum_{j=0}^{m}K_k^jf$. Then
$$\|u-u_m\|_2\le\frac{\rho^{m+1}}{1-\rho}\|f\|_2.$$
No compactness, analytic continuation, or physical uniqueness hypothesis is used in this small-norm branch.

We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
For each $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the essential-supremum result gives $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|qv\|_{L^1(D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|v\|_2$. Moreover, if $M\ge0$ and $|f|\le M$ almost everywhere, then

So $\|f\|_\infty$ is the least essential bound of $|f|$.

derivations.claim: The integral operator depends linearly on $q$, so $K_{q,k}-K_{q',k}=K_{q-q',k}$ for any $q,q'\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$. By [F2], $\|K_{q,k}-K_{q',k}\|\le C_D\|q-q'\|_\infty$. Thus $q\mapsto\rho_k(q)$ is continuous, $\mathcal U_{D,k}=\{\rho_k<1\}$ is open, and $0\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ because $K_{0,k}=0$.

Cauchy–Schwarz gives its absolute value at most $\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\|u_{q,k,d}\|_2$.

Apply [F8] to $v=u_{q,k,d}$, whose existence is established in step 1.2. It supplies continuity in observation direction and the stated uniform outgoing-wave limit estimate, so the defined data are the physical far-field amplitude for this volume branch.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set with $0<M:=|D|<\infty$, and let $k>0$. Write $S^2:=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:|v|=1\}$ and $C_D:=\sqrt{M\,\operatorname{diam}(D)/(4\pi)}$. For $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, extended by zero off $D$, set $G_k(z):=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ and $G_k(0):=0$, and let
$$K_{q,k}v(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \rho_k(q):=\|K_{q,k}\|_{L^2(D)\to L^2(D)}.$$
The **small-norm contrast class** is
$$\mathcal U_{D,k}:=\{q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C):\rho_k(q)<1\}.$$
For $d\in S^2$, put $f_{k,d}(x):=e^{ikd\cdot x}$ on $D$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, let $u_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ denote the unique solution of $u=f_{k,d}+K_{q,k}u$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, define the exact far-field data family by
$$\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)u_{q,k,d}(y)\,dy,\qquad (\theta,d)\in S^2\times S^2.$$

For $h\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, define its first Born data by
$$\mathcal B_k h(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}h(y)e^{ikd\cdot y}\,dy=\frac1{4\pi}\widehat{h_0}\!\left(\frac{k}{2\pi}(\theta-d)\right),$$
where $h_0$ is the zero extension of $h$ to $\mathbb R^3$ and $\widehat g(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}\,dy$ for $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. No uniqueness or stability outside $\mathcal U_{D,k}$ is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses and notation of the fixed-frequency far-field definition. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ put $\rho=\rho_k(q)$. Uniformly over all incident and observation directions,
$$\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}\left|\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{M}{4\pi}\|q\|_\infty\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.$$
Whenever $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, this implies
$$\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}\left|\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{M C_D}{4\pi}\frac{\|q\|_\infty^2}{1-C_D\|q\|_\infty}.$$
For each fixed $(\theta,d)$, the scalar map $q\mapsto\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)$ on the open domain $\mathcal U_{D,k}$, with $L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\mathbb C$ viewed as real Banach spaces, is Fréchet differentiable at $q=0$ and has derivative $h\mapsto\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)$. The remainder bound is uniform in $(\theta,d)$; it asserts no nonlinear uniqueness or stability result.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ have singular value decomposition
$A=U\Sigma V^*$, and let $\tau\ge0$ be a declared threshold. The
**truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau$** is

$$ A_\tau^+ := V\Sigma_\tau^+U^*, $$

where $\Sigma_\tau^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is the transposed-shape
diagonal matrix whose $i$th diagonal entry is $\sigma_i^{-1}$ when
$\sigma_i>\tau$ and is $0$ when $\sigma_i\le\tau$; every off-diagonal entry is
$0$.

The threshold is part of the definition, exactly as in
[[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]]: changing
$\tau$ changes which singular directions are retained.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear map
between real or complex Hilbert spaces, with Hilbert adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$.
Write $\mathbb N_{>0}:=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. If $R(K)$ has finite dimension
$r\in\mathbb N$, put $J=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, interpreted as empty when $r=0$;
if $R(K)$ is infinite-dimensional, put $J=\mathbb N_{>0}$. Thus $J$ indexes
exactly the positive singular values $s_j>0$ in nonincreasing order. Let
$(v_j)_{j\in J}$ and $(u_j)_{j\in J}$ be complete
orthonormal families in $N(K)^\perp$ and $\overline{R(K)}$, respectively,
with $Kv_j=s_ju_j$ and $K^*u_j=s_jv_j$. The empty sum is zero, finite $J$
uses a finite sum, and infinite $J$ uses the norm-convergent series whenever
the stated square-summability condition holds. Use inner products linear in the
first argument. Define the Picard sum
$$P_K(y):=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{|\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y|^2}{s_j^2},\qquad y\in Y.$$
Then:

1. The exact equation $Kx=y$ is solvable if and only if
   $y\perp N(K^*)$ and $P_K(y)<\infty$.

2. The domain of the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse is
   $$D(K^\dagger)=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp=\{y\in Y:P_K(y)<\infty\},$$
   and for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$,
   $$K^\dagger y=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y}{s_j}v_j.$$
   Thus the orthogonal component in $R(K)^\perp=N(K^*)$ is discarded by
   $K^\dagger$; exact range membership additionally requires that component
   to be zero.
