citations.quote:
Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be the image of a compact smooth embedded circle, and let $E:N^\perp K\to\mathbb R^3$ be the Euclidean normal-addition map $E(p,v)=p+v$. There is a real $\varepsilon>0$ such that $E$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from $\{(p,v):\|v\|<\varepsilon\}$ onto an open neighborhood $N_\varepsilon$ of $K$. Moreover, $\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $\mathbb R^3\setminus N_\varepsilon$ by pushing each nonzero normal vector radially to length $\varepsilon$. The construction uses only a finite cover of the compact circle and no choice axiom.

If $A\subset X$ is a CW subcomplex and its inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, then $X$ strongly deformation retracts onto $A$. Moreover, if $(Y,B)$ is a CW pair and $u_0,u_1:B\to Z$ are homotopic, then the adjunction spaces $Z\cup_{u_0}Y$ and $Z\cup_{u_1}Y$ are homotopy equivalent relative to their common subspace $Z$.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

Let $Q=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be pointed at $[0]$, and for $r\in\mathbb N$ put

$$W_r:=\bigvee_{j<r}(Q,[0]).$$

Then $\pi_1(W_r,w)$ is the free group on the $r$ standard loops, one traversing each circle summand once. In particular it has rank $r$ ([[def-rank-of-a-finite-rank-free-group]]). For $r=0$, $W_0$ is a point and the basis is empty.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: Cut out disjoint small underpass intervals, one in each crossing box. The remaining projected arcs are embedded and pairwise disjoint: an interior double point would have an underpassing preimage, which has been removed. Put these arcs at height $1$, their ends in the plane $z=0$, and join each pair of ends of a removed underpass below that plane. This normalization preserves the complement pair. Indeed, inside a crossing box the two branches retain a strict height inequality while their heights interpolate; away from these boxes projection is injective and vertical interpolation cannot introduce intersections. A change of height $d(q)$ on a strand extends to a local ambient map $(q,z)\mapsto(q,z+\chi(z)d(q))$, subdividing the interpolation so that $1+\chi'(z)d(q)>0$. Finitely many disjoint strip charts, smooth cutoffs and parameter subdivisions suffice. Planar bends can likewise be straightened in their disjoint strip charts. All these maps are the identity in a common high collar.

For $c=0$, first compare the actual smooth knot with a polygon, rather than identifying embeddings merely from the code. Its projection is a smooth embedded circle $\gamma$, so the knot is $(\gamma(s),g(s))$. Apply the finite compact-tube construction [F2] to the flat curve $(\gamma(s),0)$: the planar slice of its normal tube is an injective strip $\Psi(s,r)=\gamma(s)+r n(s)$, with $n$ the positive unit planar normal. In this strip the ambient map $(\Psi(s,r),z)\mapsto(\Psi(s,r),z-t\chi(r)g(s))$, with $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi$ zero near the strip boundary, is a homeomorphism for each $t$ (it is a translation on every vertical fibre), and is the identity outside the strip. It flattens the actual knot. Uniform continuity of the tangent and the finite tube bounds then give a sufficiently fine inscribed polygon: each chord stays in the strip and its projection to the circle is strictly increasing, since its tangent has positive scalar product with the nearby oriented circle tangents. The polygonal projection has one full turn, so it is bijective, and the polygon is the normal graph $r=f(s)$. Choose the subdivision so $\|f\|_\infty\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$. The fibre maps $r\mapsto r+t\chi(r)f(s)$ are strictly increasing homeomorphisms fixing the strip boundary; extended by the identity, they give an ambient planar isotopy carrying $\gamma$ to this polygon. Its product with the identity in $z$ is an ambient three-dimensional isotopy. All subdivisions and bounds use a finite cover and one sufficiently large subdivision number. This relates the actual embedding to the polygon without any later diagram-code supplier.

Here is a precise convenient tunnel model for the normalized knot. In each crossing box choose a small convex polygonal footprint $F_i$ and a convex lower cap $C_i=\{(q,z):q\in F_i,\ h_i(q)\le z\le0\},$ where $h_i$ is piecewise linear, negative inside $F_i$ and zero on its boundary. Take the lower arc to be the two straight segments from its two interior top-face endpoints to one interior point of $C_i$. This replacement of the underpass is realized by vertical interpolation of its negative graph, fixing its endpoints. Each $C_i$ is a product neighborhood of that arc: radial coordinates from the interior vertex identify $C_i$ with a ball; on its boundary send two disjoint disks around the endpoints of a diameter to small disks around the two top endpoints, and extend radially. Such a boundary map is constructed by joining the disk centers by simple polygonal arcs, taking rectangular strips around those arcs, and using affine maps on a finite common triangulation; outside the strips it is the identity. Thus it identifies a standard cylinder core with the two-segment arc and its two end disks with the designated exits. Attach product tubes along the disjoint upper arcs to those exits. The resulting neighborhood $N_*$ has one cap and one upper tube per underpass, joined in the same single cycle as $K$. The disk fibers on the caps and tubes use the specified exit-disk maps as transition maps, so they fit along the finite cyclic core to give a disk bundle over the circle; this verifies the tube structure rather than assuming an arbitrary regular neighborhood. Corners and the core bends can be rounded inside disjoint smaller charts; retain the polygonal cap boundary, which is only used topologically.

The polygon's bounded side is supplied by [F6]. Triangulate it by diagonals: at a convex vertex use its neighbor triangle if it contains no other vertex; otherwise join it to a vertex in that triangle farthest from the opposite side. The smaller open triangle contains no intervening vertex, so the diagonal is internal; induction on the vertex count yields a finite triangulation. A leaf of its triangle-adjacency tree is an ear $uvw$, with ear tip $v$ and base $uw$. Remove any collinear vertices before this step. Put $q$ in the interior of $uw$. Choose $z_+=q+(1+\eta)(v-q)$ and $z_-=q-\epsilon(v-q)$, with small positive $\eta,\epsilon$, so the convex quadrilateral $Q=(u,z_+,w,z_-)$ meets the rest of the polygon only at $u,w$. Such bounds exist because the closed ear has no other polygon points, nonadjacent edges have positive separation, and the two remaining incident edges have a positive angle away from the ear; finite determinant and distance comparisons select the bounds. Both $v$ and $q$ are interior to $Q$. Triangulate $Q$ by the fan from $v$. On each fan triangle map its apex $v$ to $v_t=(1-t)v+tq$, fix its two boundary vertices, and interpolate affinely. Since $Q$ is convex and $v_t$ is always interior, the image triangles are a nondegenerate fan partition of the same quadrilateral. The resulting map is therefore injective, surjective and piecewise linear, fixes the whole boundary, and extends by the identity to an ambient plane isotopy. At $t=1$ it sends the two ear edges $uv,vw$ onto $uq,qw$, while fixing all other polygon edges. This is an ambient straightening, not a collapse of a triangle to its base. Inductively remove the ears until a triangle remains. From an interior point of that triangle its boundary has a continuous positive radial-distance function $R(\theta)$; the plane homeomorphism multiplying each ray's radius by $1/R(\theta)$ sends it to a round circle. The products of these plane maps with the identity in $z$ identify the actual knot complement with the round-circle complement.

For $c>0$, transport the rounded product disk-bundle neighborhood $N_*$ of step 2.1 back through the ambient normalization in step 1.1 and use it as $N(K)$. In each disk fiber of this tube write the normalized radial coordinate as $r\in[0,1]$. The homotopy $r\mapsto(1-s)r+s$ fixes the fiber boundary and sends every nonzero fiber point to that boundary at $s=1$; extend it by the identity outside the tube. The formulas agree continuously at $r=1$ and fix the target pointwise, so they give a strong deformation retraction of $\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ onto $E_K$. For $c=0$, the same radial formula in the Euclidean normal coordinates of [F2] gives the stated retraction.

Take a large ball $B_R$ containing $N_*$. Outside it, the homotopy $x\mapsto((1-s)+sR/|x|)x$, with the interior fixed, retracts the exterior to its truncation $X$ in $B_R$. Its outer sphere is retained. Write $A=X\cap\{z\ge0\}$. Below the plane, the exterior is exactly $B=\{(q,z):-\sqrt{R^2-|q|^2}\le z\le h(q)\},$ where $h=h_i$ on $F_i$ and is zero elsewhere; enlarge $R$ so every cap lies above the lower hemisphere. The top plates of the caps belong to $A$ as tube-boundary faces, except for the two exits occupied by upper tubes. Thus $X=A\cup B$ and $A\cap B$ is the equatorial disk with the interiors of the $F_i$ removed. On $B$ use $(q,z)\mapsto(q,(1-s)z+s h(q))$ and on $A$ the identity. These maps agree on the overlap, remain in the indicated vertical intervals, and paste continuously because the two sets are closed in $X$. They fix their target $Y_*=A\cup\bigcup_i D_i,\qquad D_i=\{(q,h_i(q)):q\in F_i\},$ pointwise. This proves the global strong deformation retraction, including the lower region and infinity.

The upper region $A$ is a ball with the neighborhoods of $c$ disjoint boundary-parallel arcs removed. The parallelism disks are the vertical curtains beneath their disjoint projected arcs. Their strip neighborhoods are disjoint. Cutting these strips off the upper half-ball leaves a ball with finitely many boundary indentations: flatten each indentation in its rectangular strip coordinate, fixing the other faces. The strip containing an arc is a ball with a straight diameter tube removed. In cylindrical coordinates this last space is $S^1\times\{(r,z):r\ge\epsilon,\ r^2+z^2\le1\},$ whose second factor is a convex disk. Hence $A$ is a boundary connected sum of $c$ solid tori, glued through specified disks to the remaining ball. For an actual bouquet spine, cut each solid torus across a meridian disk and absorb its remaining ball into the central ball. The result is a central ball with $c$ product one-handles. Join the centers of the $2c$ attaching disks to an interior point by disjoint star arms in that ball; after flattening the finitely many boundary disks, these are radial arms from their centers to the central point. Add the one-handle core intervals. The resulting embedded graph is a bouquet of $c$ circles, since every vertex other than the central one has degree two. To specify the CW structure for the relative contraction, use a finite polyhedral ball model for the central ball. Triangulate its boundary so that each attaching disk is a subcomplex and its center is a vertex, then cone that boundary triangulation to one interior vertex. Each radial star arm is an edge of this cone triangulation. The union $C$ of the attaching disks and these star edges is a finite CW subcomplex. It is contractible by contracting each disk to its center and then the star to the interior vertex. The central ball $B_0$ and $C$ are both nonempty and contractible, so the inclusion $C\hookrightarrow B_0$ is a homotopy equivalence. By [F3], $B_0$ strongly deformation retracts onto $C$, fixing $C$ pointwise; HEP alone is not being used to assert a contraction. Next contract every attaching disk linearly to its center, and contract the transverse disk factor of each product one-handle by the same linear factor. These formulas agree on the end disks and fix the star edges and handle cores, so they paste to a strong deformation retraction onto the stated bouquet. For each drilled arc, orient its graph loop to represent the based positive meridian. In an oriented normal-disk chart along the oriented knot tangent, choose the disk orientation so that tangent followed by disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation, and traverse the disk boundary in its induced positive direction. In the complement product $S^1\times D^2$ of the drilled tube, this boundary is the $S^1$ factor; contracting the disk factor and using the retained collar access path carries it to the corresponding bouquet loop. Thus the chosen generator is the positive meridian, not its inverse. Each such loop crosses precisely its own curtain once. Consequently [F5] identifies these positively oriented meridians as the free basis, rather than merely normal generators.

Fix disk coordinates $\phi_i:\overline D^2\to D_i$ and constants $0<r_0<r_1<1$. In $Y_*$ set $V_i=\phi_i(\{|v|<r_1\})$ and let $U$ be the complement of the union of the closed disks $\phi_i(\{|v|\le r_0\})$. These sets are relative-open: the cap interiors have their ordinary disk topology, their closures away from their boundary are disjoint from $A$, and the omitted closed disks are closed in $Y_*$. They cover because $r_0<r_1$. Each $V_i$ is an open disk, different $V_i$ are disjoint, and their overlaps with $U$ are exactly the annuli $r_0<|v|<r_1$. On each outer collar, increasing its radius by $r\mapsto(1-s)r+s$ retracts $U$ to $A$, fixing $A$. Step 5.1 supplies its meridian basis. Transfer these sets and the composed homotopies back through the finite normalizations in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1. They give the stated subspace and cover in the original exterior.

For the resulting round circle use $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, $K=\{z_1=0\}$, and infinity $p=(1,0)$. Choose the angular coordinate so that increasing $t$ gives the positively oriented meridian (replace $t$ by $-t$ if the carried knot orientation requires it). The map $(w,e^{it})\longmapsto(\sqrt{1-|w|^2}e^{it},w)$ identifies $S^3\setminus K$ with $D^\circ\times S^1$, and $p$ with $(0,1)$. Choose a center-preserving homeomorphism from $D^\circ$ to $(-1,1)^2$. For $q\in(-1,1)^2$, put $r=\|q\|_\infty$ and define $$c(q)=\begin{cases}q,&r\le\tfrac12,\\[2pt]q/(2r),&r>\tfrac12.\end{cases}$$ The homotopy $C_s(q)=(1-s)q+sc(q)$ stays in the open square, fixes $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]^2$, and preserves $q=0$. Therefore $(q,z)\mapsto(C_s(q),z)$ is a strong deformation retraction of $(D^\circ\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$ onto $([-1/2,1/2]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$: when $z=1$, every point in the punctured fiber has $q\ne0$, and $C_s(q)$ is a positive scalar multiple of $q$, so the homotopy never reaches the puncture. Rescaling the square gives $([-1,1]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$. Write $S^1=[-1,1]/(-1\sim1)$ with the puncture at circle coordinate $0$. For $v\in[-1,1]^3\setminus\{0\}$, the homotopy $$H_s(v)=\left(1-s+\frac{s}{\|v\|_\infty}\right)v$$ retracts onto the cube boundary, fixes both identified end faces pointwise, and therefore descends to the product quotient. Its image $X_0$ is a finite CW complex: the lateral faces form the torus $T=\partial[-1,1]^2\times S^1$, and the two square end faces become one disk $D^2$ attached along $\ell=\partial[-1,1]^2\times\{1\}$. Give $T$ its product CW structure with $\ell$ as a subcomplex; then $D^2$ is a contractible CW subcomplex of $X_0$. By [F4], collapsing it is a homotopy equivalence, and the quotient is $T$ with $\ell$ collapsed. Cutting $T$ along $\ell$ gives a cylinder; after the two boundary copies of $\ell$ are collapsed to their common point, the quotient is a sphere with its two poles identified. To identify its homotopy type explicitly, let $Z$ be $S^2$ with an interval attached at its two distinct poles. Give $Z$ the finite CW structure in which the interval is a 1-cell and its endpoints are 0-cells, so the interval is a contractible subcomplex. Collapsing it identifies the poles, so [F4] makes $Z$ homotopy equivalent to the sphere-with-poles-identified quotient. The two endpoint maps of the interval into $S^2$ are homotopic along a fixed path; choose this path to be the $e^{it}$ meridian cut at $t=0$. By the attaching-map clause of [F3], $Z$ is homotopy equivalent to the adjunction space with both endpoints attached at one pole, namely $S^2\vee S^1$, and the new circle is the retained positive meridian. For this wedge with wedge point $w$, choose $q\in S^2\setminus\{w\}$ and $r\in S^1\setminus\{w\}$, and set $$A=S^1\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\}),\qquad B'=(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup S^2.$$ These are open in the wedge topology and cover $S^1\vee S^2$. The first deformation retracts to $S^1$, the second to $S^2$, so both are path-connected; their overlap $(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\})$ is nonempty and contracts to $w$ by contracting each punctured summand to $w$. Thus the sets and overlap satisfy the path-connected open-cover hypotheses of van Kampen [F5], which gives $\pi_1(S^1\vee S^2,w)\cong\pi_1(S^1,w)*\pi_1(S^2,w)\cong\mathbb Z*1\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the positive meridian circle. Finally step 3.1 gives the asserted retraction onto $E_K$ in both cases.

citations.quote:
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. For $c>0$, choose the closed tubular disk-bundle neighborhood $N(K)$ formed from one product cap about each underpass and one product tube along each intervening upper arc, attached in the cyclic order of the knot and rounded in disjoint charts. Put $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. There is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. With a common basepoint in the collar above the diagram and access paths in that collar extended into the arc charts, the positive under-arc meridians are its free basis. Each $V_i$ is contractible, $U\cap V_i$ is an open annulus around the $i$-th crossing attachment, and distinct $V_i$ are disjoint. Thus $V_i$ meets $U$ and any previously attached crossing pieces precisely in $U\cap V_i$.

For $c=0$, choose a sufficiently small Euclidean normal tube and let $E_K$ be its exterior. The Euclidean complement has homotopy type $S^1\vee S^2$, with the circle represented by the positive meridian. In particular its fundamental group is infinite cyclic; the extra sphere at infinity must not be discarded. In both cases the punctured chosen disk-bundle tube retracts radially to its boundary, giving a strong deformation retraction $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\to E_K$. These constructions require only finitely many charts and no choice axiom.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

For every pointed topological space $(X,x_0)$, the product

$$[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha*\beta]$$

is well defined and makes $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ a group. Its identity is the class of
the constant loop $c_{x_0}$, and $[\alpha]^{-1}=[\bar\alpha]$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

For homomorphisms $f:K\to G$ and $h:K\to H$, let $N$ be the normal closure in $G\ast H$ of $$\{j_G(f(k))j_H(h(k))^{-1}:k\in K\}.$$ Then $(G\ast H)/N$, with the induced factor maps $j_G$ and $j_H$, is a pushout of $f$ and $h$.

derivations.claim: Take ambient coordinates $(x,y,z)$ with overstrand tangent $+\partial_x$, viewing normal $+\partial_z$, and positive projection basis $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$. Source has $y<0$ and target $y>0$, with the understrand below the overstrand. Parameterize the under-core from source to target by $u$, whether or not this agrees with the knot orientation. Choose its product tube $\Phi(u,v)$ so that the oriented knot tangent followed by the ordered normal frame is ambient-positive; take the first normal-frame vector toward the positive-$z$ side of the understrand and the second to complete that orientation. Thus increasing angle from $\theta_0=0$ gives the positive meridian even when $u$ runs opposite to the knot orientation. Choose a small positive radius $r$. The path used here is the push-off $\beta(u)=\Phi(u,r(\cos\theta_0,\sin\theta_0))$, from source to target; it never lies on the knot core. The two meridian loops are the boundaries $\mu_u(\tau)=\Phi(u,r(\cos(\theta_0+2\pi\tau),\sin(\theta_0+2\pi\tau)))$, based at the endpoints of $\beta$. For exterior paths take $r$ at least the removed tube radius; shrink that radius first if necessary. Choose the product tube disjoint from the overstrand and other arc pieces, and $r$ smaller than the crossing-chart separation bounds. Choose upper-collar paths $\alpha_s,\alpha_t$ to these actual boundary points. In the normal $(y,z)$ plane of the overstrand, their concatenation $\alpha_s\beta\alpha_t^{-1}$ follows a small perturbation of the polygon $(0,H),(-d,-h),(d,-h),(0,H)$, which has positive signed area. The polygon and a sufficiently small surrounding strip avoid the origin; the chosen radius makes the perturbation lie in that strip, so its winding is still $+1$. For explicit complement control, straighten the local under-core to $x=0,z=-h$ in the product chart and take its upper push-off at $z=-h+r$. The access triangle is then entirely above $z=-h$, while the over-core projects to the origin. Radial interpolation of its positive polar-distance function to a sufficiently small circle about the origin stays inside that triangle minus the origin, hence above the under-core as well. Retain the positive-radius angular access in the under-tube until reaching these straightened paths. Thus the resulting homotopy is to one counterclockwise over-meridian and avoids both strands throughout. Thus all paths and homotopies lie in the complement, the loop represents $m_o$, and $\alpha_t\simeq m_o^{-1}\alpha_s\beta$ rel endpoints there.

The positive-radius cylinder $(u,\tau)\mapsto\Phi(u,r(\cos(\theta_0+2\pi\tau),\sin(\theta_0+2\pi\tau)))$ transports the boundary meridians, with its basepoint edge equal to $\beta$. Its image misses the knot core and, by the separated tube choice, the overstrand and every other arc. Reading the boundary of this cylinder gives $\beta\mu_t\beta^{-1}\simeq\mu_s$ in the complement; its disk orientation is transported continuously even when the source-to-target direction opposes the knot orientation. Therefore $[\alpha_t\mu_t\alpha_t^{-1}]=m_o^{-1}[\alpha_s\beta\mu_t\beta^{-1}\alpha_s^{-1}]m_o=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o$. Equivalently the annular-core word $m_o^{-1}m_sm_om_t^{-1}$ bounds the cap of [F1], consistently with [F3]. Reversing the understrand orientation inverts both its meridians, so inversion gives the same side-based equation, rather than a switch of the conjugating direction.

The under-tangent follows $n_o$ exactly when incoming is source and outgoing is target, giving the first incoming/outgoing equation. Otherwise solve the same equation for $m_s$ to obtain the second. A reversed meridian is the inverse loop by [F2]. If a common access path $\alpha$ is replaced by $\lambda\alpha$, the class $[\alpha\mu\alpha^{-1}]$ becomes $[\lambda][\alpha\mu\alpha^{-1}][\lambda]^{-1}$; this holds for each of the three meridians. These observations prove all remaining assertions.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. For $c>0$, choose the closed tubular disk-bundle neighborhood $N(K)$ formed from one product cap about each underpass and one product tube along each intervening upper arc, attached in the cyclic order of the knot and rounded in disjoint charts. Put $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. There is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. With a common basepoint in the collar above the diagram and access paths in that collar extended into the arc charts, the positive under-arc meridians are its free basis. Each $V_i$ is contractible, $U\cap V_i$ is an open annulus around the $i$-th crossing attachment, and distinct $V_i$ are disjoint. Thus $V_i$ meets $U$ and any previously attached crossing pieces precisely in $U\cap V_i$.

For $c=0$, choose a sufficiently small Euclidean normal tube and let $E_K$ be its exterior. The Euclidean complement has homotopy type $S^1\vee S^2$, with the circle represented by the positive meridian. In particular its fundamental group is infinite cyclic; the extra sphere at infinity must not be discarded. In both cases the punctured chosen disk-bundle tube retracts radially to its boundary, giving a strong deformation retraction $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\to E_K$. These constructions require only finitely many charts and no choice axiom.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

A topological space $X$ is **simply connected** when it is nonempty and
path-connected ([[def-path-connected]]) and, for every $x_0\in X$, the group
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ has exactly one element.

Requiring every basepoint avoids presuming a change-of-basepoint theorem. For a
path-connected space that later theorem shows that checking one basepoint is
equivalent, but no such result is needed for this definition. The empty space
is path-connected under the published convention, but it is not simply
connected here because nonemptiness is explicit.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]], if $U\cap V$ is simply connected, then the inclusion-induced homomorphisms give an isomorphism

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)*\pi_1(V,x_0)\cong\pi_1(X,x_0).$$

Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous and let $x_0\in X$. Composition sends a loop
$\alpha$ at $x_0$ to the loop $f\circ\alpha$ at $f(x_0)$. Using the loop
classes and fundamental group of [[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]],
the proposed
**induced homomorphism** is

$$f_*:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(Y,f(x_0)),\qquad f_*([\alpha]):=[f\circ\alpha].$$

The next theorem proves that this value is independent of the representative,
that it is a group homomorphism in the sense of [[def-group-homomorphism]], and
that induced maps respect identities, composition and homotopies that fix the
basepoint.

Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a continuous map with $f(x_0)=y_0$. Then

$$f_*([\alpha])=[f\circ\alpha]$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism. For pointed continuous maps,

$$\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id},\qquad (g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*.$$

If $f_0,f_1:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ are homotopic through a homotopy that keeps
$x_0$ at $y_0$, then $(f_0)_*=(f_1)_*$.

For every pointed topological space $(X,x_0)$, the product

$$[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha*\beta]$$

is well defined and makes $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ a group. Its identity is the class of
the constant loop $c_{x_0}$, and $[\alpha]^{-1}=[\bar\alpha]$.

derivations.claim: Since $K$ is compact, choose $R>0$ with $K$ and $b$ in the open ball $D=B_R(0)$. Put $U=S^3\setminus(K\cup\{\infty\})=\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ and $V=S^3\setminus\overline D$. Then $V$ is an open ball about infinity, disjoint from $K$, and $U\cap V=V\setminus\{\infty\}$. First verify that $U$ is path-connected without assuming a diagram code. Parameterize the smooth embedded circle by $k:S^1\to K$. For $p\in U$, the cone $$C_p=\{p+t(k(s)-p):s\in S^1,\ t\ge1\}$$ has three-dimensional outer volume zero: on each of finitely many smooth coordinate intervals of $S^1$ and each bounded interval $1\le t\le n$, the defining map is Lipschitz on a compact rectangle; subdividing into $O(N^2)$ squares of side $1/N$ covers its image by balls of radius $O(1/N)$, whose total three-dimensional volume is $O(1/N)$. Thus each truncated image has outer volume zero. For each $n$, the finite chart and derivative bounds give an explicit cover volume $A_n/N$ after mesh size $1/N$; choosing $N_n>2^{n+2}A_n/\epsilon$ makes the $n$th truncated images of both cones have total cover volume below $\epsilon 2^{-n-1}$. These formula-defined mesh sizes give a cover of $C_p\cup C_q$ with total volume below $\epsilon$ for every $\epsilon>0$, so the union has outer volume zero without a choice of covers. An open ball contains a cube of positive volume, so choose $r$ in an open ball outside $C_p\cup C_q$. If the segment $[p,r]$ met $K$ at $k(s)$, then $r=p+t(k(s)-p)$ for some $t\ge1$, contrary to $r\notin C_p$; similarly $[q,r]$ misses $K$. The broken line from $p$ to $r$ to $q$ lies in $U$. Under inversion $J(x)=x/\|x\|^2$, extended by $J(\infty)=0$, the set $V$ is the open ball of radius $1/R$ about $0$. The radial homotopy $y\mapsto(1-t)y$ contracts it to $0$, so it is nonempty and path-connected. Since this ball is convex, every based loop contracts to its own basepoint by the straight-line homotopy inside the ball; [F3] therefore makes $V$ simply connected. The same inversion identifies $U\cap V$ with $0<\|y\|<1/R$. Fix $\rho=1/(2R)$; the puncture-preserving radial homotopy $$y\longmapsto\left((1-t)+t\frac{\rho}{\|y\|}\right)y$$ is a strong deformation retraction of this punctured ball onto the sphere $S^2_\rho$. The punctured ball is path-connected. Choose $y_0\in S^2_\rho$, let $i:S^2_\rho\hookrightarrow U\cap V$ be inclusion, and let $r$ be the radial retraction. Since the radial deformation fixes $S^2_\rho$ pointwise, [F7] and functoriality make $i_*$ and $r_*$ inverse isomorphisms at $y_0$. By [F2], $\pi_1(S^2_\rho,y_0)$ is trivial. For any other basepoint $y$ in the punctured ball, choose a path $\gamma$ from $y$ to $y_0$ and use $[\alpha]\mapsto[\bar\gamma*\alpha*\gamma]$. Concatenation and reparameterization preserve endpoint-fixed homotopies, so this is a well-defined homomorphism. The inverse uses $\bar\gamma$; the inserted pairs $\gamma*\bar\gamma$ and $\bar\gamma*\gamma$ contract by the piecewise retracing homotopy, so the homomorphism is an isomorphism. Thus every basepoint group of the overlap is trivial; its nonemptiness and path-connectedness with [F3] make $U\cap V$ simply connected.

Choose $b_0\in U\cap V$. The open sets $U,V$ cover $S^3\setminus K$; [F4] applies by the path-connectedness in step 1.1. Since $V$ and $U\cap V$ are simply connected by step 1.1, the special case [F5] shows that inclusion induces an isomorphism $\pi_1(U,b_0)\to\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b_0)$.

The inclusion induces the based map by [F6]. Choose a path $\gamma$ in $U$ from $b$ to $b_0$, which exists by step 1.1. The formula $[\alpha]\mapsto[\bar\gamma*\alpha*\gamma]$ defines isomorphisms between the fundamental groups at these basepoints by the concatenation and retracing argument in step 1.1. Using the same path in $S^3\setminus K$ makes the square with inclusion commute, since postcomposing the concatenated path gives the same loop. Thus the inclusion map at $b$ is conjugate by isomorphisms to the isomorphism at $b_0$.

Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$

Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. $$n\longmapsto[\omega_n].$$

$$[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha*\beta]$$

Read the over-arc $a_o$ and append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. This rule uses the positive in-plane normal, which points counterclockwise from the oriented over-tangent, and does not depend on the under-strand direction. The orientation of each positive meridian is fixed by requiring the oriented knot tangent followed by its normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and one relator per crossing.

Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

Let $F(X)$ be a free group and let $R\subseteq F(X)$ be a set of words, called
**relations**. The group with presentation

$$\langle X\mid R\rangle:=F(X)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(X)}$$

is the quotient by the normal closure of $R$. The members of $X$ are its
**generators**. In this quotient, every relation in $R$ becomes the identity,
as do all consequences forced by normality.

A **free group on a set $X$** is a group $F(X)$ together with a map
$i:X\to F(X)$ such that, for every group $G$ and every function $u:X\to G$,
there is a unique group homomorphism $\widehat u:F(X)\to G$ satisfying

$$\widehat u\circ i=u.$$

The reduced-word construction supplies such a group; the construction and its
universal property are established in [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]].
When no ambiguity arises, $x\in X$ is identified with its image $i(x)$.

A homomorphism that kills a normal subgroup factors uniquely through the quotient group.

If $N\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}G$, $f:G\to H$ is a homomorphism, and
$N\subseteq\ker f$, then there is a unique homomorphism $\bar f:G/N\to H$
such that $\bar f(gN)=f(g)$ and $f=\bar f\circ\pi$.

Let $G$ be a group. For $g,h\in G$, their **commutator** is

$$[g,h]:=ghg^{-1}h^{-1}.$$

This convention is fixed throughout; some sources use its inverse. By the
inverse laws of [[lem-group-inverse-laws]], one has
$[g,h]^{-1}=hgh^{-1}g^{-1}=[h,g]$.

The **commutator subgroup**, or **derived subgroup**, is the subgroup generated
by all commutators:

$$[G,G]:=\langle\{[g,h]:g,h\in G\}\rangle.$$

The generated subgroup notation is that of [[def-generated-subgroup]].

For every group $G$, the derived subgroup $G'=[G,G]$ is characteristic, hence normal. The quotient $G^{\mathrm{ab}}:=G/G'$ is abelian and has the following universal property: for every homomorphism $f:G\to A$ into an abelian group, there is a unique homomorphism $\bar f:G^{\mathrm{ab}}\to A$ with $f=\bar f\circ q$, where $q:G\to G/G'$ is the quotient map.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice,
an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid $\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous and let $x_0\in X$. Composition sends a loop
$\alpha$ at $x_0$ to the loop $f\circ\alpha$ at $f(x_0)$. Using the loop
classes and fundamental group of [[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]],
the proposed
**induced homomorphism** is

$$f_*:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(Y,f(x_0)),\qquad f_*([\alpha]):=[f\circ\alpha].$$

The next theorem proves that this value is independent of the representative,
that it is a group homomorphism in the sense of [[def-group-homomorphism]], and
that induced maps respect identities, composition and homotopies that fix the
basepoint.

Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a continuous map with $f(x_0)=y_0$. Then

$$f_*([\alpha])=[f\circ\alpha]$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism. For pointed continuous maps,

$$\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id},\qquad (g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*.$$

If $f_0,f_1:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ are homotopic through a homotopy that keeps
$x_0$ at $y_0$, then $(f_0)_*=(f_1)_*$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F3], the crossing-free unknot group is $\langle x\mid\ \rangle$, the free group on one generator. By [F5] it is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$, whose abelianization is itself by [F7].

The trefoil's displayed crossing triples and [F2] give $b=cac^{-1}$, $a=bcb^{-1}$, and $c=aba^{-1}$. Substituting the last into the second yields $a=bab a^{-1}b^{-1}$; right multiplication by $ba$ gives $aba=bab$. Under this relation, $cac^{-1}=a b a b^{-1}a^{-1}=b$, so the first equation follows. Thus eliminating $c$ gives $\langle a,b\mid aba=bab\rangle$, and [F3] identifies it with $G_T$.

In the abelianization, written additively by [F7], $aba=bab$ gives $2[a]+[b]=[a]+2[b]$, hence $[a]=[b]$ and the abelianization is generated by $[a]$. The map $G_T\to\mathbb Z$ sending $a,b$ to $1$ respects the relator and is surjective; by [F8] it factors through the abelianization. The map $\mathbb Z\to G_T^{\mathrm{ab}}$ sending $1$ to $[a]$ is inverse, so $G_T^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb Z$.

The map $a\mapsto(12)$, $b\mapsto(23)$ respects $aba=bab$, since both sides equal $(13)$. Its image contains two adjacent transpositions and hence all six elements of $S_3$, so it is surjective by [F4] and [F6]. Since $S_3$ is nonabelian, $G_T$ is nonabelian; every quotient of the cyclic group $\mathbb Z$ is cyclic, so $G_T\not\cong\mathbb Z\cong G_U$.

If $U$ and $T$ were ambient isotopic, [F9] would give a homeomorphism of their complements; [F10] and [F11] would induce a fundamental-group isomorphism. Step 2.2 rules this out. Their abelianizations nevertheless agree by steps 1.1 and 2.1, proving the stated counterexample.

Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

The input is a finite record $D$ and a designated starting under-arc $a_0$ of one oriented knot. First check that the vertex, edge, and segment lists are finite; that every vertex, bend, and point on an edge polyline has rational coordinates; and that each polyline has the prescribed incident endpoints. Before geometric tests, delete consecutive repeated coordinates from each polyline; reject an edge with no positive-length segment or a crossing with a zero-length incident ray. Check that every crossing has four incident half-edges, a recorded cyclic order and a pairing into alternating opposite branches, and one designated over-branch; every other vertex must be a valence-two bend. Check that edge orientations agree at bends and continue coherently through each paired branch, and that following these pairings and bends traces one oriented circle. If $a_0$ is not one of the resulting under-arcs, or any structural check fails, return invalid-input.

For every unordered pair of line segments, compute the determinant of their rational direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate intersection equations over $\mathbb{Q}$ and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Reject every self-intersection, every positive-length overlap, and every intersection except a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence. At each crossing, sort the four nonzero incident rays by half-plane and exact determinant comparisons; reject the input if two rays have the same direction, if this geometric cyclic order disagrees with the recorded order, or if the paired branches do not alternate. These checks are finite.

At each crossing, let the outgoing over-half-edge be the ray in the direction of the oriented over-tangent. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and one relator per crossing.

Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. derivations.claim: The eight stated routes give 24 segments, 16 degree-two ports and four crossing vertices. Here is an exact reproducible intersection test for the displayed integers. For segments $a+tu,b+sv$, with $u=a'-a,v=b'-b$ and $\Delta=\det(u,v)\ne0$, their intersection parameters are $$t=\det(b-a,v)/\Delta,\qquad s=\det(b-a,u)/\Delta.$$ Retain the intersection just when $0\le t,s\le1$. If $\Delta=0$, the test $\det(b-a,u)=0$ detects collinearity, and comparison of the two closed endpoint intervals in either nonconstant coordinate detects overlap. Applying these formulas to the table gives 276 unordered segment pairs: precisely 40 meet, each solely at its common declared endpoint, and the other 236 are disjoint. The 40 consist of one pair at each of the 16 ports and six pairs at each of the four crossing centers. No pair overlaps in positive length. At each center the $Oi,C,Oo$ and $Ui,C,Uo$ triples are collinear with the center strictly between the ports. The determinants of the full oriented over/under vectors are respectively $-69696,3168,3168,-69696$, so those are transverse opposite pairs with exactly the stated cyclic orders. The cyclic visit list uses every branch once, and following the paired branches gives that single list, not several circles. Hence every validity condition in [F1] holds. Finitely many nonincident compact segments have positive distance, so sufficiently small disjoint bend disks introduce no new crossing; over/under height separation in the crossing disks realizes the smooth knot.

The geometric figure-eight admission can be checked without inferring knot type from a group presentation. Draw the downward three-strand braid with successive crossings $\sigma_1,\sigma_2^{-1},\sigma_1,\sigma_2^{-1}$, where a positive generator has its left strand over, and close corresponding endpoints outside the braid rectangle without additional crossings. Number its successive crossings $1,2,4,3$. Following its first top strand through the closure gives exactly $1O,2U,3O,1U,4O,3U,2O,4U$. In right/up plane coordinates its positive-generator over and under tangents point respectively down-right and down-left, giving negative determinant; the negative generator reverses that sign. Thus the four labeled determinants are $-,+,+,-$. Together with the visit list these determine precisely the cyclic orders in the statement. For an additional check, the six face boundary cycles, listing each departure port and then taking the next counterclockwise port after traversing its edge, are $$(1Oo,2Oo,4Oi),\ (1Ui,3Uo,2Ui),\ (1Oi,4Oo,3Oo),\ (1Uo,4Uo),\ (2Uo,3Ui,4Ui),\ (2Oi,3Oi).$$ These are the same two bigons and four triangular faces of that closed braid drawing; the table merely subdivides its eight edges at their ports. To see that this comparison concerns embeddings, take small crossing disks and narrow edge rectangles in each drawing. The identical cyclic orders identify these neighborhoods respecting over/under pairs. The six face boundaries are simple polygonal circles. Their disk coordinates can be obtained by the elementary finite polygon construction: use the vertical-slab convex-cell triangulation of [F6] and peel boundary triangles to identify the filled polygon with a disk. At each peeling step a triangle with one boundary edge and interior opposite vertex leaves a disk; if all vertices of the remaining triangulation are on its boundary, the dual is a finite tree and a leaf triangle has two boundary edges. Reversing these elementary triangle attachments gives disk coordinates with the prescribed boundary parametrization. Matching the resulting boundary circle coordinates extends over the disk by $(r,z)\mapsto(r,h(z))$. Applying this to each paired face extends the neighborhood identification over every face; the exterior is treated as a disk on the sphere. After rounding, this is the same regular spherical diagram, and choosing the same outer face gives the planar diagram. The closed braid just described is the standard two-clasp four-crossing figure-eight diagram (equivalently its usual alternating closed-three-braid description). This verifies admission by the full embedded diagram, not solely its under-arc relators.

Cutting the oriented visit circle at its four $U$ visits gives the four claimed under-arcs. The intervening $O$ visits put $O1$ on $x_1$, $O3$ on $x_2$, $O4$ on $x_3$, and $O2$ on $x_4$. For a direct side check, let $o_r=rOo-rOi$. The values of $\det(o_r,rUi-C_r)$ are $15840,-2376,-2376,15840$; those of $\det(o_r,rUo-C_r)$ are $-53856,792,792,-53856$. Positive values are the left side. This proves every entry of the crossing table, including which underpass follows the positive normal. By [F2] and [F3], $x_o^{-1}x_Rx_ox_L^{-1}=1$ is equivalently $x_ox_L=x_Rx_o$. Substitution of the four rows gives exactly $R_1,R_2,R_3,R_4$ as displayed. By [F4] these are the actual complement group and positive meridians. Starting at $x_1$ the underpasses are $R_2,R_1,R_3,R_4$ and the corresponding crossing signs sum to $1-1+1-1=0$.

In the group with the first three relators, left-multiply $R_3$ by $x_1$ and then use $R_1$ and $R_2$ to obtain $$x_1x_3x_2=x_1x_2x_4=x_3x_1x_4=x_3x_4x_2.$$ Right cancellation gives $x_1x_3=x_3x_4$, which is precisely $R_4$. Conversely imposing all four imposes the first three, so [F5] gives inverse identity-on-generator quotient maps. Thus deletion of the fourth relator changes neither the group nor the meridian assignment.

The square is a simple crossing-free polygon with coherent counterclockwise orientation and one component, so it is a valid code with a single under-arc and no crossing scan. Rounding it gives the ordinary planar unknot. By [F2] and [F4] its complement group is $\langle x\mid\ \rangle$. Define the homomorphism from this free group to $\mathbb Z$ by $x\mapsto1$, using [F5], and the homomorphism back by $n\mapsto x^n$. Their composites fix the generator and all integers, respectively, and are identities; the first claim also follows from uniqueness in [F5]. charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and

[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),

$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept

irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:

symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice,
an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid $\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Let $S\subseteq M$ be an embedded submanifold.

Equip $S$ with the smooth structure supplied by
[[lem-slice-chart-restrictions-form-a-smooth-atlas]]. The inclusion
$i:S\hookrightarrow M$ is then a smooth embedding by
[[prop-the-inclusion-of-an-embedded-submanifold-is-a-smooth-embedding]], so its
differential is defined. Identify $T_pS$ with the linear subspace
$di_p(T_pS)\subseteq T_pM$. Here the notation
$$TM|_S:=\coprod_{p\in S}T_pM,\qquad T^*M|_S:=\coprod_{p\in S}T_p^*M$$
means the fibrewise restriction of these disjoint unions to base points in
$S$; it does not invoke restriction to an open subset.

The **normal-bundle set** of $S$ in $M$ is the fibrewise quotient

$$\nu(S):=\coprod_{p\in S}T_pM/T_pS.$$

The **conormal-bundle set** of $S$ in $M$ is the fibrewise annihilator

$$N^*S:=\{\xi\in T^*M|_S:\xi|_{T_pS}=0\text{ for the base point }p\}.$$

Both are intrinsic constructions attached to the embedding $S\hookrightarrow M$.
The next proposition supplies their smooth vector-bundle structures.

Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume countable choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, there are an oriented normal-bundle trivialization, a tubular map $\Phi$ defined on an open neighbourhood containing $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, and a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. This $N(K)$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, its boundary $T_K$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^1$, and its exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with boundary $T_K$. The open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $E_K$.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\geq 0$ and
every abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:
$$H_n(f_\#)=H_n(g_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$

Assume countable choice. For a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, let $\mu$ be the positive fibre meridian and let $\sigma$ be the product section $s\mapsto(s,1)$ of $T_K=\partial N(K)\cong S^1\times S^1$. Then $T_K=\partial E_K$ is a torus and $[\mu],[\sigma]$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. The curve $\sigma$ is a product section; this statement does not assert that it is the preferred zero-homology longitude.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Write $D_r^2=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:|z|\le r\}$ in the product coordinates and set $U=\Phi(S^1\times\{|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$ and $V=S^3\setminus\Phi(S^1\times D^2_{\epsilon/2})$. The set $U$ is open because its source is open in the tubular domain and $\Phi$ maps that domain diffeomorphically onto an open set. The removed disk image is compact, hence closed in Hausdorff $S^3$, so $V$ is open. They cover $S^3$, and $U\cap V=\Phi(S^1\times\{\epsilon/2<|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$.

Radial homotopies retract $U$ onto $N(K)$ by replacing each fibre radius $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\min(r,\epsilon)$, fixing the zero vector; retract $V$ onto $E_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\max(r,\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon/2<r\le2\epsilon$ and fixing points outside the closed radius-$2\epsilon$ product tube; and retract $U\cap V$ onto $T_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\epsilon$. Each formula remains within its domain, agrees with the identity at the relevant boundary, and fixes its target. Thus these are deformation retractions.

On the overlap, composing its inclusion into $U$ with the first retraction gives radius $\min(r,\epsilon)$, while retracting first to $T_K$ and including into $N(K)$ gives radius $\epsilon$; linear interpolation stays in $N(K)$. For the inclusion into $V$, the corresponding radii are $\max(r,\epsilon)$ and $\epsilon$, and their interpolation stays in $E_K$. Hence, after the deformation-retraction identifications, the two maps in Mayer–Vietoris are the maps induced by $T_K\hookrightarrow N(K)$ and $T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$. By [F7], homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism on homology.

By [F9], the Mayer–Vietoris sequence for the open cover of step 1.2 has the segment $$H_2(S^3;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(U\cap V;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(U;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(S^3;\mathbb Z).$$ The outer groups vanish by [F6], so the middle map is an isomorphism. Under the identifications of step 3.1, it is induced by the two boundary inclusions.

By [F8], $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ with basis $([\mu],[\sigma])$. The product tube $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$ retracts to its core $S^1$ by contraction in each disk fibre, so homotopy invariance [F7] and [F6] give $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Put $H=H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Steps 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 give $\mathbb Z^2\cong\mathbb Z\oplus H$. The isomorphism embeds $H$ as a subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$. Every subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$ is free of rank at most two: projection to one coordinate has cyclic image; if nonzero, choose a preimage of its positive generator to split it off, and the kernel is a subgroup of $\mathbb Z$; if zero, the subgroup already lies in $\mathbb Z$. Since the complementary $\mathbb Z$ has rank one and the total rank is two, $H$ has rank one. Therefore $H\cong\mathbb Z$.

Choose $c$ to be the first component of the Mayer–Vietoris image of $[\sigma]$; it is a generator of $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)$ because the product section projects with degree one to the core of the product tube [F5, F8]. Choose a generator $h$ of $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, which exists by step 5.1. The meridian maps to zero in the $N(K)$ component because it bounds its fibre disk. In the bases $([\mu],[\sigma])$ and $(c,h)$, the Mayer–Vietoris isomorphism of step 4.1 has first column $(0,a)$ for some integer $a$ and second column whose first coordinate is $1$. Its determinant is therefore $\pm a$; since the map is an isomorphism over $\mathbb Z$, $a=\pm1$. Thus $[\mu]$ generates $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer with $i_*[\sigma]=k[\mu]$, and put $[\lambda]=[\sigma]-k[\mu]$. Then $i_*[\lambda]=0$, $p_*[\lambda]=1$, and the change from the basis $([\mu],[\sigma])$ to $([\mu],[\lambda])$ has determinant $1$. In the new basis, $i_*(a[\mu]+b[\lambda])=a[\mu]$, so the kernel is exactly $\mathbb Z[\lambda]$, a primitive rank-one direct summand. Every degree-one class is $[\sigma]+a[\mu]$ and maps to zero exactly when $a=-k$, proving uniqueness. The curve $t\mapsto(e^{2\pi it},e^{-2\pi ikt})$ is embedded in $S^1\times S^1$ because its first coordinate is injective on $S^1$; it represents $[\lambda]$ and is a preferred longitude.
