Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, let $p$ be a nondegenerate critical point of
$f$, and let $\lambda$ be the index of $p$. If $n=\dim M$, then there are local
coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ centered at $p$ in which

$$f=f(p)-\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda}(x^i)^2+\sum_{i=\lambda+1}^{n}(x^i)^2.$$

For $n=0$, both sums are empty.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: On a compact height band without critical points, the restriction of height to the surface has a smooth field $X$ with $dz(X)=1$: in any surface chart divide a coordinate field by its nonzero height derivative, and combine finitely many such fields by a smooth partition near the compact band. Its flow carries the level circles through the band. Existence for the entire height interval follows by covering the compact band by finitely many flow charts, choosing a common positive short time, and restarting; the trajectory remains in the band until its height reaches an endpoint. Projecting each moving circle to its horizontal plane gives a smooth isotopy of disjoint plane curves. Its velocity has a smooth planar extension near the circles by their normal collar charts; finitely many cutoffs give a compactly supported extension. Its planar flow therefore straightens these curves simultaneously, level by level. In ambient coordinates use $(x,z)\mapsto(g_z(x),z)$ for these plane diffeomorphisms, cutting it off beyond the end levels. Consequently every regular end of the piece can be made vertical. The construction can be made fixed near its attachment to a critical neighborhood.

Move the horizontal caps toward the critical level, stopping in a sufficiently thin slab about that level; in a regular collar this is exactly shortening a vertical cylinder and translating its cap. With nested caps perform the move on the innermost disk first and keep the stopping heights distinct in the order imposed by disjointness. This prevents intersections: outside the moving collar the only possible obstruction is another cap over a nested planar disk, and that cap has already been moved to a nearer stopping height or is kept beyond the moving one. Use positive, strictly monotone changes of the height coordinate along each cylinder, constant near its fixed end, to implement these moves; on the cap use the corresponding translation. Smooth corner rounding is done in disjoint collar neighborhoods. These are isotopies of the capped surface, and [F2] extends them ambiently. The same shortening applies in a component with no critical point, using any intermediate level.

At a saddle use the chart $z=z(p)+u^2-v^2$. Outside a small rectangle about the saddle the regular sheets can be made vertical by step 1.1. Viewed in the horizontal plane, the two circles on the two-component side are joined by the projected saddle rectangle; its interior misses those circles. There are exactly two possibilities: their bounded disks are disjoint, or one disk lies inside the other. To justify completeness, each circle bounds the unique disk in the plane by [F1]. The connected second circle avoids the first and hence lies entirely in its disk interior or its exterior; applying the same argument with the two interchanged gives precisely disjoint or nested disks. The rectangle lies in the region adjacent to both of its attaching arcs: outside both disks in the disjoint case and in the annulus between them in the nested case. A different region would force it to cross one of the two circles. The saddle's other level circle is the boundary obtained by the band reconnection. Reverse height if necessary so this is the one-component side.

With no critical point the connected uncapped piece is a cylinder: the flow in step 1.1 identifies it with one level circle times an interval. After shortening and straightening it is the vertical wall over a plane circle, with one disk cap at each end. Its bounded region is $D^2\times I$ in the disk coordinates from [F1]. This is a ball after rounding: replace the product corners in the disk-radius/height half-plane by circular arcs; the rounded solid is a smooth convex cylinder with rounded ends, radially parametrizable from its center. If there is a maximum or a minimum, the critical chart in [F2] is a paraboloid disk. The regular part is a cylinder attached to its boundary, by step 1.1. Shorten that cylinder into the chart. The paraboloid and its opposite planar cap bound a region $\{(u,v,t):0\le t\le c-u^2-v^2\}$, or its reflection. It is a ball, since rounding its edge gives a convex solid with a smooth radial parametrization; a radial rescaling is constant linear near the center and adjusted near the boundary. Thus these three cases give standard balls.

In the disjoint-disk case, straighten the two attaching arcs in the boundary collars of their planar disks. The projected union of the two disks and the connecting rectangle is a disk: shrink the disks in their parametrizations to end caps, straighten the rectangle in its product coordinates, and round to a stadium. All remaining interval parametrizations extend over their collars by increasing interpolation, so this is an actual disk parametrization. The capped saddle bounds the solid made from the two short disk cylinders by a single thickened rectangle joining one disk window of each. Indeed, away from the rectangle its boundary is exactly the two vertical walls and their horizontal caps; across the rectangle its boundary has the reconnection prescribed by $u^2-v^2$. Rounding the rectangle's two lower or upper edges produces that saddle chart, and rounding the other edges gives precisely the cap collars. The two cylinders are balls by step 3.1. The thickened rectangle is a ball meeting the first cylinder in one disk, and its union with that cylinder meets the second cylinder in one disk. Two applications of [F3] therefore make this solid a ball.

In the nested-disk case let $D_i\subset\operatorname{Int}D_o$ be the inner and outer disks. Their intervening closed annulus is a smooth annulus by the two marked-disk/annulus construction of numbered clauses 12.1–13.1 of [F1]'s smooth-input normal-form proof. The joining rectangle is a crosscut of this annulus. Cutting along its central joining arc leaves a connected surface: a path can be rerouted from one side of the cut to the other around either of the two boundary circles before their marked attaching intervals are removed. Its boundary is one circle and its Euler characteristic is $0+1=1$, since cutting the rectangle replaces one band by two boundary intervals. The finite surface normal form in [F1] therefore gives a topological disk, and its smooth-input construction gives a smooth disk. Equivalently the curve on the one-component side bounds the annulus slit along the joining rectangle. The bounded solid of the capped saddle is an outer short disk cylinder with an inner short disk cylinder indented into one end; the indent's boundary window is opened to the outer wall by the thickened joining rectangle. The indented cylinder together with that rectangle is a ball meeting the outer cylinder's boundary in one disk: this window is the union of its inner disk window and the strip running to the outer boundary, rounded along their shared interval. This description is checked fiberwise away from the rectangle: a point of $D_o\setminus D_i$ has the full outer vertical interval and a point of $D_i$ has that interval shortened by the inner cap. Along the rectangle these intervals join at their endpoints in the single local reconnection $u^2-v^2$; rounding gives the prescribed saddle. The indented cylinder and joining rectangle are balls glued along one window, hence their union is a ball by [F3]. Removing this boundary-attached ball from the outer cylinder leaves a ball by [F3]. This proves the nested case.

A connected regular piece has one circle at each end; an extremum piece has one; and a saddle piece has the three boundary circles just analyzed. There are no additional ends in the connected component: the regular flow supplies cylinders and the single critical chart supplies respectively the disk or the single band. Thus steps 4.1–4.2 exhaust the capped components that are spheres. Every straightening used an embedding isotopy, so it carries the constructed ball back to a smooth embedded standard ball bounded by the original capped sphere. For surgeries performed successively at finitely many regular levels, the innermost choice ensures that each cap interior misses the remaining surface, and sufficiently small distinct collar widths keep all new caps disjoint. Their components have exactly the form used in steps 1.1–2.1, so the final assertion follows as well.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The reflection image $r^{-1}(U)$ is a round circle and hence a standard unknot; if its orientation is reversed, a half-turn in its plane is an orientation-preserving isotopy to the chosen orientation. Thus $K$ would be trivial, contrary to [F1], and $r(K)$ is nontrivial.

Suppose $r(K)=J\#L$ with both $J,L$ nontrivial. Reflect the connected-sum model. By [F2], its image is the connected sum of the reflected summands, $K=r^{-1}(J)\#r^{-1}(L)$ up to oriented ambient isotopy. Reflection preserves nontriviality by the argument in step 1.1, contradicting primeness of $K$. Hence $r(K)$ is prime.

derivations.claim: For commutativity, choose the symmetric standard two-ball model in [F1]. The orientation-preserving half-turn exchanging its two lobes carries each oriented knot tangle to the corresponding tangle in the swapped model and carries the fixed joining map to itself. It therefore gives an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy between the model outputs for $K\#J$ and $J\#K$; [F2] transfers this equality to arbitrary connected-sum data.

For associativity, place representatives of $K,J,L$ in three disjoint standard ball-arc pieces in a row and join consecutive pieces by the same fixed gluing. The constructions $(K\#J)\#L$ and $K\#(J\#L)$ then use the same three pieces and the same two joining maps; only the order in which the two gluings are performed differs. Since the gluings have disjoint boundary spheres, their order does not change the resulting oriented manifold or knot. By [F2], this common model represents both bracketings for arbitrary data.

For the identity, choose the standard unknot summand with a small ball meeting it in a trivial arc. Its spanning disk shows that the complementary arc is boundary-parallel and hence trivial. The connected-sum gluing replaces a short trivial arc of $K$ by another standard trivial arc. The ball-arc isotopy of [F2] identifies the output with $K$. Reversing the order gives the same argument for the left identity.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Delete a small straight subarc of $T$ in a coordinate ball. Identify its complementary ball with $B^3$ and parametrize the remaining oriented arc by a smooth embedding $a:[0,1]\to B^3$ with endpoints on $S^2$, interior in the open ball, and transverse radial endpoint collars. These are the standard ball-arc data of [F2]. Move the arc slightly if necessary so that it misses the origin; this is possible by a small translation on its interior, fixed on endpoint collars, since a smooth compact arc in three-space has empty interior and its endpoint collars can be kept outside a small ball about the origin. Put $f(s)=|a(s)|^2>0$, with $f(0)=f(1)=1$ and $f<1$ in the interior; transversality gives $f'(0)<0<f'(1)$.

Arrange that $f$ is Morse away from its endpoint collars, without changing the arc type. Here are finite perturbation details. The zeros of $f'$ lie in a compact subinterval. Cover that zero set by finitely many smaller open intervals on each of which a compactly supported smooth function $\phi_i$ has derivative $1$. For the family $f_u=f+\sum_i u_i\phi_i$, the map $(s,u)\mapsto f'_u(s)$ is a submersion near this zero set because one parameter derivative is $1$; on its compact complement $f'$ is bounded away from zero, so small parameters create no further zeros. Apply [F3] to this finite family and zero in $\mathbb R$. Choose arbitrarily small good $u$, so every zero of $f'_u$ is simple. Endpoint collars stay fixed and $0<f_u<1$ inside. Replace $a(s)$ by $\sqrt{f_u(s)/f(s)}a(s)$. For sufficiently small parameters this is an isotopy of embeddings, since on a finite chart cover immersion and local injectivity persist in $C^1$, while compact pairs outside the chart diagonals have a positive separation margin. Its squared radius is $f_u$. Rename this arc $a$ and this function $f$; the finitely many simple critical points lie in a compact subinterval, so there are only finitely many.

In $B^4=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R:|x|^2+t^2\le1\}$ take the surface $D=\{(a(s),t):0\le s\le1,\ t^2\le1-f(s)\}$. The strip map $(s,t)\mapsto(a(s),t)$ is an embedding. Its parameter domain is explicitly a smooth disk: the ellipse $v^2\le s(1-s)$ maps onto it by $(s,v)\mapsto(s,v\sqrt{q(s)})$, where $q(s)=(1-f(s))/(s(1-s))$ extends smoothly and positively to both endpoints because $f$ has simple transverse endpoint zeros of $1-f$. This map and its inverse are smooth, and every interior vertical fibre is an interval of positive length. Smoothness at those endpoints follows from the implicit function theorem applied to $f(s)+t^2=1$, because $f'$ is nonzero there; the domain boundary is locally $s=s(t)$ rather than a corner. Equivalently $D$ is the regular sublevel of $f(s)+t^2$ in a slightly extended embedded strip. Consequently it is a smooth compact properly embedded disk, its boundary lies in $S^3$, its interior lies in the open four-ball, and its intersection with $S^3$ is transverse.

The two boundary arcs of $D$ are $(a(s),\sqrt{1-f(s)})$ and $(a(s),-\sqrt{1-f(s)})$. The equatorial sphere $t=0$ meets their union only at $s=0,1$. The hemispheres are standard three-balls; projection to $x$ identifies their interiors with the interior of $B^3$, and their lifted arcs represent the original ball-arc pair by [F2]. To see this without a boundary-singular projection, first use transverse endpoint collars to straighten the arcs in smooth hemisphere collars, and then use projection on the compact remaining subarcs; the collar interpolation is an isotopy of the arcs fixing endpoints. Reflection $(x,t)\mapsto(x,-t)$ exchanges the hemispheres and reverses the boundary orientation of $S^3$. The orientation induced on $\partial D$ runs along one lifted arc with increasing $s$ and along the other with decreasing $s$. Thus the capped oriented boundary arcs are $T$ and $-T^*$, with the fixed mirror reflection transported by positive coordinate frames as in [F2]. Gluing these standard hemispherical arc data gives $\partial D=T\#(-T^*)$ as an oriented knot.

On $D$ the squared radial function is $\rho(s,t)=f(s)+t^2$. Its interior critical points are exactly $(s,0)$ with $f'(s)=0$, and their Hessians are $\operatorname{diag}(f''(s),2)$. They are nondegenerate, with index $0$ or $1$, never $2$. Since $\rho>0$, taking its square root preserves these critical indices. Hence the standard radial function makes $D$ a ribbon disk by [F1], proving the full conclusion.

Let $M\subseteq\mathbb R^N$ be a compact embedded smooth manifold.

- If $N=1$, then every nonzero linear functional on $\mathbb R$ restricts to a
  Morse function on $M$.
- If $N\ge2$, then there is a subset $E\subseteq S^{N-1}$ that is
  $\mathcal A$-null for every smooth atlas $\mathcal A$ of $S^{N-1}$
  ([[def-null-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold]]), such that for
  every $u\in S^{N-1}\setminus E$, the height function
  $$h_u:M\to\mathbb R,\qquad h_u(x)=u\cdot x$$
  is Morse.

Thus restricted linear heights are Morse for generic directions.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold and let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be Morse. Then
every $C^\infty$ neighbourhood $\mathcal U$ of $f$ contains a smooth function
$g$ such that:

- $g$ has the same critical points as $f$;
- the Hessian of $g$ at each critical point equals the Hessian of $f$ there; and
- distinct critical points of $g$ have distinct critical values.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Assume countable choice. Let a smoothly embedded surface in a horizontal slab of $\mathbb R^3$ have regular boundary on the two boundary planes and have at most one critical point of the height function, a nondegenerate one. Cut off its regular end collars and cap every resulting boundary circle by its planar disk, at slightly separated heights when disks are nested, rounding the seams. Every connected component of the resulting closed surface that is a sphere bounds a smoothly embedded standard $3$-ball. This includes the caps obtained by successively doing innermost horizontal-disk surgeries on a smooth sphere at finitely many regular levels separating all its critical values.

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

statement.

derivations.claim: Choose a point of $S^3$ outside $S$ and use its stereographic chart to regard $S$ as a compact smoothly embedded sphere in $\mathbb R^3$. By [F1] choose a direction whose restricted height is Morse, and rotate it to the $z$ direction. Separate its finitely many critical values by the finite small perturbation in [F1]. Realize that perturbation geometrically by retaining the $x,y$ coordinates and changing only $z$. A sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation and its straight interpolation are embeddings: finitely many graph charts retain a nonzero rank-two minor and local injectivity, while pairs of source points outside those chart neighborhoods have a positive image-separation minimum by compactness. Choose the perturbation below both bounds. By [F5] this is an ambient isotopy of $S^3$, supported away from the stereographic point. It therefore suffices to prove that the resulting sphere, with excellent Morse height, bounds a smooth standard ball in $\mathbb R^3$.

Choose finitely many regular heights between consecutive critical values. A level meets the sphere in finitely many smooth disjoint circles: its preimage is a compact regular one-manifold, and finitely many connected local interval charts cover it. Each circle bounds a planar smooth disk by [F2]. Choose an innermost circle, so that this disk's interior misses every other level circle and hence misses the sphere. In a sufficiently thin regular band around the level remove the sphere's annular collar of that circle and replace it by the two horizontal disks at the band's ends. The level curves vary smoothly, so their disks at nearby heights remain disjoint from the rest of the surface after a sufficiently small band shrink. Round the two seams in that band. This is surgery on the sphere along a disk whose interior misses the surface.

Every such surgery replaces one smooth sphere by two smooth spheres. Indeed its circle splits that sphere into two disk regions by [F2], and each region, with the added cap, is a smooth sphere: the boundary gluing is a smooth circle map and extends over a disk by the angular interpolation used in [F2]'s normal-form construction. Now repeat step 1.2 on each remaining circle of that regular level, always innermost among the remaining circles and with a new sufficiently small collar width. Earlier horizontal caps are kept at distinct nearby levels, and the new width is chosen smaller than their positive distances from the chosen level. There are finitely many circles. Then repeat at the finitely many other chosen regular levels, with disjoint level neighborhoods. The outcome is a finite disjoint collection of smooth spheres, each made from a connected piece of the original sphere between successive cutting levels, together with horizontal caps. Each such piece contains at most one height critical point.

By [F3] each final sphere bounds a smooth embedded standard ball. We shall reverse the surgeries and prove inductively that each sphere then present bounds a smooth embedded standard ball. No assertion that all their chosen balls are disjoint is needed: balls bounded by disjoint spheres may be nested.

Consider the reverse of the last unreversed surgery, whose two output spheres bound balls $A$ and $B$ by the inductive assertion. In its product disk neighborhood the two added cap disks can be moved toward each other until both occupy the original surgery disk $D$; equivalently shrink the normal coordinate of the deleted annular collar to zero. Their remaining boundaries are disjoint. The move is an isotopy up to its endpoint on each individual ball, because the cap has a product collar and its boundary annulus is shortened monotonically; at the endpoint it merely meets the other ball's boundary in $D$. An arbitrarily small corner rounding reverses this motion and recovers the pre-surgery sphere. The balls now have either disjoint interiors and intersection exactly $D$, or one is contained in the other, with their boundaries meeting exactly in $D$. To check that these alternatives exhaust the possibilities, first take their disjoint cap positions. The complement of a known embedded ball in $\mathbb R^3$ is connected: [F4] carries that ball to a round one by a compactly supported ambient isotopy. Hence each connected sphere disjoint from the other's boundary lies wholly inside or wholly outside its ball. If neither ball contains the other's boundary, their interiors are disjoint; otherwise one ball is inside the other. The product cap motion preserves the corresponding alternative and makes their boundary contact exactly $D$.

In the disjoint-interior case the pre-surgery sphere is the rounded boundary of $A\cup_D B$. This union is a ball by disk absorption [F4]. In the nested case, relabel so that $B\subset A$; the pre-surgery sphere is the rounded boundary of $A\setminus\operatorname{Int}B$, where $B$ meets $\partial A$ in the disk $D$. Disk removal [F4] says that this too is a ball. These boundary identifications can be checked in $D\times[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$: the pre-surgery annular wall is the side $\partial D\times[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$, whereas surgery inserts the faces $D\times\{-\varepsilon,\varepsilon\}$; all surfaces agree outside that neighborhood. Thus the induction gives a smooth standard ball bounded by the original excellent-height sphere. Undoing the initial small ambient isotopy gives a smooth embedded standard ball bounded by the given $S$.

Apply [F4] to that parametrized embedded ball, using the stereographic chart, to carry it by an ambient isotopy to a small Euclidean round ball. Translation and positive dilation in $\mathbb R^3$ extend smoothly across its compactifying point: they are the usual stereographic conformal transformations of $S^3$, and their parameter paths give smooth ambient isotopies. They carry the round boundary sphere to the unit sphere, the standard equator in this stereographic convention. Concatenate with the preceding isotopies, using smooth stationary reparametrizations. This gives the claimed $H_t$, starting at the identity. The two components and both ball diffeomorphisms are now the inverse images of the two standard open hemispheres and their closures under $H_1$. The two restrictions agree on $S$ because they restrict one ambient diffeomorphism, and pulling back the standard equator's two-sided collar gives a common collar with the same property.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

If a TOP product collar of the boundary, together with a finite PL structure on its boundary surface, has already been supplied, the new PL structure may be chosen equal to that product PL structure on a smaller boundary neighborhood. No smooth marking or smooth ambient isotopy is asserted. Full AC remains the hypothesis of this theorem; no choice-free theorem is obtained by omitting that premise.

Assume full AC. Put $B^j=[-1,1]^j$. Let $k+n=3$, $0\le k\le3$, and let $h:B^k\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^3$ be a topological embedding which is PL on a neighborhood of $\partial B^k\times\mathbb R^n$. There is an isotopy of embeddings $h_t$, $0\le t\le1$, starting at $h$, such that $h_1$ is PL on a neighborhood of $B^k\times B^n$, and
$$h_t=h\quad\text{on}\quad(\partial B^k\times\mathbb R^n)\cup\bigl(B^k\times(\mathbb R^n\setminus\operatorname{Int}(2B^n))\bigr).$$
For $n=0$ this means a boundary-relative straightening of the whole three-ball. More precisely $h_t=hP_t$ for an ambient TOP isotopy of the source with jointly continuous inverses and the displayed fixed set. No smooth isotopy is asserted.

This is a full-AC-qualified TOP-to-PL handle statement, including handles whose interior was only topologically parametrized. It does not by itself provide a finite triangulation of an arbitrary compact TOP manifold or discharge an original choice-free consumer.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable PL three-manifold supplied with a finite PL triangulation, possibly with nonempty boundary. There are finitely many compact connected orientable PL three-manifolds $P_1,\ldots,P_q$, $q\ge1$, each **prime**, and a finite PL connected-sum presentation
$$M\cong P_1\mathbin\#\cdots\mathbin\# P_q.$$
Here prime means that a PL connected-sum factorization has a standard PL three-sphere as one factor. Connected sum removes interiors of parametrized PL balls and glues their boundary spheres by supplied finite PL maps. The presentation supplies the cut spheres, cap-ball parameters and gluing maps, and identifies every original boundary component of $M$ with its boundary component in exactly one factor. Original sphere boundary components are allowed; their ball factors are not discarded. The presentation can be chosen with non-irreducible factors only standard $S^1\times S^2$; every other prime factor is PL irreducible.

This is existence in an already supplied finite PL manifold. No uniqueness, TOP triangulation, TOP-to-PL compatibility, Poincare conjecture, or statement that an arbitrary TOP ball is a PL ball is asserted. No choice axiom is required.

A supplied finite PL embedding of the standard PL two-sphere in $\mathbb R^3$ bounds a compact parametrized PL three-ball; its two complementary components are the bounded ball interior and a connected unbounded exterior. A supplied finite PL embedding of the standard PL two-sphere in the standard PL three-sphere bounds two parametrized PL three-balls, and a PL homeomorphism of that three-sphere carries it to the common boundary in a standard double of a convex three-ball. All parameters and homeomorphisms are finite PL on the compact spaces in question. No choice hypothesis is introduced.

This is a PL assertion in already supplied standard PL ambient spaces. It does not assert triangulability of arbitrary topological three-manifolds or tame arbitrary wild sphere embeddings.

Here a parametrized PL ball means a finite polyhedron supplied with a piecewise linear homeomorphism, with piecewise linear inverse, to a convex polyhedral ball of the stated dimension. All subpolyhedra and maps in the following assertions are finite.

(a) Let $B_1,B_2$ be parametrized PL three-balls and $D_i\subset\partial B_i$ parametrized PL two-disks. Every PL homeomorphism $f:D_1\to D_2$ extends to a PL homeomorphism $B_1\to B_2$.

(b) The space obtained by gluing two parametrized PL three-balls along parametrized PL two-disks in their boundaries, by a specified PL homeomorphism, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

(c) Let $B$ and $A\subset B$ be parametrized PL three-balls, with $A\ne B$. Suppose $A\cap\partial B=\partial A\cap\partial B=D$ is a parametrized PL two-disk and $A\setminus D\subset\operatorname{Int}B$. Impose the following standard boundary-window condition at $C=\partial D$: every point of $C$ has a PL coordinate neighborhood in which
$$B=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0\},\qquad A=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0,\ v\le0\},\qquad D=\{w=0,\ v\le0\}.$$
The equalities are understood after intersection with the coordinate neighborhood, and $C$ corresponds to $v=w=0$. Then $Q=\overline{B\setminus A}$, with closure in $B$, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

No assertion about a sphere in an arbitrary PL three-manifold is assumed. In (c) the closure of the set difference is essential: $B\setminus\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb R^3}A$ would retain the interior of the contact disk as an extra sheet. These statements introduce no choice hypothesis.

Every finite convex cell complex has a compatible finite simplicial triangulation. Choose one relative interior point in each nonempty cell; triangulate the boundary in increasing dimension and cone from that point. This construction agrees on every common face and preserves each cell as a subpolyhedron.

Let $M$ be a compact topological three-manifold with boundary $P$. Suppose a finite combinatorial PL surface $P_0$ and a homeomorphism $P_0\to P$ are given. Then there is a TOP embedding $c:P\times[0,1]\to M$ with $c(x,0)=x$ such that $c(P\times[0,1))$ is a relatively open neighborhood of $P$ in $M$. If $P$ is empty the empty embedding has this property.

The boundary PL structure is used to organize finitely many local pushes only. No PL structure on $M$, and no PL or smooth property of the resulting collar, is asserted or assumed.

For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.
When the vertex set has a supplied total order, it is induced by the
simplicial-to-singular chain map of [[def-simplicial-to-singular-chain-map]],
extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.
For an arbitrary vertex set, the isomorphism is defined compatibly on its
finite subcomplexes and requires no choice principle.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

derivations.claim: Fix the finite PL structure on $M$ supplied by [F1]. We give the compatibility operation needed below, rather than assume that an arbitrary TOP sphere was PL in this structure. For a finite disjoint locally flat sphere system, cut along its spheres using their local flat charts. The orientation of each sphere and of $M$ labels the two local sides consistently; the cut space is therefore a compact TOP manifold with two boundary copies of each sphere, and its old boundary unchanged. Assign the standard finite sphere PL parameter to one copy and the identical parameter under the cutting identification to the other. These finitely many new boundary components have collars by [F5]; keep also the old PL boundary collar of $M$, choosing all collars disjoint. Apply the relative assertion of [F1] to each cut component. On the smaller new boundary collars the cutting identification is the identity in the assigned sphere parameters, so gluing the collars gives an actual PL product across each seam. Finite product-cell subdivisions give a finite PL structure $\Sigma'$ on the original $M$ in which every sphere of the system is PL. It agrees with the original structure $\Sigma$ near $\partial M$. This operation also applies to any finite TOP connected-sum presentation: each gluing sphere receives matching parameters, and its cap balls have the cone parameters of [F4].

Two such finite PL structures $\Sigma,\Sigma'$ on $M$ agreeing near its boundary are related by a homeomorphism $u:(M,\Sigma)\to(M,\Sigma')$ TOP isotopic to the identity, fixed on a smaller boundary collar. Here is the needed relative comparison construction. Cover the compact remainder of that collar by $\Sigma'$ coordinate domains. Subdivide the finite $\Sigma$ triangulation so finely that the closed thirty-two-fold star of each simplex meeting the remainder is in one of these domains; finite cover shrinking and the geometric mesh decrease give this subdivision. Form the vertex, edge, face and tetrahedron handles of [F1], Proof1.1, with all transverse extensions inside these stars. At each index straighten the current identity map in the chosen $\Sigma'$ coordinate chart using [F2]. Its source parameter is a $\Sigma$ PL handle; for positive index its attaching band lies in the already straightened region. Protect smaller earlier core neighborhoods and trim the attaching bands exactly as in [F1], Proof2.1. Here the coordinate control is finite and explicit. Choose the transverse extensions inside the closed two-fold star of their core simplex; at a fixed index their nonidentity supports are disjoint, after trimming the protected attaching bands. A correction can therefore carry a point only between simplices at most four adjacency steps apart, and at most one correction of that index moves it. Before the last index there have been at most three such stages. Consequently the current image of a handle and its transverse extension stays in the closed thirty-two-fold star of its core simplex, inside its chosen target coordinate domain. A sufficiently fine subdivision has this property because each fixed finite iterate of the star has mesh tending to zero. Thus every coordinate embedding to which [F2] is applied really has its whole domain in the chosen chart; no PL compatibility of the original TOP transition maps is assumed. Each correction is the identity on its attaching boundary and outside its own compact twice-core, so extends to all of $M$. Subsequent widths are chosen inside the remaining PL neighborhoods. The index-zero through index-three cores and their protected bands cover the remainder, just as in [F1], Proof2.1. At the endpoint the map is locally PL everywhere, including the unchanged boundary collar. Its inverse is locally PL on the same finite image subdivisions, hence it is a PL homeomorphism. Concatenating the finitely many supported isotopies gives $u$ and its TOP ambient isotopy. In particular, pulling the system of step1.1 back by $u$ makes it a PL sphere system in the ORIGINAL structure by an actual TOP ambient isotopy; this statement does not assert a smooth isotopy.

Consequently PL primeness and PL irreducibility for a finite PL manifold agree with their TOP tame versions. One recognition detail is needed in the reverse direction: if a closed finite PL manifold is TOP homeomorphic to $S^3$, pull its PL structure to standard $S^3$ and apply step2.1 (there is no boundary collar condition) to obtain a PL homeomorphism to standard PL $S^3$. If a finite PL manifold with sphere boundary is a TOP ball, its PL double is TOP $S^3$; the preceding recognition and [F4] make each half a PL ball. Thus neither a TOP sphere factor nor a TOP ball side is silently being recognized as PL without the comparison construction. Indeed a TOP splitting sphere can be moved to a PL sphere by steps1.1 and2.1, and the ambient homeomorphism identifies its two cut components. If its PL side is a parametrized ball, its TOP side is a parametrized TOP ball; conversely every PL splitting is an admitted TOP splitting. The same argument compares every finite TOP connected-sum presentation with a finite PL presentation. Capping choices do not affect the homeomorphism types: conjugate any boundary identification to a sphere map and extend by the cone formula $[x,t]\mapsto[f(x),t]$, which is a homeomorphism even when $f$ is only TOP. No assertion that a TOP ball parameter was PL in the old structure is used. Now apply [F3] to the fixed finite triangulation of $M$. It gives a finite connected sum of factors prime in the full tame TOP sense, with boundary allowed and every original boundary mark retained. This proves existence. It also proves the asserted prime-but-not-irreducible exception: [F3] proves $S^1\times S^2$ PL prime, hence TOP prime by this step, and $\{*\}\times S^2$ is nonseparating and cannot bound a ball. Every other prime is irreducible by [F3] and this same compatibility operation.

We prove uniqueness first for finite PL presentations in one fixed PL manifold. A system $S$ will be said to reduce $M$ to a list $P_1,\ldots,P_k$ if cutting along $S$ and capping its cut faces gives precisely these manifolds together with some standard three-spheres having no original boundary marks. All original boundary components remain assigned to their cut component. Each $P_i$ is irreducible and is not $S^3$; balls and other factors with original boundary are retained. Given a prime presentation, take its separating connected-sum spheres and add one standard nonseparating sphere in each $S^1\times S^2$ summand. Their finite collars and the marked model in [F3], Proof3.1, show that they reduce $M$ to its irreducible nonspherical prime factors: cutting and capping the added sphere turns that summand into $S^3$. The cap-ball avoidance construction [F3], Proof1.1, realizes all these spheres disjointly in the original manifold. Conversely, if $S$ reduces to this list, adding any finite PL spheres disjoint from $S$ leaves the list unchanged. In a capped irreducible component each new sphere bounds a ball. Its cut-and-cap operation leaves that component and an unmarked $S^3$; in a capped $S^3$ this follows from [F4]. Move cap balls off the sphere as in [F3], Proof1.1, to carry out the cutting, or equivalently keep track of the cap balls as punctures on their respective sides. They introduce only extra punctures and do not erase an original boundary component. Induction over the finite added spheres proves the assertion.

Let $S$ and $T$ be systems reducing $M$ to the irreducible lists from two prime presentations. Make their intersection transverse by a finite PL perturbation of one system. To see the finiteness and the local condition, take finite common subdivisions of their surface charts and ambient stars, and move their vertices by sufficiently small generic displacements in the finite linear charts. Avoid the finitely many affine incidences giving coincident vertices, tangencies or edge/face degeneracies; choose them one at a time outside these proper affine subsets. Finite compact disjoint simplices retain their positive separation, and the transverse link disks retain their embedding under such small moves. Use the boundary-fixed face-cone extensions in the ambient little stars to realize the moves, or just keep the parametrized perturbed surfaces; no factor changes. The intersection is now a compact one-manifold with a finite triangulation, hence finitely many disjoint polygonal circles. If there are no circles, keep the two systems. Otherwise choose a circle innermost on a component of $T$, bounding a PL disk $D$ whose interior misses $S$. The disk exists because a polygonal circle on a PL sphere bounds two parametrized disks by [F4]'s sphere boundary-disk construction.

Suppose $\partial D\subset S_j$. Surger $S_j$ along $D$: its two complementary disks capped by two close parallel copies of $D$ give spheres $S'_j,S''_j$. Small product pushes make both disjoint from $S_j$ and from all the other spheres of $S$. These are actual finite PL surfaces: in the finite disk and circle collar charts take two levels, triangulate the product strips, and flatten their quadrant corners by finite face-cone maps. The three spheres $S_j,S'_j,S''_j$ bound a parametrized three-punctured sphere $P$. For its parameter, take the collar of $S_j$ on the $D$ side and the narrow disk prism thickening $D$; it is the standard collar with a disk two-handle on one end. Cut the sphere parameter along the common circle into its two parametrized disks. The two disk prisms and their circle strip give, by the marked window gluing of [F4], a ball with two disjoint parametrized interior balls removed. This verifies the three-punctured-sphere description with its three specified boundary components, not just its homology. Add both new spheres to $S$. By step4.1 this enlarged system reduces to the same list. Then delete $S_j$. This attaches $P$ to the component on the other side of $S_j$ along exactly that one boundary sphere; the other two boundary spheres stay cut. After capping these two faces, the operation just fills the old $S_j$ face by a parametrized ball. Thus the capped component is unchanged, and all other capped components are unchanged. This remains true if the two sides belonged to the same component before adding the new spheres, since $P$ is an isolated component AFTER the two new cuts. The new system therefore reduces to the same list.

The surgery reduces the number of intersections with $T$. Choose its disk levels on opposite sides of $D\subset T$ and the circle collar so that the two cap disks miss $T$. Every remaining old intersection circle lies in one of the two complementary disks of $S_j$ and is merely carried to the corresponding new sphere. The chosen circle disappears, and no new one is created; all other members of $S$ are unchanged. Repeat step6.1 until the finite nonnegative intersection count is zero. The resulting $S^*$ is disjoint from $T$ and reduces to precisely the original $P_i$ list. Their union is now an enlargement both of $S^*$ and of $T$. Step4.1 says its capped components consist of the $P_i$ together with unmarked $S^3$'s and also of the $Q_i$ together with unmarked $S^3$'s. Hence the nonspherical irreducible factors occur with identical multiplicity and homeomorphism types, up to permutation. Original boundary marks may be retained throughout, though the Statement does not require that stronger marking.

The remaining number of $S^1\times S^2$ factors is also determined. Work over $\mathbb Q$. The finite triangulation and [F6] make $b_1(M)=\dim H_1(M;\mathbb Q)$ finite. For a separating connected-sum sphere, use its collar to form an open two-set cover; the intersection retracts to $S^2$. This sphere has $H_1=0$ and connected $H_0=\mathbb Q$, and its map to the two connected sides' $H_0$ groups is $a\mapsto(a,-a)$, injective. Exactness in [F6] gives $H_1(M;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(P;\mathbb Q)\oplus H_1(Q;\mathbb Q)$; filling the boundary spheres has no effect on $H_1$ by the same cover sequence with a ball. For $S^1\times S^2$ use two proper overlapping open circle arcs whose intersection has two interval components, and multiply by $S^2$. Each of the two open sets retracts to $S^2$ and the overlap retracts to two copies of $S^2$. The sphere has zero $H_1$ by its finite boundary-of-a-tetrahedron chain complex in [F6]. The degree-zero map $\mathbb Q^2\to\mathbb Q^2$ sends both component generators to $(1,-1)$, so its kernel is one-dimensional. The same exact sequence gives $b_1(S^1\times S^2)=1$. Thus a presentation with irreducible list $P_i$ and $\ell$ such factors satisfies $b_1(M)=\sum_i b_1(P_i)+\ell$. Step7.1 identifies the sum for the two presentations, so their numbers $\ell$ are equal.

Finally take any two admitted finite tame TOP prime presentations of the original $M$. By steps1.1 and2.1 move each of their finite cutting systems to a PL system in the fixed structure. Their capped factors are homeomorphic to the original factors by step3.1. TOP prime factors become PL prime, so [F3]'s prime-versus-irreducible assertion applies; the explicit nonseparating handle model identifies the possible $S^1\times S^2$ factors. Steps4.1–8.1 therefore compare these two presentations and give precisely the required equality of prime factors up to order and insertion or deletion of $S^3$. A single-factor presentation and $M=S^3$ are included: the reducing system may be empty and its only capped component may be an unmarked $S^3$; the same refinement argument forces every nonspherical irreducible list to be empty, and step8.1 forces zero handle factors. Existence and the exceptional prime factor were proved in step3.1. All boundary cuts and cap maps used actual parameters, the only TOP-to-PL compatibility used the explicit relative operation of steps1.1 and2.1, and full AC entered through [A1], [F1] and [F2] exactly as declared.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] and carry the knot through the same ambient isotopy. We now have the two standard hemispherical balls, each containing one proper arc of the knot. Cap each arc by a simple boundary arc, pushed slightly into a boundary collar; orient the cap to close the oriented original arc. Boundary caps give the same capped knot class: two simple arcs in a two-sphere joining the same two points are isotopic keeping the endpoints, with no other marked points to avoid. One explicit reduction puts the arcs transverse, removes an outermost bigon successively, and then slides the resulting disjoint arcs across the disk they cobound; all moves take place in surface disks and extend to their ball collars.

A small collar neighbourhood of each cap arc is a ball meeting the capped knot in one trivial arc. Delete these two ball-arc neighbourhoods. The remaining arcs are precisely the original two knot pieces, with endpoint collars on the common equator. Gluing by the fixed orientation-matching two-ball convention recovers $K$; the simultaneous boundary parametrization in [F1] makes the two sides agree. Straighten the cap collar and its positive local frame before gluing, which is a change of the local data allowed by [F2]. Hence this is the connected sum $K_1\#K_2$ in the stated convention. Transporting back through the original ambient isotopy proves the assertion. No extension of an arbitrary prescribed sphere diffeomorphism is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $F$ is any spanning surface for $K$, its image $r(F)$ is a connected compact smooth surface with boundary $r(K)$. Push the orientation of $F$ forward to orient $r(F)$; reversing the boundary orientation instead is achieved by reversing the orientation on $r(F)$. By [F2], all these surfaces have genus $g(F)$. Thus every genus admissible for $K$ is admissible with the same value for $r(K)$ and $-K$.
Apply the same argument using $r^{-1}=r$ and orientation reversal again. This gives the reverse inclusion of the sets of admissible genera, so their minima agree for all four knots.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

derivations.claim: If $K$ is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, carry its planar spanning disk through the isotopy. This is a genus-zero spanning surface, and nonnegativity gives $g(K)=0$.

Conversely, use [F1] to let a smooth embedding $e:D^2\to S^3$ parametrize a genus-zero spanning surface with oriented boundary $K$. For $0<r\le1$ the circles $x\mapsto e(rx)$, $x\in S^1$, are embedded and form a smooth isotopy from $K$ to a sufficiently small circle about $e(0)$. This contracts circles inside the embedded disk; it does not contract the final circle to a point. Choose a point outside this spanning disk and the fixed standard disk; their union has empty interior, since finitely many surface slice charts cover each compact disk. Its stereographic complement is one common positive chart $\mathbb R^3$ containing both disks. Write $p$ for the chart image of $e(0)$ and $E$ for the expression of $e$ translated by $-p$, so $E(0)=0$. For small fixed $r>0$, the maps $x\mapsto E(trx)/t$ for $0<t\le1$, continued at $t=0$ by $r\,dE_0(x)$, are an isotopy of embedded circles in that chart. Indeed Taylor's formula gives the smooth extension and, on a small disk, the derivatives are uniformly close to the injective linear map $r\,dE_0$; projection onto its image plane gives a uniform injectivity estimate by integration along line segments. Their images lie in the chart after decreasing $r$.

The final linear ellipse is isotopic to an oriented round circle in its plane: use the positive square root of its two-dimensional Gram matrix to deform its ordered independent spanning vectors to an orthonormal pair. Complete that pair by its positive normal to a positive ambient frame. Apply the same shrinking and linearization to the fixed standard disk in the common stereographic chart, obtaining an oriented round circle about its interior point $q$. Join the two round circles explicitly in this $\mathbb R^3$: move the center along the segment from $p$ to $q$, interpolate their positive radii, and rotate the first positive frame to the second through rotations in $SO(3)$ (successive rotations about coordinate axes suffice). Each intermediate circle is embedded, and the whole finite track is compact in the chart. A half-turn about a diameter reverses a circle orientation if required while preserving the ambient orientation. Reverse the standard disk shrinking to finish at the fixed standard unknot. Extend the concatenated circle isotopies by [F2]; each ambient diffeomorphism preserves orientation since it starts at the identity. Thus $K$ is the standard oriented unknot.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F$ be a compact smooth surface with boundary, let $M$ be a smooth three-manifold without boundary, and let $S\subset M$ be a closed embedded smooth surface. If $i:F\to M$ is a smooth embedding whose boundary restriction $i|_{\partial F}$ is transverse to $S$, then there is a smooth isotopy $i_t:F\to M$ through embeddings, fixed on a neighbourhood of $\partial F$, such that $i_1(F)$ is transverse to $S$.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $S\subset S^3$ be a smoothly embedded sphere transverse to $K$ in exactly two points. Cutting along $S$ gives two properly embedded arcs; cap each arc by an orientation-compatible simple arc on $S$, pushed slightly into the corresponding boundary collar to obtain oriented knots $K_1$ and $K_2$. Then the oriented isotopy class of $K$ is the connected sum $K_1\#K_2$.
