Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

Let $F_n=\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ be the free group of
[[def-free-group]], identified with $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ through the
standard meridians by
[[thm-the-punctured-disk-fundamental-group-is-free-on-standard-meridians]]. For
$1\le i\le n-1$, $\rho(\sigma_i)\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ is the automorphism
given on the basis by
$$\rho(\sigma_i)(x_i)=x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)(x_{i+1})=x_i, \qquad \rho(\sigma_i)(x_j)=x_j\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$
Its inverse is
$$\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_i)=x_{i+1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_{i+1})=x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_j)=x_j\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$
Products use ordinary function composition: the leftmost factor is the
outermost map and the rightmost factor acts first. Also
$\rho(\sigma_i^{-1}):=\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}$.

**The assignments are automorphisms, and the displayed formulas are inverse.**
By the universal property of the free group
([[def-free-group]], [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]]) the displayed
values on the free basis extend to a unique endomorphism
$\rho(\sigma_i):F_n\to F_n$, and likewise the displayed inverse formulas extend
to an endomorphism $\theta:F_n\to F_n$. Substituting,
$$\theta\bigl(\rho(\sigma_i)(x_i)\bigr)=\theta(x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1}) =\theta(x_i)\,\theta(x_{i+1})\,\theta(x_i)^{-1} =x_{i+1}\,\bigl(x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1}\bigr)\,x_{i+1}^{-1}=x_i,$$
$$\theta\bigl(\rho(\sigma_i)(x_{i+1})\bigr)=\theta(x_i)=x_{i+1},$$
and both composites fix every other basis element; so
$\theta\circ\rho(\sigma_i)=\operatorname{id}_{F_n}$ on a basis, hence as
endomorphisms. Symmetrically $\rho(\sigma_i)\circ\theta=
\operatorname{id}_{F_n}$. Therefore $\rho(\sigma_i)$ is a bijection with the
displayed inverse, i.e. an automorphism
([[def-group-isomorphism-and-automorphism]]).

**Convention note.** The displayed formulas are Artin's equations (14) and (15)
with the letter $\sigma_i$ and its inverse interchanged; under the frozen
geometric conventions of this library the *positive* half twist is the
anticlockwise supported half rotation (see
`def-elementary-geometric-half-twist` and
`thm-braid-group-is-the-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-the-punctured-disk`),
and
`prop-the-geometric-action-on-meridians-is-the-artin-representation` proves
that its action on the standard meridians is exactly the substitution frozen
above. The interchange is a convention, not a change of mathematical content:
$\rho$ and Artin's substitution generate the same subgroup of
$\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ and satisfy the same braid relations, and the
companion page shows that the mirror (clockwise) half rotation realizes
Artin's displayed formulas verbatim.

By [[lem-artin-automorphisms-satisfy-the-braid-relations]] the assignment
$\sigma_i\mapsto\rho(\sigma_i)$ satisfies the defining relations of the
presented braid group $B_n$ of
[[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]], so von Dyck's theorem
[[thm-von-dyck]] yields a unique homomorphism
$$\rho:B_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(F_n).$$
This is the **Artin representation**; it is the frozen convention for every
later statement of the page.

**Uniqueness and effectivity.** The homomorphism is unique because it is
prescribed on the generating set $\{\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\}$, and it is
computed on a braid word by composing the finitely many automorphisms
$\rho(\sigma_i)^{\pm1}$ attached to its letters, as frozen in
[[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]]. No choice principle and no
geometric input are used in the construction; von Dyck's theorem
[[thm-von-dyck]] supplies existence and uniqueness of the extension.

Assume AC. Let $G_n$ be the geometric braid group,
$\varphi_n:B_n\to G_n$ the published surjection of
[[prop-the-artin-presentation-surjects-onto-geometric-braids]], and
$$\Psi:G_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}(D^2,Q_n;\partial D^2)$$
the isomorphism of
[[thm-braid-group-is-the-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-the-punctured-disk]].
Identifying $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ with $F_n$ by the standard meridians of
[[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]], the automorphism of $F_n$
induced by the mapping class $\Psi(\varphi_n(\beta))$ equals $\rho(\beta)$ for
every braid word $\beta$. In particular the geometric half twist $\sigma_i$ acts
as the Nielsen automorphism of
[[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]].

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $D^2=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le1\}$ and
$Q_n=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the closed unit disk and the base configuration of
[[def-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-a-punctured-disk]], so that
$q_1<\dots<q_n$ are distinct points of the real axis of
$\operatorname{int}D^2$. Fix the boundary basepoint
$$d:=(0,1)\in\partial D^2 .$$
For $1\le i\le n$ let $s_i\colon[0,1]\to D^2$ be the **straight stem**
$$s_i(t):=(1-t)\,d+t\,q_i ,$$
the straight segment from $d$ to $q_i$, and choose a round circle $C_i$ in
$D^2\setminus Q_n$ centred at $q_i$, of radius $0<\varepsilon_i<d(q_i,\partial D^2)$
so small that the closed disks $B_i$ bounded by the circles are pairwise disjoint, that each circle meets only its own stem, and that it meets $s_i$ exactly once, at
$p_i:=s_i(1-\varepsilon_i/L_i)$ where $L_i:=|d-q_i|$, and meets no other stem
$s_j$ with $j\ne i$. Write $c_i\colon[0,1]\to D^2\setminus Q_n$ for $C_i$
traversed once **positively** (counterclockwise), from $p_i$ back to $p_i$.
The **standard meridian loops** are the loops based at $d$
$$x_i:=s_i\,c_i\,s_i^{-1},\qquad 1\le i\le n,$$
read as $s_i$ from $d$ to $p_i$, then $c_i$, then $s_i$ from $p_i$ back to $d$
([[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]]). Further, $\partial$ denotes the
**positively oriented boundary loop**
$$\partial(t):=d\,e^{2\pi i t},\qquad t\in[0,1],$$
of $D^2$ based at $d$: it traverses $\partial D^2$ once counterclockwise,
starting and ending at $d$.

**Existence and independence of the choices.** The straight segments $s_i$
leave $d$ in pairwise distinct directions (the points $q_1,\dots,q_n$ are
distinct and lie strictly below $d$) and meet one another only at $d$; the
segments $s_i$ meet the real axis only at their endpoints $q_i$. An explicit choice-free family is given by
$$\varepsilon_i=\frac14\min\left(\{1-|q_i|\}\cup\left\{|q_i-q_j|,\frac{|q_i-q_j|}{\sqrt{1+q_j^2}}:j\ne i\right\}\right).$$
The finite set inside the minimum is nonempty and contains only positive
numbers. The distance from $q_i$ to the line through $d,q_j$ is
$|q_i-q_j|/\sqrt{1+q_j^2}$, so $B_i$ misses every other stem. Also
$\varepsilon_i+\varepsilon_j\le|q_i-q_j|/2<|q_i-q_j|$, proving disjointness
of the **closed** disks, and $\varepsilon_i<1-|q_i|$ keeps each disk inside
$D^2$. The radius is less than $|d-q_i|$, giving exactly the displayed contact
with its own stem. For $n=1$ the minimum has only its boundary-margin entry;
for $n=0$ the family is empty. Any family satisfying these conditions may be
fixed; this formula witnesses its existence without any choice axiom.

The class $[x_i]\in\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ is independent of
all admissible radii, including the old broader convention requiring only
avoidance of the other stems. Such a circle encloses no $q_j$ with $j\ne i$:
otherwise the other stem from $d$, which lies outside the circle, to $q_j$
would cross it (or have $q_j$ on it). Thus the larger disk of any two admissible
concentric circles still contains no other puncture. Interpolate their radii
and their tether contact points radially; this is a based lasso homotopy in
$D^2\setminus Q_n$ ([[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]]).
It does not require the intermediate circle to be disjoint from the other
circles, so the class argument does not circularly assume the newly explicit
representative convention. Fix once and
for all one such family of circles; every statement on this page uses that
fixed family.

**Frozen conventions of the page.** The stems and the basepoint transport are
fixed once and for all by the choices above; the stems are indexed so that the
positively oriented boundary loop $\partial$, as seen from $d$, meets the
directions of the stems in the order $s_1,s_2,\dots,s_n$. Products of braid
automorphisms use ordinary function composition: the leftmost factor is the
outermost map, so the rightmost factor acts first. No relation of the braid presentation and no choice principle
is used in this definition.

Let $F_n=\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ be the free group of
[[def-free-group]] on $n$ letters. The assignment $x_i\mapsto[x_i]$ extends to
a group isomorphism $F_n\to\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$; equivalently, the
classes $[x_1],\dots,[x_n]$ of the standard meridians of
[[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]] form a free basis of
$\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$.

Let $X$ be the based presentation $2$-complex with one vertex, oriented $1$-cells $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, and oriented $2$-cells attached along words $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ in the free group $F_n$. Let $G=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be its presented fundamental group, let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation, and let $\psi:G\to H$ be the declared free-abelian deck map. For $\Phi:\mathbb F[F_n]\to M_d(Q)$ induced by $x_j\mapsto\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)$, the twisted differential $\partial_1$ has blocks $\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d$, and the $i$th block row of $\partial_2$ is

$$\left(\Phi\left(\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial x_1}\right),\ldots,\Phi\left(\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial x_n}\right)\right),$$

where coefficient vectors are written as rows and differentials act on the right: the matrix of $\partial_1$ is the stacked column of blocks $\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d$, while the matrix of $\partial_2$ is the $md$-by-$nd$ block matrix whose $i$th row is the displayed Fox row. The Fox derivatives use the product and inverse recursions in the Wada definition. Thus the evaluated Fox-Jacobian blocks are exactly the cellular boundary blocks of the based twisted complex of this presentation $2$-complex.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

If $D$ is an integral domain, then $D\setminus\{0\}$ is multiplicative. Its localisation
$$ \operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D $$
is the **field of fractions** of $D$. Thus its elements are fractions $a/b$ with $a,b\in D$ and $b\ne0$, modulo the localisation equivalence relation.

For every integral domain $D$, the localisation $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is a field. Its canonical map
$$ D\longrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}(D),\qquad d\longmapsto d/1, $$
is an injective unital ring homomorphism.

derivations.claim: Let $\alpha(g)=\rho(g)\psi(g)$ denote the coefficient matrix. Under [A1], the supplied filling certificate and [F7] identify $\pi_1(X)$ as the quotient of $\pi_1(Y)$ that kills the axis meridian $x$. Pulling the coefficient system back from $X$ therefore gives $\alpha(x)=I_d$ and $\psi(x)=1$; the core of $V$ is represented on $T$ by $g_n$, with matrix $M_n$. The algorithm forms the full positive-meridian basis on $X$ before applying $\chi$, while the compatible filling certificate specifies the resulting pulled-back or extended coefficient systems on $Y,T,V$ and makes them agree on overlaps. The map $\pi_1(Y)\to\pi_1(X)$ is surjective, so the pulled-back deck map on $Y$ is still onto and the coefficient-unit images for the two exteriors agree. Since $D\ne0$, $M_n-I_d$ is invertible.

First compute the core-circle spine $V_{\mathrm{core}}$ with one $0$-cell and one $1$-cell for $g_n$. Its twisted boundary is $M_n-I_d$, so this core complex is acyclic and its torsion is $D^{-1}$. This core is not used as a CW pair containing $T$; a separate relative model and its torsion comparison are established before applying the gluing sequence. Give $T$ the standard one-vertex CW structure with $1$-cells $x,g_n$ and one commutator $2$-cell $xg_nx^{-1}g_n^{-1}$. The Fox boundary blocks are $d_1=(0,M_n-I_d)^\mathsf{T}$ and $d_2=(I_d-M_n,0)$: hence $d_1$ is onto, $d_2$ is injective onto $\ker d_1$, and $T$ is acyclic. In the torsion determinant product, the factors $\det(I_d-M_n)$ and $\det((M_n-I_d)^{-1})$ cancel up to $(-1)^d$, so $\tau(T)=(-1)^d$.

For $X$, Fox differentiation of $r_i=g_i^{-1}\beta_*(g_i)$ gives block row $M_i^{-1}(\widetilde B_{i,*}-e_i)$, where $e_i$ is the $i$th identity block row and $M_i=\rho(g_i)\psi(g_i)$. Thus, after deleting the $g_n$ column, the Fox block is $\operatorname{diag}(M_1^{-1},\ldots,M_{n-1}^{-1})(\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I)$, whose determinant is $\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\det(M_i^{-1})\right)N$. The prefactor is a nonzero coefficient unit. The $d_1$ block for $g_n$ is $M_n-I_d$, which is invertible, so $d_1$ is onto and projection from $\ker d_1$ to the first $n-1$ coordinate blocks is an isomorphism. By [F5], the projected $d_2$ is the displayed deleted Fox block. Therefore $N\ne0$ implies $d_2$ injective and, by dimensions and $d_1d_2=0$, the complex is acyclic; if the complex is acyclic, the same projection makes $d_2$ injective and forces $N\ne0$. Hence nonacyclicity is equivalent to $N=0$.

Give $D^2$ its boundary vertex, boundary edge $x$, and meridian disk cell $a$, and give $S^1$ its vertex and core edge $g_n$. Their product is a finite CW model $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ of the actual solid torus containing exactly the specified torus CW structure as its boundary subcomplex. Besides the cells of $T$, it has the $2$-cell $a\times\{*\}$, still denoted $a$, and the $3$-cell $b=a\times g_n$. Put $A=M_n-I_d$ and let $q$ denote the torus $2$-cell, with the orientation in step 2.1. For a coefficient row $v$, the product boundaries are $$\partial a(v)=x(v),\qquad \partial q(v)=x(-vA),\qquad \partial b(v)=q(v)+a(vA).$$ The first formula is the meridian disk boundary, the second is the torus Fox boundary from step 2.1, and the third is the oriented boundary of disk times core edge; its two terms have cancelling images under $\partial$. Replace the degree-two block $q(v)$ by $q'(v)=q(v)+a(vA)$. This block-triangular basis change has determinant one, $\partial q'=0$, and $\partial b(v)=q'(v)$. Split off the unit two-term pair $(b,q')$, then the unit pair $(a,x)$. The remaining based complex is exactly the core complex with $\partial g_n(v)=vA$. Each split pair has identity incidence and torsion one up to the sign unit, and the triangular change contributes determinant one. Hence $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ has the same homology and torsion class as $V_{\mathrm{core}}$, so it is acyclic and its torsion is $D^{-1}$ up to the declared units. This calculation supplies the missing based comparison while retaining $T$ in the actual gluing model.

Use the relative-cellular gluing operation [F9] for the actual decomposition in the supplied certificate. For $V$ use $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ from step 3.1, not its core spine. For the exterior pieces the operation uses the compatible relative CW representatives and the supplied based simple-spine comparisons. Equivalently, a boundary map into a spine is represented by its finite cellular mapping cylinder: each added prism over a torus cell pairs with its source face, with lifted incidence a unit; these pairs are removed in decreasing cell dimension. Their torsion changes lie in the declared unit subgroup. Thus the based torsion classes used below are those of the supplied spines, without identifying the boundary torus with a subcomplex of a core circle or of an abstract presentation. In the common relative models each cell of $T$ occurs in both pieces, and each other cell occurs in exactly one. Inclusion into the first piece and its negative into the second, followed by the difference quotient to the union, therefore give the degreewise split short exact sequence $$0\longrightarrow C_*(T)\longrightarrow C_*(Y_{\mathrm{rel}})\oplus C_*(V_{\mathrm{rel}})\longrightarrow C_*(X_{\mathrm{rel}})\longrightarrow0.$$ Choose the shared lifts compatibly; any permitted adjustment changes only the declared determinant/deck units. Since $T$ and $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ are acyclic by steps 2.1 and 3.1, the long exact homology sequence identifies $H_*(Y;Q^d)$ with $H_*(X;Q^d)$. Thus $Y$ is acyclic exactly when $X$ is. Subsequent references to the gluing sequence mean these relative models and their certified based comparisons.

In the acyclic case, choose boundary bases in the short exact sequence compatibly: lift a basis of each quotient boundary space, append a basis of the subcomplex boundary space, and lift the resulting boundary bases to chain groups. The change-of-basis matrices are block triangular with diagonal blocks the matrices for the subcomplex and quotient, so their determinants multiply degree by degree; the alternating torsion product therefore gives $\tau(Y)\tau(V)=\pm\tau(T)\tau(X)$. As $\tau(T)=\pm1$ and both signs lie in the declared unit subgroup, step 2.1 yields $\tau(Y)\doteq\tau(X)D$.

Suppose $X$ and hence $Y$ are acyclic over $Q$. The finite based chain modules over $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$ are free. If $z\in C_1(Y;\Lambda^d)$ is a $1$-cycle, acyclicity over $Q$ gives $z/1=d_2(y)/s$ for some $y\in C_2(Y;\Lambda^d)$ and nonzero $s\in\Lambda$. By [F8], equality in the fraction field means that some nonzero $u\in\Lambda$ annihilates $sz-d_2(y)$; since $C_1(Y;\Lambda^d)$ is free over the domain $\Lambda$, multiplication by $u$ is injective, so $sz=d_2(y)$. Every degree-one homology class is therefore killed by a nonzero element of $\Lambda$.

Apply [F2] to the certified spine of $Y$ and delete the $g_n$ column, whose denominator is $D\ne0$. For $s_i=\beta_*(g_i)(x^{-1}g_ix)^{-1}$, the $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ Fox blocks evaluate to $\widetilde B-I$, where $\widetilde B$ is the full cumulative-meridian Fox matrix, and the $x$-column blocks are $I_d-M_i$ with $M_i=\rho(g_i)\psi(g_i)$. Because $\beta_*(g_n)=g_n$, the last row of $\widetilde B-I$ is zero; after deleting its $g_n$ column, the remaining matrix has upper-left block $\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I$, arbitrary upper-right block, zero lower-left block, and lower-right block $I_d-M_n$. It is block upper triangular, so its determinant is $(-1)^dND$. Dividing by $D$ gives $(-1)^dN$, which represents $N$ modulo the sign unit. Consequently $\tau(Y)\doteq N$.

If the complex is acyclic, combine steps 5.1 and 6.1 to obtain $\tau(X)D\doteq N$, hence $\tau(X)\doteq N/D$. If it is nonacyclic, step 2.2 gives $N=0$, and the declared convention sets $\tau(X)=0=N/D$. This proves the statement in both branches.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the maximal-abelian-cover convention. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link, with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L$ formed by deleting the interiors of pairwise-disjoint chosen closed normal-disk tubes, and basepoint $b\in E_L$. For a knot, $r=1$ and $E_L=E_K$. The full meridian abelianization group is $H_L=H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, with the positive normal-disk meridians as its ordered basis. Choose a finite-rank free abelian group $H$ of positive rank and an epimorphism $\chi:H_L\to H$; write $\psi=\chi\circ\mathrm{ab}:G\to H$ for the induced map from $G=\pi_1(E_L,b)$. The identity choice $H=H_L$ is the full multivariable deck map; a coloring may identify its variables only through the explicitly stated map $\chi$. Let $\mathbb F$ be a field, let $d\ge1$, and let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$, the commutative Laurent-polynomial ring with monomial basis $H$, and $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$. On row vectors define the right $\mathbb F[G]$ action by $v\cdot g=v\rho(g)\psi(g)$, where $\psi(g)$ is central multiplication by its monomial in $\Lambda$. For a chosen finite based CW structure $X$ on $E_L$, orient and order its cells and choose one lift of each cell to the universal cover $\widetilde X$. The twisted cellular complex is

$$C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)=\Lambda^d\otimes_{\mathbb F[G]}C_*(\widetilde X;\mathbb F),$$

and its fraction-field complex is $C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;Q^d)=Q\otimes_{\Lambda}C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)$. The lifted cell bases and the standard coordinate basis of $\mathbb F^d$ give the based $Q$-vector-space bases. If this fraction-field complex is not acyclic, define its twisted torsion to be $0$. If it is acyclic, choose in each degree a basis $\mathbf b_i$ of $B_i=\operatorname{im}\partial_{i+1}$ and lifts $\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}$ of $\mathbf b_{i-1}$ under $\partial_i$; with $\mathbf c_i$ the based cellular basis, set

Attaching a $1$-cell $x$ at the vertex and a $2$-cell with attaching word $x$ is an elementary expansion: the new $1$-cell is a free face of the new $2$-cell, so collapsing this pair returns the original circle spine. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the maximal-abelian-cover convention. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link, with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L$ formed by deleting the interiors of pairwise-disjoint chosen closed normal-disk tubes, and basepoint $b\in E_L$. For a knot, $r=1$ and $E_L=E_K$. The full meridian abelianization group is $H_L=H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, with the positive normal-disk meridians as its ordered basis. Choose a finite-rank free abelian group $H$ of positive rank and an epimorphism $\chi:H_L\to H$; write $\psi=\chi\circ\mathrm{ab}:G\to H$ for the induced map from $G=\pi_1(E_L,b)$. The identity choice $H=H_L$ is the full multivariable deck map; a coloring may identify its variables only through the explicitly stated map $\chi$. Let $\mathbb F$ be a field, let $d\ge1$, and let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$, the commutative Laurent-polynomial ring with monomial basis $H$, and $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$. On row vectors define the right $\mathbb F[G]$ action by $v\cdot g=v\rho(g)\psi(g)$, where $\psi(g)$ is central multiplication by its monomial in $\Lambda$. For a chosen finite based CW structure $X$ on $E_L$, orient and order its cells and choose one lift of each cell to the universal cover $\widetilde X$. The twisted cellular complex is

$$C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)=\Lambda^d\otimes_{\mathbb F[G]}C_*(\widetilde X;\mathbb F),$$

and its fraction-field complex is $C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;Q^d)=Q\otimes_{\Lambda}C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)$. The lifted cell bases and the standard coordinate basis of $\mathbb F^d$ give the based $Q$-vector-space bases. If this fraction-field complex is not acyclic, define its twisted torsion to be $0$. If it is acyclic, choose in each degree a basis $\mathbf b_i$ of $B_i=\operatorname{im}\partial_{i+1}$ and lifts $\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}$ of $\mathbf b_{i-1}$ under $\partial_i$; with $\mathbf c_i$ the based cellular basis, set

$$\tau(C_*,\mathbf c)=\prod_i[\mathbf b_i,\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}/\mathbf c_i]^{(-1)^{i+1}}\in Q^\times,$$

where brackets denote the determinant of the change-of-basis matrix. The twisted Reidemeister torsion is this value modulo the subgroup $\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}=\{\pm\det(\rho(g))\psi(g)^d:g\in G\}\subset Q^\times$. This exact determinant image is contained in the commonly used coarser unit subgroup $\{\pm a h:a\in\det(\rho(G)),\ h\in H\}$. The choice-free statement uses the full abelianization chain model first and specializes it only by the declared coefficient map $\chi$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice convention of the twisted-chain definition. Let $L$ be a nonempty oriented link, let $E_L$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $X$ be a finite based two-dimensional CW complex with one $0$-cell, $n\ge2$ oriented $1$-cells $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, and $n-1$ oriented $2$-cells attached by based words $r_1,\ldots,r_{n-1}$. The supplied data include a based cellular spine certificate: a finite sequence of elementary cellular expansions and collapses identifying the simple-homotopy type of $X$ with the selected finite CW structure on $E_L$. Thus an abstract group isomorphism $\pi_1(X)\cong\pi_1(E_L)$ alone is not a spine certificate. Let $G=\pi_1(E_L)$, let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ and $\psi:G\twoheadrightarrow H$ be the representation and declared free-abelian deck map, and put $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb F[H])$. The associated deficiency-one presentation is $\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_{n-1}\rangle$ through the certified spine map. For $w\in F_n$, define Fox derivatives recursively by $\partial x_k/\partial x_j=\delta_{kj}$, $\partial(uv)/\partial x_j=\partial u/\partial x_j+u\,\partial v/\partial x_j$, and $\partial x_k^{-1}/\partial x_j=-x_k^{-1}\delta_{kj}$. Extend them linearly to the group ring and let $\Phi:\mathbb F[F_n]\to M_d(Q)$ be the ring homomorphism induced by $x_k\mapsto\rho(x_k)\psi(x_k)$. Form the block Fox matrix $J=(\Phi(\partial r_i/\partial x_k))_{i,k}$, of size $(n-1)d$ by $nd$. Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Let a finite colored geometric braid, a field with exact arithmetic, a representation of the closure exterior group, the full positive-meridian abelianization followed by a declared surjective color map, and compatible based spine and axis-filling certificates satisfy all input conditions of the colored twisted Burau procedure. Under [A1], let $A$ be the annulus left on the Heegaard torus after removing an open annular neighborhood of the $(2,3)$ curve. The torus-knot model identifies its core with the common source circle $c$ in the finite spine $X=M_2\cup_c M_3$, where $M_2$ and $M_3$ are mapping cylinders of the degree-two and degree-three maps of a circle and their target core circles are $a$ and $b$. By [F7], the compact exterior is the mapping cylinder of an explicit map from its boundary torus to $X$. Choose finite cell structures compatible with this map and the two degree maps, and take the unique vertex of $X$ as basepoint. In the resulting mapping-cylinder CW structure, each prism over a boundary-torus cell $\sigma$ pairs with its unglued face $\sigma\times\{0\}$; removing these pairs in decreasing cell dimension gives a finite sequence of elementary collapses onto $X$, fixing $X$ and its chosen basepoint. Thus this specific exterior-to-$X$ equivalence is simple. Give $X$ its natural finite CW structure with one vertex, core edges $a,b,c$, and $2$-cells $\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ attached by $r_2=a^2c^{-1}$ and $r_3=b^3c^{-1}$. Slide $\lambda_3$ over the oppositely oriented $\lambda_2$, replacing its attaching word by
$$r_3r_2^{-1}=(b^3c^{-1})(a^2c^{-1})^{-1}=b^3a^{-2}.$$
This elementary based $2$-cell slide removes $c$ from that attaching map. The edge $c$ now occurs exactly once in the boundary of $\lambda_2$ and nowhere else, so $(c,\lambda_2)$ is a free $1$- and $2$-cell pair and collapses. Reversing the orientation of the remaining $2$-cell gives the attaching word $a^2b^{-3}$. Thus the resulting one-vertex complex with core edges $a,b$ and one $2$-cell is based simple-homotopy equivalent to the chosen compact exterior and supplies the required certificate.

The abelianization of this spine has generators $[a],[b]$ and relation $2[a]-3[b]=0$. By [F6], the positive meridian class $[m]$ generates $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Write $[a]=p[m]$ and $[b]=q[m]$; the relation gives $2p=3q$, and $a,b$ generate the abelianization, so $\gcd(p,q)=1$. Hence $(p,q)=(3,2)$ or $(-3,-2)$; orient the two core generators consistently with the positive meridian to choose $(3,2)$. Thus the full positive-meridian deck map sends $a\mapsto t^3$ and $b\mapsto t^2$.

For $r=a^2b^{-3}$, the Fox product and inverse rules give $\partial r/\partial a=1+a$ and $\partial r/\partial b=-a^2(b^{-1}+b^{-2}+b^{-3})$. Evaluating at $a=t^3$, $b=t^2$ gives $1+t^3$ and $-(t^4+t^2+1)$. The $a$ denominator is $t^3-1\ne0$, so the deleted-$a$ quotient is $-(t^4+t^2+1)/(t^3-1)$. Factoring $t^4+t^2+1=(t^2+t+1)(t^2-t+1)$ and $t^3-1=(t-1)(t^2+t+1)$ reduces it to $(t^2-t+1)/(1-t)$.

In the cumulative basis, $g_1=x_1$ and $g_2=x_1x_2$. The positive Artin rule gives $\sigma_1(g_1)=g_2g_1^{-1}$ and fixes $g_2$. The Fox row of $g_2g_1^{-1}$ is $(-g_2g_1^{-1},1)$, which evaluates to $(-t,1)$ under the trivial representation and equal strand colors; the fixed boundary word contributes the second row $(0,1)$. Therefore the reduced block for $\sigma_1$ is $[-t]$. For automorphisms $\beta,\gamma$ of the free group, the product and inverse recursions imply $\partial(\beta(u))/\partial g_j=\sum_k\beta(\partial u/\partial g_k)\,\partial(\beta(g_k))/\partial g_j$: it holds for generators and inverses, and the product rule extends it to every word by induction. After evaluation, the braid-preserved color map makes coefficient substitution by $\beta$ leave the coefficients unchanged, so the full Fox matrices compose by matrix multiplication; their block form has bottom row $(0,1)$, so the reduced scalar blocks multiply. The two strands close to one component, hence this coloring is preserved, and the reduced block for $\sigma_1^3$ is $[-t]^3=[-t^3]$.

The fraction-field $d_1$ has the invertible block $t^3-1$, so it is onto. The deleted Fox minor from step 3.1 is nonzero, so $d_2$ is injective; since the chain dimensions are $1,2,1$ and $d_1d_2=0$, its image is the one-dimensional kernel of $d_1$. The complex is acyclic. Moreover, any Laurent-ring $1$-cycle becomes a boundary over $\mathbb Q(t)$; clearing its denominator and using that the chain module is free over the domain $\mathbb Q[t^{\pm1}]$ shows that the cycle's homology class is annihilated by a nonzero Laurent polynomial. Thus the degree-one Laurent-ring homology is torsion, and the hypotheses of the exterior-spine Wada theorem hold.

Apply [F2] to the certified spine and admissible $a$ column. Its Wada quotient from step 3.1 represents the twisted torsion class. This identifies the displayed rational function with the torsion computed from the torus-spine certificate.

The Burau numerator and boundary denominator are $N=\det([-t^3]-[1])=-(t^3+1)$ and $D=t^2-1$. Hence $N/D=-(t^3+1)/(t^2-1)=-((t+1)(t^2-t+1))/((t-1)(t+1))=(t^2-t+1)/(1-t)$. This is exactly the quotient in step 3.1, so the finite determinant calculation equals the based-spine torsion value. If the compatible axis-filling certificate is supplied as well, [F5] identifies the same ratio with the procedure output.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, the codomain and image are both the zero group, so the cokernel is trivial and has order $1=|\det A|$. Now suppose $n>0$. Multiplication on the left or right by an integer matrix with determinant $\pm1$ preserves the isomorphism type of the cokernel and preserves the absolute determinant: left multiplication changes the basis of the target, and right multiplication changes the basis of the domain.

Whenever the current remaining square submatrix is nonzero, among all matrices obtained from it by such row and column operations choose one whose least nonzero absolute entry is as small as possible; by swaps and a sign change, place that positive entry $d$ in position $(1,1)$. If any entry in its first row or column is not divisible by $d$, Euclidean division and a row or column subtraction produce a nonzero remainder strictly between $0$ and $d$, which contradicts the minimality of $d$. Clear the first row and column by subtracting multiples of the first column and row. If an entry $b$ in the remaining submatrix were not divisible by $d$, add its row to the first row, write $b=kd+r$ with $0<r<d$, and subtract $k$ times the first column from its column; swapping that column with the first would again give a smaller nonzero pivot. Hence $d$ divides the remaining submatrix.

Apply the same finite pivot procedure to each remaining square submatrix. If a remaining submatrix is zero, stop and retain it unchanged as part of the zero block. Since every nonzero pivot removes one row and one column, induction gives a diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0,\ldots,0)$ with each $d_i>0$, obtained by unimodular row and column operations. Its cokernel is $\bigoplus_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z/d_i\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z^{n-r}$. Thus it is finite exactly when $r=n$, equivalently when $\det A\ne0$; then its order is $\prod_i d_i=|\det A|$. The operations in step 1.1 preserve both conclusions for the original matrix.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice,
an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid $\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link (a finite disjoint union of oriented smoothly embedded circles,
[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]) with $r\ge1$ components,
and let $X_L:=S^3\setminus L$. Then $X_L$ is a connected smooth $3$-manifold
without boundary, and in particular is path-connected, locally path-connected
and semilocally simply connected; moreover $X_L$ has the homotopy type of a
finite CW complex
([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]). Consequently the
covering-space classification
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]) applies to $X_L$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

derivations.claim: Radial motion in each punctured normal disk gives a deformation retraction from $S^3\setminus J$ to $X$. By [F1], Alexander duality identifies $H_1(S^3\setminus J;\mathbb Z)$ with $\widetilde H^1(J;\mathbb Z)=\bigoplus_iH^1(J_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n$. The inclusion of the compact exterior induces the same homology isomorphism by the retraction in [F2]. Thus $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n$.

The boundary of a small positive normal disk to $J_i$ maps to the $i$-th Alexander-duality coordinate generator: it meets $J_i$ once positively and misses every other component. Hence $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_n]$ are the coordinate basis, with the positive orientation normalized as in [F3]. The $i$-th coordinate of $[\lambda_i]$ is zero by its zero self-linking convention, and for $j\ne i$ its $j$-th coordinate is the defined linking number $\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$. Therefore $[\delta_i]=[\lambda_i+f_i\mu_i]=\sum_jA_{ij}[\mu_j]$.

In Mayer–Vietoris for the filling, the map $H_1(\partial V_i)\to H_1(V_i)$ is onto and its kernel is generated by the meridian-disk boundary $\delta_i$. The map $H_0(\bigsqcup_i\partial V_i)\to H_0(X)\oplus H_0(\bigsqcup_iV_i)$ is injective: in coordinates it sends $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ to $(\sum_i a_i,-a_1,\ldots,-a_n)$. Exactness therefore gives $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$.

Since $A$ is invertible over $\mathbb Q$, for every $x\in\mathbb Z^n$ some positive integer $m$ clears the denominators of $A^{-1}x$, so $mx\in A\mathbb Z^n$ and each class is torsion. If $F,F'$ bound $mC,m'C$, pass to a common multiple $M$; the difference $(M/m)F-(M/m')F'$ is a 2-cycle $Z$. If $r[D]=0$, write $rD=\partial G$; the chain boundary identity gives $r(Z\mathbin{\cdot}D)=Z\mathbin{\cdot}\partial G=\partial Z\mathbin{\cdot}G=0$, hence $Z\mathbin{\cdot}D=0$. Thus the quotient is independent of the chosen bounding chain and multiple modulo integers. Replacing either cycle representative by a homologous one adds an integer by the same boundary identity.

Let $B$ be the slope-coordinate matrix $[\delta]=B[\mu]$ in $H_1(X;\mathbb Q)$; step 2.1 gives $B=A$. In the reverse filling, the slope-coordinate matrix is $B^{-1}$. Let $\widetilde J_i$ denote the core of the attached solid torus, oriented so the boundary longitude $\ell_i$ mapping to it satisfies $\delta_i\mathbin{\cdot}\ell_i=1$. Since $\delta_i\mathbin{\cdot}\mu_i=-1$, the image of $\mu_i$ in that solid torus is $-[\widetilde J_i]$. Define $H_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_Y(\widetilde J_i,\widetilde J_j)$ for $i\ne j$, and let $H_{ii}$ be the reverse-surgery framing determined by the slope $\mu_i$. For $i\ne j$, clear denominators in $[\mu_i]=\sum_k(B^{-1})_{ik}[\delta_k]$ and cap each $\delta_k$ by its meridian disk. The chain in $X$ realizing this homology relation misses every core; with $\delta_k\mathbin{\cdot}\ell_k=+1$, the capped disk in $V_k$ meets the oriented core $\widetilde J_j$ once positively if $k=j$ and not at all otherwise. Hence $(B^{-1})_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_Y(\mu_i,\widetilde J_j)=-H_{ij}$. The reverse diagonal framing is the reverse slope coefficient divided by $\delta_i\mathbin{\cdot}\mu_i=-1$, so $H_{ii}=-(B^{-1})_{ii}$. Therefore $H=-B^{-1}=-A^{-1}$.

Each old meridian $\mu_i$ represents $-\widetilde J_i$ in its attached solid torus. Hence for distinct indices their linking equals the core-linking entry $H_{ij}$; for a self-pairing, a parallel meridian maps to the parallel core specified by the reverse framing, also giving $H_{ii}$. Thus $\lambda_Y([\mu_i],[\mu_j])=-(A^{-1})_{ij}$. The chain formula is additive in both cycles, by taking common multiples and summing bounding chains, so its matrix on the meridian basis gives $\lambda_Y([x],[y])=-x^TA^{-1}y\pmod{\mathbb Z}$. If $x$ is replaced by $x+Az$, the value changes by $-z^Ty$; if $y$ is replaced by $y+Az$, it changes by $-x^Tz$, both integers because $A$ is symmetric and integral.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, choose its compact exterior $E_K$ with boundary torus $T_K$, and let $\mu$ and $\lambda$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude. The exterior homology theorem gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z$ be the composite of abelianization with the homomorphism $[\mu]\mapsto1$. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $\phi_q$ be the composite $\pi_1(E_K)\xrightarrow{\phi}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, and let $p_q:E_q\to E_K$ be the connected cover classified by $\ker\phi_q$. On $T_K$, the homomorphism sends $[\mu]\mapsto1$ and $[\lambda]\mapsto0$, so the preimage of $T_K$ is a connected torus cover whose fundamental group corresponds to $\langle\mu^q,\lambda\rangle$. Let $\widetilde\mu$ be the closed lift of $\mu^q$. Attach a solid torus to $E_q$ with its meridian identified with $\widetilde\mu$; the resulting oriented closed $3$-manifold is the $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$. In tubular coordinates near $K$, the extended map to $S^3$ has local form $(s,w)\mapsto(s,w^q)$, and the deck group $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ acts by $w\mapsto e^{2\pi i/q}w$.

Assume countable choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, there are an oriented normal-bundle trivialization, a tubular map $\Phi$ defined on an open neighbourhood containing $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, and a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. This $N(K)$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, its boundary $T_K$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^1$, and its exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with boundary $T_K$. The open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $E_K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

If $A$ is a deformation retract of a topological space $X$, then for every
$n\geq 0$ and every abelian group $G$ the inclusion $i:A\hookrightarrow X$
induces an isomorphism
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(i_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(A;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G).$$

derivations.claim: By [F2], inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups and identifies the positive meridian classes. The total-linking homomorphism in [F3] therefore corresponds to $\phi$; by [F4], $A_K$ is isomorphic to $N^{\mathrm{ab}}$ with the action induced by conjugation by a positive meridian, up to replacing that action by its inverse according to the left-versus-right lift convention.

Put $G_q=\ker(\phi\bmod q)$. For $g\in G_q$, write $\phi(g)=qk$ and set $n=g s^{-qk}\in N$. Then $g=n s^{qk}$, and the expression is unique because $\phi(s^{qk})=qk$. Thus $G_q$ is the split extension of $N$ by the infinite cyclic group generated by $s^q$, acting on $N$ by conjugation. By [F5] and [F1], $G_q$ is the fundamental group of $E_q$.

Abelianizing this split extension kills the commutators in $N$ and the relations $s^qns^{-q}=n$ for $n\in N$. By [F3], those relations impose $(t^q-1)A_K=0$ on $N^{\mathrm{ab}}$; if the inverse deck convention is used, $t^{-q}-1=-t^{-q}(t^q-1)$ generates the same submodule. The homomorphism $G_q\to\mathbb Z$, $g\mapsto\phi(g)/q$, splits by $1\mapsto s^q$, so $H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)\cong A_K/(t^q-1)A_K\oplus\mathbb Z[s^q]$.

The boundary of $E_q$ is a torus cover with basis the lift $\widetilde\mu$ of $\mu^q$ and a lifted longitude. Thicken $E_q$ and the filling solid torus by collars to form an open cover. By [F6], its Mayer–Vietoris map presents $H_1(\Sigma_q(K))$ as $H_1(E_q)$ modulo $[\widetilde\mu]$: the longitude lift maps to the core generator of the attached solid torus and eliminates that generator, while the filling meridian maps to zero there. The class $[\widetilde\mu]$ is $[s^q]$, the generator of the displayed free summand in step 3.1. Quotienting by it gives the stated isomorphism.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, choose its compact exterior $E_K$ with boundary torus $T_K$, and let $\mu$ and $\lambda$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $\phi_q$ be the composite $\pi_1(E_K)\xrightarrow{\phi}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, and let $p_q:E_q\to E_K$ be the connected cover classified by $\ker\phi_q$. On $T_K$, the homomorphism sends $[\mu]\mapsto1$ and $[\lambda]\mapsto0$, so the preimage of $T_K$ is a connected torus cover whose fundamental group corresponds to $\langle\mu^q,\lambda\rangle$. Let $\widetilde\mu$ be the closed lift of $\mu^q$. Attach a solid torus to $E_q$ with its meridian identified with $\widetilde\mu$; the resulting oriented closed $3$-manifold is the $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$. In tubular coordinates near $K$, the extended map to $S^3$ has local form $(s,w)\mapsto(s,w^q)$, and the deck group $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ acts by $w\mapsto e^{2\pi i/q}w$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], cut $B^4$ along the thickening of the pushed-in disk-band surface, producing cut copies $B_1^4,\ldots,B_q^4$. First glue these copies only along the disk $0$-handle of the branch surface. A disk thickening is a $3$-ball in the boundary of each cut $4$-ball; joining the two face balls for consecutive copies is the standard boundary-connected-sum operation, so the resulting $4$-manifold is again a $4$-ball with one $0$-handle. For each surface band, the positive face of copy $k$ glued to the negative face of copy $k+1$ joins the two band-core arcs; its regular neighborhood is a $2$-handle $D^2\times D^2$ attached along $S^1\times D^2$. There are $q-1$ such seams and $2g$ bands, so the construction gives $2g(q-1)$ $2$-handles and no other handles.

For band $a_i$ and seam $k$, the attaching circle $C_{i,k}$ is obtained by joining its oriented core arc in the positive face of copy $k$ to the core arc in the negative face of copy $k+1$, with endpoints joined through the common disk $0$-handle. In the collar of $F$, closing either face arc through that disk gives the corresponding positive or negative push-off of the closed core cycle $a_i$. Simultaneously moving $a_i^-$ and $a_j$ through the product collar to $a_i$ and $a_j^+$ preserves linking, so symmetry of linking and [F3] give $\operatorname{lk}(a_i^-,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_j^+,a_i)=V_{ji}$. For two handles at the same seam, the positive-face and negative-face contributions are therefore $V_{ij}$ and $V_{ji}$, giving $V_{ij}+V_{ji}$; for the self-entry this is framing $2V_{ii}$. For handles at consecutive seams, only their common sheet contributes, and the reflection reverses one normal direction, giving $-\operatorname{lk}(a_j^+,a_i)=-V_{ji}$ in the upper block; symmetry gives $-V_{ij}$ in the lower block. If the seams are separated by at least one unused seam, the attaching circles lie in disjoint sheet neighborhoods, so their linking is zero. These cases exhaust all pairs and give exactly $M_q(V)$.

In a normal disk to the branch surface, the $q$ cut sheets form the standard cyclic degree-$q$ branched disk; its map is $w\mapsto w^q$. Away from the branch locus, a positive meridian moves through the $q$ sheets cyclically, so the boundary exterior cover is the connected cover classified by the homomorphism $\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z/q$ sending $\mu$ to $1$. Its meridian boundary is the closed lift of $\mu^q$, which bounds the filling disk. By [F4] and uniqueness of the classified connected cover, the boundary with its branch marking is $\Sigma_q(K)$.
For $q=2$ there is one seam, so the block matrix has only its diagonal block $V+V^T$, as stated.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, choose its compact exterior $E_K$ with boundary torus $T_K$, and let $\mu$ and $\lambda$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude. The exterior homology theorem gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z$ be the composite of abelianization with the homomorphism $[\mu]\mapsto1$. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $\phi_q$ be the composite $\pi_1(E_K)\xrightarrow{\phi}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, and let $p_q:E_q\to E_K$ be the connected cover classified by $\ker\phi_q$. On $T_K$, the homomorphism sends $[\mu]\mapsto1$ and $[\lambda]\mapsto0$, so the preimage of $T_K$ is a connected torus cover whose fundamental group corresponds to $\langle\mu^q,\lambda\rangle$. Let $\widetilde\mu$ be the closed lift of $\mu^q$. Attach a solid torus to $E_q$ with its meridian identified with $\widetilde\mu$; the resulting oriented closed $3$-manifold is the $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$. In tubular coordinates near $K$, the extended map to $S^3$ has local form $(s,w)\mapsto(s,w^q)$, and the deck group $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ acts by $w\mapsto e^{2\pi i/q}w$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F$ be a connected compact oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and choose any ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with positive-push Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $M_q(V)$ be the symmetric block matrix of size $2g(q-1)$ whose $2g\times2g$ block in position $(k,\ell)$, for $1\le k,\ell\le q-1$, is $V+V^T$ if $k=\ell$, $-V^T$ if $\ell=k+1$, $-V$ if $k=\ell+1$, and $0$ if $|k-\ell|\ge2$. Then
$$
H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{coker}(M_q(V)).
$$
For $q=2$ this presentation matrix is $V+V^T$; when $g=0$ the empty matrix has trivial cokernel.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $X_K=S^3\setminus K$, and let $q\ge2$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde X_K;\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module with the positive-meridian deck action $t$. Then, as abelian groups,
$$
H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\cong A_K/(t^q-1)A_K.
$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary orientation equal to that of $K$, let $g$ satisfy $\chi(F)=1-2g$, and choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Use the positive normal convention $(n,u,v)>0$ and define $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde X_K;\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module of the knot complement $X_K=S^3\setminus K$, where the cover is classified by the total-linking homomorphism and $t$ acts by the deck transformation corresponding to the positive meridian. Then there is an isomorphism of $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$-modules
$$A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}\bigl(V-tV^T:\Lambda^{2g}\to\Lambda^{2g}\bigr).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with integer entries. Define $\operatorname{coker}(A)=\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$. Then $\operatorname{coker}(A)$ is finite if and only if $\det A\ne0$, and in that case its order is $|\det A|$. For the empty $0\times0$ matrix, take $\det A=1$ and $\operatorname{coker}(A)=0$.

derivations.claim: Quotienting the module presentation in [F2] by $(t^q-1)A_K$ gives $A_K/(t^q-1)A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}(V-tV^T:R_q^{2g}\to R_q^{2g})$ as abelian groups. The group $R_q^{2g}$ is free abelian of rank $2gq$ on $t^ka_i$ for $0\le k<q$ and $1\le i\le2g$, so this map is represented by a square integer matrix $Q_q$.

After tensoring with $\mathbb C$, multiplication by $t$ on $R_q\otimes\mathbb C$ is diagonalizable: its eigenvalues are the $q$ distinct roots $\zeta_q^j$ for $0\le j<q$, each with one-dimensional eigenspace. On the corresponding $2g$-dimensional summand, $Q_q$ acts by $V-\zeta_q^jV^T$. Therefore $\det Q_q=\prod_{j=0}^{q-1}\det(V-\zeta_q^jV^T)$. The $j=0$ factor is $\det(V-V^T)=\pm1$ by [F3]. Thus $\det Q_q\ne0$ exactly when every factor with $1\le j<q$ is nonzero, and its absolute value is the product of the absolute values of those factors.

By [F1], the group in question is $\operatorname{coker}(Q_q)$. Applying [F5] shows it is finite exactly when $\det Q_q\ne0$, with order $|\det Q_q|$; if any nontrivial-root factor vanishes, the square integer cokernel has positive free rank and is infinite.

By [F4], $D(t)=\pm t^k\Delta_K(t)$ for some integer $k$. At every root of unity, $|\pm(\zeta_q^j)^k|=1$, so $|D(\zeta_q^j)|=|\Delta_K(\zeta_q^j)|$. Hence the determinant-root criterion and product from step 3.1 give exactly the Alexander-polynomial criterion and order in the Statement, including the empty-matrix case $g=0$.
