The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. It supplies countable choice for the chosen tubular data: for any sequence of nonempty sets, apply full choice to its range and compose with the index map. Let $L=\bigcup_{i\in I}K_i$ be a finite oriented link in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, where $I$ is a finite index set. For each component $K_i$, choose a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K_i)$, with the neighbourhoods pairwise disjoint, and include its exterior $E_{K_i}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K_i)$, the positive meridian $\mu_i$, and the preferred longitude $\lambda_i$; the longitude is the degree-one parallel class in $H_1(\partial E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$ that maps to zero in $H_1(E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$. For each $i\in I$, choose an integer $n_i$. The resulting **integral framed-link surgery diagram** is this link and integer family, with the surgery result defined by removing the interiors of all $N(K_i)$ and gluing an oriented solid torus to each boundary torus so that its meridian maps to $n_i[\mu_i]+[\lambda_i]$. If $I=\varnothing$, the surgery result is $S^3$. A diagram is considered up to orientation-preserving ambient isotopy carrying each component framing; a planar projection is only a way of drawing the link.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integral framed link diagram, **Kirby move equivalence** is the equivalence relation generated by the following operations.

1. Apply an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy to the framed link in $S^3$.

2. **Handle slide:** choose distinct components $K_i,K_j$, a parallel $K_j^+$ determined by the framing of $K_j$, and an embedded band whose ends attach to $K_i$ and $K_j^+$ and whose interior misses every link component. Replace $K_i$ by the band sum of $K_i$ with $K_j^+$ and keep the framing obtained by carrying the normal framing across the band. Orient the new component by the band-sum orientation.

3. **Stabilization or destabilization:** add or remove an unknot with framing $+1$ or $-1$ that lies in a $3$-ball disjoint from all the other components.

The integer framing of a component is measured from its preferred longitude as in the integral surgery definition. A planar link projection is not part of the move data; any drawing below is schematic.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact smooth $n$-manifold with collared boundary, let $M\subseteq\partial_+W$ be a connected boundary region, and let $h_1,h_2$ be $k$-handles attached to $M$ by embeddings $f_1,f_2$ with disjoint images, where $1\le k\le n-2$. A **slide of $h_1$ over $h_2$** is determined by a band datum: points $x_i$ in the attaching spheres $f_i(S^{k-1}\times\{0\})$, trivializations of the normal bundles of the attaching spheres near $x_i$ compatible with the framings of $f_i$, and an embedded band $\beta$ whose rank-$(n-k-1)$ normal framing matches the sphere framings after quotienting out the transverse band direction, as supplied by the band lemma. The datum also includes the full framing gluing convention described below; quotient compatibility alone is insufficient. The slid handle $h_1'$ is the $k$-handle attached to $M$ by the embedding $f_1'$ whose core sphere is obtained from $f_1(S^{k-1}\times\{0\})\setminus\operatorname{int}\beta_0$ and from $f_2(S^{k-1}\times\{0\})\setminus\operatorname{int}\beta_1$ pushed off along the band framing, where $\beta_0,\beta_1$ are the two end discs, together with the side $\partial D^{k-1}\times I$ of the band, smoothed along the gluing circles; the framing of $f_1'$ is built from the framing of $f_1$, the signed framing of the parallel copy of $f_2$, and the band framing, and extends to an embedding of the attaching region. Equivalently, in the band-sum picture, the attaching sphere of $h_1'$ is the connected sum of the attaching sphere of $h_1$ with a signed framed parallel copy of the attaching sphere of $h_2$ along the band, so that the slid attachment is disjoint from the attachment of $h_2$. Different band data may give different slides; all of them are called slides of $h_1$ over $h_2$. For $k=1$ the general formula is read in the $0$-dimensional sense: the band is an arc joining a point of the first attaching $0$-sphere to a framed parallel point of the second, and the slid attaching $0$-sphere is obtained from the first by replacing that point with a parallel copy of the other point of the second attaching $0$-sphere.

For $k\ge2$, write the old ordered normal framings as $(v_{i1},\ldots,v_{iq})$, $q=n-k$, choosing the first normal line to be the transverse band line at each end. The band framing matches the classes of $(v_{i2},\ldots,v_{iq})$. Round the seams in the two-dimensional plane formed by the end disk's radial direction and the transverse band direction. The first normal to the rounded sphere is the complementary normal in this plane; choose its sign to match $v_{11}$ on the first sphere. At the other end it agrees with $\sigma v_{21}$ for a uniquely determined $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$. Use $(\sigma v_{21},v_{22},\ldots,v_{2q})$ on the entire parallel copy of the second sphere. Equivalently, when $\sigma=-1$, precompose its normal disk coordinate with $(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_q)\mapsto(-z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_q)$. This reflection concerns the copy used in the band sum; the retained handle $h_2$ keeps its original attaching embedding. Require these full ordered frames to glue across the rounded seams, rather than requiring agreement with both unreflected old frames. In an oriented boundary, this is the usual condition that the orientations induced on the two removed end disks by the framed spheres and the band have opposite boundary-gluing signs. Both addition and subtraction are allowed by the choice of band-end coordinates and this sign convention.

The seam rotation in the indicated plane, together with the remaining band normal vectors, gives a full framing agreeing with the first old framing and the signed second-copy framing. A sufficiently thin normal thickening is then an attaching embedding; take the parallel copy outside the retained attaching region and the thickening small enough to be disjoint from it. For $k=1$, use the full normal framing transported when the chosen foot is pushed along the band and across the parallel interval core of $h_2$ to its other foot; this fixes the analogous sign convention without using a positive-dimensional seam. The band lemma supplies the embedded band and its quotient framing, while the full-frame convention supplies the additional gluing data. No uniqueness of the slide is asserted. Countable Choice is inherited through the band-existence and smooth-attachment conventions.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $h_1,h_2$ be $k$-handles attached to $M\subseteq\partial_+W$ as in the slide definition, with $1\le k\le n-2$, and let $h_1'$ be a slide of $h_1$ over $h_2$ (the slid handle attached to $M$ by the band move). Then $W\cup_{f_1}h_1\cup_{f_2}h_2$ and $W\cup_{f_1'}h_1'\cup_{f_2}h_2$ are diffeomorphic relative to $\partial_0W$; more precisely there is a diffeomorphism supported in a neighbourhood of the two handles and the band region carrying the first presentation to the second. Consequently a handle slide does not change the diffeomorphism type of the presented manifold and may be performed on any of two equal-index handles.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $M$ be a closed
smooth $m$-manifold, $0\le p\le m-1$, $q=m-p$, and let
$\varphi:S^p\times D^q\hookrightarrow M$ be a framed embedded surgery sphere
([[def-framed-embedded-surgery-sphere]]). Regard $\varphi$ in the upper face
$M\times\{1\}$ of the cylinder $M\times[0,1]$ as the embedding
$\varphi\times\{1\}$, whose image is contained in the interior of that face. The
**surgery trace cobordism** of $\varphi$ is the compact smooth
$(m+1)$-manifold
$$W_\varphi=(M\times[0,1])\cup_{\varphi\times\{1\}}(D^{p+1}\times D^q),$$
that is, the cylinder $M\times[0,1]$ with the standard $(p+1)$-handle
$D^{p+1}\times D^q$ attached along the framed sphere, the corner along
$\varphi(S^p\times\partial D^q)$ being rounded in the standard way
([[def-attaching-a-smooth-handle-with-corner-rounding]]). The index shift is
part of the construction: a surgery datum of sphere dimension $p$ produces a
handle of index $p+1$, whose attaching region is $S^p\times D^q$ and whose
outgoing region is $D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}$
([[def-k-handle-core-cocore-attaching-region-and-belt-sphere]]).

The cylinder is the product cobordism with the empty handle presentation, whose
incoming face is $M_0=M\times\{0\}$ and whose outgoing face is
$M\times\{1\}$; the product presentation and its, possibly empty, collar
structure are those of
[[lem-product-cobordisms-have-critical-point-free-presentations]], and the
collar of the incoming face is the one used whenever the trace is recorded as a
cobordism ([[def-smooth-collar-of-a-manifold-boundary]],
[[def-smooth-cobordism-triad-for-morse-theory]]).

The trace carries the following fixed pieces of structure, which are not
choices made afterwards:

- the **incoming face** $M\times\{0\}$, identified with $M$ by the product
  structure;
- the **core disk** $D^{p+1}\times\{0\}$ of the attached handle;
- the **cocore disk** $\{0\}\times D^q$ of the attached handle;
- the **belt sphere** $\{0\}\times S^{q-1}\subseteq D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}$,
  a copy of which lies in the outgoing face of $W_\varphi$.

When $M$ is oriented, an oriented trace additionally requires compatibility
of the framing with the orientation: choose the handle orientation so its
attaching identification reverses the induced boundary orientations of the
handle and the cylinder. The orientation then glues, and $W_\varphi$ is an oriented
bordism from $M$ to its outgoing face, the outgoing face carrying the induced
boundary orientation and the incoming face the negative of the orientation of
$M$, in the outward-normal-first convention of
[[def-induced-boundary-orientation]]; this is the oriented bordism relation of
[[def-oriented-smooth-cobordism]], and the orientation of $M$ determines the extending orientation when this compatibility
holds. For $p\ge1$ the attaching region is connected, so the handle
orientation can always be chosen to match it. For $p=0$ its two components
must both match that one handle orientation; an arbitrary pair of interval
framings need not do so, and the unoriented trace remains defined in that case.
The supplied orientation is the only ambient orientation used ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

Nothing is proved here. In particular, the identification of the outgoing face
with the surgered manifold $M_\varphi$ of
[[def-p-surgery-on-a-smooth-m-manifold]] is the content of the upper-boundary
theorem of this page, and the deformation retractions of the trace are not part
of the definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $M$ be a closed
smooth $m$-manifold, $0\le p\le m-1$, $q=m-p$, let $\varphi$ be a framed
embedded surgery sphere in $M$, let $W_\varphi$ be its trace and let
$M_\varphi$ be the $p$-surgery on $M$ along $\varphi$. Then:

(i) $\partial W_\varphi$ is the disjoint union of the two closed faces
$M\times\{0\}\cong M$ (the incoming face) and the outgoing face, and the
outgoing face is diffeomorphic to $M_\varphi$, with compatible collar choices the identification
being the identity on $M\setminus\varphi(S^p\times\operatorname{int}D^q)$ and
carrying the belt sphere of the handle to the belt sphere of the surgery;

(ii) there are homotopy equivalences of pairs relative to the indicated faces,
$$(W_\varphi,M)\simeq(M\cup_{\varphi_0}D^{p+1},M),\qquad (W_\varphi,M_\varphi)\simeq(M_\varphi\cup_{\beta}D^q,M_\varphi),$$
where $\beta$ is the belt-sphere embedding. The characteristic disks in these
models include the collar paths from the attaching spheres to the respective
faces; the raw core disk in the upper handle does not have boundary in the
incoming face;

(iii) in particular the trace is a bordism from $M$ to $M_\varphi$, as the
definition of the trace asserts.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For an ambient isotopy, carry each component neighbourhood, meridian, and preferred longitude along the isotopy. The endpoint diffeomorphism of $S^3$ therefore maps every filling meridian to the same framed slope on the corresponding endpoint torus. Extend it over each attached solid torus by the product identification used in the filling. The resulting map is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of the filled manifolds.

Applying [A1] to the family of values of any sequence $(X_n)$ in [F8] gives a choice function on that range; composing it with $n\mapsto X_n$ supplies the choice function required by [F8]. Thus the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis of [F3]–[F6] holds. For a diagram $D$, form its $4$-dimensional surgery trace from $S^3\times[0,1]$ by attaching one $2$-handle for each framed link component. Orient the product by $dt$ followed by the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient each handle so its attaching identification reverses the induced boundary orientations of the handle and cylinder, as required by [F5]; this is possible because each attaching region $S^1\times D^2$ is connected. The trace is connected. On the outgoing face, the unaltered part $E_D=S^3\setminus\bigcup_i\operatorname{int}N(K_i)$ has the standard $S^3$ orientation from the upper product face, exactly the orientation that the filling conventions [F1, F7] extend over the attached solid tori. The link exterior is nonempty and connected (paths in $S^3$ can be perturbed off the one-dimensional link; for the empty diagram $E_D=S^3$). Thus the identity-on-$E_D$ identification in [F6] preserves the surgery orientation. The link slide of [F2] is exactly the $k=2$ handle slide of [F3], including its full transported normal framing. Since $1\le2\le4-2$, [F4] supplies a diffeomorphism between the two traces relative to the incoming $S^3$ face. Both traces have the product orientation there and the diffeomorphism fixes that face; its tangent derivative is the identity and its normal derivative preserves the interior side, so it preserves the trace orientation. Its restriction preserves the induced orientations on the outgoing faces. Composing with the identifications in [F6] gives the required orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of surgery results.

Suppose a split unknot is added with coefficient $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ in a ball disjoint from the rest of the link. The separating sphere shows that the filled manifold is the connected sum of the old surgery result with the filling of the unknot exterior along $\varepsilon[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$. For the standard unknot, take $E_U=\{|z_2|\ge1/\sqrt2\}\subset S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, identified with $D^2\times S^1$ by $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,z_2/|z_2|)$. Its preferred longitude $\lambda_U$ is the meridian of this solid torus, and $\mu_U$ is its core longitude. The diffeomorphism $g_\varepsilon(z,w)=(w^{-\varepsilon}z,w)$ of $D^2\times S^1$ preserves orientation, fixes $[\lambda_U]$, and sends $[\mu_U]$ to $[\mu_U]-\varepsilon[\lambda_U]$; hence it sends the slope $\varepsilon[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$ to the unoriented meridional slope $[\mu_U]$. Choose the $S^3$ gluing with meridian $[\mu_U]$ and the $\varepsilon$-filling gluing as its pullback by $g_\varepsilon^{-1}$. The map $g_\varepsilon$ on the exterior and the identity on the attached solid torus then give an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism between the two fillings. Filling along $[\mu_U]$ restores the original unknot neighbourhood, so the $\varepsilon$-framed unknot filling is orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic to $S^3$. Hence the connected sum is the original manifold: deleting a ball and regluing the complementary ball of $S^3$ restores the same manifold. Removing a split $\varepsilon$-framed unknot is the inverse operation.

Each allowed move preserves the oriented surgery manifold by steps 1.1–1.3. Composing the finitely many orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms along a move sequence proves the assertion for Kirby-move-equivalent diagrams.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. It supplies countable choice for the chosen tubular data: for any sequence of nonempty sets, apply full choice to its range and compose with the index map. Let $L=\bigcup_{i\in I}K_i$ be a finite oriented link in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, where $I$ is a finite index set. For each component $K_i$, choose a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K_i)$, with the neighbourhoods pairwise disjoint, and include its exterior $E_{K_i}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K_i)$, the positive meridian $\mu_i$, and the preferred longitude $\lambda_i$; the longitude is the degree-one parallel class in $H_1(\partial E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$ that maps to zero in $H_1(E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$. For each $i\in I$, choose an integer $n_i$. The resulting **integral framed-link surgery diagram** is this link and integer family, with the surgery result defined by removing the interiors of all $N(K_i)$ and gluing an oriented solid torus to each boundary torus so that its meridian maps to $n_i[\mu_i]+[\lambda_i]$. If $I=\varnothing$, the surgery result is $S^3$. A diagram is considered up to orientation-preserving ambient isotopy carrying each component framing; a planar projection is only a way of drawing the link.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integral framed link diagram, **Kirby move equivalence** is the equivalence relation generated by the following operations.

1. Apply an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy to the framed link in $S^3$.

2. **Handle slide:** choose distinct components $K_i,K_j$, a parallel $K_j^+$ determined by the framing of $K_j$, and an embedded band whose ends attach to $K_i$ and $K_j^+$ and whose interior misses every link component. Replace $K_i$ by the band sum of $K_i$ with $K_j^+$ and keep the framing obtained by carrying the normal framing across the band. Orient the new component by the band-sum orientation.

3. **Stabilization or destabilization:** add or remove an unknot with framing $+1$ or $-1$ that lies in a $3$-ball disjoint from all the other components.

The integer framing of a component is measured from its preferred longitude as in the integral surgery definition. A planar link projection is not part of the move data; any drawing below is schematic.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice,
an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid $\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

derivations.claim: **Framing bookkeeping from bands.** For disjoint oriented components $X,Y$, write $\operatorname{lk}(X,Y)$ for the coefficient of $[Y]$ in $H_1(E_X;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_X]$, using the positive meridian convention in [F1]. A parallel representing integer framing $a$ has class $[\lambda_X]+a[\mu_X]$, so its linking with $X$ is $a$. This linking number is symmetric: choose transverse 2-chains bounding $X$ and $Y$ in $S^3$ (they exist since $H_1(S^3)=0$); the boundary formula for their intersection 1-chain gives $\operatorname{lk}(X,Y)=\operatorname{lk}(Y,X)$. For oriented components $A,B$ with framings $a,b$ and linking number $l$, a slide of $A$ over the signed parallel $sB$, $s=\pm1$, has framing $a+b+2sl$. Indeed the band sum and its framing parallel are homologous, in the complement of the other curve, to the sums of the corresponding old parallels; additivity gives the two cross-linkings $sl,sl$. Its linking with a third component $C$ is $\operatorname{lk}(A,C)+s\operatorname{lk}(B,C)$, because the band sum represents $[A]+s[B]$ in the complement of $C$. These are consequences of the actual parallel-and-band construction, not permissions to replace a geometric link by a matrix. We use bands with no added full twist; an existing twist of any component is carried with its strip.

**The zero-meridian crossing operation.** A slide over $U$ can switch a crossing of a selected strand with the strand of $K$ encircled by $U$. Here is the local construction. Take the disk of $U$ transverse to the latter strand, and take a thin band from the selected strand to a disk-parallel copy of $U$. Put the interior of the band off the disk and all the link. In a cross-section perpendicular to the encircled strand, the band sum replaces a short detour on one side of the origin by that detour followed by one signed circuit about the origin. Round its two band corners. The result is the detour on the other side: the region between the circuit with its return segment and this detour is a disk in the punctured cross-section, so pushing across its product with the short strand interval is an ambient isotopy relative to the ends. Thus precisely the chosen crossing changes. Use the opposite band side for the opposite crossing. The disk-parallel framing of $U$ has no twist, so the strip is the transported framing of this operation, including any change of self-linking prescribed by step 1.1. The operation is valid when the selected strand is another part of $K$: use distinct disjoint short arcs as the two band ends. The encircled arc is unchanged, so $U$ remains its small zero-framed meridian. To use a different arc, move this meridian along a thin tubular neighbourhood of $K$; a meridional disk slides along the product tube, so this is an isotopy of $U$ in the complement of $K\cup L$, with its disk framing. The bands and their corners have smooth rounded product neighbourhoods; the disk pushes extend by a cutoff in those neighbourhoods to smooth orientation-preserving ambient isotopies.

**Signed-unit blowdown as allowed moves.** Suppose an unknotted component $J$ has framing $\varepsilon=\pm1$ and a spanning disk $D$ transverse to the other strands. At a piercing of sign $d$, slide that strand over $-\varepsilon d$ times the oriented framed parallel of $J$. Route its band beside $D$. The parallel makes exactly $\varepsilon$ full turns around the disk-normal direction, so this banded detour removes that piercing and gives one signed twist of the remaining disk-piercing strands. This is a geometric disk operation: cut the strands at their small piercing intervals, carry their cut ends along disjoint narrow radial strips of $D$ to its boundary, and use the framed parallel there to join the ends on the same side of $D$. Nested radial strips are used one at a time; corners are rounded in the disk-normal product. After all piercings have been removed, $J$ bounds a disk missing the remaining link, so a small neighbourhood of that disk is a ball separating $J$. Delete it by [F2]. The remaining strands have acquired $-\varepsilon$ full twist about $D$; reversing this construction gives the corresponding blowup. The framing/linking updates are $a_i'=a_i-\varepsilon l_i^2$ and $l_{ij}'=l_{ij}-\varepsilon l_il_j$, where $l_i=\operatorname{lk}(A_i,J)$: apply step 1.1 successively to the signed slides, or count the crossings of the parallel strips in the displayed full twist. In the applications below each remaining component crosses $D$ only once. A full twist of one such strand is a curl of an unknotted arc; of two such strands it is their two-strand full twist. Thus this operation has an explicit geometric meaning, as well as the displayed integer update.

**Splitting the pair from the old link.** Choose a regular finite projection of the compact smooth link, keeping a small meridional arc marked. Such a projection can be obtained by replacing finitely many short arcs inside disjoint tubular charts by polygonal arcs and rounding, followed by a small generic change of direction; the replacements are isotopies in their product tubes, and finitely many nonadjacent projected line segments have only finitely many transverse intersections after that change. At every mixed crossing of $K$ with $L$, use step 2.1 on the strand of $L$ to put $K$ above that strand. Its framing does not change: that component has linking zero with the small meridian $U$, and $U$ has framing zero, so step 1.1 gives the same integer. The local replacement changes no crossing between two strands of $L$. Consequently the old framed link, considered by itself, is still its original framed isotopy class. Once $K$ is above $L$ at every mixed crossing, lift $K$ and its very small meridian in the projection direction above a slab containing $L$, and move them into a ball disjoint from $L$. This lift has no obstruction at a mixed crossing because their height order was chosen precisely this way. From now on all operations are in that ball.

**Unknotting the companion.** Fix a base point away from the meridional arc. Switch self-crossings of $K$ by step 2.1 until its based diagram is descending: on traversing from the base point, the first encounter with each crossing is the overpass. A descending diagram is an unknot by the following explicit disk construction. Cut at the base point, and straighten the arc in traversal order, lifting each initial segment above all later segments; each lift is possible because the initial segment is the overpass at every first encounter. Join the endpoints by the short base-point arc outside the projection. This gives a simple planar circle after a final height isotopy, hence an embedded spanning disk. There are finitely many crossings, so these are finitely many moves and disk pushes. Keep $U$ tiny at an unchanged arc during each crossing operation and carry it by the subsequent isotopies. The result is the standard Hopf pair $K_n,U_0$ in the disjoint ball, for some integer $n$. Changes of $n$ have been carried by the strips; we do not assert that crossing changes preserve $n$.

Sliding $K$ over either signed disk-parallel of $U$ changes $n$ by $+2$ or $-2$ by step 1.1. The curves $((1-t)r w^{\pm1},w)$, $0\le t\le1$, are embedded for every $t$, since the second coordinate is $w$. They give an isotopy to the core, supported away from the exterior boundary and hence away from $U$. Extend its velocity in a small tube by a cutoff to obtain an ambient isotopy; the full normal strip is transported. Thus the pair is again a Hopf pair, rather than merely having the same linking matrix. Repeating gives $K_0,U_0$ if $n$ is even and $K_1,U_0$ if $n$ is odd. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $N,M$ be connected nonempty compact oriented smooth three-manifolds, with their boundaries identified with the same oriented surface $\Sigma$ in the bordism convention and with fixed compatible product collars. There is a finite framed link in $\operatorname{int}N$ whose surgery is diffeomorphic to $M$ with the prescribed external boundary parametrization. It may be realized as a four-dimensional two-handle trace with those marked horizontal faces and vertical collar $\Sigma\times[0,1]$. More generally this holds componentwise for a specified common component partition; empty input is treated by the empty union. In particular a fixed connected standard base with the required boundary may be chosen on each component, and a closed component may use $N=S^3$. An explicit connected standard base is the complement in $S^3$ of standard handlebodies placed in pairwise disjoint balls, one for each boundary component with its specified genus, with the given surface parametrizations attached to these boundary copies. This is relative surgery existence, not equivalence or completeness of surgery moves. Decorations may be carried by the resulting actual diffeomorphism; a complete decorated move theorem is a separate assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. It supplies countable choice for the chosen tubular data: for any sequence of nonempty sets, apply full choice to its range and compose with the index map. Let $L=\bigcup_{i\in I}K_i$ be a finite oriented link in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, where $I$ is a finite index set. For each component $K_i$, choose a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K_i)$, with the neighbourhoods pairwise disjoint, and include its exterior $E_{K_i}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K_i)$, the positive meridian $\mu_i$, and the preferred longitude $\lambda_i$; the longitude is the degree-one parallel class in $H_1(\partial E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$ that maps to zero in $H_1(E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$. The standard unknotted Heegaard torus is $T_r=\{|z_1|=r,\ |z_2|=\sqrt{1-r^2}\}$; its two sides are solid tori. In the angular coordinates $(u,v)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$ given by $(u,v)\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i u},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i v})$, let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the first and second coordinate classes in $H_1(T_r;\mathbb Z)$. For coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the **oriented torus knot** $T(p,q)$ is the image of $s\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i p s},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i q s})$, for $s\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, oriented by increasing $s$; it represents the primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$. The mirror convention is the reflection $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,\overline{z_2})$, which sends $T(p,q)$ to $T(p,-q)$ with image orientation, and reversing the knot orientation gives $T(-p,-q)$. For nonzero $p,q$ with $d=\gcd(|p|,|q|)>1$, the corresponding torus link is the union of $d$ disjoint parallel copies of the primitive slope $(p/d,q/d)$; it is not a single embedded curve of class $p\alpha+q\beta$. The exterior is $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ for a chosen closed tubular neighborhood. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and a preferred longitude is a degree-one class on $\partial E_K$ whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Choose $N(K)$ to be a sufficiently small closed metric tube around the orbit $K$ for the round metric; this tube is invariant because $\rho_t$ is isometric and preserves $K$. Set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. Then

$$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The common element $h=x^p=y^q$ is central and represents a regular fiber of a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ over a disk. The fibration has two distinguished core fibers of multiplicities $|p|$ and $|q|$; a fiber of multiplicity one is regular, and a fiber of multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. Thus there are exactly two exceptional fibers when $|p|,|q|>1$, and one is regular when one absolute parameter is $1$.

For any integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, compatible based paths identify the positive normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude in the peripheral system as

$$\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta,\qquad \lambda=h\mu^{-pq}.$$

Here the positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and the preferred longitude has degree one around $K$ and maps to zero in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Their homology classes form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so both classes are primitive.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume countable choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, there are an oriented normal-bundle trivialization, a tubular map $\Phi$ defined on an open neighbourhood containing $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, and a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. This $N(K)$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, its boundary $T_K$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^1$, and its exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with boundary $T_K$. The open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $E_K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $M$ be a
finitely presented $R$-module ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]),
so that there are $m,n\in\mathbb N$ and a presentation

$$R^m\xrightarrow{\ A\ }R^n\xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }M\longrightarrow0 .$$

Fix the standard bases $e_1,\dots,e_m$ of $R^m$ and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $R^n$
([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]) and let $A=(a_{ij})$ be the
$n\times m$ matrix of the $R$-linear map $\alpha$ with respect to them: the
$j$-th column of $A$ is the coordinate vector of $\alpha(e_j)$, so
$\alpha(e_j)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij}f_i$. Such a matrix is called a **presentation
matrix** of $M$ (for the chosen presentation). A **minor** of $A$ of size
$r\times r$ is the determinant $\det(a_{i_sj_t})_{s,t=1}^r$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]) of the square submatrix obtained by
choosing rows $i_1<\dots<i_r$ and columns $j_1<\dots<j_r$; determinants of
$1\times1$ and $0\times0$ submatrices are allowed, with the empty determinant
equal to $1$.

For $k\ge0$ the **$k$-th elementary ideal** $E_k(M)$ of the presented module $M$
is the ideal of $R$ generated by the determinants of **all**
$(n-k)\times(n-k)$ minors of $A$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]): if $n-k>n$ or $n-k>m$ there is no such
minor, and the ideal generated by the empty set is $0$. In particular no minor
is nonzero-by-convention: the conventions are
$$E_k(M)=R\quad\text{for }k\ge n,\qquad E_k(M)=0\quad\text{for }k<n-m .$$
For $0\le k\le\min(n,m)$ the ideal $E_k(M)$ is the ideal generated by the
$(n-k)\times(n-k)$ minors; e.g. $E_1(M)$ is generated by the
$(n-1)\times(n-1)$ minors of $A$, and $E_n(M)=R$ because the $0\times0$ minor
is $1$. This is the $k$-th **Fitting ideal** $\operatorname{Fit}_k(M)$ of the
Stacks Project (Tag 07Z6, Lemma 15.8.2 and Definition 15.8.3), which is
indexed by the size $n-k$ of the complementary minors; the two conventions
$0=E_{-1}\subset E_0\subset\cdots$ agree on the range $0\le k\le\min(n,m)$.

**Caveats.** (i) The notation $E_k(M)$ suppresses the chosen presentation; the
ideal defined here is a priori attached to the presentation and it is the
content of [[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]] that
it is in fact an invariant of $M$. (ii) The conventions in the degenerate
ranges are conventions, not theorems; they are the ones compatible with the
Stacks numbering and with independence of the presentation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, so that the Alexander module $A_L$ of an oriented
nonempty link $L$ is defined and finitely presented over
$\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]],
[[lem-the-alexander-module-of-a-link-complement-is-finitely-presented]]). Let
$r$ be the number of components of $L$. Define the **one-variable Alexander
polynomial** $\Delta_L(t)\in\Lambda$ to be a greatest common divisor of the zeroth
elementary ideal $E_0(A_L)$
([[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]]), i.e. a generator of
the smallest principal ideal of $\Lambda$ containing $E_0(A_L)$
([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]],
[[def-unique-factorisation-domain]]); it is well defined up to multiplication
by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$
([[lem-units-and-powers-of-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]). The **Alexander
invariant** is the normalisation
$$D_L(t):=\begin{cases}\Delta_L(t),&r>1,\\[2pt] \dfrac{\Delta_L(t)}{1-t},&r=1,\end{cases}$$
understood for a knot as an element of the fraction field of $\Lambda$ when
$(1-t)\nmid\Delta_L(t)$; for the integer-valued link formulas of this page the
distinction matters and is stated with each use.

**Caveats.** The ideal $E_0(A_L)$ is a well-defined invariant of $L$ because
$A_L$ is finitely presented and elementary ideals are independent of the
presentation
([[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]]); a greatest
common divisor in a unique factorisation domain is well defined up to units, and
the units of $\Lambda$ are $\pm t^k$. For every link the absolute one-variable Alexander module admits a square
presentation, so $E_0(A_L)$ is principal, generated by its determinant (the
standard link fact recorded in [F3]). For a knot ($r=1$), every gcd
representative satisfies $\Delta_L(1)=\pm1$. These standard presentation and
normalisation facts are recorded here; the gcd definition itself uses only
finite presentability and unique factorisation.

The Laurent polynomial ring $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ of
[[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]] is Noetherian, hence every ideal of
$\Lambda$ is finitely generated, and $\Lambda$ is a unique factorisation
domain; its units are $\pm t^k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, and $t$ is prime in $\mathbb Z[t]$ but becomes a unit in $\Lambda$.

derivations.claim: Abelianizing the presentation in [F1] gives the relation $p[x]=q[y]$. The map $\phi(x)=q$, $\phi(y)=p$ is onto because $\gcd(p,q)=1$; its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(p,-q)$, exactly the abelianized relation vector, so the abelianization is $\mathbb Z$. The meridian in [F1] maps to $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, so the epimorphism $\phi$ in the Statement is precisely the positive total-linking homomorphism that classifies the cover in [F4].

For every integer $n$, $(z^n-1)/(z-1)$ is a finite Laurent sum; for $n<0$ it equals $-(z^{-1}+\cdots+z^n)$. In the lifted attaching word, a positive edge contributes the current deck translate and a negative edge contributes the negative of the preceding translate. The $x^p$ block therefore contributes $(x^p-1)/(x-1)$ to the $x$-edge coordinate. The following $y^{-q}$ block starts after the $x^p$ translate and contributes $x^p(y^{-q}-1)/(y-1)$ to the $y$-edge coordinate. These are the complete signed edge contributions of the two-cell in $\widetilde P_\phi$.

The cyclic cover in the Statement has cellular chain groups $C_2=\Lambda$, $C_1=\Lambda^2$, $C_0=\Lambda$. Its first boundary is $d_1=(t^q-1,\ t^p-1)$ because lifted $x$- and $y$-edges end $q$ and $p$ deck steps from their starts. Evaluating the two edge contributions in step 1.2 at $x=t^q$, $y=t^p$ gives the second boundary column; the $y$-coordinate is $t^{pq}(t^{-pq}-1)/(t^p-1)=-(t^{pq}-1)/(t^p-1)$:
$$d_2(1)=\left(\frac{t^{pq}-1}{t^q-1},\ -\frac{t^{pq}-1}{t^p-1}\right)^T.$$
This is the cellular boundary of the lifted two-cell.

In $\Lambda$, $\gcd(t^p-1,t^q-1)\doteq t-1$: for positive exponents the Euclidean algorithm gives this because $\gcd(|p|,|q|)=1$, and negative exponents differ from the positive ones by units. Hence $a=(t^q-1)/(t-1)$ and $b=(t^p-1)/(t-1)$ are coprime. The kernel of $d_1$ is the free rank-one submodule generated by $(b,-a)^T$: if $au+bv=0$, unique factorization implies $a\mid v$, and then $(u,v)$ is a multiple of $(b,-a)$. The column in step 2.1 is $\delta_{p,q}(b,-a)^T$. To show $\delta_{p,q}\in\Lambda$, replace signed exponents by $m=|p|$, $n=|q|$, which changes each factor only by a unit. Set $A=(t^m-1)/(t-1)$ and $B=(t^n-1)/(t-1)$. They are coprime; since $m,n$ divide $mn$, both divide $(t^{mn}-1)/(t-1)$. Unique factorization gives $AB\mid(t^{mn}-1)/(t-1)$, hence $\delta_{m,n}=((t^{mn}-1)/(t-1))/(AB)\in\Lambda$, and the signed quotient is a unit multiple. If $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, this quotient is a unit, so the same cyclic presentation gives $A_K=0$.

By [F5], $H_1$ of the cyclic cover of $P_{p,q}$ is $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_2\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$. The presentation complex and $E_K$ have the same fundamental group and the same homomorphism $\phi$; the fundamental groups of their cyclic covers are the corresponding kernels, and the deck action on their abelianizations is conjugation by a preimage of $1\in\mathbb Z$. Hurewicz therefore identifies their first-homology $\Lambda$-modules. Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3] by [L1]; the deformation retraction then identifies the cyclic-cover homology of $E_K$ with that of $S^3\setminus K$. Thus $A_K\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$.

The one-by-one presentation $[\delta_{p,q}]$ of $\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$ has $E_0$ generated by its sole $1\times1$ minor, namely $\delta_{p,q}$. Isomorphism invariance of the Alexander module and the definition [F6] give $E_0(A_K)=(\delta_{p,q})$ and hence $\Delta_K\doteq\delta_{p,q}$.

citations.quote: Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

An essential smooth embedded circle in the standard torus $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ represents a nonzero primitive integral homology class. A finite disjoint family of essential smooth circles can be carried by a jointly smooth ambient isotopy of $T$ to parallel affine circles. Two essential circles with the same primitive unoriented class are smoothly ambient isotopic. The components between disjoint essential circles have smooth annulus parameters, with prescribed product collars on their boundary circles. No choice axiom is assumed.

Likewise two smooth spanning arcs of a parametrized annulus with the same endpoints and relative winding number are smoothly ambient isotopic relative to any collars on which they already agree. When disjoint, they have a smooth disk-strip parameter; disjoint essential circles in a parametrized annulus have smooth annulus-strip parameters. All isotopies may be stationary near their time endpoints.

For $n=2,3$, a given smooth ball embedding $e:D^n\to N$ into a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold is isotopic through embeddings to a small coordinate round ball, and that embedding isotopy extends ambiently with compact support. For a parametrized smooth $n$-ball $B$ and a parametrized smooth boundary $(n-1)$-disk $W$, the pair $(B,W)$ is diffeomorphic to the standard ball with a hemispherical window. The diffeomorphism can retain the specified window parameter, using stereographic parameters on the standard hemisphere and allowing the necessary orientation of that parameter. No choice axiom is assumed.

Consequently, attaching a parametrized smooth $n$-ball to a smooth $n$-manifold along such a window does not change its diffeomorphism type, provided an attaching collar and corner rounding are supplied. The resulting diffeomorphism is supported in the added ball and an arbitrarily small receiving collar. The inverse assertion holds for removing a ball that meets the boundary in exactly one such window with the supplied collar charts. In dimension two the windows are intervals.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

Let $F_0=f(F)$ be a compact two-sided smoothly embedded surface in a compact smooth three-manifold, with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$, and let $F_1,H_1$ be its angular neatification from [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]]. The ambient manifold may be nonorientable. If $F_1$ has a smooth compressing disk or smooth boundary-compressing disk, then $F_0$ has a disk of the same type. Boundary-compressing disks can also be transported in the opposite direction: if $F_0$ has one, then $F_1$ has one. Consequently absence of either kind of smooth disk passes from $F_0$ to $F_1$.

Here the boundary-compressing witness has one boundary arc in the surface and the other in $\partial M$, its interior missing both. The construction allows the broader convention of ordinary smooth disk embeddings with tangential endpoint contact, and also gives smooth corner-disk witnesses with transverse surface arcs when that convention is used. No smooth ambient removal of an original surface tangency is asserted.

derivations.claim: First apply [F9] to the given surface, fixed pointwise on its boundary. The resulting surface is neat. Incompressibility passes to it, and a boundary-compressing witness passes in either direction; absence of boundary compressions therefore passes as well. Work with this neat representative for the following smooth collar constructions. The boundary-fixing topological ambient extension pulls any resulting boundary-parallel product back to the actual original surface. Thus this preparation does not add a neatness hypothesis to the Statement. Write $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha$ is the essential proper arc in $A$ and $\beta$ lies in a boundary torus $T$. In an annulus every essential proper arc joins its two boundary circles: cut along a radial spanning arc and use a lift to the strip; an arc returning to the same boundary cuts off a disk there. Consequently both boundary circles of $A$ lie on this same $T$. They are essential on $T$: otherwise choose an innermost disk bounded by one of them in $T$, push it inward off the annulus collar, and obtain a compression of $A$. By [F2] the two circles cut $T$ into two parametrized annuli. The interior of $\beta$ misses them and joins them, so it spans one of these annuli, denoted $A_0$.

Push the interior of $A_0$ a little into its inward collar, keeping its rim on $A$, and round the rim. The union $S=A\cup A_0$ is a torus with a displayed corner before rounding. The curve $\alpha\cup\beta$ on it meets a core of $A$ once algebraically, not merely modulo two: $\alpha$ is a spanning arc of the annulus. It is therefore a nonseparating essential circle. Compress $S$ along $D$, taking two parallel copies of $D$ in its disk neighborhood; the result is a sphere. Irreducibility supplies a parametrized ball bounded by it. The disk neighborhood lies outside this ball: its strip along $\beta$ is joined to $\partial M$ through the gap left when that strip was removed from $A_0$, without crossing the compressed sphere. A ball in the interior cannot contain that boundary collar. Restoring the disk neighborhood therefore attaches one marked $1$-handle to the ball, rather than removing a possibly knotted handle from it. Its two attaching disk windows have the actual parallel-copy parameters of $D$. They can be put in standard positions by [F3]: standardize one window, shrink the other in the connected complement of the first on the boundary sphere, and move it to the opposite standard disk by the finite supported construction in [F3]'s Proof 1.1–2.1, fixing the first. Thus the restored region $U$ is a smooth solid torus with meridian disk the cocore of this handle. Its boundary is the displayed $S$; all corner changes are restored by the original quadrant collars.

The marking is essential. In the product coordinates $U=D^2\times S^1$ supplied by that ball and handle, let $(\mu,\lambda)$ denote the meridian-longitude basis of its boundary. Each rim circle of $A$ meets the cocore boundary once algebraically, because it meets $\alpha\cup\beta$ once. Hence its slope is $p\mu+q\lambda$ with $q=\pm1$. By [F2] normalize the two rim circles to affine circles of that slope. The entire boundary isotopy extends into a radial annulus of $D^2\times S^1$: in the boundary radial coordinate use the same formula $(r,x)\mapsto(r,h_{\eta(r)t}(x))$ as [F3], identity near the inner solid torus. The product diffeomorphism $(z,e^{i\theta})\mapsto(e^{ip\theta}z,e^{iq\theta})$, with inverse $(z,e^{i\varphi})\mapsto(e^{-ipq\varphi}z,e^{iq\varphi})$, carries longitudinal circles to that slope, up to replacing $p$ by its negative according to the chosen inverse. Apply its inverse. The two complementary boundary annuli now correspond to the two arcs between two points on $\partial D^2$, times $S^1$. The disk with one of these marked arcs is a rectangle with its bottom edge marked, with the usual rounded-corner interpretation, by [F3] in dimension two. Taking its product with $S^1$ gives a product between the corresponding annuli: the first is $A\times\{0\}$, and $A\times\{1\}\cup\partial A\times[0,1]$ is the second annulus $A_0$. Restore the retained quadrant collars to get this product for the actual original $A$ and boundary annulus in $\partial M$. This proves boundary-parallelity in [F1]'s precise sense. The winding-one condition from $D$ is what justifies this product; complementary annuli in an arbitrary solid torus do not suffice. All selected charts, windows and curve moves were finite, and [F2]–[F3] require no choice.
