The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let
$(M,g)$ be a connected, boundaryless, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold
that is complete and whose sectional curvature satisfies $K\le0$ at every
tangent two-plane. Then for every $p\in M$:

1. the exponential map $\exp_p:T_pM\to M$ is a smooth covering map when its
   domain carries the pulled-back metric $\tilde g:=\exp_p^*g$;
2. $(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is complete and $T_pM$ is simply connected, so $\exp_p$ is
   a **universal cover** of $M$;
3. if in addition $M$ is simply connected, then $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism
   for every $p$, and $M$ is diffeomorphic to the Euclidean space $T_pM$.

The curvature sign is the one of [[def-sectional-curvature]], so $K\le0$
includes the flat case; no lower bound on curvature, no compactness and no
dimension restriction (other than finiteness) are assumed. The completeness of
$(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is a conclusion, not a hypothesis: without it the pulled-back
metric need not be complete even for a local diffeomorphism of a complete
manifold.

Assume exactly $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian
manifold without boundary, let $p\in M$, let $v\in\mathcal E_p$ be in the
domain of $\exp_p$, and let $w\in T_pM$. Define
$$\gamma:[0,1]\to M,\qquad \gamma(t)=\exp_p(tv).$$
There is a unique Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ with
$$J(0)=0,\qquad D_tJ(0)=w,$$
where the derivative at $0$ is one-sided. For every $t\in[0,1]$,
$$J(t)=d(\exp_p)_{tv}(tw),$$
using the canonical identification $T_{tv}(\mathcal E_p)\cong T_pM$,
and in particular $d(\exp_p)_v(w)=J(1)$. The exponential differential is
evaluated at points $tv\in\mathcal E_p$, as ensured by the geodesic-time
scaling property. Constant central geodesics, zero initial data, and dimension
zero are included. No completeness hypothesis is imposed.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]]; the tensor-determination argument is choice-free.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as inherited through
[[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]]; the algebraic proof below
uses no additional choice. A Riemannian manifold has constant sectional
curvature $K$ if and only if

$$R(X,Y)Z=K\bigl(g(Y,Z)X-g(X,Z)Y\bigr).$$

Equivalently,

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)=K\bigl(g(Y,Z)g(X,W)-g(X,Z)g(Y,W)\bigr).$$

Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be smooth on an interval, with smooth one-sided data at included endpoints. For every $t_0\in I$ and $v_0\in E_{\gamma(t_0)}$ there is exactly one parallel section $V$ on all of $I$ with $V(t_0)=v_0$. The same holds for a piecewise smooth curve on a compact interval, with continuity at its finitely many corners. A singleton carries its prescribed vector. No AC is required for a supplied connection and curve.

Let $(M,g)$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$
be an interval with nonempty interior, and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an
affinely parametrized geodesic. For every $a\in I$ and every
$v,w\in T_{\gamma(a)}M$, there is exactly one smooth Jacobi field $J$ along
all of $\gamma$ such that
$$J(a)=v,\qquad D_tJ(a)=w.$$
If $a$ is an included endpoint, $D_tJ(a)$ is interpreted one-sided. Constant
geodesics and dimension zero are included. The result requires no completeness,
compactness of $I$, or axiom of choice.

Levi–Civita parallel transport preserves inner products, lengths, angles of nonzero vectors, and Riemannian volume density. If the manifold is oriented, it also preserves its oriented Riemannian volume form. Without a supplied global orientation only density preservation is claimed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,s):z\in\mathbb C,\ s>0\}$ use the metric $s^{-2}(|dz|^2+ds^2)$. Suppose $f:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ is a quasi-isometry with constants $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$:
$$\lambda^{-1}d(x,y)-\varepsilon\le d(f(x),f(y))\le\lambda d(x,y)+\varepsilon,$$
and with coarsely dense image. Then it induces an ideal-boundary homeomorphism $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$. There is $H=H(\lambda,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that, after postcomposition by any Möbius transformation carrying $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$, its plane restriction satisfies
$$\max_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\le H\min_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\qquad(z\in\mathbb C,\ r>0).$$
Here $h$ in that inequality denotes the normalized map. If the boundary homeomorphism preserves orientation, it is analytically quasiconformal in sphere charts, with constant at most $H$. If it reverses orientation, postcomposition with complex conjugation is quasiconformal with that constant. If $f$ is equivariant for a homomorphism between groups of hyperbolic isometries, its boundary map is equivariant for their boundary actions.

derivations.claim: Choose $p\in M$ and an oriented orthonormal identification $T_pM\cong\mathbb R^3$. By [F1], the pulled-back metric on this whole tangent space is complete and covers $M$. In polar coordinates $(r,\omega)$, let $T$ be the unit radial velocity and extend $v\perp\omega$ to a parallel field $E$ along that radial geodesic by [F2]. Parallel transport preserves inner products, so $E\perp T$ and $|E|=|v|$. The explicit field $J(r)=\sinh r\,E(r)$ has $J(0)=0$, $D_rJ(0)=v$, and $D_r^2J=\sinh r\,E$ while $R(J,T)T=-J$; hence $D_r^2J+R(J,T)T=0$. Jacobi initial-data uniqueness and the exponential differential formula in [F2] identify this field with the angular variation. Its length is therefore $\sinh r\,|v|$. Its inner products are $\sinh^2r$ times the sphere metric because parallel transport preserves inner products. Radial velocity has length one and is orthogonal to these normal fields. Thus the pulled-back metric is exactly $dr^2+\sinh^2r\,d\omega^2$. The map $(r,\omega)\mapsto(\cosh r,\sinh r\,\omega)$ identifies it with the future unit hyperboloid of Minkowski space; differentiation gives that same metric, and it extends smoothly and bijectively at the origin. The hyperboloid is the upper half-space model via $y=1/(x_0-x_3)$ and $z=(x_1+ix_2)/(x_0-x_3)$, whose inverse is obtained by solving these equations and $x_0^2-|x'|^2=1$; direct differentiation gives the upper half-space metric. Thus [F1]'s source is isometric to $\mathbb H^3$.

We verify the full orientation-preserving isometry group. Identify the hyperboloid with the positive Hermitian determinant-one matrices by $x\mapsto x_0I+x_1\sigma_1+x_2\sigma_2+x_3\sigma_3$, where the Pauli matrices satisfy $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$. The determinant is $x_0^2-|x'|^2$. The action $X\mapsto AXA^*$ of $A\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb C)$ preserves the future hyperboloid and its metric; its kernel is $\{I,-I\}$. It is transitive, because every positive Hermitian determinant-one matrix has a positive Hermitian square root of determinant one, obtained by diagonalizing a two-by-two Hermitian matrix. The stabilizer of $I$ is $\mathrm{SU}(2)$. On the tangent space of traceless Hermitian matrices it realizes every rotation. Indeed, for a real unit vector $n$, the matrix $U=\cos(\theta/2)I+i\sin(\theta/2)\,n\cdot\sigma$ is unitary of determinant one; the displayed Pauli identity shows its conjugation gives the rotation about $n$ through angle $-\theta$. Every three-dimensional proper orthogonal matrix has an axis and is a planar rotation on its orthogonal complement, so these realize all of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. An isometry fixing a point and its tangent frame fixes every geodesic from that point, hence every point by the polar description in step 1.1. Therefore every orientation-preserving model isometry comes from this projective matrix group. Its boundary action on rank-one Hermitian matrices $vv^*$ is $[v]\mapsto[Av]$, the usual fractional linear action on $\mathbb{CP}^1$. This is the Möbius action in [F3].

The deck group of [F1]'s universal cover acts by isometries of the pulled-back metric and preserves its pulled-back orientation. It is therefore a subgroup of the group in step 2.1. It acts freely, since a deck transformation fixing one point fixes every lifted path from that point, hence the connected cover. It is discrete and properly discontinuous: an evenly covered neighborhood has disjoint lifted neighborhoods and a deck transformation intersecting one with itself must be the identity. Such transformations form an isolated neighborhood of the identity in the matrix topology by continuity of evaluation at a point. The group is torsion-free: a finite-order model isometry has a fixed point. In the hyperboloid model, sum the finitely many orbit vectors of any point and normalize their future timelike sum; this is a fixed point. Finally, universal covering path lifting identifies the deck group with $\pi_1(M)$ and its orbit quotient with $M$. Under this identification the metric and orientation descend exactly to the given ones, proving the assertion.

Use the upper half-space model
$$\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are
$$z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z},$$
each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

For $0<\zeta<\pi/2$, let
$$\mathcal O_\zeta= \{(x+iy,t)\in\mathbb H^3: 0\le x\le\cos\zeta,\quad 0\le y\le x\tan\zeta,\quad t\ge\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}\}.$$
Its hyperbolic volume in the upper half-space metric is $\frac12\Lambda(\zeta)$.

For every real $\theta$, $\Lambda$ is continuous, odd, and $\pi$-periodic, with $\Lambda(\pi/2)=0$ and
$$\Lambda(2\theta)=2\Lambda(\theta)+2\Lambda(\theta+\pi/2).$$
For $0\le\theta\le\pi$,
$$\Lambda(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sin(2n\theta)}{n^2}.$$
In particular,
$$\Lambda(\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).$$
For every integer $N\ge1$, the positive remainder after the terms $k=0,\ldots,N$ is at most $\sqrt3/(72N^2)$.

derivations.claim: Apply a Euclidean similarity of the boundary plane, extended by the same scaling of height, sending the circumcircle of the three finite ideal vertices to the unit circle centered at $0$; this upper half-space isometry fixes $\infty$. The three vertices become points $p,q,r$ on that circle and remain equilateral. Hence $(0,0)$ lies in the interior of their triangle, so the vertical ray from $(0,0,1)$ to $\infty$ lies inside the tetrahedron.

On the unit-hemisphere face, draw the perpendicular arcs from $(0,0,1)$ to its three edges and the arcs from $(0,0,1)$ to $p,q,r$. Cone the six resulting sectors to $\infty$. Because the vertical ray lies in the tetrahedron, the six simplices have disjoint interiors and cover the tetrahedron; their common faces have three-dimensional volume zero. Each simplex has two finite vertices and two ideal vertices. Its three right dihedral angles come from the perpendicular cuts; among its other angles, two equal the corresponding original tetrahedron edge angle $\zeta$ and the third is $\pi/2-\zeta$. The tetrahedron is regular, so [F2] gives $\zeta=\pi/3$ for each of the six simplices.

Normalize one simplex by a hyperbolic isometry so its ideal vertices are $\infty$ and $(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$ and one finite vertex is $(0,0,1)$. The three right angles place the projected right-angle vertex at $(\cos\zeta,0)$: the two legs are horizontal and vertical. The angle at the origin is $\zeta$, so the other ideal point has coordinates $(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$. The projected triangle is the intersection of the half-planes $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$, $x\le\cos\zeta$ and $y\le x\tan\zeta$. The unit hemisphere through $(0,0,1)$ has equation $x^2+y^2+t^2=1$, and the tetrahedral side is above it. Thus the simplex is exactly $\mathcal O_\zeta$ from [F3] with $\zeta=\pi/3$.

By [F3], each of the six simplices has volume $\frac12\Lambda(\pi/3)$. Their interiors are disjoint and their union is the tetrahedron up to faces of volume zero, so additivity gives $\operatorname{Vol}=6\cdot\frac12\Lambda(\pi/3)=3\Lambda(\pi/3)$. Substitution of the absolutely convergent series in [F4] gives the second displayed expression; absolute convergence follows by comparison with $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}$.

The same formula with $g,h$ reversed bounds the inverse commutator, so $\rho([g,h])\le C\rho(g)\rho(h)$ on $U_r$, for one fixed $C$. Choose $r$ with $Cr\le1/2$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Use the upper half-space model $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,y):z\in\mathbb C,y>0\}$ with metric $(|dz|^2+dy^2)/y^2$. Let $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be discrete and torsion-free, and suppose that it contains a subgroup $A\cong\mathbb Z^2$. Then $A$ fixes a unique ideal point. After conjugating that point to infinity, its full stabilizer $P=\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(\infty)$ consists of translations by a lattice $\Lambda\le\mathbb C$ of rank two. It is the unique maximal abelian subgroup containing $A$.

For a sufficiently large $R$, the quotient of the closed horoball $\{y\ge R\}$ by $P$ embeds properly in $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$. Its boundary is a compact torus, its interior is a cusp, and its volume is $\operatorname{area}(\mathbb C/\Lambda)/(2R^2)$. If $M$ has exactly one topological end, the complement of the open cusp has compact closure.

No finite-volume thin decomposition, abstract peripheral recognition, or rigidity theorem is assumed or concluded here. The rank-two subgroup and the quotient presentation of $M$ are hypotheses.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a **nonempty**, connected,
boundaryless Riemannian manifold, and let $d=d_g$ be its Riemannian distance.
The following conditions are equivalent.

1. The metric space $(M,d)$ is complete.
2. The Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is geodesically complete.
3. For every $p\in M$, the fibre exponential domain is all of the tangent
   space: $\mathcal E_p=T_pM$.
4. There is a point $p_0\in M$ for which $\mathcal E_{p_0}=T_{p_0}M$.
5. Every closed bounded subset of the metric space $(M,d)$ is compact.

Whenever these conditions hold, every $x,y\in M$ are joined by a minimizing
geodesic. More exactly, there is $v\in T_xM$ with
$$
\exp_x(v)=y,\qquad |v|_{g_x}=d(x,y),
$$
and $t\mapsto\exp_x(tv)$ on $[0,1]$ has length $d(x,y)$.

The nonemptiness hypothesis is essential for this formulation: on the empty
manifold conditions 1--3 and 5 are vacuous, whereas condition 4 is false.

derivations.claim: We prove the needed uniform small-matrix fact. In a neighborhood of the identity of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ choose the unique determinant-one lift near $I$, and put $\rho(g)=\max\{\|g-I\|,\|g^{-1}-I\|\}$ for a fixed matrix operator norm. For small $r$, the symmetric neighborhood $U_r=\{\rho<r\}$ has compact closure. Writing $g=I+X,h=I+Y$ gives $[g,h]-I=(XY-YX)g^{-1}h^{-1}$. The same formula with $g,h$ reversed bounds the inverse commutator, so $\rho([g,h])\le C\rho(g)\rho(h)$ on $U_r$, for one fixed $C$. Choose $r$ with $Cr\le1/2$. For any discrete subgroup $D$, the finite set $S=D\cap U_r$ generates a nilpotent subgroup. Indeed, every left-nested commutator of $n$ elements of $S$ has $\rho\le r2^{-(n-1)}$, by induction, and remains in $U_r$. Since the identity is isolated in $D$, all such commutators vanish for one common sufficiently large $n$. To justify the nilpotence conclusion, argue by induction on this common bound: the commutators of length $n-1$ commute with every generator, hence generate a central subgroup; quotient by it and use the induction hypothesis. The initial bound $n=1$ is the trivial group. Thus the group has a finite central series. Compactness makes $D\cap U_r$ finite, since a discrete subgroup is closed as in [F2]'s elementary proof.

We pass from small matrices to small point displacement, including the finite-index step. Fix a model point $o$ and a compact neighborhood $Q$ of its compact stabilizer $K$. Choose an identity neighborhood $V$ so that $qVq^{-1}\subset U_r$ for every $q\in Q$, possible by uniform continuity on compact $Q$. Cover $K$ by finitely many open sets $W_1,\ldots,W_N$ with $W_j^{-1}W_j\subset V$. There is $\eta_0>0$ such that every $g$ with $d(o,go)<\eta_0$ lies in $Q\cap\bigcup_jW_j$. To verify this last assertion, the inverse image of the closed unit ball under the frame projection $G\to\mathbb H^3$ is compact: use finitely many local trivializations over that ball with compact fiber $K$. A contrary sequence with displacement tending to zero therefore has a subsequence converging into $K$, a contradiction. Choose $0<\eta<\eta_0/(N+1)$. For a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma$ let $D$ be generated by the elements moving $o$ by less than $\eta$; there are finitely many such elements, again by the compact frame fiber. Set $H=\langle D\cap U_r\rangle$, nilpotent by step 1.1. In any word of length greater than $N$, its first $N+1$ prefixes lie in $Q\cap\bigcup_jW_j$, by the triangle inequality. Two prefixes $w_i,w_j$, $i<j$, lie in the same $W_j$, so $h=w_i^{-1}w_j\in V\cap D$ and $w_ihw_i^{-1}\in U_r\cap D\subset H$. If the rest of the word is $v$, then $w_jv=(w_ihw_i^{-1})w_iv$. Deleting this positive-length block therefore gives a shorter representative of the same left coset modulo $H$. Iteration shows every left coset has a representative of length at most $N$, proving $[D:H]<\infty$.

Such a $D$ preserves either a unique ideal point or a pair of ideal points, unless trivial. If $H$ is trivial, finite index and torsion-freeness make $D$ trivial. Otherwise its normal core in $D$ has finite index and is nontrivial and nilpotent. A nontrivial nilpotent group has a nontrivial center, by its central series; choose a central element $z$. Its centralizer from [F2] puts that normal core into either the translations fixing the parabolic point of $z$ or the diagonal group fixing its loxodromic pair. It is abelian and has that unique common fixed set. Normality makes $D$ preserve that set. A discrete torsion-free group preserving a pair is cyclic: an element interchanging the pair has order two, and the remaining diagonal group is cyclic by [F2]. A group preserving one point consists either of translations or is cyclic loxodromic. For the latter assertion, conjugate a loxodromic element fixing that point to a dilation fixing infinity and zero. Its commutator with any affine map fixing infinity is a translation. A nonzero such translation, conjugated by contracting powers of the dilation, tends to the identity, impossible in a discrete group. Thus all affine maps commute with the dilation and lie in the cyclic diagonal group. This proves the assertion and also that $D$ is abelian. By model homogeneity, the same $\eta$ works at every point.

Consider the open displacement regions $U_g=\{x:d(x,gx)<\eta\}$ for nonidentity $g\in\Gamma$. If two meet, step 3.1 applied at an intersection point says that their elements have the same parabolic fixed point or the same loxodromic pair. This propagates along every intersection chain. Each $U_g$ is connected: for a translation it is a horoball, since $\sinh(d((z,y),(z+\lambda,y))/2)=|\lambda|/(2y)$; for a loxodromic with translation length $\ell>0$ and rotation angle $\alpha$, cylindrical coordinates about its axis give $\sinh^2(d(x,gx)/2)=\sinh^2(\ell/2)\cosh^2r+\sin^2(\alpha/2)\sinh^2r$, so it is an axis tube or empty. This formula follows from the hyperboloid coordinates $(\cosh r\cosh t,\cosh r\sinh t,\sinh r\cos\varphi,\sinh r\sin\varphi)$ and the shift $(t,\varphi)\mapsto(t+\ell,\varphi+\alpha)$. Thus every component of $\bigcup_gU_g$ is associated to exactly one fixed point or pair. Its stabilizer is the full elementary subgroup with that fixed set, by step 3.1. It is precisely invariant under this stabilizer: an intersecting translate gives an intersection chain and hence the same fixed set.

A parabolic component is one horoball: its stabilizer is a nontrivial discrete translation lattice of rank one or two, with a shortest nonzero translation vector, and the union of the corresponding concentric horoballs is the horoball for that shortest vector. A loxodromic component is an axis tube of finite radius. Its stabilizer is generated by one screw motion with positive translation length $\ell$. Only finitely many of its powers satisfy $|n|\ell<\eta$; the formula in step 4.1 gives one finite tube radius for each such power, and their union has the largest of these finite radii. The quotient of its closed tube is compact, since the angular coordinate is a circle, the axis coordinate is taken modulo $\ell$ with a possible rotation, and the radial coordinate lies in a bounded closed interval. Thus the thin open subset of $M$ has precisely the claimed tube and horocusp component models. Its complement is the closed set on which injectivity radius is at least $\eta/2$, since injectivity radius in a simply connected hyperbolic cover is half the infimum of the nontrivial deck displacements.

This thick complement is compact. Otherwise properness [F3] lets us choose infinitely many points there mutually separated by at least $\eta/4$: successively avoid finitely many compact closed balls. Their radius-$\eta/8$ balls are disjoint and are isometric embedded hyperbolic balls, since the injectivity radius at each center is at least $\eta/2$. Each has the same positive volume, contradicting finite total volume. The thick set is nonempty. If empty, connectedness of $M$ puts its entire cover into one component of the thin set from step 4.1; $\Gamma$ is then elementary. A translation rank-two quotient has infinite volume by integrating $y^{-3}$ down to zero over a fundamental parallelogram; rank-one quotients have an infinite transverse horizontal direction. A cyclic loxodromic quotient has infinite volume by integrating $\sinh r\cosh r\,dr\,d\varphi\,dt$ over unbounded $r$ and an axis fundamental interval. The trivial quotient is also infinite-volume. All contradict the hypothesis.

Only finitely many thin components occur. To prove the required local finiteness near the compact thick set, choose a small lifted metric ball about any one of its points. Every displacement region $U_g$ meeting a radius-$a$ ball about its center $x$ has $d(x,gx)<\eta+2a$ by the triangle inequality. There are finitely many such $g$, because the inverse image of a bounded displacement ball in the model frame bundle is compact and its intersection with the discrete group is finite. Each $U_g$ belongs to a single component, so only finitely many components meet this neighborhood. Finitely many such neighborhoods cover the thick set. Every thin component has boundary in that set, since it is a proper component of the open thin locus and the displacement descriptions in steps 4.1–5.1 supply a boundary. Therefore every component occurs in that finite list.

A rank-one horocusp has infinite volume: a translation fundamental strip has an infinite transverse Euclidean direction, and integrating $y^{-3}$ over any finite nonempty height interval already gives infinite volume. It is excluded. The remaining finitely many horocusps are rank two and have standard compact torus cross-sections. We justify the closed boundaries before taking their complement. Choose $\eta<\eta'<\eta_0/(N+1)$ and rerun steps 2.1–3.1 at $\eta'$; their finite-index and elementary-group conclusions still hold. At a common point of two closed $\eta$-displacement regions the two generators move that point by at most $\eta<\eta'$, so they have the same elementary fixed set. Consequently distinct closed thin components cannot touch, and each closure is precisely invariant under its stabilizer. The closed tube quotients embed because they are compact and injective; the closed rank-two horoball quotients embed properly by [F2], whose explicit properness proof applies to every precisely invariant closed horoball with compact torus cross-section. Their boundaries are thus disjoint embedded smooth model tori. Add the finitely many compact tube closures from step 5.1 to the compact thick set from step 6.1. This is exactly the complement of those open rank-two horocusps, hence compact. Each cusp boundary is a smooth horotorus by its explicit model, and its attached product end is the horoball quotient. Clamping each product end to its boundary gives a deformation retraction onto the complement, so this is a compact core in the homotopy sense as well. This constructs the claimed finite standard cusp decomposition, including the zero-cusp compact case.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$
that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

derivations.claim: Since $f$ is an isometry, $f^*g_N=g_M$. In any coordinate charts, if $J=Df$ is the coordinate derivative, then the metric matrices satisfy $G_M=J^{\mathsf T}(G_N\circ f)J$. Taking determinants gives $\sqrt{\det G_M}=|\det J|\sqrt{\det(G_N\circ f)}$. Thus $f$ pulls the Riemannian volume density of $N$ back to that of $M$, regardless of whether it preserves orientation.

Consider the set of ALL coordinate-neighborhood pairs $(U,V)$ with $f(U)\subset V$. It covers $M$. Fix a countable basis of $M$; for each basis member contained in some such $U$, use [A1] to select one containing pair. Their selected $U$ neighborhoods form a countable cover $(U_j)_{j\ge1}$, with corresponding $V_j$. Thus no point-indexed choice of charts is required. Make it disjoint by setting $A_1=U_1$ and $A_j=U_j\setminus\bigcup_{i<j}U_i$; these are Borel, disjoint and cover $M$. In coordinates on $U_j,V_j$, apply [F2] to the nonnegative measurable function equal to the target density times the indicator of $f(A_j)$. The Jacobian identity in step 1.1 yields $\operatorname{Vol}_M(A_j)=\operatorname{Vol}_N(f(A_j))$. The sets $f(A_j)$ are disjoint and cover $N$.

The indicators of the finite unions $\bigcup_{j\le n}A_j$ increase to $1_M$. By [F3] and [F4], the volume of $M$ is the limit of the sums $\sum_{j\le n}\operatorname{Vol}_M(A_j)$, and the same holds for $N$ and the sets $f(A_j)$. These finite sums agree term by term by step 2.1; their limits therefore agree in $[0,\infty]$. If one volume is finite, their common value is finite.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with a chosen closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and let $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Every smoothly embedded two-sphere in the interior of $E_K$ bounds a smoothly embedded closed three-ball contained in $E_K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot that is not ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, let $E_K$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $T_K=\partial E_K$. There is no properly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose boundary is a simple closed curve in $T_K$ that is not null-homotopic in $T_K$.

derivations.claim: By [A1], the countable-choice hypothesis of [F1] holds. Its chosen tube and exterior are precisely those in the Statement. Apply [F1] to each specified interior sphere to obtain a smooth embedded ball in $E_K$ with that boundary, proving the first conclusion.

The full-AC and nontrivial-knot hypotheses of [F2] are exactly supplied. A disk of the kind excluded in the Statement has its interior in the exterior interior and its boundary on $T_K$, so it is one of the boundary-preimage smooth disks excluded by [F2]. Apply that result to prove the second conclusion. Neither argument uses atoroidality, a hyperbolic metric or an extra torus-classification premise.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)$, and set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and $T_K=\partial E_K$. If $K$ is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot, then every smoothly embedded $2$-sphere in $\operatorname{int}E_K$ bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $E_K$, and there is no smoothly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose interior misses $T_K$ and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in $T_K$.

derivations.claim: Put $M=E_K$ and $T=\partial M$. By hypothesis $M$ is compact, connected, orientable and irreducible, and $T$ is its single torus boundary component. If $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(M)$ had nontrivial kernel, [F1] would supply an essential simple curve in $T$ bounding a proper disk in $M$, contradicting boundary incompressibility. Hence $\pi_1(M)$ contains the injected group $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ and is infinite.

The given embedded-torus atoroidality and the hypothesis that $M$ is not Seifert-fibered allow [F2] to be applied. Therefore every $\pi_1$-injective torus map is homotopic into $\partial M$. Together with the incompressible torus boundary and infinite $\pi_1$ from step 1.1, these are the actual hypotheses of [F3]: AFW supplies hyperbolization, and the finite-volume conclusion for this incompressible-boundary case is the separately cited Rubinstein statement. Thus $\operatorname{int}(M)$ admits a complete finite-volume metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$. This applies to fibered knot exteriors as well as nonfibered ones; no additional non-interval-bundle assumption has been introduced.

The interior of a compact connected manifold with one connected boundary component has one end: a boundary collar gives a cofinal family of connected complements of compact subsets, namely $T\times(0,\epsilon)$. By [F4], every end of the metric from step 2.1 is a rank-two horoball quotient, so there is exactly one torus cusp. It belongs to the unique original boundary end. This is an existence assertion for a metric on the original interior; no prescribed horosphere scale, meridian–longitude translation vectors, or separately marked peripheral conjugacy is asserted. No conclusion is used outside the four topological hypotheses of the Statement.

Use the upper half-space model
$$\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are
$$z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z},$$
each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

Let an orientable finite ideal triangulation have exactly one ideal vertex, whose link is a torus. Suppose its tetrahedra carry positive shapes whose edge products equal $1$ and whose dihedral angles sum to $2\pi$ around every edge. If the cusp multipliers $H(\alpha)$ and $H(\beta)$ are $1$ for a basis $\alpha,\beta$ of the torus fundamental group, then the glued hyperbolic metric is complete at that cusp.

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb C$ be a rank-two lattice acting on $\mathbb H^3$ by horizontal translations, and let
$$
C=\{(x+iy,t):t\ge1\}/\Gamma
$$
be the quotient of the horoball $t\ge1$. If $A$ is the Euclidean area of a fundamental parallelogram for $\Gamma$, then the end is at infinite hyperbolic distance and $\operatorname{Vol}(C)=A/2$.

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3) =\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).$$

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice. For a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, let $\mu$ be the positive fibre meridian and let $\sigma$ be the product section $s\mapsto(s,1)$ of $T_K=\partial N(K)\cong S^1\times S^1$. Then $T_K=\partial E_K$ is a torus and $[\mu],[\sigma]$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. The curve $\sigma$ is a product section; this statement does not assert that it is the preferred zero-homology longitude.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]]. Write

$$G_n:=\{[\beta]:\beta\ \text{a braid based at}\ Q\}$$

for the set of braid isotopy classes relative to the top and bottom
([[def-braid-isotopy-relative-top-and-bottom]]), and let $[\gamma][\beta]:
=[\gamma\star\beta]$ be the stacking of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]]. Then:

**(a)** $G_n$ is a group ([[def-group]]) with this operation. Its identity is
the class $[e]$ of the trivial braid $e_j(t):=q_j$, and the inverse of
$[\beta]$, for $\beta=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ with endpoint permutation $\pi(\beta)$,
is the class of the **reversed braid**

$$\overline\beta_j(t):=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)\qquad(t\in I,\ 1\le j\le n).$$

**(b)** The endpoint permutation map

$$\pi\colon G_n\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad[\beta]\longmapsto\pi(\beta),$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]).

The construction is choice-free: all motions and reparametrisations used are
given by explicit formulas.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

derivations.claim: The endpoint permutation of $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$ is $(12)(23)(12)(23)=(1\ 3\ 2)$, because each half twist has the adjacent transposition as endpoint permutation and inverse has the same transposition. By [F8], its closure is one component. Cut the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram along its projection regions and four crossing arcs. Above and below the diagram this produces two ideal balls: each crossing arc has four face-side copies, and every face is a diagram region. Gluing upper and lower faces with the same region label restores the cut-open complement, because each cut face and crossing-arc side is identified with exactly its original mate; the only unfilled points are the deleted knot arcs, which are ideal vertices. Collapsing the two bigon faces gives two tetrahedra. Recording the vertex matches on their four faces gives exactly the four maps in the statement.

By [F2], at $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ every edge parameter is $\omega$. The first edge class has product $\omega^6=1$, and the second has product $\omega^6=1$; each class contains six edge copies, so its total dihedral angle is $6(\pi/3)=2\pi$.

Applying the four vertex maps identifies all eight tetrahedron vertices into one ideal vertex and the twelve tetrahedron edges into the two six-edge classes in the statement. To check the link vertices explicitly, write $u|v$ for the truncation corner at ideal vertex $u$ on edge $uv$. The four corner classes are $\{0|1,0|2,3|2,3'|1',3'|2',0'|1'\}$, $\{1|0,1'|3',2|0,2'|3',1'|0',2|3\}$, $\{1|2,1'|2',0|3,0'|2',1|3,0'|3'\}$, and $\{2|1,2'|1',3|0,2'|0',3|1,3'|0'\}$; these are disjoint and contain all $24$ link corners. The eight link triangles have their $24$ sides identified in $12$ pairs, so $\chi=4-12+8=0$. The four face maps give a connected adjacency graph on the eight link triangles; their induced boundary-orientation signs are respectively negative, negative, negative, negative. Hence the link is connected, closed and orientable, and therefore is a torus.

Writing $\phi_i$ for the face map whose source face omits vertex $i$, the strip triangles are $a=0$, $h=0'$, $b=1$, $g=1'$, $c=2$, $f=2'$, $d=3$, and $e=3'$. The $\alpha$ corner trace is $0|2,0'|3',1|2,1'|3',2|0,2'|1',3|0,3'|1'$, with factors $z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1},z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1}$. The link side crossed after each corner is paired with the next triangle by $\phi_1,\phi_0,\phi_3,\phi_1,\phi_3,\phi_2,\phi_1,\phi_3$, the last closing $e$ to $a$. The $\beta$ trace cuts off $0|3$ on the right and $0'|1'$ on the left, giving $H(\beta)=z_2^{-1}w_1$. Cutting along $\alpha$ leaves $\beta$ joining the two boundary copies with one positive crossing, so $([\alpha],[\beta])$ is a homology basis and hence a $\pi_1$ basis on the torus. At the regular shape both multipliers equal $1$.

The edge conditions in step 1.2, torus link in step 2.1, and basis cusp multipliers in step 3.1 satisfy [F3], so the glued metric is complete at its unique torus cusp. The face maps are hyperbolic face isometries; the $2\pi$ edge-angle sums make the metric smooth across every edge, and the only omitted locus is the single ideal vertex. Thus completeness at this cusp is completeness of the whole glued complement. Each tetrahedron has volume $v_3$ by [F5], so additivity gives total volume $2v_3<\infty$; its horospherical cusp truncation also has finite volume by [F4]. The induced metric on the figure-eight complement is therefore complete and finite-volume with one peripheral torus cusp.

boundaries.evidence: Nonempty manifolds make the finite Haar quotient measure positive; the boundary rigidity theorem is not applied with zero total measure. Proof, step 1.1: First use [F5] to write $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ and $N=\Gamma'\backslash\mathbb H^3$ with the standard cusp decompositions, identifying their deck groups with the fundamental groups and transporting $\theta$ accordingly. We verify the finite-Haar hypothesis of [F3], rather than infer it from a citation. Put $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ and $K=\mathrm{SO}(3)$, the stabilizer of a point in $\mathbb H^3$. The action identifies $G$ with the oriented orthonormal frame bundle: in the ball model an orientation-preserving isometry can send the center to any point by an upper half-space affine map after Cayley conjugation, and its stabilizer acts as every rotation; an isometry fixing a frame fixes each geodesic with its initial velocity and is the identity. Give $K$ normalized bi-invariant volume from the Ad-invariant inner product $-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. Integrating this probability measure on each frame fiber against hyperbolic volume defines a smooth positive measure on $G$. It is independent of the local frame section, since changes of section are rotations, and is left-$G$-invariant, since $G$ acts isometrically on the base and by rotations on the fibers. It is also right invariant: in left-invariant tangent coordinates the Jacobian of right translation is $|\det_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{Ad}(g^{-1})|$. On $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ the complex determinant of Ad is one. For diagonal matrices its eigenvalues are $a^2,1,a^{-2}$; for upper and lower unipotent matrices Ad is triangular with diagonal entries one. These matrices generate $G$ by Gaussian elimination, so the determinant assertion holds for every $g$. The real determinant is the squared modulus of the complex one. Thus the displayed frame measure is Haar on both sides. Its quotient on $\Gamma\backslash G$ is the locally transported right invariant Radon measure required in [F3]. Local product integration and a disjoint countable chart decomposition give its total mass exactly $\operatorname{Vol}(M)$, since the fiber mass is one. It is finite and positive. [A1, F5, given, algebra]

One cusp and knot exteriors are special cases; no one-cusp assumption enters the general theorem. Elementary cyclic or parabolic groups are excluded by explicit infinite-volume integrals, rather than assumed nonelementary. Proof, step 1.2: We give the uniqueness argument, including orientation reversal. First, $\Gamma$ is not elementary. If nontrivial it gives, by conjugation with contracting powers, nontrivial elements tending to the identity. All these quotients have infinite volume. For rank-two translations integrate $y^{-3}$ over a Euclidean fundamental parallelogram and $y\downarrow0$; rank-one translations have in addition an infinite horizontal direction. A cyclic loxodromic quotient has cylindrical density $\sinh r\cosh r\,dr\,d\varphi\,dt$ about its axis, with $t$ taken modulo its positive translation length, so integrating over $r\to\infty$ diverges even if its generator rotates the cylinder. Horoballs are geodesically convex, so the pointwise geodesic homotopy from $\widetilde g$ to $\widetilde I$ stays inside that arbitrarily deep target horoball on sufficiently deep source tails. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ and finite volume. Then $M$ is a compact core together with finitely many pairwise disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Each end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ of a horoball by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of these open ends is compact. The number of cusps may be zero. In particular, the standard cusp decomposition in the general rigidity construction follows from the complete finite-volume metric, with no knot or triangulation assumption.

Assume AC. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ and $N=\Gamma'\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be connected orientable hyperbolic manifolds, with discrete torsion-free groups. Suppose each is a compact core together with finitely many disjoint standard torus cusp ends: an end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of the union of these ends is compact. Zero ends are allowed, in which case the manifold is compact.

Every group isomorphism $\theta:\Gamma\to\Gamma'$ permutes the conjugacy classes of the peripheral cusp groups. There is a smooth $\theta$-equivariant quasi-isometry $F:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ which on every sufficiently deep lifted cusp is affine in its horizontal coordinates and preserves cusp depth after a constant height rescaling. It has a smooth equivariant quasi-inverse with inverse affine cusp maps. On quotient manifolds these maps are proper homotopy equivalences.

The standard cusp decomposition is a supplied hypothesis here; this lemma does not derive it merely from finite volume.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,s):z\in\mathbb C,\ s>0\}$ use the metric $s^{-2}(|dz|^2+ds^2)$. Suppose $f:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ is a quasi-isometry with constants $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$:
$$\lambda^{-1}d(x,y)-\varepsilon\le d(f(x),f(y))\le\lambda d(x,y)+\varepsilon,$$
and with coarsely dense image. Then it induces an ideal-boundary homeomorphism $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$. There is $H=H(\lambda,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that, after postcomposition by any Möbius transformation carrying $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$, its plane restriction satisfies
$$\max_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\le H\min_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\qquad(z\in\mathbb C,\ r>0).$$
Here $h$ in that inequality denotes the normalized map. If the boundary homeomorphism preserves orientation, it is analytically quasiconformal in sphere charts, with constant at most $H$. If it reverses orientation, postcomposition with complex conjugation is quasiconformal with that constant. If $f$ is equivariant for a homomorphism between groups of hyperbolic isometries, its boundary map is equivariant for their boundary actions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ act on the Riemann sphere by Möbius transformations. Let $\Gamma\le G$ be discrete, with finite nonzero Haar quotient measure $\nu$ on $X=\Gamma\backslash G$. Here Haar quotient measure means the right invariant Radon measure obtained by locally transporting Haar measure through the covering projection $G\to X$; its normalization is immaterial. Let $\theta:\Gamma\to G$ be a homomorphism, and let $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be an orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphism satisfying $h\circ\gamma=\theta(\gamma)\circ h$ for every $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Then $h$ is Möbius.

This statement assumes the existence of the quasiconformal boundary conjugacy. It does not assert that an abstract group isomorphism or a quasi-isometry produces one.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ and $N$ be second-countable oriented hyperbolic three-manifolds, and let $f:M\to N$ be an isometry. Then
$$
\int_M d\operatorname{vol}_M=\int_N d\operatorname{vol}_N.
$$
In particular, if either volume is finite, then both are finite and the values agree.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E_K$ be the compact connected orientable exterior of a smooth knot in $S^3$, with one torus boundary component. If $E_K$ is irreducible, its boundary is incompressible, $E_K$ is atoroidal, and $E_K$ is not Seifert-fibered, then $\operatorname{int}(E_K)$ admits a complete finite-volume Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$ with one torus cusp. No conclusion is asserted for a torus or satellite knot unless its exterior satisfies all four topological hypotheses.

derivations.claim: The action preserves $|z|^2+|w|^2$, so it acts smoothly on $S^3$. The orbit of $(2^{-1/2},2^{-1/2})$ is exactly $K$. A group element stabilizes this point only if $3\theta$ and $2\theta$ are both multiples of $2\pi$; coprimality of $2$ and $3$ makes the stabilizer trivial. The regions $|z|\le|w|$ and $|w|\le|z|$ are solid tori, parametrized respectively by $(z,w)=(z,\sqrt{1-|z|^2}\eta)$ and $(z,w)=(\sqrt{1-|w|^2}\eta,w)$ with the disk coordinate bounded by $2^{-1/2}$ and $\eta\in S^1$. The $w$ coordinate is the core direction of the first solid torus and winds twice along $K$; the $z$ coordinate is the core direction of the second and winds three times. This proves the claimed $(3,2)$ torus-knot type. On the axis $z=0$ the stabilizer has order $2$, and on the axis $w=0$ it has order $3$.

On $zw\ne0$, write $\alpha=\arg z$ and $\beta=\arg w$ modulo $2\pi$. The integer coordinate change $\theta=\alpha-\beta$, $\phi=2\alpha-3\beta$ has determinant $-1$ and is invertible on the phase torus. The circle action changes $\theta$ by its parameter and fixes $\phi$, while $r=|z|\in(0,1)$ is fixed; thus the quotient of this open set is the cylinder with coordinates $(r,\phi)$, and the inverse image of any disk $D$ around $q(K)$ in it is explicitly $S^1_\theta\times D$. At $r=0$ and $r=1$ the phase circle collapses to one point at each end, so the full orbit space is a sphere; the two axis orbits have stabilizer orders $2$ and $3$. The complement of $D$ is a disk with those two cone points. Its orbits give the fibers of $E_K$, and [F2] identifies the axis fibers as exceptional of orders $2$ and $3$.

Choose a basepoint $x$ on a regular fiber, let $h$ be that fiber loop, and let $\gamma$ be any loop in $E_K$ based at $x$. The map $F:[0,1]^2\to E_K$ defined by $F(s,t)=g_{2\pi s}(\gamma(t))$ is well-defined because the tube is invariant. Its boundary represents $h\gamma h^{-1}\gamma^{-1}$: the two vertical sides are $\gamma$ and $\gamma^{-1}$ since $g_0=g_{2\pi}=\operatorname{id}$, and the horizontal sides are the fiber loop and its reverse. The square contracts its boundary, so $h$ commutes with $[\gamma]$. Since $\gamma$ was arbitrary, the regular fiber class is central in $\pi_1(E_K)$.

By [F3], a Seifert-fibered exterior does not satisfy the required non-Seifert-fibered hypothesis. Step 2.1 establishes that $E_K$ is Seifert-fibered, so this example refutes the statement that every knot exterior is non-Seifert-fibered and also fails that hypothesis of the hyperbolization contract.

Define the standard figure-eight knot $K_8$ to be the oriented closure of the three-strand geometric braid $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$. Its endpoint permutation is a $3$-cycle, so this closure has one component.

Let $\Delta_0=[0,1,2,3]$ and $\Delta_1=[0',1',2',3']$ be oriented ideal tetrahedra with orientation-reversing affine face maps
$$[0,1,2]\to[3',1',2'],\quad [0,1,3]\to[0',1',2'],\quad [0,2,3]\to[0',1',3'],\quad [1,2,3]\to[0',2',3'].$$
This is the two-tetrahedron ideal triangulation obtained from the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram by cutting along crossing arcs, identifying upper and lower polyhedron faces with equal region labels, and collapsing the two bigon faces. Its edge classes are
$$\{01,02,23,0'1',1'3',2'3'\},\qquad \{12,03,13,1'2',0'2',0'3'\};$$
each has valence six, and the unique ideal vertex link is a torus. Put shape $z_1$ on $01,23$, shape $z_2$ on $03,12$, and shape $z_3$ on $02,13$ in $\Delta_0$; put shape $w_1$ on $0'1',2'3'$, shape $w_2$ on $0'3',1'2'$, and shape $w_3$ on $0'2',1'3'$ in $\Delta_1$. Unfold the eight cusp-link triangles by the face maps into the standard rectangular strip. Its upper-row labels are $a,b,c,d$ and its lower-row labels are $h,g,f,e$, both read from left to right; the corner trace across the strip is therefore $a,h,b,g,c,f,d,e$. Identify the strip boundary sides as prescribed by those same maps. Let $\alpha$ be the edge path across the strip from the left side of $a$ on the left boundary to the left side of $a$ on the right boundary, and let $\beta$ be the edge path on the left boundary from the base of $a$ to the top of $h$. Their ordered corner factors are respectively $z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1},z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1}$ and $z_2^{-1},w_1$. The face-pairing incidence check gives one positive transverse intersection, so their homology classes form a basis of $H_1$ and the loops form a basis of $\pi_1$ of the torus link. The two edge products are $z_1^2z_3w_1^2w_3$ and $z_2^2z_3w_2^2w_3$, while
$$H(\alpha)=\left(\frac{z_2z_3}{w_2w_3}\right)^2,\qquad H(\beta)=\frac{w_1}{z_2}.$$
For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, assigning $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ makes both edge products and both cusp multipliers equal to $1$ and gives total angle $2\pi$ around each edge. The gluing therefore gives the figure-eight complement a complete finite-volume curvature $-1$ metric with one peripheral torus cusp.

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3) =\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ and $N$ be interiors of compact connected oriented knot exteriors carrying complete finite-volume hyperbolic metrics. Every isomorphism $\pi_1(M)\to\pi_1(N)$, considered up to the conjugacy induced by basepoint changes, is realized by a unique isometry in the corresponding proper homotopy class. If the isomorphism is induced by an orientation-preserving proper homotopy equivalence, the isometry preserves orientation. In particular, the two metrics have equal volume, where volume is the integral of their Riemannian volume densities.

For every real $\theta$, $\Lambda$ is continuous, odd, and $\pi$-periodic, with $\Lambda(\pi/2)=0$ and
$$\Lambda(2\theta)=2\Lambda(\theta)+2\Lambda(\theta+\pi/2).$$
For $0\le\theta\le\pi$,
$$\Lambda(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sin(2n\theta)}{n^2}.$$
In particular,
$$\Lambda(\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).$$
For every integer $N\ge1$, the positive remainder after the terms $k=0,\ldots,N$ is at most $\sqrt3/(72N^2)$.
