citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ bounds a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ whose oriented boundary is $K$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact oriented smooth $1$-manifold and give $\partial W$ the outward-normal-first orientation ([[def-induced-boundary-orientation]]). The boundary is a finite $0$-manifold, so its orientation at a boundary point $p$ is a sign $\varepsilon(p)\in\{+1,-1\}$; then $$\sum_{p\in\partial W}\varepsilon(p)=0.$$ On each closed-interval component the two boundary points carry opposite signs; circle components contribute nothing. With the standard orientation of $[a,b]$ the outward-normal-first convention gives $\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}$.

If $X$ is a nonempty contractible topological space, then for every $n\geq 0$
and every abelian group $G$,
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\cong H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(\ast;G),$$
where $\ast$ denotes a one-point space.

Let $X$ be a compact oriented smooth $x$-manifold without boundary, let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $Z\subseteq M$ be a closed oriented embedded $z$-submanifold with $x+z=n$ ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]). For a smooth $f:X\to M$ transverse to $Z$, the **oriented intersection number** is the finite sum

$$I(f,Z):=\sum_{p\in f^{-1}(Z)}\varepsilon(p)\in\mathbb Z,$$

with the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]; the sum is finite by [[lem-compact-transverse-complementary-intersections-are-finite]]. For an arbitrary smooth $g:X\to M$, choose a transverse $f$ homotopic to $g$ ([[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], under Countable Choice; the homotopy is a smooth family in the sense of [[def-smooth-family-of-maps-and-evaluation-map]]) and set $I(g,Z):=I(f,Z)$; independence of the choice is [[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]], not assumed here. For compact oriented complementary-dimensional submanifolds $A,B\subseteq M$, where one is compact and the other closed, one sets $I(A,B):=I(i_A,B)$ with $i_A$ the inclusion, so the first factor is the submanifold $A$. If the source is not compact, or the target submanifold is not closed, the sum may fail to be finite or invariant; the safe extension by properness with compact trace is recorded in the remark on properness later on this page. Countable Choice is assumed for selecting transverse representatives and for the classification used to prove independence of that selection; the signs, the finite sum and the empty case (which contributes $0$) are choice-free.

For transverse maps $f:X^x\to M$, $g:Z^z\to M$ with compact oriented boundaryless sources and $x+z=\dim M$, define $I(f,g)$ as the sum of the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]] over $X\times_MZ$. This set is closed in the compact product because $M$ is Hausdorff, and discrete by [[def-transverse-complementary-dimensional-intersection-set]], so the sum is finite. If $g$ is an inclusion this recovers $I(f,Z)$. Ambient compactness is unnecessary in either construction.

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $f:X^x\to M$ and $g:Z^z\to M$ be smooth maps from oriented smooth manifolds, with $x+z=n$ and $f,g$ transverse in the sense of [[def-transverse-smooth-maps]]. Let $a\in X$, $b\in Z$ satisfy $f(a)=g(b)=y$. Then $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ and $T_yM$ have the same dimension, and transversality says that

$$(df_a,dg_b):T_aX\oplus T_bZ\longrightarrow T_yM,\qquad (v,w)\mapsto df_a(v)+dg_b(w),$$

is surjective, hence a linear isomorphism ([[def-transverse-linear-subspaces]]); the sum is direct because the dimensions add up. The ordered direct sum $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ carries the product orientation with the first factor $T_aX$ and the second factor $T_bZ$ ([[def-product-orientation]]), and the three tangent spaces carry their manifold orientations ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

The **local oriented intersection sign** $\varepsilon(a,b)\in\{+1,-1\}$ is $+1$ when this isomorphism carries the product orientation of $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ to the orientation of $T_yM$, and $-1$ otherwise; equivalently it is the orientation sign of the induced isomorphism of determinant lines ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]], [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

For transverse oriented embedded submanifolds $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ with $a+b=n$ one takes $f$ and $g$ to be the inclusion maps ([[def-transverse-embedded-submanifolds]]); the sign at $p\in A\cap B$ then compares $T_pA\oplus T_pB\to T_pM$ with $A$ first. The empty intersection is allowed and carries no signs. In dimension zero the sign compares the two orientation rays directly, and for $x=z=n=0$ it is $\varepsilon_X(a)\varepsilon_Z(b)\varepsilon_M(y)$, the product of the two source point signs and the ambient point sign. The factor order is part of the definition: with the two factors exchanged the signs are multiplied by $(-1)^{ab}$, exactly the graded-commutativity sign measured later on this page by the factor-interchange theorem. No compactness, closedness hypothesis or choice axiom is used in this local definition.

For an oriented manifold with boundary, orient $T_p\partial M$ by the **outward-normal-first** rule: an outward vector first, followed by a positive boundary determinant, is a positive determinant of $T_pM$.

For oriented vector spaces use the ordered determinant isomorphism $\det(V\oplus W)\cong\det V\otimes\det W$ and take the tensor product of the selected rays. Fibrewise this defines the product orientation.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary. Let $f:D=\Delta^n\to N$ be continuous. On each codimension-one face $D_i$, prescribe a smooth simplex $g_i$ and a continuous homotopy $H_i:D_i\times[0,1]\to N$ from $f|_{D_i}$ to $g_i$. Require the homotopies to agree on every common face at every time. Then there are a smooth simplex $g:D\to N$ and a continuous homotopy $H$ from $f$ to $g$ whose restriction to each $D_i\times[0,1]$ is exactly $H_i$, with unchanged time parameter. If $f$ is already smooth and every $H_i$ is constant, one may take $g=f$ and $H$ constant. The boundaryless hypothesis cannot be removed: for the boundary target $[0,\infty)$ there are compatible smooth faces of a $3$-simplex, an explicit continuous filling, and compatible constant prescribed face homotopies, for which no filling with a $C^2$ scalar extension to an affine neighbourhood exists. In particular there is no smooth filling in the sense of [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. This counterexample requires no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: **Finite-chain model and independence.** Write each rational chain as a finite rational sum of parametrized singular simplices. Within each labeled intersection factor, take the finite family of its simplices and iterated faces, identifying equal parametrized faces so that cancellations remain exact. Never identify simplices across the two factors merely because their maps agree: their perturbations must be independent. Preserve the given smooth product end collars and truncate at a smaller positive collar level. The remaining target is the boundaryless interior $B^{4\circ}$. Apply [F7] inductively over the finite face family, extending compatible face homotopies and fixing prescribed smooth faces. This gives a smooth chain replacement respecting the boundary operator, with the same rational coefficients; the homotopy prisms give relative homology. Applying [F7] with any prescribed open neighborhood as target keeps the replacement there. For general position, keep the two labeled families separate and make each pair of their open face strata transverse to the diagonal in $B^{4\circ}\times B^{4\circ}$. Choose faces in increasing dimension, fixing their previously treated subfaces. In Euclidean coordinates a cutoff-supported translation of the unfixed map is submersive in its parameter where the cutoff is positive; near the fixed part the pair is already transverse. The relative and parametric clauses of [F6] therefore give the required perturbation. Extend a chosen face homotopy consistently to all incident simplices in that factor, but not to the other factor. Finitely many face-pair conditions can be imposed simultaneously. Subdivision into finitely many compact coordinate pieces and sufficiently small parameters keep all changes inside prescribed open neighborhoods and away from the end collars. For complementary two-chains the diagonal preimages are finite signed sets; lower-dimensional face pairs are empty. Define the intersection by summing these signs with the rational product coefficients. This agrees with the given transverse interior count. Now fix $Q$ and two choices $P,P'$ bounding $\alpha$, using facewise-transverse representatives with their identical end collars. Their difference $C=P-P'$ is a smooth rational two-cycle compactly supported in $B^{4\circ}$. By [F3], choose a finite continuous rational three-chain $Z$ there with $\partial Z=C$. Smooth $Z$ relative to its prescribed boundary $C$ by [F7], identifying faces within the $Z$ family only. Keeping $Q$ independent and fixed, perturb the remaining $Z$ faces relative to $C$, whose intersections with $Q$ are already transverse. Each simplex-pair diagonal preimage is a compact oriented one-manifold; codimension-one faces give its endpoints, while codimension-two faces have negative expected dimension. The local half-space model and [F4] give the boundary signs. Sum with the rational product coefficients: internal face endpoints cancel because the same face map occurs with opposite boundary coefficients. What remains is $(\partial Z)\cdot Q=C\cdot Q$, together with the term from $Z$ and $\partial Q$. That latter term is empty since $Z$ is compactly supported in the interior and $\partial Q=\beta\subset S^3$. By [F2] the total signed boundary count is zero, so $P\cdot Q=P'\cdot Q$. Apply the same finite construction to homotopy prisms to obtain independence of the replacements. Interchanging the two two-dimensional factors introduces no sign and proves independence of the second chain. All operations are rational-linear, giving the same assertions for finite rational combinations. No embedded-manifold realization of $Z$ is used.

By [F5], choose an oriented Seifert surface $S_\beta\subset S^3$ for each knot component of $\beta$, and similarly choose a cap for each component of $\alpha$. It suffices by bilinearity to consider one knot component of each. Choose a collar depth $0<\epsilon$ in $B^4$. Make $Q$ a graph of $S_\beta$ in the boundary collar with depth zero on $\beta$ and strictly between $0$ and $\epsilon/2$ on its interior. To give this graph a literal product end collar, choose $0<\delta<\epsilon/2$, attach $\beta\times[0,\delta]$, and join its inner edge to the graph inside a tubular neighborhood of $\beta$ disjoint from $\alpha$, leaving the graph unchanged outside that neighborhood; choose the join below depth $\epsilon/2$. This adds no intersections with $P$ and changes none of the signs computed below. Make $P$ consist of the product collar $\alpha\times[0,\epsilon]$ followed by a cap at depth $\epsilon$. Then $P$ and $Q$ intersect exactly above $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. At each such point, the oriented tangent basis of the collar of $P$ is $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a)$, where $a$ is the positive tangent to $\alpha$ and $n_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outward normal of $B^4$; the tangent basis of $Q$ is a positive basis $(s_1,s_2)$ of $S_\beta$, up to radial components which do not change the determinant. By [F4], $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive exactly when $(a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive in the boundary orientation. Thus the $4$-dimensional intersection sign is exactly the $3$-dimensional sign of $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. Hence $P\cdot Q=\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ by [F1].

Hence the equality holds for all such $P,Q$ when the boundaries are knots. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be disjoint finite rational $1$-cycles in the boundary $S^3$ of the standard oriented $4$-ball $B^4$, each represented as a finite rational linear combination of oriented knots. Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ with $\partial P=\alpha$ and $\partial Q=\beta$, with common standard product collars at their respective boundaries and with their interiors in general position. Then the signed interior intersection number $P\cdot Q$ equals the bilinear extension of the linking number $\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ defined by positive meridians in $S^3$.

Let $H$ be a free abelian group of rank $2g$ and let $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ be a bilinear form. Write $H_{\mathbb Q}=H\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and extend $V$ $\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to $H_{\mathbb Q}$. If $L\subset H_{\mathbb Q}$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace of dimension $g$ and $V(x,y)=0$ for all $x,y\in L$, then $M=H\cap L$ is a rank-$g$ direct summand of $H$ and $V|_{M\times M}=0$.

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$ with boundary an oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected oriented Seifert surface for $K$. After matching product collars and pushing the interior of $F$ slightly into $B^4$, the closed locally flat surface $\Sigma=F\cup_KD$ bounds a compact connected oriented locally flat three-manifold $R\subset B^4$. The conclusion includes an oriented ambient product neighborhood of $R$ on both sides, with the positive normal push-off along the $F$ portion of $\partial R=\Sigma$ lying on the complementary side of $R$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, the inclusion of smooth into continuous real singular chains induces an isomorphism
$$H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H_k^{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$$
in every integer degree. This isomorphism is natural for smooth maps. The proof smooths only finitely many simplices at a time. For boundary targets it moves a finite compact set into the interior; it does not prescribe arbitrary boundary faces during smoothing.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

If a TOP product collar of the boundary, together with a finite PL structure on its boundary surface, has already been supplied, the new PL structure may be chosen equal to that product PL structure on a smaller boundary neighborhood. No smooth marking or smooth ambient isotopy is asserted. Full AC remains the hypothesis of this theorem; no choice-free theorem is obtained by omitting that premise.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

If $M$ is a compact topological manifold with boundary $A=\partial M$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $A$ and a homeomorphism
$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$
Consequently $A\hookrightarrow M$ is an unbased cofibration, and $M\setminus A\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. The manifold is Hausdorff and second countable by convention. All three conclusions require no AC.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.
For a finite CW complex, $\chi(X)=\sum_n(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

derivations.claim: Construct the compact oriented locally flat $R$ by [F5], and write $\Sigma=\partial R=F\cup D$ after matching collars. The Axiom of Choice [A1] is the hypothesis under which the supplied Seifert-pairing and duality interfaces are invoked. Capping the sole boundary circle of $F$ by a disk does not change $H_1$ because that circle is already the boundary of the oriented fundamental $2$-chain of $F$; by [F9] and exactness [F10], $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $2g$. In the pair sequence [F10], $H_0(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_0(R;\mathbb Q)$ is an isomorphism because both are connected. Exactness therefore makes $H_1(R;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ surjective. By [F2] and [F14], the target has dimension $b_2(R)$, so the image of $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $b_1(R)-b_2(R)$.

Let $\widehat R$ be the double of $R$ along $\Sigma$, with the second copy oppositely oriented so the orientations glue. Its two copies have open collar thickenings with intersection retracting to $\Sigma$, so [F11] gives $\chi(\widehat R)=2\chi(R)-\chi(\Sigma)$. By [F12] and [F13], $\chi(\widehat R)=0$, and by [F9], $\chi(\Sigma)=2-2g$; hence $\chi(R)=1-g$. Also [F2] gives $H_3(R;\mathbb Q)\cong H^0(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)=0$: a relative zero-cocycle is locally constant on the connected $R$ and vanishes on the nonempty connected $\Sigma$, so it is zero. With $b_0(R)=1$, the rational Euler-characteristic identity [F13] implies $b_1(R)-b_2(R)=g$. Thus the kernel $L=\ker(H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q))$, identified with a subspace of $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, has dimension $2g-g=g$.

Represent $x,y\in L$ by finite rational smooth cycles in the given $F$, away from $K$, and choose finite rational continuous bounding chains in $R$. Use its pre-collar-push model and the actual positive normal product of [F5]. Push the first chain into the positive complementary side, with boundary the actual positive Seifert push $x^+$; leave the second chain in $R$ with boundary $y$. An intrinsic boundary-collar push of their interiors and the common product near $F$ give the usual collared bounding chains in $B^4$, missing the corner $K$. Their supports are disjoint compact sets by the actual two-sided product. Choose disjoint relatively open smooth ambient neighborhoods $U,V\subset B^4$ of those supports, including their boundary cycles; these are smooth manifolds with boundary as open subsets of the standard smooth ball. In $U$, [F6] makes the smooth cycle $x^+$ bound a finite smooth real chain, since it bounds continuously there; likewise $y$ bounds in $V$. In each finite set of occurring simplices the equations for the boundary coefficients are rational, so rational Gaussian elimination replaces the real coefficients by rational ones without enlarging support. Near $S^3$, move the interiors inward and attach the standard product of the fixed boundary cycle with the collar interval. This puts both chains in common standard end collars, still in disjoint $U,V$. They therefore have empty interior intersection, and [F3] gives $V_{\mathbb Q}(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)=0$. The smoothing here concerns only chains in the disjoint smooth ambient regions; it assumes no smooth structure on $R$ or its TOP normal chart.

Apply the integral-saturation result [F4] to this $g$-dimensional rational isotropic subspace: $M=H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\cap L$ is a primitive rank-$g$ direct summand with $V|_{M\times M}=0$. By [F8] the pairing is on an integral Seifert lattice, so the metabolic-form definition makes $M$ a metabolizer. This proves the Statement for every locally flat slice disk, including every smooth slice disk.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a

$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological

$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings

derivations.claim: If $g=0$, $V$ is the empty matrix and a disk with its empty homology basis realizes it. Assume $g>0$. Put $J=V-V^T$ and $H=\mathbb Z^{2g}$. Choose a primitive vector $e\in H$. For every $x\in H$, the vector $x'=x-J(x,f)e+J(x,e)f$ satisfies $J(x',e)=J(x',f)=0$. Thus $H=\langle e,f\rangle\oplus\langle e,f\rangle^\perp$, and the restricted alternating form on the second summand is unimodular. Induction gives a basis with matrix $J_0=\bigoplus_{k=1}^g\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Let $P\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be the corresponding change of basis and put $W=P^TVP$; then $W-W^T=J_0$.

Start with a disk and attach $2g$ oriented bands in the standard one-boundary handle pattern. Their core curves form an integral basis with intersection matrix $J_0$. The result is a connected compact smooth oriented surface with one boundary component. Write $W_0$ for its positive-push matrix; by [F1], $W_0-W_0^T=J_0$.

For each band core, inserting an integer number of full twists in a small subarc changes only its self-linking entry by the chosen integer. The twist box is disjoint from the other core arcs, and the surface intersection matrix is unchanged. Perform these finitely many modifications to make every diagonal entry of $W_0$ equal the corresponding diagonal entry of $W$.

For each pair $i<j$, choose subarcs of bands $i$ and $j$ in a ball disjoint from every other core and every earlier modification. Insert the oriented local clasp whose two new mixed crossings between $a_i^+$ and $a_j$ have the same sign $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$. By [F2], their signed sum changes by $2\varepsilon$, so $W_{ij}$ changes by $\varepsilon$. The clasp preserves the abstract surface intersection form; by [F1], $W_{ij}-W_{ji}$ is unchanged, and therefore $W_{ji}$ also changes by $\varepsilon$. The move is supported away from every other core, so all other pair entries and all diagonal entries stay fixed. The target equation $W-W_0=(W-W_0)^T$ off the diagonal holds because both skew parts are $J_0$. A finite number of positive or negative clasps thus sets both entries to their target values for each pair, without changing previously treated pairs. The resulting surface has positive-push matrix exactly $W$.

The basis change $P^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ on this surface changes its matrix from $W$ to $(P^{-1})^TW P^{-1}=V$. The constructed surface has one boundary component, so its boundary is an oriented knot and the matrix is a Seifert matrix for that knot.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. An integral Seifert lattice is a pair $(H,V)$ in which $H$ is a free abelian group of rank $2g$ for some $g\geq0$, and $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ is bilinear with $V-V^T$ unimodular. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

derivations.claim: In $(H,V)\oplus(H,-V)$, the diagonal subgroup $\Delta H=\{(x,x):x\in H\}$ is a direct summand: it is the kernel of the surjection $(x,y)\mapsto x-y$ and that surjection has section $z\mapsto(z,0)$. Its rank is $\operatorname{rank}H$, half the rank of $H\oplus H$. For $x,y\in H$, $(V\oplus(-V))((x,x),(y,y))=V(x,y)-V(x,y)=0$, so $\Delta H$ is a metabolizer.
By [F1], the metabolic direct sum in step 1.1 represents zero, while the direct-sum relation identifies its class with $[V]+[-V]$. Hence $[-V]=-[V]$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. derivations.claim: The standard plumbing has the three crossing bands of the positive two-strand three-crossing closure: its two annular strips use successive pairs of the three bands, and their common disk is the plumbing square with its four alternating attaching edges. In oriented braid coordinates $(x,y,t)$ use $(X,Y,Z)=(x,-t,y)$, of determinant $+1$, to draw the closure on the $(X,Y)$ page with viewer $+Z$. The overpass runs down-left and the underpass down-right at each of the three crossings, while the two outside closure arcs are crossing-free. This is precisely the right-hand trefoil diagram of Rolfsen printed146, identified as right-hand on printed201; the comparison fixes the handedness using actual crossing data. The two core classes have intersection number $a\cdot_F b=1$ by [F2]. Since $F$ has genus one and one boundary component, its first homology has rank two; the intersection matrix in the core classes has determinant $1$. Therefore $a,b$ form an integral basis.

By [F1], each diagonal is the self-linking of a Hopf core. Equally oriented parallel cores transport to the two boundary components with one orientation reversed, so their linking is minus the boundary linking, namely $-1$. A small positive normal push returns to the first core through curves disjoint from the second. Thus $V_{11}=V_{22}=-1$. The disk specified in [F2] bounds $a^+$ in the complement of $b$, hence $\operatorname{lk}(a^+,b)=0$ and $V_{12}=0$. By [F3], $V_{12}-V_{21}=a\cdot_F b=1$, so $V_{21}=-1$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when an integral Seifert lattice comes from a knot's positive-push pairing. For an integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, its integral Witt class is its class in $G_{\mathbb Z}$ from the definition of metabolic Seifert form and algebraic knot concordance. An isomorphism $(W,B,T)\to(W',B',T')$ of rational isometric structures is a rational-linear bijection $P:W\to W'$ such that $B'(Px,Py)=B(x,y)$ and $PT=T'P$. A rational isometric structure is a triple $(W,B,T)$ in which $W$ is a finite-dimensional even-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space, $B:W\times W\to\mathbb Q$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T:W\to W$ is an invertible linear map satisfying $B(Tx,Ty)=B(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in W$, and $I-T$ is invertible. Such a structure is metabolic if it has a $T$-invariant subspace $L\subset W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=\frac12\dim_{\mathbb Q}W$ and $B|_{L\times L}=0$. Define the rational Witt group $G_{\mathbb Q}$ by direct sum of isomorphism classes, with metabolic structures set equal to zero. For a nonsingular integral Seifert matrix $V$, the associated matrix pair is $(B,T)=(V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)$; whether this pair is a rational isometric structure is established separately.

The definition concerns finite-rank bilinear forms and isometry data. It does not identify the unrelated Witt Lie algebra with either $G_{\mathbb Z}$ or $G_{\mathbb Q}$.

derivations.claim: The matrix $B=V+V^T$ is symmetric. Modulo $2$, $V+V^T\equiv V-V^T$; by [F1] the determinant of $V-V^T$ is odd, so $\det B$ is odd and in particular nonzero. Thus $B$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb Q$.

Since $V$ and $V^T$ are invertible over $\mathbb Q$, $T=V^{-1}V^T$ is invertible. Direct multiplication gives $$ T^TBT=V(V^T)^{-1}(V+V^T)V^{-1}V^T=V+V^T=B, $$ because the two summands in the middle expression simplify respectively to $V$ and $V^T$. Therefore $T$ is a $B$-isometry.
Finally $I-T=V^{-1}(V-V^T)$, which is invertible by invertibility of $V$ and [F1]. The three defining conditions in [F2] hold, proving the claim.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ bounds a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ whose oriented boundary is $K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. An integral Seifert lattice is a pair $(H,V)$ in which $H$ is a free abelian group of rank $2g$ for some $g\geq0$, and $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ is bilinear with $V-V^T$ unimodular. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

Assume full AC when the form is obtained from a knot. For every integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, the class represented by $(H,-V)$ is the additive inverse of the class represented by $(H,V)$ in $G_{\mathbb Z}$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $g\geq0$ and let $V\in M_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ satisfy $\det(V-V^T)=\pm1$, where the empty skew matrix has determinant $1$. There is a connected compact smooth oriented surface $F\subset S^3$ with one boundary component and an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ whose positive-push Seifert matrix is exactly $V$.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, and let $F,F'$ be any connected compact smooth oriented spanning surfaces for $K$. For any ordered integral bases of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and $H_1(F';\mathbb Z)$, the matrices of the positive-push Seifert pairing are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular congruences and the two rank-two elementary Seifert enlargements or their reverses.

Assume full AC for any knot-derived Seifert matrix. Let $V$ be an integral Seifert matrix and let $E_0(V;x,y,z)$ or $E_1(V;x,y,z)$ be either elementary enlargement in the definition of S-equivalence, where $x,y\in\mathbb Z^{2g}$ and $z\in\mathbb Z$. Then $E_0(V;x,y,z)$ and $E_1(V;x,y,z)$ are integral Seifert lattices, and each represents the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$ as $V$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(K,F)$ and $(K',F')$ be oriented knot and spanning-surface pairs in the oriented standard three-sphere, and let $h_t:S^3\to S^3$ be a smooth ambient isotopy with $h_0$ the identity, $h_1(K)=K'$, and $h_1(F)=F'$, preserving the given orientations. If $V$ and $V'$ are their Seifert matrices in any integral bases, then the basis transported by $h_1$ has matrix $V$, and any other target basis with transition matrix $P$ has matrix $V'=P^TVP$. Hence $V$ and $V'$ are S-equivalent, meaning they are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular congruences and the two elementary rank-two enlargement moves or their reverses.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The set of smooth oriented knot concordance classes in the standard three-sphere is an abelian group under connected sum, with identity the standard unknot and inverse of $[K]$ represented by the reverse mirror $K^\dagger$. Separately, the set of locally flat topological oriented knot concordance classes is an abelian group under connected sum, with the same identity and inverse convention.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in the unit four-ball $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ if and only if it is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $D\subset B^4$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk with oriented boundary $K$. Then the positive-push Seifert lattice $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is metabolic: it has a rank-$g$ primitive direct summand on which $V$ vanishes identically.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $D\subset B^4$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk with oriented boundary $K$. Then the positive-push Seifert lattice $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is metabolic: it has a rank-$g$ primitive direct summand on which $V$ vanishes identically.

derivations.claim: For a smooth oriented knot $K$, choose a surface and basis from [F1] and define $a(K)=[V_F]\in G_{\mathbb Z}$. The class is independent of this choice: [F4] relates any two such matrices by finitely many congruences and elementary enlargements or their inverses. A congruence is an isomorphism of the integral lattice, and each enlargement preserves the class. This also handles every integral basis choice. Applied to a transported surface under an oriented ambient isotopy, the same surface-independence statement and the pairing convention give a function on oriented knot types. This part is proved without a slice-disk premise.

Put representatives of $K,J$ and their chosen surfaces in separated balls, and join the surfaces by the connected-sum band away from the old basis curves. Their old first-homology bases together form a basis of the boundary-connected sum: collapsing the connecting band gives the wedge of the two surfaces, so first homology is their direct sum. Positive push-offs and the curves from opposite balls have linking number zero, since any curve in one ball bounds a rational, indeed integral, singular two-chain there, disjoint from the other ball. Thus the matrix is $V_K\oplus V_J$, and [F2] gives $a(K\#J)=a(K)+a(J)$. The unknot has its disk surface with empty matrix and hence $a(U)=0$. By step 1.1 these calculations are independent of the separated representatives and chosen surfaces.

Work first in the smooth category. A knot smoothly concordant to $U$ bounds a smooth proper disk by [F6], so [F8] gives $a(K)=0$. The inverse of $[J]$ is represented by $J^\dagger$, and therefore $J\#J^\dagger$ is concordant to $U$. Step 2.1 gives $a(J^\dagger)=-a(J)$. If $K$ and $J$ are smoothly concordant, their group difference $K\#J^\dagger$ is concordant to $U$, so $0=a(K\#J^\dagger)=a(K)-a(J)$. Hence $a$ descends to a well-defined map $\Phi_{\mathrm{sm}}$ on smooth concordance classes. Step 2.1 proves that this map is a group homomorphism. Here [F8] applies the proved locally flat metabolizer argument to the smooth slice disk.

The smooth homomorphism is onto. Each positive generator $[V]$ of $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the image of the realizing knot from [F3]. The image of a group homomorphism is a subgroup, so it also contains the negative of every such generator. Every element of the presented integral group is a finite sum of signed generators, hence is in the image. This proves the entire smooth surjective-homomorphism assertion.

In the locally flat category, [F10] supplies the group law and inverse needed for descent. If $K$ is TOP concordant to $U$, cap the unknot end of its collared annulus with the standard disk in a standard ball. Gluing that ball to $S^3\times I$ adds a radial collar to the ball, and the matching end product charts make the result a locally flat proper slice disk. By [F9] its Seifert form is metabolic, so $a(K)=0$ by [F2]. For TOP-concordant $K,J$, their group difference $K\#J^\dagger$ is TOP concordant to $U$. The smooth inverse calculation in step 3.1 already gives $a(J^\dagger)=-a(J)$, and step 2.1 therefore yields $0=a(K\#J^\dagger)=a(K)-a(J)$. Hence $a$ descends to $\Phi_{\mathrm{top}}$. Step 2.1 proves additivity, and the same realization argument as in step 4.1 makes its image contain every signed generator, hence all of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This proves the TOP surjective-homomorphism assertion under the unchanged full-AC hypothesis, using the explicitly external group input and the exact TOP metabolizer interface rather than the former conditional hold.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. An integral Seifert lattice is a pair $(H,V)$ in which $H$ is a free abelian group of rank $2g$ for some $g\geq0$, and $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ is bilinear with $V-V^T$ unimodular. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when an integral Seifert lattice comes from a knot's positive-push pairing. For an integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, its integral Witt class is its class in $G_{\mathbb Z}$ from the definition of metabolic Seifert form and algebraic knot concordance. An isomorphism $(W,B,T)\to(W',B',T')$ of rational isometric structures is a rational-linear bijection $P:W\to W'$ such that $B'(Px,Py)=B(x,y)$ and $PT=T'P$. A rational isometric structure is a triple $(W,B,T)$ in which $W$ is a finite-dimensional even-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space, $B:W\times W\to\mathbb Q$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T:W\to W$ is an invertible linear map satisfying $B(Tx,Ty)=B(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in W$, and $I-T$ is invertible. Such a structure is metabolic if it has a $T$-invariant subspace $L\subset W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=\frac12\dim_{\mathbb Q}W$ and $B|_{L\times L}=0$. Define the rational Witt group $G_{\mathbb Q}$ by direct sum of isomorphism classes, with metabolic structures set equal to zero. For a nonsingular integral Seifert matrix $V$, the associated matrix pair is $(B,T)=(V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)$; whether this pair is a rational isometric structure is established separately.

The definition concerns finite-rank bilinear forms and isometry data. It does not identify the unrelated Witt Lie algebra with either $G_{\mathbb Z}$ or $G_{\mathbb Q}$.

Every element of the integral algebraic concordance group has an invertible integral Seifert-matrix representative, allowing the empty matrix for the zero-rank representative. If $V$ is any such representative, the rule
$$
[V]\longmapsto[(\mathbb Q^{\operatorname{rank}V},V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)]
$$
defines an injective homomorphism into the rational isometric Witt group. An integral Seifert form represents zero in the integral group if and only if it is itself metabolic. These are finite algebraic assertions and require no choice principle; knot-derived forms retain their separately stated choice assumptions.

For a monic irreducible polynomial $p\in\mathbb Q[t]$ with $p(0)\ne0$, put $p^*(t)=p(0)^{-1}t^{\deg p}p(t^{-1})$. For each such self-reciprocal polynomial $p=p^*$ other than $t-1$, let $G_p$ be the subgroup of the rational isometric Witt group generated by structures whose characteristic polynomial is a power of $p$. Then restriction to the generalized primary subspaces induces an isomorphism
$$
G_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{p=p^*,\ p\ne t-1}G_p.
$$
A pair of distinct reciprocal primary factors contributes a metabolic structure and therefore contributes zero. Only finitely many components of any given class are nonzero. No choice principle is needed.

Let $p\in\mathbb Q[t]$ be monic, irreducible, and self-reciprocal, with $p(0)
e0$ and $p
e t-1$. Put $E=\mathbb Q[t]/(p)$, write $\alpha=t+(p)$, and give $E$ the involution $\iota(\alpha)=\alpha^{-1}$. If $p
e t+1$, the primary component $G_p$ of the rational isometric Witt group is isomorphic to the hermitian Witt group of $E$ with this involution. Here the latter group is generated by finite-dimensional nonsingular hermitian forms, with orthogonal direct sum as addition and forms having an isotropic half-dimensional $E$-subspace set to zero. If $p=t+1$, the same conclusion holds with the group generated by even-dimensional nonsingular symmetric forms over $\mathbb Q$, modulo metabolic forms. For a semisimple primary isometry, the comparison sends a hermitian form $h$ to $(\operatorname{Tr}_{E/\mathbb Q}h,\alpha)$ on its underlying rational vector space. These comparisons require no choice principle.

Let $E/F$ be a quadratic extension of number fields with its nontrivial involution. In the hermitian Witt group $W(E/F)$, the kernel of all signatures is killed by $4$. The joint signature image is a free abelian subgroup of $\mathbb Z^s$ of rank at most $s$, where $s$ is the number of real places of $F$ at which $E$ becomes complex. No choice principle is required.

Let $W(\mathbb Q)$ denote the Witt group of nonsingular symmetric bilinear forms over $\mathbb Q$, with orthogonal sum as addition and metabolic forms set to zero. For every such form $q$, four times its Witt class equals its signature times the class of the four-dimensional identity form. In particular, the kernel of the signature is killed by $4$, including its restriction to the subgroup of even-dimensional classes. The signature image is $\mathbb Z$ on the full group and $2\mathbb Z$ on the even-dimensional subgroup.

In the integral algebraic concordance group put
$$
F_b=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_n=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-n^2\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q_q=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-(3q-1)/4\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $b,n$ range over positive integers and $q$ ranges over primes congruent to $3$ modulo $4$ other than $3$. The classes $[F_b]$ are independent of infinite order, each $[P_n]$ has exact order two, and each $[Q_q]$ has exact order four. The three families together generate their direct sum, isomorphic to
$$
\mathbb Z^{(\mathbb N)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^{(\mathbb N)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)^{(\mathbb N)}.
$$
Moreover the classes $[P_n]$ have linearly independent images in $G_{\mathbb Z}/2G_{\mathbb Z}$. These are pure algebraic assertions about the displayed forms; no choice principle is required.

Assume full AC. Let $G$ be a countable abelian group and $s:G\to\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb Z$ a homomorphism whose kernel $K$ satisfies $4K=0$. Then $K$ is precisely the torsion subgroup of $G$, and for cardinals $r,u,v\le\aleph_0$,
$$G\cong\mathbb Z^{(r)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^{(u)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)^{(v)}.$$
If $G$ contains elements $f_i,p_i,q_i$, indexed by positive integers, such that the $f_i$ are integer-linearly independent, the order-two elements $p_i$ have linearly independent images in $G/2G$, and the $2q_i$ are linearly independent order-two elements with $4q_i=0$, then $r=u=v=\aleph_0$.

derivations.claim: Both groups in [F1] are countable. A rational structure is specified, after one finite basis choice, by its dimension and two finite rational matrices; the isometry and nonsingularity conditions select a subset of this countable set. An integral Seifert lattice is likewise specified by a finite integer matrix. The corresponding presented groups are quotients of the countable sets of finite signed lists of these matrices: finite lists of rationals or integers have explicit natural-number codes, so a countable union over their lengths is countable. Quotients are countable by the surjection from these codes. This argument does not identify the two types of object. Use the injection [F2] to regard $G_{\mathbb Z}$ as a subgroup of $G_{\mathbb Q}$ for the rest of the proof.

For each primary group of [F3] other than $t+1$, the involution on $E$ is nontrivial. Indeed if its distinguished generator equalled its inverse, its irreducible polynomial would divide $t^2-1$; $t-1$ is excluded by invertibility of $I-T$ and $t+1$ was separated. If $F=E^{\sigma}$, choose $0\ne\delta$ with $\sigma\delta=-\delta$. Every $z\in E$ has the unique decomposition $(z+\sigma z)/2+\delta(z-\sigma z)/(2\delta)$ with coefficients in $F$, so $E/F$ is quadratic. Take all hermitian signatures at real places of $F$ where $E$ becomes complex, and take the ordinary rational signature on the $t+1$ component. These form a homomorphism $s:G_{\mathbb Q}\to\bigoplus_{j\in J}\mathbb Z$. The index set $J$ is at most countable: there are countably many rational irreducible polynomials and finitely many real places for each number field. Each individual class has only finitely many primary components, so its total signature has finite support. With [A1] fix an enumeration of this index set, adding zero coordinates if needed, to put the target inside $\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb Z$.

If $s(x)=0$, each of the finitely many nonzero primary components of $x$ has all its signatures zero. By [F4] four times each such component is zero; the primary direct-sum isomorphism [F3] gives $4x=0$. Thus $4\ker s=0$. The same holds for the kernel of $s\iota$ on $G_{\mathbb Z}$, since $\iota$ is injective. Applying [F6] separately to these two countable groups gives decompositions of each with at most countable free, order-two and order-four multiplicities. In particular every torsion class has order dividing four; the proof has used signatures to identify all torsion, rather than merely exhibiting some finite-order classes.

In either group, the elements $F_b,P_n,Q_q$ of [F5] meet the three infinitude tests of [F6]. A finite nonzero integer combination of the $F_b$ cannot be torsion: if some nonzero multiple vanished, projection to each distinct primary factor would contradict the infinite order of its $F_b$. The $2Q_q$ are independent order-two elements, by distinct primary factors and exact order four. For the rational quotient by doubles, project to the quadratic primary factor of $P_n$, identified with a hermitian Witt group by [F3], and then take hermitian rank modulo two. This is a homomorphism because metabolic hermitian forms have even rank. The two-dimensional rational structure of $P_n$ has rank one over its quadratic field, so the homomorphism takes value one there; it vanishes on the other $P_m$ by their distinct primary factors, and on every double by its target $\mathbb Z/2$. Hence the $P_n$ are independent modulo doubles in $G_{\mathbb Q}$ as well as in $G_{\mathbb Z}$, the latter also following directly from [F5]. Thus the $P_n$ are independent in the quotient by doubles in each group. This last condition forces independent order-two summands after splitting; independent order-two elements alone would not suffice, since doubles of order-four elements also have order two. There are infinitely many indicated primes $q$ by the finite Euclidean argument in [F5].

By [F6] and step 4.1, all three multiplicities in both decompositions from step 3.1 are infinite, and their countable upper bounds make them precisely $\aleph_0$. This is the displayed abstract group isomorphism for each of $G_{\mathbb Q}$ and $G_{\mathbb Z}$. The integral result here follows from its proved injection, the shared exponent bound, the splitting argument and the actual integral families. No assertion that primary summands split integrally, no identification of the rational group with its integral subgroup, and no unspecified integral localization or coupling theorem is needed for this abstract isomorphism. In particular the allowed $t+1$ component of the original rational Definition has been retained throughout.

derivations.claim: The disk has $H_1=0$, so its Seifert matrix is the empty matrix. The subgroup $M=0$ has rank zero, is a direct summand, and the pairing vanishes on it. By [F1], this is metabolic and represents the identity class.

By [F2] and [F3], the trefoil's rational structure has symmetric form $B=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix}$. For a vector $(m,n)\in\mathbb Q^2$, $B((m,n),(m,n))= -2(m^2+mn+n^2)=-2(m+n/2)^2-3n^2/2$, which is negative whenever $(m,n)\ne(0,0)$. Thus the rational structure has no nonzero isotropic line. For an integral vector the Seifert self-pairing is $-(m^2+mn+n^2)<0$, so no rank-one subgroup has identically zero Seifert pairing, and [F4] rules out an integral metabolizer.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose two boundary components, with their induced orientations, have linking number $+1$. Let $F$ be the genus-one Seifert surface obtained by plumbing two positive Hopf bands in a square, with oriented core curves $a,b$ forming a positive handle basis, and choose the plumbing side so that $a^+$ bounds a disk in $S^3$ disjoint from $b$. The oriented boundary of this standard positive two-band plumbing is the right-handed trefoil. In the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ with ordered basis $(a,b)$, the Seifert matrix is
$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Fix the orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ chosen for the mirror convention in the oriented connected-sum definition. If $K$ is a smooth oriented knot, its mirror $r(K)$ carries the orientation induced from $K$ by $r$. The reverse mirror of $K$, denoted $K^\dagger$, is the image $r(K)$ with its knot orientation reversed. Thus $K^\dagger$ changes both the ambient orientation convention and the orientation of the knot.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the stated full-AC hypothesis supplies $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Apply [F5] to $T$; its conclusion gives the required smooth proper disk for $S=T\#T^\dagger$ and the stated radial critical-point indices.

The reverse-mirror surface is $-r(F)$, so its positive normal is the reflected original positive normal: the ambient reflection and surface reversal cancel in the normal orientation. Thus the transported basis has matrix $-V$, since reflection negates linking. For this particular trefoil matrix put $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; direct multiplication gives $P^TVP=V^T$. Rechoose the basis of the reverse-mirror surface by $P$. Its matrix is then $-V^T$. This is a specified trefoil basis change, not a general image-basis formula for reverse mirrors.

Form the boundary-connected-sum Seifert surface in the two summand balls. Cycles from different summands have zero linking because each bounds a $2$-chain in its own ball, disjoint from the other summand. The combined basis therefore has matrix $W=\operatorname{diag}(V,-V^T)$.

Let $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Direct multiplication gives $P^TV^TP=V$. The graph $M=\{(x,Px):x\in\mathbb Z^2\}$ is spanned by $e_1+e_4$ and $e_2+e_3$; projection onto the first factor identifies it with $\mathbb Z^2$, so it is a rank-$2$ direct summand. For any $x,y\in\mathbb Z^2$, $(x,Px)^TW(y,Py)=x^T(V-P^TV^TP)y=0$. Thus $M$ is a metabolizer.

The two blocks give $\det(V-tV^T)=(1-t)^2+t=t^2-t+1$ and $\det(-V^T+tV)=(t-1)^2+t=t^2-t+1$. Hence $\det(W-tW^T)=(t^2-t+1)^2$. For $f(t)=t^2-t+1$, one has $f(t^{-1})=t^{-2}f(t)$, so $\det(W-tW^T)=t^2f(t)f(t^{-1})$. By [F6], this is the claimed Fox–Milnor norm factorization of $\Delta_S$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], $\Delta_T(t)\doteq\det(V-tV^T)=(1-t)^2+t=t^2-t+1$. Thus $|\Delta_T(-1)|=3$, since every Laurent unit $\pm t^k$ evaluates to $\pm1$ at $-1$.

By [F6] and step2.1, the trefoil does not bound a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball. Independently, if such a disk existed then [F5] would give a metabolic Seifert form, contradicting the signature calculation in step2.2 and [F4].
