citations.quote: Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the analytic existence and invariant chain-comparison assertions. Let a balanced sutured manifold be taut. For a specified coherent orientation class, its integral sutured Floer homology has a direct summand isomorphic to the integers. More precisely, a finite good taut hierarchy terminating in product balls induces a split inclusion of the terminal product homology into the original homology, with orientation classes induced along the cuts.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a null-homologous knot in a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$, let $F$ be a genus-$g$ Seifert surface, and let $(M,\gamma)$ be the balanced sutured manifold obtained by cutting the compact exterior of $K$ along $F$. For a surface-adapted admissible sutured Heegaard diagram, the generator correspondence between the top Alexander summand of the knot Floer complex and the sutured Floer disk-count module identifies their disk-count differentials. Under the hypotheses of a horizontal decomposition, the induced chain map realizes Ni's horizontal decomposition formula. For an essential separating product annulus with connected $R_+$ and $R_-$ whose decomposition has two balanced pieces, the induced chain map realizes Ni's product-annulus tensor formula. These assertions use the specified basepoint domains, periodic-domain admissibility, and exact characteristic-product-region hypotheses; they make no claim that generic Heegaard disk existence alone supplies the decomposition maps.

For the actual marked Seifert surface of genus g, oriented as minus the fiber for the cut, an adapted generator x has Alexander degree g minus the number of its interior polygon coordinates. Thus the top degree-g generators are exactly the outer generators and correspond to the cut diagram generators with their ordered intersection signs. If the integral top homology is one copy of the integers, the actual cut incidence matrix is unimodular, the cut is an integral homology product, and its periodic-domain group vanishes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an actual weakly admissible balanced sutured diagram on a surface with boundary, the integral disk complex exists for each specified coherent orientation class. Its disk, triangle and quadrilateral moduli spaces admit finite signed counts and the corresponding oriented boundary identities on actual weakly admissible multidiagrams. Sphere and one-torus boundary bubbles are excluded by the zero boundary-region multiplicities. Orientation classes are transported rather than declared equivalent.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix a finite collection of admitted compact marked sutured diagrams, a finite sequence of diagram moves or surface cuts, and finite-dimensional parameter families of dimension at most two. Suppose the local Fredholm, finite-dimensional Sard, compactness and gluing constructions are supplied for their actual Cauchy–Riemann operators, including the prescribed endpoint and protected-neighborhood conditions. All selections needed to apply those constructions, choose coherent determinant orientations, and obtain simultaneous regular data can then be made under Countable Choice. In particular no uncountable choice of analytic charts or regular data is needed for these fixed finite integral Floer constructions.

derivations.claim: Choose a Seifert surface F realizing the least genus g=g(K), and let E be the compact exterior. The exterior is irreducible: a sphere in its interior bounds two balls in S³ by F1; the connected knot neighborhood lies entirely on one side, so the other ball is disjoint from it and lies in E. A small oriented meridian loop meets F once, so F is nonseparating: a separating two-sided surface would have algebraic intersection zero with every closed loop. Cut E along the connected F to obtain connected M with the product annular suture and the two F faces. Their Euler characteristics agree and the boundary meets that suture, so M is balanced. A sphere in M is disjoint from F in E. Its E-ball is also disjoint from F: since F is connected, disjoint from the sphere, and has its boundary on ∂E outside that interior ball, it lies entirely on the other side. Thus that ball remains a ball in M. This proves irreducibility of the actual cut without a general-Y irreducibility assertion.

The two faces are incompressible. A compression of F along a nonseparating essential circle produces a connected Seifert surface of genus g−1. A separating compression produces a boundary-bearing Seifert component and a closed component. The latter has positive genus, since otherwise the original compression circle bounded a disk on F; discarding it again gives a Seifert surface of genus strictly less than g. Both contradict minimality. A face compression in M would be such a compression in E. For g=0 the disk has no essential compression circle.

To prove the actual sutured norm-minimality, take any compact oriented properly embedded competitor T representing the positive face class in H₂(M,γ;Z). Its total oriented boundary in H₁(γ;Z) is one copy of the longitude. Put its boundary circles in the interior of the annular suture. Cap an innermost contractible boundary circle by its disk in the annulus, pushed into the boundary collar; this operation increases Euler characteristic and cannot increase the Thurston complexity. Continue until every boundary circle is essential. Whenever both orientations remain, choose an adjacent opposite pair. The annulus between them contains no other boundary circle. Glue it to T in a thin boundary collar and round the corners. This gives an embedded oriented surface and removes the pair. Euler characteristic is unchanged; if two components merge, the inequality max(0,−(χ₁+χ₂))≤max(0,−χ₁)+max(0,−χ₂) shows that total complexity cannot increase. For two circles on one component its Euler characteristic, hence complexity, is unchanged. The finite sequence ends with exactly one essential boundary circle, since its total winding is one. Delete all closed components, which also cannot increase complexity. The remaining connected surface embeds in E and extends across the knot collar to an actual Seifert surface for K of the same genus. Its genus is at least g by minimality. For g≥1 its complexity is therefore at least 2g−1=x(F); for g=0 it is at least zero=x(F). It follows that x(T)≥x(F). The same argument applies to the negative face. Thus M is the actual taut balanced sutured manifold, by irreducibility and norm-minimality. The boundary cancellations were used only to derive a lower bound and need not preserve the competitor's relative class after it is mapped to E.

Work under the full-Choice analytic framework F6 on the actual fixed finite hierarchy and marked adapted diagram. Its admitted sutured operator problems retain the boundary/divisor barriers, periodic-domain and area conditions and the specified coherent orientation class. With the regular data and compactification/gluing construction supplied at that scope, apply F3 to the marked Seifert surface F. Its meridional frame, rather than an unspecified closure framing, gives an admissible adapted representative. By F4 every generator has Alexander degree g−n_P(x), with n_P(x) a nonnegative integer. Hence its whole integral chain complex has no generator, and thus no homology, in a grading greater than g.

The entire degree-g summand is the outer summand, and F3 identifies its signed differential with the actual cut complex of M. Since M is taut, F2 gives that this cut homology contains a split copy of Z for the orientation class induced by the given knot complex. Consequently the integral knot Floer group at degree g is nonzero. This also covers g=0: the taut cut argument and the same signed chain map apply to the minimum disk, without a genus-one connected-sum or field-coefficient substitution.

Degree g is nonzero and every larger degree is zero, so the maximum of the stated nonvanishing degree set is exactly g(K). The proof uses only the literal S³ ball-side and minimum-Seifert-genus arguments above; it makes no claim of arbitrary general-Y Thurston norm detection.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the analytic existence and invariant chain-comparison assertions. An actual good decomposing surface admits an adapted admissible nice diagram. For a specified coherent orientation class on the exterior complex, the outer summand of that diagram is integrally chain isomorphic to the cut diagram with the induced orientation class; nonzero periodic domains are retained by pullback of characters. When the surface separates into two balanced pieces, every generator is outer and the full complex is identified with the graded tensor product of the two component complexes. In particular the usual two-piece horizontal decomposition has this chain formula. It gives the homology tensor formula over every field; over the integers it gives the graded Künneth exact sequence including Tor.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the analytic existence and invariant chain-comparison assertions. Let a balanced sutured manifold have connected positive and negative boundary faces. An essential separating product-annulus decomposition into balanced pieces admits a graded integral tensor chain equivalence, with coherent orientation classes induced from the specified class. This realizes the homology tensor formula over every field and the integral Künneth formula with Tor. Product-disk decompositions and product one-handle additions have literal integral complex identifications. The closure construction for any connected pair of faces identifies its top knot complex with the actual sutured disk complex using the specified marking and orientation class.

Let $Y$ be a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold, let $K\subset Y$ be a smooth oriented null-homologous knot, and let $F\subset Y$ be a compact connected oriented embedded surface with oriented boundary $K$. Choose a closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, put $M=Y\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, and let $\gamma_\mu$ be the union of two disjoint annuli on $\partial M$ whose core sutures are parallel meridians of $K$ with opposite orientations. Delete a collar of $\partial F$ to regard $F$ as a properly embedded surface in $(M,\gamma_\mu)$, with relative class $[F]\in H_2(M,\partial M;\mathbb Z)$. Let $t_\mu$ be the meridional boundary trivialization of the oriented plane field used in the relative Spin-c definition. For $\mathfrak{s}\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(M,\gamma_\mu)$, its Alexander grading is

$$A_F(\mathfrak{s})=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak{s},t_\mu),[F]\right\rangle,$$

with the standard sign convention that gives the usual Alexander grading for knots in $S^3$. For a balanced admissible sutured Heegaard diagram of $(M,\gamma_\mu)$, the Spin-c summand $SFH(M,\gamma_\mu,\mathfrak{s};\mathbb Z)$ is the homology of the integral sutured Floer disk-count complex generated by the Heegaard generators assigned to $\mathfrak{s}$. Define the integral knot Floer group in Alexander grading $i$ by

$$\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(Y,K,[F],i;\mathbb Z)=\bigoplus_{\substack{\mathfrak{s}\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(M,\gamma_\mu)\\ A_F(\mathfrak{s})=i}}SFH(M,\gamma_\mu,\mathfrak{s};\mathbb Z).$$

This fixes the integral coefficient convention. The equivalent associated-graded closed Heegaard-complex presentation, invariance under changing diagrams, and comparison with the mod-two grid complex are separate theorems; this definition supplies none of their proofs or a coefficient-change map.

For the actual marked Seifert surface of genus g, oriented as minus the fiber for the cut, an adapted generator x has Alexander degree g minus the number of its interior polygon coordinates. Thus the top degree-g generators are exactly the outer generators and correspond to the cut diagram generators with their ordered intersection signs. If the integral top homology is one copy of the integers, the actual cut incidence matrix is unimodular, the cut is an integral homology product, and its periodic-domain group vanishes.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Construct the actual marked closure/adapted surface diagram from the relative Morse handles, carrying the page longitude and meridional boundary frame. Positive boundary fingers, the uniform relative windings, and permissible niceification give the admitted diagram. The Chern obstruction formula evaluates on minus F as minus 2g plus twice the number of interior polygon coordinates. Consequently its degree-g generators are exactly its outer generators. Each index-one disk is an exhausted embedded bigon or rectangle and lifts uniquely in the cut/double surface. The literal Fredholm conjugacies and the pullback of the specified periodic-domain orientation character align every coefficient after generator signs. Thus this generator correspondence identifies the full disk-count differentials over the integers. Signed relative moves transport the identification to the defining complexes, with their markings and coherent orientation classes.

For a horizontal decomposition, the cut components are balanced. In its adapted diagram there is no reverse cross-family intersection from side two to side one; the equal row and column counts force every perfect-matching generator to avoid the polygon. Thus the whole complex is the outer complex. The cut surface is a disjoint union, so each index-one disk has exactly one nonconstant factor. Ordering determinant factors gives the Koszul differential ∂(x1⊗x2)=∂x1⊗x2+(−1)^|x1|x1⊗∂x2. This is the horizontal chain map and the complete integral chain formula. Taking homology over any field gives Ni's horizontal formula. Taking homology over the integers instead gives the Künneth exact sequence including Tor; no unqualified integral homology tensor formula is asserted.

For an essential separating product annulus with connected R+ and R− and two balanced cut pieces, form the two rounded horizontal surfaces from opposite boundary faces and the annulus. Their actual cobordism regions give the required relative class and their Euler sums give the horizontal equality. This reduces the operation to attachment of a product region. A rooted cut-arc forest removes a product region meeting the sutures by literal product-disk identifications. For an interior essential product region, the explicit once-punctured-torus block forces its two fixed coordinates and isolates the only possible extra genus-one two-corner domain, whose Maslov index is minus one; it cannot contribute. Both comparison diagrams therefore have precisely the same supported disks and conjugate oriented operators in the unchanged complement. The resulting integral chain identification, followed by the remaining product-disk cuts, gives the full separating-annulus graded tensor operation. It gives Ni's field formula and the integral Künneth/Tor formulation as above. All constructions keep the stated basepoint zero regions, actual periodic lattices and essential-annulus hypotheses. They apply when the specified characteristic product region supplies those actual surfaces; they do not infer its geometry from generic disk existence.

It is balanced: both faces have Euler characteristic $1-2g$, no component is closed, and every boundary component meets the vertical annulus. A meridian intersects $F$ algebraically once, so $F$ is nonseparating and the cut is connected.

The signed cut comparison gives $\operatorname{SFH}(M,\gamma;\mathbb Z)\cong\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(Y,K,[F],g;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. The grading uses the supplied class $[F]$ and genus of this actual surface; no genus-detection theorem for a different ambient manifold is substituted.

The irreducibility assumption applies to $E$: pushing away the deleted-knot end identifies every compact sphere question with that in $Y\setminus K$. A sphere in the interior of $M$ is therefore a sphere disjoint from $F$ in $E$ and bounds a ball in $E$. Since $F$ is connected and disjoint from this sphere, if it entered the ball it would lie wholly in its interior, contradicting $\partial F\subset\partial E$. The ball is consequently disjoint from $F$; shrink the cut collar if necessary to obtain the same ball in $M$. Thus $M$ is irreducible.

If $(M,\gamma)$ were not taut, its integral sutured Floer homology would vanish by the external vanishing input, contradicting step 1.2. Therefore it is taut. This is the contrapositive of F2, not a reversal of taut hierarchy nonvanishing.

If the taut balanced $(M,\gamma)$ were not a product, F3 would give $\mathbb Z^2\hookrightarrow\operatorname{SFH}(M,\gamma;\mathbb Z)$. Such an injection into $\mathbb Z$ is impossible: images $a,b$ of its two basis vectors satisfy the nontrivial integer relation $b a-a b=0$ when either is nonzero, and an image zero itself contradicts injectivity. The two disjoint outer summands in the source argument therefore contradict step 1.2. Hence the actual $F$-cut exterior is a product sutured manifold. This includes $g=0$ and uses the corrected characteristic-pair qualification F4.

citations.quote: Let a null-homologous knot in a closed connected oriented three-manifold be fibered with a specified connected oriented Seifert fiber. Its compact exterior with two meridional sutures admits a good surface-adapted balanced diagram carrying that actual Seifert surface, its boundary longitude, and the meridional boundary trivialization. For a fiber of an actual open book the cut/double diagram represents the marked product obtained by cutting along the fiber, with the original monodromy retained in regluing.

A good admissible surface-adapted balanced diagram can be made nice by a finite sequence of permissible fingers and own-family disk slides preserving its surface marking. Weak admissibility is preserved. Every complementary region of the underlying diagram disjoint from its true boundary is a bigon or square.

Two balanced Heegaard diagrams of the same marked sutured manifold are connected by relative attaching-circle isotopies, own-family disk slides, and ordinary stabilizations and destabilizations. An ordinary stabilization can be moved by such slides to the true boundary region. Under the Axiom of Choice, these moves induce integral chain homotopy equivalences for the transported coherent orientation class, and the product sutured manifold has integral homology equal to one copy of the integers. For supplied actual coherent systems on a homology-product branch, the periodic-domain character ambiguity vanishes.

For the actual marked Seifert surface of genus g, oriented as minus the fiber for the cut, an adapted generator x has Alexander degree g minus the number of its interior polygon coordinates. Thus the top degree-g generators are exactly the outer generators and correspond to the cut diagram generators with their ordered intersection signs. If the integral top homology is one copy of the integers, the actual cut incidence matrix is unimodular, the cut is an integral homology product, and its periodic-domain group vanishes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the analytic existence and invariant chain-comparison assertions. For an actual nice admissible good surface diagram whose cut has zero periodic-domain group, the outer differential and the cut differential are identified over the integers after changing generator signs. This identifies the top Alexander homology with the integral homology of the cut diagram when the surface is the marked Seifert surface and the outer degree is its genus. The conclusion applies in particular to a fiber cut and to the rank-one branch of the cut Euler-matrix reduction.

derivations.claim: Use the actual binding bridge and drilling construction to represent the exterior with two meridional sutures, carrying the actual page longitude and the class of F. The adapted surface cut is literally the result of cutting this mapping torus along its fiber, hence is F times an interval with its product sutures. Apply the finite permissible niceification. Signed relative diagram moves compare the resulting complex to the chosen defining complex, with its specified coherent orientation class transported. No restriction on Y or change of coefficient ring is made.

In this marked adapted diagram the local Euler obstruction is minus 2g plus twice the number of interior polygon coordinates when evaluated on minus F. Therefore the Alexander degree is g minus that number: degree g is precisely the outer generator set, and no higher degree occurs. The product cut has zero periodic-domain group, either directly from its empty product diagram and the relative handle description, or from its vanishing relative integral homology. The signed cut comparison consequently identifies the whole degree-g differential with the cut differential, after harmless changes of generator signs.

The empty diagram of the actual product has one empty-tuple generator and no nonconstant disk, so its integral chain complex is Z with zero differential. The signed relative move equivalences identify its homology with that of the actual cut diagram. Combining with the full top-summand chain identification gives the asserted integral group isomorphism. The exterior orientation character restricts trivially to the zero-periodic cut, so this conclusion holds for the specified defining class without asserting equivalence of arbitrary orientation systems on the uncut exterior.

citations.quote: Let $K$ be a null-homologous knot in a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$, let $Y\setminus K$ be irreducible, and let $F$ be a genus-$g$ Seifert surface. If the integral top Alexander group $\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(Y,K,[F],g;\mathbb Z)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$, then the sutured manifold obtained by cutting the compact knot exterior along $F$ is a product sutured manifold. The argument uses Ni's homology-product reduction, the horizontal and separating product-annulus decompositions, the characteristic product region, and Gabai's taut-foliation input under their stated hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Apply F1 to the actual class $[F]$, the actual genus $g$ and the given integral group. The cut exterior is a product $F\times[0,1]$ as a sutured manifold. In particular the two horizontal faces correspond to the two copies of the original $F$, rather than to a surface selected only by a genus or homology calculation.

To restore the exterior, identify those two faces using their actual gluing map. In product coordinates this is $(x,1)\sim(h(x),0)$ for a self-homeomorphism $h:F\to F$. Thus the exterior is the mapping torus of $h$. Its projection to $[0,1]/(0\sim1)=S^1$ is a surface bundle, and the seam is precisely the original embedded $F$.

The vertical boundary is the mapping torus of $\partial F$. Its boundary collar extends this bundle over the deleted-knot end, giving the fibration of $Y\setminus K$ with fiber the interior of $F$, or equivalently with compact fiber $F$ in the compact exterior. This proves the stated fiberedness with the prescribed surface, for arbitrary $Y$ and also for genus zero.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $I^*$ be the binary icosahedral group, the group of $120$ unit quaternions acting on the unit sphere $S^3$ by left multiplication, and put $P=S^3/I^*$. The quotient is a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold with universal cover $S^3$ and deck group $I^*$. Then $H_*(P;\mathbb Z)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Z)$ and $\pi_1(P)\cong I^*$ is nontrivial.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The unknot $U$ bounds its spanning disk inside $B_0$, so $[U]=0$ in $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. For $X=P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3$, use the collar enlargements [F5] of $X$ and $B^3$ in $P$. They form an open cover, retract to those pieces, and have intersection retracting to $S^2$; apply [F2] to this open cover. Since $H_1(S^2)=0$ by [F3], exactness injects $H_1(X)$ into $H_1(P)=0$, so $H_1(X)=0$. The same exact sequence in degree zero, using $H_1(P)=0$ and $H_0(P)=H_0(S^2)=H_0(B^3)=\mathbb Z$, gives $0\to\mathbb Z\to H_0(X)\oplus\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\to0$. Rank comparison yields $H_0(X)\cong\mathbb Z$, so each punctured summand is connected with $H_1=0$.

Put $A=B_0\setminus U$ and let $C$ be the closed ball on the other side of $\partial B_0$ in $S^3$. Identify $B_0$ with the unit ball and $U$ with a round circle in the plane $z=0$. From every point of $A$, the vertical segment in the direction of the sign of its $z$-coordinate reaches $\partial B_0$ without meeting $U$; when $z=0$, the starting point is not on $U$ and the upward segment meets the plane only there. Since $\partial B_0$ is path-connected, $A$ is path-connected. Thicken $A$ and $C$ by collars to obtain an open cover of $S^3\setminus U$ whose overlap retracts to $S^2$. The map on $H_0(S^2)$ is the injection $1\mapsto(1,-1)$. Since $H_1(S^2)=0$ and $C$ is contractible, [F2] identifies $H_1(A;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(S^3\setminus U;\mathbb Z)$; [F3] identifies the latter with $\mathbb Z$.

Apply [F2] to the open collar enlargements [F5] of the two punctured summands in $Y$; the pieces and intersection retract to the punctured summands and $S^2$, respectively. By step 1.1 both summands are connected and have zero $H_1$, and the map $H_0(S^2;\mathbb Z)\to H_0(P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_0(P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3;\mathbb Z)$ sends $1$ to $(1,-1)$ and is injective. Exactness gives $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$. Since $Y$ is closed, connected, and oriented, [F4] gives $H_2(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$ and $H_0(Y;\mathbb Z)=H_3(Y;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$. Hence $Y$ is an integral homology sphere. The duality and UCT uses are under [A1].

The side of $S$ in the second summand is $P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3$, which is not a $3$-ball: capping it with a ball would identify $P$ with $S^3$, contrary to [F1]. The other side is the union of $P\setminus\operatorname{int}(B^3\cup B_0)$ and $A$, glued along $\partial B_0$. Apply [F5] to obtain an open cover of this side, relative to its remaining boundary, with intersection retracting to that sphere and pieces retracting to the two named sets. Since $H_1(S^2)=0$ by [F3], exactness in [F2] makes the map from the direct sum of the two pieces' $H_1$ groups into the union's $H_1$ injective. Step 1.2 therefore makes this side's $H_1$ nonzero. Neither side is a $3$-ball, so $S$ cannot bound a $3$-ball in $Y\setminus U$.

Therefore $Y\setminus U$ is reducible and the displayed universal assertion is false. The diagram records the separation and location of $U$; the proof uses the homology and homotopy arguments above, not the diagram.

derivations.claim: Since $v$ is primitive, Bezout's identity gives $w\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ with $\det(v,w)=1$. The linear torus diffeomorphism taking the basis $(v,w)$ to the standard basis takes both curves to curves of class $(1,0)$. It is enough to prove the claim for that class.

Put the two curves in transverse position. If they intersect, lift them to the annular cover $A=\mathbb R^2/\langle(1,0)\rangle$. Each lift is an essential embedded circle, and the deck translates of each one are disjoint. In the universal cover of $A$, a lift of either circle is a proper line invariant under horizontal unit translation and contained in a bounded horizontal strip; all such lines have the same two ends. The signed intersection sum in a fundamental period is zero because both curves have class $(1,0)$. Thus intersections have both signs. Two successive intersections of opposite sign cut off a bounded region between subarcs of the two lines. Choose among such regions one with the least number of interior intersections and, among those, least horizontal width modulo deck translation. If a lifted arc entered the region, its first entry and exit would cut off a region with fewer interior intersections; if a nontrivial deck translate met it, the overlap would yield a region of smaller horizontal width. Hence its interior is disjoint from all lifted arcs and translates, and its projection is an embedded bigon in $T$. Isotoping one arc across the bigon removes two intersections and creates none. Compactness and transversality give finitely many intersections, so finitely many such isotopies make the curves disjoint.

The disjoint curves still have primitive class $(1,0)$, so neither bounds a disk. Cutting the torus along the second curve gives a connected orientable surface with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero, hence an annulus. The first curve remains essential in that annulus. Cutting the annulus along it gives two annuli, so it is parallel to the second curve and isotopic to it. Composing this isotopy with the finite bigon-removal isotopies in step 2.1 proves the assertion for the original pair; undoing the linear diffeomorphism proves it for $v$.

citations.quote:
Assume [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]], let $n\ge1$, and let
$1\le j\le n$. On $L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ define the $j$-th **Riesz
transform** $R_j$ by its Fourier multiplier

$$m_j(\xi):=\begin{cases}-i\,\xi_j/|\xi|,&\xi\ne0,\\0,&\xi=0,\end{cases}\qquad \widehat{R_jf}=m_j\,\widehat f ,$$

where the Fourier transform is the unitary Plancherel extension $\mathcal F_2$
of [[thm-plancherel]] and the multiplier acts by
$R_j=\mathcal F_2^{-1}M_{m_j}\mathcal F_2$. The symbol $m_j$ is measurable and
$|m_j(\xi)|\le1$ for every $\xi$ on account of $|\xi_j|\le|\xi|$, so the
published $L^2$ multiplier theorem
[[lem-ltwo-fourier-multiplier-bound]] applies with essential supremum at most
one: $R_j$ is a well-defined bounded complex-linear operator on
$L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, it depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $m_j$,
and in particular the assigned value $m_j(0)=0$ has no effect on the operator.
The theorem also identifies $R_j$ on Schwartz functions with the regular
distribution of $\mathcal F_2^{-1}(m_j\mathcal F_2f)$, and gives $\|R_j\|\le1$.

The **Riesz kernel** attached to this definition is the function on
$\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$

$$K_j(x):=c_n\,\frac{x_j}{|x|^{n+1}},\qquad c_n:=\frac{\Gamma\bigl((n+1)/2\bigr)}{\pi^{(n+1)/2}} ,$$

with [[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral|$\Gamma$]] the Euler
integral. Since $(n+1)/2>0$, the published convergence theorem
[[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]] gives $0<\Gamma((n+1)/2)<\infty$,
so $c_n$ is a positive finite constant and $K_j$ is a smooth function on
$\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, odd under $x\mapsto-x$ and homogeneous of degree
$-n$: $K_j(tx)=t^{-n}K_j(x)$ for $t>0$.

This definition asserts only the multiplier description. It does not assert
that the principal value $\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{|y|>\varepsilon}
K_j(y)f(x-y)\,dy$ exists for any particular $f$ or $x$; that statement is
proved separately for Schwartz functions, as is the identification of the limit
with the $L^2$ class $R_jf$. In dimension $n=1$ the constant collapses to
$c_1=\Gamma(1)/\pi=1/\pi$, by the value $\Gamma(1)=1$ of
[[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]], and $K_1(x)=1/(\pi x)$ is the
line Hilbert kernel; the comparison of $R_1$ with the Hilbert transform of the
line is worked out on the examples page. The Fourier convention is the
$e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}$ convention of $\mathcal F_2$. Replacing its phase by
$e^{-ix\cdot\xi}$ leaves both $m_j$ and $c_n$ unchanged: the frequency
rescaling $\xi\mapsto\xi/(2\pi)$ preserves $\xi_j/|\xi|$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$ and $1\le j\le n$. The $j$-th Riesz
transform $R_j$ of [[def-riesz-transforms-on-euclidean-space]] extends uniquely
to a bounded operator on $L^p(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for every
$1<p<\infty$, with norm at most $C_{n,p}$, a constant depending only on $n$
and $p$: the Riesz kernel $K_j(x)=c_nx_j/|x|^{n+1}$ is a standard $1$-Hölder
Calderón–Zygmund kernel with constant $C_n=c_n2^{n+1}(3n+4)$, so that
$$\|R_jf\|_p\le C_{n,p}\bigl(1+|S^{n-1}|2^{-1}C_n\bigr) \max\bigl(p,(p-1)^{-1}\bigr)\|f\|_p \qquad(f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)).$$

Assume Countable Choice.  For $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every
multi-index $\alpha$,

$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha u) =(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu, \qquad \mathcal F(x^\alpha u) =\left(-\frac1{2\pi i}\right)^{|\alpha|} \partial_\xi^\alpha\mathcal Fu.$$

Every operation and equality is in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in
$\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and therefore depend only on the corresponding
almost-everywhere classes.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the intersection
$$C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)\cap W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
is dense in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is a function
$v\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$\|v-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ and no
extension of $u$ beyond $\Omega$ is assumed. The exponent $p=\infty$ is
excluded, as the companion remark records.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain
([[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]) and let
$1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is compactly embedded in
$L^p(\Omega)$: every sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ has a subsequence
converging in $L^p(\Omega)$. Every bounded $C^1$ domain is an example.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain with a bounded extension operator $E$, and let $1\le p<n$, $p\le q\le p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously:
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)).$$
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If $f\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$ and $\Delta T_f=0$, then $f=h$ almost everywhere for a unique smooth harmonic $h$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (and hence Countable Choice and Dependent Choice). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected $W^{1,p}$-extension domain. Then there exists $C_P=C_P(n,p,\Omega,\mathbb K)$ such that $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_P\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with its quotient norm, is complete. Equivalently, every Cauchy
sequence in the metric induced by that norm converges in $L^p(\mu)$.

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere relative to $\mu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: **The whole-space first-order estimate.** For a compactly supported smooth one-form $b$ on $\mathbb R^4$ put $f_{ij}=\partial_i b_j-\partial_j b_i$ for all ordered indices and $g=\sum_i\partial_i b_i$. The identity $\Delta b_j=\sum_i\partial_i f_{ij}+\partial_j g$ and [F1] give $\partial_k b_j=-\sum_iR_kR_if_{ij}-R_kR_jg$: multiplication of the Fourier symbols proves equality away from zero frequency, hence almost everywhere in the $L^2$ transforms, and Plancherel injectivity identifies the functions. Riesz boundedness now gives $\|\nabla b\|_p\le C_{p,V}(\|db\|_p+\|d^*b\|_p)$. Approximate compactly supported $W^{1,p}$ forms by compactly supported smooth ones using [F2]; all displayed first derivatives converge in $L^p$, so the estimate extends to them.

**Reflection of a tangential one-form.** For smooth $a$ on $\overline B_1$ with $a(
u)=0$, put $\jmath(x)=x/|x|^2$ on $1<|x|<2$ and $b=\jmath^*a=D\jmath^T a(\jmath x)$ there, and put $b=a$ inside $B_1$. On the sphere $D\jmath=I-2
u\otimes
u$, so the boundary values match. This continuous piecewise smooth form has its piecewise first derivatives as weak derivatives, by cancelling the value-jump terms in integration by parts. Outside the sphere, differentiating and cancelling the symmetric second derivatives of $\jmath$ gives $db=\jmath^*(da)$. Also $D\jmath D\jmath^T=|x|^{-4}I$ and $\Delta\jmath_j=-4|x|^{-4}x_j$, whence $\operatorname{div}b=|x|^{-4}(\operatorname{div}a)(\jmath x)+4|x|^{-2}x\cdot b$. The inversion Jacobian is $|x|^{-8}$; these formulas on the bounded annulus show that its $b,db,d^*b$ norms are controlled by the respective inside $a,da,d^*a$ norms, with an additional $C\|a\|_p$ in the codifferential estimate.

**The estimate with a compact lower-order term.** Multiply the reflected form by a fixed cutoff equal to one near $\overline B_1$ and supported in $B_2$. Its exterior derivative and codifferential acquire only bounded smooth multiples of $b$. Apply step 1.1 to the resulting compactly supported $W^{1,p}$ form and restrict to $B_1$, using step 1.2 and the product rule. This yields $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,V}(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p+\|a\|_p)$. It extends to $Y_p$ by its defining strong approximation. For the same approximants, integration by parts and zero normal value give $\int\langle a_j,d\phi\rangle=\int\langle d^*a_j,\phi\rangle$; passing to the limit proves the claimed identity for $a\in Y_p$.

**The kernel has no nonzero elements.** Suppose $a\in Y_p$ has $da=d^*a=0$. The identity used in step 1.1 makes each component of $a$ distributionally harmonic, hence smooth in the ball by [F4]. Closedness gives a smooth $V$-valued potential $u(x)=\int_0^1\sum_i x_i a_i(tx)\,dt$: differentiating under the integral and using $\partial_j a_i=\partial_i a_j$ makes $\partial_j u$ the integral of $\frac{d}{dt}(t a_j(tx))$, so $du=a$. Normalize $u$ to have zero mean on $B_{1/2}$. For $1/2<R<1$, Poincare on $B_R$ gives $\|u-u_{B_R}\|_{L^2(B_R)}\le PR\|a\|_2$. Taking the mean over $B_{1/2}$ bounds $|u_{B_R}|\le |B_{1/2}|^{-1/2}P\|a\|_2$. Consequently $\|u\|_{L^2(B_R)}\le C\|a\|_2$, uniformly in $R$. Here $a\in L^2$ since $p\ge2$ and the ball has finite volume. Monotone convergence [F5] gives $u\in W^{1,2}(B_1)$ with $du=a$. The zero-normal identity of step 2.1 extends to every $W^{1,2}$ scalar test by [F5], since $a\in L^2$ and $d^*a=0$. Test with $u$ to obtain $\|a\|_2^2=0$. Thus $a=0$.

**Removing the lower-order term.** If no constant bounded the $W^{1,p}$ norm by $\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p$ on $Y_p$, choose $a_j\in Y_p$ with $\|a_j\|_{W^{1,p}}=1$ and $\|da_j\|_p+\|d^*a_j\|_p<1/j$. By [F3] a subsequence converges in $L^p$. Apply step 2.1 to its pairwise differences; their first-order data tend to zero, so the subsequence is Cauchy in $W^{1,p}$. Completeness follows componentwise from [F5] by passing the derivative test identities to the $L^p$ limits. The strong limit $a\in Y_p$ therefore has norm one, but $da=d^*a=0$, contrary to step 3.1. This proves $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,V}(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p)$ on the unit ball.

**Critical nonlinear absorption.** For $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$, the Frobenius matrix inequality gives $|[X,Y]|\le2|X||Y|$ and hence $|a\wedge a|\le2|a|^2$. Fix $2\le p<4$ and let $p^*=4p/(4-p)$. By [F3] there is $S_p$ with $\|a\|_{p^*}\le S_p\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}$. For $d^*a=0$, step 4.1 and Holder give $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,V}(\|F_a\|_p+2\|a\|_4\|a\|_{p^*})$, since $1/p=1/4+1/p^*$. Choose $\rho_p=(4C_{p,V}S_p)^{-1}$. Then $\|a\|_4\le\rho_p$ absorbs the last term and gives $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le2C_{p,V}\|F_a\|_p$. All curvature products are in $L^p$, since $p^*\ge2p$ for $p\ge2$ on a finite-volume ball.

**All radii and conclusion.** Pull back by $y\mapsto ry$, so $b(y)=r a(ry)$. Smooth zero-normal forms pull back to smooth zero-normal forms, and strong approximation shows that $Y_p$ pulls back to $Y_p$. The $L^p$ norms of $\nabla b,db,d^*b$ scale by $r^{2-4/p}$, while $\|b\|_p=r^{1-4/p}\|a\|_p$. Also $F_b(y)=r^2F_a(ry)$ and $\|b\|_4=\|a\|_4$. Dividing the unit-ball estimates of steps 4.1–5.1 by $r^{2-4/p}$ proves both stated bounds. The integration identity rescales directly, and the kernel assertion follows from the estimate. Full AC is used through the exact Fourier, compactness and approximation suppliers [F1]–[F6], including the sequential choices in step 4.1.

citations.quote: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (and hence Countable Choice and Dependent Choice). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected $W^{1,p}$-extension domain. Then there exists $C_P=C_P(n,p,\Omega,\mathbb K)$ such that $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_P\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u$.
Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $A\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$ be a unital subalgebra which separates points. Then $A$ is dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$ for the supremum metric.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with its quotient norm, is complete. Equivalently, every Cauchy
sequence in the metric induced by that norm converges in $L^p(\mu)$.

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere relative to $\mu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the intersection
$$C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)\cap W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
is dense in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is a function
$v\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$\|v-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ and no
extension of $u$ beyond $\Omega$ is assumed. The exponent $p=\infty$ is
excluded, as the companion remark records.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: **A finite harmonic decomposition.** If $p$ is homogeneous of degree $d$ on $\mathbb R^4$, put $N=\lfloor d/2\rfloor$, $c_0=1$, and $c_j=-c_{j-1}/(4j(d-j+1))$ for $1\le j\le N$. Define $H=\sum_{j=0}^Nc_j|x|^{2j}\Delta^jp$. For homogeneous $Q$ of degree $d-2j$, product differentiation and Euler's identity give $\Delta(|x|^{2j}Q)=4j(d-j+1)|x|^{2j-2}Q+|x|^{2j}\Delta Q$. Hence successive terms cancel in $\Delta H$, and $\Delta^{N+1}p=0$ gives $\Delta H=0$. All denominators are positive in their stated range. Moreover $p-H$ is divisible by $|x|^2$. Induction on $d$, starting with degrees zero and one, therefore writes $p$ as a finite sum $\sum_k|x|^{2k}H_{d-2k}$ with homogeneous harmonic $H_{d-2k}$. Decomposing each homogeneous piece of an arbitrary polynomial and then restricting to the unit sphere writes its restriction as $\sum_{l=0}^L G_l|_{\partial B_1}$ with each $G_l$ homogeneous harmonic of degree $l$. All constructions apply coefficientwise to $V$.

**A polynomial antiderivative of the Laplacian.** On a monomial $x_1^a x_2^{b_2}x_3^{b_3}x_4^{b_4}$ define $I$ to multiply by $x_1^2/((a+1)(a+2))$; extend linearly to polynomials. Then $\partial_1^2I=\mathrm{id}$, and $I$ commutes with $\Delta'=\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2+\partial_4^2$. For a polynomial $f$, choose $M$ so that $(\Delta')^{M+1}f=0$ and set $p=-\sum_{k=0}^M(-1)^kI^{k+1}(\Delta')^kf$. Applying $\partial_1^2+\Delta'$ telescopes the finite sum and gives $\Delta p=-f$.

**Mean-zero polynomial density.** Given an $L^2$ function on $B_1$, first approximate it in $L^2$ by a compactly supported smooth function using [F3]. Extend this smooth function by zero near the boundary; it is continuous on the compact closed ball. Apply the polynomial density of [F3] uniformly, which also gives $L^2$ approximation by [F4]. Thus polynomials are dense in $L^2(B_1)$, coefficientwise for $V$. For mean-zero $f$, take polynomial approximants $p_j\to f$ and replace $p_j$ by $f_j=p_j-(p_j)_{B_1}$. Holder gives $\|(p_j)_{B_1}\|\,|B_1|^{1/2}\le\|p_j-f\|_2$, so these mean-zero polynomials still converge to $f$ in $L^2$. Full AC permits this sequential selection.

**The normal correction for polynomial data.** Suppose the polynomial $f$ has zero mean on $B_1$, choose $p$ from step 1.2, and let $g=-x\cdot
abla p$ restricted to $\partial B_1$. By [F1], $\int_{\partial B_1}g=-\int_{B_1}\Delta p=\int_{B_1}f=0$. Decompose $g=\sum_lG_l|_{\partial B_1}$ by step 1.1. For $l\ge1$, Euler's identity and [F1] give $l\int_{\partial B_1}G_l=\int_{\partial B_1}\partial_
u G_l=\int_{B_1}\Delta G_l=0$. Thus the constant $G_0$ is zero: its sphere integral vanishes and the sphere has positive area, since [F1] applied to $x$ gives $|\partial B_1|=4|B_1|>0$. The harmonic polynomial $h=\sum_{l\ge1}G_l/l$ satisfies $\partial_
u h=g$ on the sphere. Hence $u=p+h$ satisfies $-\Delta u=f$ and $\partial_
u u=0$. Subtracting its volume mean preserves these equations and gives a mean-zero polynomial solution.

**The exact boundary Hessian estimate.** For a scalar smooth $u$ with $\partial_
u u=0$ on $\partial B_1$, consider $Z=(\Delta u)
abla u-D^2u\,
abla u$. Direct differentiation cancels the third derivatives and gives $\operatorname{div}Z=(\Delta u)^2-|D^2u|^2$. On the sphere $
abla u$ is tangential. Differentiating $
abla u\cdot
u=0$ in that tangential direction gives $D^2u(
abla u,
u)=-|
abla u|^2$, because $
abla_{
abla u}
u=
abla u$ there. Thus $Z\cdot
u=|
abla u|^2$. By [F1], $\|\Delta u\|_2^2=\|D^2u\|_2^2+\int_{\partial B_1}|
abla u|^2$. Sum the identity over an orthonormal basis of $V$. In particular every polynomial solution of step 2.1 satisfies $\|D^2u\|_2\le\|f\|_2$.

**The remaining terms and the weak identity.** Integration by parts [F1] for a mean-zero polynomial solution gives $\|
abla u\|_2^2=\int\langle f,uangle\le\|f\|_2\|u\|_2\le P\|f\|_2\|
abla u\|_2$ by [F2] and [F4]. Dividing when the gradient norm is nonzero, and treating zero separately, gives $\|
abla u\|_2\le P\|f\|_2$ and $\|u\|_2\le P^2\|f\|_2$. Together with step 3.1 this yields $\|u\|_2+\|
abla u\|_2+\|D^2u\|_2\le(1+P+P^2)\|f\|_2$. The all-test-function weak identity first holds for tests smooth near the closed ball by [F1], since the normal term vanishes; it then holds for every $W^{1,2}$ test by [F4]–[F5].

**Completion constructs the strong inverse.** For each $f_j$ choose the polynomial mean-zero solution $u_j$ of step 2.1. Their differences are polynomial mean-zero solutions for $f_j-f_k$, so steps 3.1–4.1 make $u_j$, all its first derivatives and all its second derivatives Cauchy in $L^2$. Completeness [F4] gives limits for each of these finitely many components. Passing in the weak derivative identities against a compactly supported smooth test identifies the first-derivative limits as the weak derivatives of the limit $u$, and then identifies the second-derivative limits as derivatives of those first derivatives. Hence $u\in W^{2,2}(B_1)$ and $u_j\to u$ strongly in that space. Its mean is zero by Holder. Passing to the limit in the weak identity of step 4.1 gives the displayed equation for every $W^{1,2}$ test. Norm continuity passes both estimates of steps 3.1–4.1 to $u$, including the constant-one Hessian bound.

**Uniqueness, linearity and compatibility.** If two mean-zero $W^{1,2}$ solutions have the same datum, test their difference equation with the difference itself. Its gradient has zero $L^2$ norm; [F2] makes its $L^2$ norm zero, so the solutions agree. This proves uniqueness in the claimed $W^{2,2}$ class as well. Linear combinations satisfy the same linear weak identity and mean-zero normalization; uniqueness proves linearity of the inverse. Testing any weak solution with each constant vector in $V$ gives $\int f=0$, proving necessity. The polynomial solution of step 2.1 equals the completed solution by this uniqueness.

**Every radius.** For data $f$ on $B_r$, put $f_r(y)=r^2f(ry)$ on $B_1$ and solve there for $v$ by step 5.1. Set $u(x)=v(x/r)$. Changing variables in the weak identity proves the required identity and mean-zero normalization on $B_r$. In four dimensions, $\|f_r\|_{L^2(B_1)}=\|f\|_{L^2(B_r)}$, $\|D^2v\|_2=\|D^2u\|_2$, $\|\nabla v\|_2=r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_2$, and $\|v\|_2=r^{-2}\|u\|_2$. Thus the bounds follow with $C=1+P+P^2$, independent of $r$. The construction preserves polynomiality for polynomial data.

**Given finite equivariance and conclusion.** For $\gamma\in\Gamma$ let $T_\gamma u(x)=\sigma(\gamma)^{-1}u(\gamma x)$. Orthogonal changes of variables preserve the ball, volume, the gradient pairing and the zero mean; orthogonality of $\sigma(\gamma)$ preserves the target pairing. Therefore $T_\gamma u$ solves the same weak equation as $u$ when $T_\gamma f=f$. Uniqueness from step 6.1, rescaled as in step 7.1, gives $T_\gamma u=u$. This proves the equivariance for every element of the given finite group, including the stated Lie-algebra case. All existence, uniqueness and estimate claims are proved; full AC enters only through the analytic suppliers and the sequential approximation choices [F2]–[F6].

Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a fixed finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let $r>0$, and write $B_r=B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^4$. For each $f\in L^2(B_r;V)$ with $\int_{B_r}f=0$ there exists a unique $u\in W^{2,2}(B_r;V)$ with $\int_{B_r}u=0$ satisfying the Neumann problem in the weak form
$$\int_{B_r}\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{B_r}\langle f,v\rangle\qquad\bigl(v\in W^{1,2}(B_r;V)\bigr).$$
Thus $-\Delta u=f$ distributionally, and the zero-normal boundary condition is included in the displayed all-test-function identity. The inverse $f\mapsto u$ is linear and obeys
$$\|D^2u\|_2\le\|f\|_2,\qquad r^{-2}\|u\|_2+r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_2+\|D^2u\|_2\le C\|f\|_2,$$
with $C$ independent of $r$ and $f$. The Hessian norm is the Euclidean norm on all ordered second derivatives. If $f$ is the restriction of a polynomial and has mean zero, then $u$ is the restriction of a polynomial with classical $\partial_\nu u=0$ on $\partial B_r$.

If a fixed finite $\Gamma\le O(4)$ and an orthogonal representation $\sigma:\Gamma\to O(V)$ satisfy $f(\gamma x)=\sigma(\gamma)f(x)$ almost everywhere, the unique solution satisfies $u(\gamma x)=\sigma(\gamma)u(x)$ almost everywhere. This includes $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with its Frobenius norm and a prescribed action by orthogonal Lie-algebra automorphisms.

The compatibility $\int f=0$ is necessary. This is a linear $L^2$ boundary-solvability result; higher-$L^p$ Neumann estimates and nonlinear Coulomb-gauge existence are separate assertions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and $1<p<\infty$. Then there is $C=C(n,p)<\infty$ such that every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies
$$\|D^2u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|\Delta u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)},\qquad \|\partial_i\partial_ju\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|\Delta u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)},$$
for all $i,j$, where $\|D^2u\|_{L^p}:=\max_{|\beta|=2}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p}$; by density the bound extends to every $u\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ (for which $\Delta u\in L^p$ holds automatically). The constant may be taken as the square of the Riesz-transform bound of [[cor-riesz-transforms-are-bounded-on-lp]], hence is finite throughout $1<p<\infty$, including $p=2$. No sharp endpoint growth rate is claimed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$ and $1<p<\infty$, and for a function with the relevant weak derivatives write $\|Du\|_{L^p}:=\max_{|\beta|=1}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p}$ and $\|D^2u\|_{L^p}:=\max_{|\beta|=2}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p}$, equivalent to the sum-form Sobolev norms of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] up to constants depending on $n$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C=C(n,p,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that every $u\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies
$$\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le\varepsilon\|D^2u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}+C\|u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}.$$
The scaled form on balls, with the norm over the doubled ball on the right, is
$$\|Du\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}\le\varepsilon R\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_{2R}(x_0))}+C R^{-1}\|u\|_{L^p(B_{2R}(x_0))}\qquad\bigl(u\in W^{2,p}(B_{2R}(x_0))\bigr),$$
with $C$ independent of $R$ and $x_0$. This is the absorption inequality used in the frozen-coefficient $W^{2,p}$ estimates. The result is asserted for the strict range $1<p<\infty$ only; the form with the same ball on both sides is not claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.
Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $A\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$ be a unital subalgebra which separates points. Then $A$ is dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$ for the supremum metric.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the intersection
$$C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)\cap W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
is dense in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is a function
$v\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$\|v-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ and no
extension of $u$ beyond $\Omega$ is assumed. The exponent $p=\infty$ is
excluded, as the companion remark records.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with its quotient norm, is complete. Equivalently, every Cauchy
sequence in the metric induced by that norm converges in $L^p(\mu)$.

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere relative to $\mu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim:
**Reflection matching.** Let $u$ be smooth near $\overline B_1$ with $\partial_
u u=0$. On $1<|x|<2$ put $\jmath(x)=x/|x|^2$ and $v(x)=u(\jmath(x))$, and put $v=u$ on $B_1$. At $|x|=1$, $D\jmath=I-2
u\otimes
u$; since $
abla u$ is tangential, the outside gradient $D\jmath^T
abla u$ equals the inside gradient. The values match as well. Thus $v$ is $C^1$ across the sphere, smooth on each side, and has locally bounded piecewise second derivatives. Integration by parts on the two sides cancels the interface terms for $v$ and its first derivatives, so these piecewise derivatives are its weak derivatives through order two.

**The reflected equation.** Writing $s=|x|$, one has $D\jmath=s^{-2}(I-2x\otimes x/s^2)$, $D\jmath D\jmath^T=s^{-4}I$, and $\Delta\jmath_j=-4s^{-4}x_j$ in four dimensions. The chain rule therefore gives $\Delta v=s^{-4}(\Delta u)(\jmath x)-4s^{-4}x\cdot(
abla u)(\jmath x)$. Since $x\cdot
abla v=-s^{-2}x\cdot(
abla u)(\jmath x)$, this is $\Delta v=s^{-4}(\Delta u)(\jmath x)+4s^{-2}x\cdot
abla v$. All coefficients are bounded on the annulus. The inversion Jacobian has absolute value $s^{-8}$ and maps that annulus into $B_1\setminus\overline B_{1/2}$, so change of variables bounds its reflected $u$, first-derivative and Laplacian norms by constant multiples of their norms on $B_1$.

**A whole-space estimate for the extension.** Choose the cutoff $\chi$ of [F5] equal to one near $\overline B_1$, and define $Eu=\chi v$ on $B_2$, zero elsewhere. Step 1.1 gives $Eu\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^4)$ with compact support. Step 2.1 and $\Delta(\chi v)=\chi\Delta v+2
abla\chi\cdot
abla v+(\Delta\chi)v$ give $\|Eu\|_p\le C\|u\|_p$ and $\|\Delta Eu\|_p\le C_p(\|\Delta u\|_p+\|
abla u\|_p+\|u\|_p)$. Since $Eu=u$ on $B_1$, $\|
abla u\|_p\le\|
abla Eu\|_p$. Apply [F2] to obtain $\|D^2Eu\|_p\le C_p(\|\Delta u\|_p+\|
abla Eu\|_p+\|u\|_p)$. Interpolate the middle term by [F2] with $\eta>0$ chosen so $C_p\eta\le1/2$, and absorb it. Then interpolate once more for the first derivatives and restrict to $B_1$. The result is $\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(B_1)}\le C_p(\|\Delta u\|_p+\|u\|_p)$. No estimate was applied before the reflected function's $W^{2,p}$ membership was proved.

**Removing the zeroth-order term for Neumann solutions.** For mean-zero polynomial $f$, [F1] gives a polynomial mean-zero solution $u$ with classical zero normal derivative and $\|u\|_{W^{2,2}}\le C\|f\|_2$. By [F3], $\|u\|_p\le C_p\|f\|_2\le C_p|B_1|^{1/2-1/p}\|f\|_p$, where the final Holder bound uses $p\ge2$. Substitution in step 3.1, with $-\Delta u=f$, proves $\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(B_1)}\le C_{p,V}\|f\|_p$ for these polynomial solutions, uniformly in their degrees.

**Construction for all mean-zero Lp data.** Extend $f$ by zero to $\mathbb R^4$, approximate in $L^p$ by smooth functions using [F4], and restrict to the closed ball. Each approximant is continuous there and hence uniformly approximable by polynomials by [F4]. A choice of uniform error tending to zero gives polynomial approximants in $L^p$; subtract their means to obtain mean-zero $f_j\to f$ in $L^p$, since $\|(f_j-f)_{B_1}\|\,|B_1|^{1/p}\le\|f_j-f\|_p$ before normalization. Let $u_j$ be the polynomial solutions from [F1]. Applying step 4.1 to their differences makes all derivative components through order two Cauchy in $L^p$. Completeness [F4] and passage in the weak-derivative test identities give a limit $u\in W^{2,p}$ with $u_j\to u$ strongly and the same bound. Finite volume and $p\ge2$ imply $u_j\to u$ in $W^{1,2}$ and $f_j\to f$ in $L^2$; their weak Neumann identities pass to the limit for every $W^{1,2}$ test. Thus the solution is the unique $L^2$ Neumann solution of [F1], now with the stronger regularity and norm estimate.

**The complete normalized domain.** By step 5.1 the inverse maps into $X_p^0$ and is bounded there. Conversely let $u\in X_p^0$ and choose polynomial zero-normal approximants $u_j\to u$ in $W^{2,p}$. Subtracting their means preserves the normal condition and convergence. The sources $f_j=-\Delta u_j$ have zero mean, by the polynomial weak identity of [F1], and converge to $f=-\Delta u\in L^p_0$. Each $u_j$ is the normalized solution for $f_j$, so the bounded inverse from step 5.1 sends $f$ to $u$. This proves bijectivity. Also $\|\Delta u\|_p\le C\|u\|_{W^{2,p}}$ and the inverse bound gives the reverse norm comparison. The zero-mean subspace of $L^p$ is closed, since its mean functional is bounded by Holder, hence complete by [F4]. Its isomorphism with $X_p^0$ gives completeness for $\|\Delta u\|_p$.

**Scaling, uniqueness and symmetry.** For $B_r$ put $f_r(y)=r^2f(ry)$, solve on $B_1$ and set $u(x)=u_r(x/r)$. Direct change of variables gives $\|f_r\|_p=r^{2-4/p}\|f\|_p$, $\|D^2u_r\|_p=r^{2-4/p}\|D^2u\|_p$, $\|\nabla u_r\|_p=r^{1-4/p}\|\nabla u\|_p$, and $\|u_r\|_p=r^{-4/p}\|u\|_p$. Divide the unit-ball bound of step 5.1 by $r^{2-4/p}$ to obtain the displayed estimate; polynomial approximations rescale as well. The weak identity passes by change of variables. Uniqueness, linearity and preservation of prescribed finite orthogonal equivariance follow from [F1], since all these solutions belong to its unique mean-zero $W^{1,2}$ solution class. Full AC is inherited through [F2]–[F5] and the sequential approximation choices.
