Assume full AC. Derivative tensors carry their Euclidean norms, and Sobolev norms are sums of the resulting $L^p$ norms. Fix a finite-dimensional real inner-product space $V$, $2\le p<\infty$, and $r>0$. Every $f\in L^p(B_r(0);V)$ with zero volume mean has a unique mean-zero $u\in W^{2,p}(B_r;V)$ satisfying
$$\int_{B_r}\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{B_r}\langle f,v\rangle\qquad(v\in W^{1,2}(B_r;V)).$$
The inverse is linear and obeys
$$r^{-2}\|u\|_p+r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_p+\|D^2u\|_p\le C_{p,V}\|f\|_p,$$
with $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ and $f$. Its solution is the $W^{2,p}$ limit of mean-zero polynomial solutions with classical zero normal derivative. In particular it belongs to the $W^{2,p}$ closure of smooth zero-normal-derivative functions on the closed ball.

On $B_1$, let $X_p$ be the $W^{2,p}$ closure of the $V$-valued polynomials with zero normal derivative on the sphere, and let $X_p^0$ be its mean-zero subspace. Then $-\Delta:X_p^0\to L^p_0(B_1;V)$ is a bounded bijection with the above inverse. Here $L^p_0$ denotes the zero-mean subspace; $X_p^0$ is complete for the equivalent norm $\|u\|_{X_p^0}=\|\Delta u\|_p$. A prescribed finite orthogonal equivariance of $f$ is preserved by the inverse, as in the $L^2$ case. No endpoint $p=\infty$ or nonlinear gauge existence is asserted.

Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a fixed finite-dimensional real inner-product space, $2\le p<\infty$, let $r>0$, and put $B_r=B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^4$. Let $Y_p(B_r;V)$ be the $W^{1,p}$ closure of smooth $V$-valued one-forms on the closed ball satisfying $a(\nu)=0$ on the sphere. Write $d^*a=-\sum_i\partial_i a_i$ and $(da)_{ij}=\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i$ for $i<j$. There is $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ such that every $a\in Y_p(B_r;V)$ satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_{p,V}\bigl(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p\bigr).$$
Every such $a$ satisfies the zero-normal integration identity $\int\langle a,d\phi\rangle=\int\langle d^*a,\phi\rangle$ for smooth $\phi$ on the closed ball. If $da=d^*a=0$, then $a=0$.

For $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with the Frobenius norm and $2\le p<4$, there exist $\rho_p>0$ and $C_p$ independent of $r$ such that, whenever $a\in Y_p$ satisfies $d^*a=0$ and $\|a\|_4\le\rho_p$, its curvature $F_a=da+a\wedge a$, $(a\wedge a)_{ij}=[a_i,a_j]$, satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_p\|F_a\|_p.$$
All norms here are Euclidean coefficient norms; the class $Y_p$ states precisely the boundary approximation hypothesis.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain with a bounded extension operator $E$, and let $1\le p<n$, $p\le q\le p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously:
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the intersection

is dense in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

derivations.claim: **Sobolev matrix algebra and boundary approximation.** By [F3]–[F4] and the weak product rule obtained by smooth approximation, $\|vw\|_{W^{2,3}}\le K_A\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}\|w\|_{W^{2,3}}$: the second-derivative cross terms obey $\|DvDw\|_3\le\|Dv\|_6\|Dw\|_6$, and [F3] controls both $L^6$ norms. Similarly $\|cv\|_{W^{1,3}}+\|vc\|_{W^{1,3}}\le K_A\|c\|_{W^{1,3}}\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. Passing the derivative test identities to $L^3$ limits proves completeness of the ambient Sobolev spaces from [F4]. The power series for $e^u$ therefore converges in $W^{2,3}$, locally uniformly in that norm, and defines a continuously differentiable composition there; termwise differentiation is justified by the convergent exponential majorants. For $u\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$ pointwise, $u^2=-s^2I$ for a real $s$, so $e^u=\cos s\,I+(\sin s/s)u$ (with the continuous value at zero) is unitary with determinant one. Polynomial Neumann approximants to $u\in X$ exponentiate to smooth $SU(2)$ maps with zero normal derivative; continuity gives $e^u\in\mathcal G_N$. Products of maps in $\mathcal G_N$ remain in it, and inverse is matrix adjoint and hence continuous. Gauge transformation by such maps sends $Y$ to $Y$, by approximating both inputs with smooth zero-normal inputs and using the above product estimates. Also $du\in Y$ for $u\in X$.

**The exact nonlinear remainder.** Put $h=e^u$ and define $R(u)=h^{-1}dh-du+h^{-1}(a+\lambda)h-a$. By step 1.1, $R(u)\in Y$ whenever $u\in X$. Let $E(u)=e^{-u}d(e^u)-du$. Differentiating the convergent matrix series, or integrating the series termwise, gives $e^{-u}d(e^u)=\int_0^1e^{-tu}(du)e^{tu}\,dt$, hence $E(u)=A(u)du$ where $A(0)=0$ and $A$ and its first two matrix derivatives are uniformly bounded for $|u|\le1$. More precisely $|A(u)|\le C|u|$ there. Thus $R(u)=E(u)+(e^{-u}ae^u-a)+e^{-u}\lambda e^u$, with $R(0)=\lambda$.

**The quadratic differential term.** Suppose $\|u\|_{W^{2,3}},\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\eta$ with $\eta$ small enough that [F3] gives $|u|,|v|\le1$. The formula in step 2.1 gives $|d^*E(u)|\le C(|u||D^2u|+|Du|^2)$. Subtracting the two formulas, using bounded first and second derivatives of $A$, and applying [F3]–[F4] gives $\|d^*E(u)\|_3\le C\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}^2$ and $\|d^*(E(u)-E(v))\|_3\le C\eta\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. Indeed terms with two first derivatives use $L^6\cdot L^6\subset L^3$, while a second derivative is paired with an $L^\infty$ factor; differences of coefficients are bounded by $C|u-v|$, and the resulting terms use the same two estimates. These formulas hold for the Sobolev classes by the smooth approximation and product continuity of step 1.1.

**The critical Coulomb coefficient and the perturbation.** In $d^*(e^{-u}ae^u-a)$ the term $e^{-u}(d^*a)e^u-d^*a$ vanishes. Only derivatives falling on the exponentials remain, so their pointwise norm is at most $C|a||Du|$ for $|u|\le1$. Subtracting at $u,v$ gives at most $C|a|(|D(u-v)|+|u-v|(|Du|+|Dv|))$. By $L^4\cdot L^{12}\subset L^3$, this gives a difference bound $C\|a\|_4\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$ when $\eta\le1$. The contracted derivative of $e^{-u}\lambda e^u$ consists of $e^{-u}(d^*\lambda)e^u$ and terms bounded by $C|\lambda||Du|$. The same subtraction, [F3] and Holder give a difference bound $C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. Thus, after choosing one universal $C_0$, the preceding estimates prove $\|d^*(R(u)-R(v))\|_3\le C_0(\eta+\|a\|_4+\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}})\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. The cancellation of $d^*a$ is why no higher norm of $a$ occurs in this bound.

**A well-defined contraction, including compatibility.** Define $T(u)=S(-d^*R(u))$ on the closed radius-$\eta$ ball in $X$. Step 2.1 and [F2] show $-d^*R(u)\in L^3_0$, so the Neumann solve is well defined for every iterate. Choose positive $\eta,\rho$ so that $\eta\le1$, the $L^\infty$ restriction of step 3.1 holds, and $K_NC_0(\eta+\rho)\le1/4$. Then choose $\delta>0$ so small that $K_NC_0\delta\le1/4$ and $K_N\|d^*\lambda\|_3\le\eta/4$ whenever $\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\le\delta$; the latter follows from the fixed finite coefficient bound for $d^*$. For $\|a\|_4\le\rho$ and such $\lambda$, step 4.1 gives contraction constant at most $1/2$, and $\|T(0)\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\eta/4$. Hence $\|T(u)\|_{W^{2,3}}\le3\eta/4$ on that ball. It is a complete metric space by [F1] and the equivalence of its domain norm with $W^{2,3}$.

**The correction and uniqueness.** By [F4], $u_{j+1}=T(u_j)$ starting at zero converges to the unique fixed point $u$ in that ball. The equation $-\Delta u=-d^*R(u)$ and $d^*du=-\Delta u$ give $d^*(du+R(u))=0$. Since $d^*a=0$, the form $b=a+du+R(u)=h^{-1}dh+h^{-1}(a+\lambda)h$ is Coulomb and belongs to $Y$ by step 1.1. Conversely any $u\in X$ in the stated ball for which $b$ is Coulomb satisfies this same Neumann equation, so uniqueness of [F1] makes it a fixed point and thus this $u$. Also $\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\|T(0)\|_{W^{2,3}}+\tfrac12\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le K_N\|d^*\lambda\|_3+\tfrac12\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}$, giving the first quantitative bound.

**The correction size in the connection norm.** The matrix power series and product estimates of step 1.1 imply $\|e^{-u}d(e^u)\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}$, $\|e^{-u}ae^u-a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}$, and $\|e^{-u}\lambda e^u\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}$ on the fixed small ball. For the middle bound, write $e^{-u}ae^u-a=(e^{-u}-1)ae^u+a(e^u-1)$; the terms with derivatives on $a$ have a factor bounded by $C\|u\|_\infty$, and the other terms use $L^4\cdot L^{12}\subset L^3$. Adding the three bounds and using step 6.1 proves the claimed estimate for $b-a$, with $C$ independent of $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}$.

**Prescribed finite equivariance.** Orthogonal pullback preserves the Laplacian, codifferential, means and all the domain norms. Constant unitary conjugation preserves matrix products, the Frobenius norm and the exponential. Therefore the transformation $u(x)\mapsto d\tau_\gamma^{-1}(u(\gamma x))$ preserves $X$ and commutes with $T$ when $a,\lambda$ have the stated equivariance; this uses the equivariant inverse of [F1]. The zero starting iterate is invariant, so every iterate and its limit are invariant. Exponentiation gives the assertion for $h$. A central unitary scalar acts trivially by conjugation, which explains why a $PU(2)$ action suffices. The existence, uniqueness, estimates and boundary compatibility are all supplied in steps 5.1–7.1; full AC is inherited as stated in [F5].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $S^3\setminus S$ has two components. The connected set $K$ is disjoint from $S$, so it lies in one component. The connected neighborhood $N(K)$ is also disjoint from $S$ and contains $K$, hence it lies in that same component.
The closure of the other component is a smooth three-ball disjoint from $N(K)$, so it is contained in $E_K$ and has boundary $S$. This proves irreducibility of the chosen exterior.

Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a fixed finite-dimensional real inner-product space, $2\le p<\infty$, let $r>0$, and put $B_r=B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^4$. Let $Y_p(B_r;V)$ be the $W^{1,p}$ closure of smooth $V$-valued one-forms on the closed ball satisfying $a(\nu)=0$ on the sphere. Write $d^*a=-\sum_i\partial_i a_i$ and $(da)_{ij}=\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i$ for $i<j$. There is $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ such that every $a\in Y_p(B_r;V)$ satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_{p,V}\bigl(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p\bigr).$$
Every such $a$ satisfies the zero-normal integration identity $\int\langle a,d\phi\rangle=\int\langle d^*a,\phi\rangle$ for smooth $\phi$ on the closed ball. If $da=d^*a=0$, then $a=0$.

For $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with the Frobenius norm and $2\le p<4$, there exist $\rho_p>0$ and $C_p$ independent of $r$ such that, whenever $a\in Y_p$ satisfies $d^*a=0$ and $\|a\|_4\le\rho_p$, its curvature $F_a=da+a\wedge a$, $(a\wedge a)_{ij}=[a_i,a_j]$, satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_p\|F_a\|_p.$$
All norms here are Euclidean coefficient norms; the class $Y_p$ states precisely the boundary approximation hypothesis.

Assume full AC and work on the closed Euclidean unit ball in four dimensions. Use sums of $L^p$ norms of Euclidean ordered derivative tensors for Sobolev norms; these are equivalent to the cited scalar Sobolev norms and invariant under orthogonal coordinate changes. Let $X$ be the mean-zero $W^{2,3}$ closure of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued polynomials with zero normal derivative on the sphere. Let $Y$ be the $W^{1,3}$ closure of smooth $\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued one-forms with zero normal component on the sphere. Let $\mathcal G_N$ be the $W^{2,3}$ closure of smooth maps to $SU(2)$ with zero normal derivative on the sphere.

There exist fixed positive constants $\rho,\eta,\delta,C$ such that, if $a\in Y$ satisfies $d^*a=0$, $\|a\|_4\le\rho$, and $\lambda\in Y$ satisfies $\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\le\delta$, there exists $u\in X$, unique among $\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\eta$, such that $h=e^u\in\mathcal G_N$ and
$$b=h^{-1}dh+h^{-1}(a+\lambda)h\in Y,\qquad d^*b=0.$$
Moreover
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}},\qquad \|b-a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C(1+\|a\|_{W^{1,3}})\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}.$$
All constants are independent of the higher norm of $a$.

Given a finite $\Gamma\le O(4)$ and an action $\tau$ of $\Gamma$ on $SU(2)$ by constant unitary conjugations, suppose $\gamma^*a=d\tau_\gamma(a)$ and $\gamma^*\lambda=d\tau_\gamma(\lambda)$. Then $u(\gamma x)=d\tau_\gamma(u(x))$ and $h(\gamma x)=\tau_\gamma(h(x))$. A representation into $PU(2)$ supplies such a conjugation action; no lift of that representation to $SU(2)$ is required.

Assume full AC. Derivative tensors carry their Euclidean norms, and Sobolev norms are sums of the resulting $L^p$ norms. Fix a finite-dimensional real inner-product space $V$, $2\le p<\infty$, and $r>0$. Every $f\in L^p(B_r(0);V)$ with zero volume mean has a unique mean-zero $u\in W^{2,p}(B_r;V)$ satisfying
$$\int_{B_r}\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{B_r}\langle f,v\rangle\qquad(v\in W^{1,2}(B_r;V)).$$
The inverse is linear and obeys
$$r^{-2}\|u\|_p+r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_p+\|D^2u\|_p\le C_{p,V}\|f\|_p,$$
with $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ and $f$. Its solution is the $W^{2,p}$ limit of mean-zero polynomial solutions with classical zero normal derivative. In particular it belongs to the $W^{2,p}$ closure of smooth zero-normal-derivative functions on the closed ball.

On $B_1$, let $X_p$ be the $W^{2,p}$ closure of the $V$-valued polynomials with zero normal derivative on the sphere, and let $X_p^0$ be its mean-zero subspace. Then $-\Delta:X_p^0\to L^p_0(B_1;V)$ is a bounded bijection with the above inverse. Here $L^p_0$ denotes the zero-mean subspace; $X_p^0$ is complete for the equivalent norm $\|u\|_{X_p^0}=\|\Delta u\|_p$. A prescribed finite orthogonal equivariance of $f$ is preserved by the inverse, as in the $L^2$ case. No endpoint $p=\infty$ or nonlinear gauge existence is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain with a bounded extension operator $E$, and let $1\le p<n$, $p\le q\le p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously:
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the intersection
$$C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)\cap W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
is dense in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is a function
$v\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$\|v-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ and no
extension of $u$ beyond $\Omega$ is assumed. The exponent $p=\infty$ is
excluded, as the companion remark records.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: **A constructed radial gauge.** Put $M(s,x)=\sum_i x_iA_i(sx)$ and define $P(s,x)$ by the convergent iterated-integral series $I+\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^k\int_{0<t_k<\cdots<t_1<s}M(t_1,x)\cdots M(t_k,x)\,dt_k\cdots dt_1$. On the compact parameter set every term has norm at most $L^k/k!$; any fixed number $N$ of spatial derivatives is bounded by $C_N k^N L_N^k/k!$. Uniform convergence of these derivative series, followed by the coordinate-segment fundamental theorem, identifies them as the derivatives of the sum. The series also gives the integral equation $P(s,x)=I-\int_0^sM(t,x)P(t,x)\,dt$, which also gives smoothness in $s$. It satisfies $\partial_sP=-MP$, $P(0,x)=I$. Since $M$ is skew-Hermitian and trace zero, differentiation gives $\partial_s(P^*P)=0$; thus $P$ is unitary, and the two-by-two determinant derivative gives $\partial_s\det P=-\operatorname{tr}(M)\det P=0$, so $P\in SU(2)$. Uniqueness of the integral equation follows by iterating its difference estimate $k$ times and taking $k\to\infty$ using $L^k/k!\to0$. Set $U(x)=P(1,x)$. Rescaling the integration parameters gives $U(sx)=P(s,x)$, so $x\cdot dU=-(x\cdot A)U$. Therefore $C=A^U$ is smooth and $x\cdot C=0$.

**Gauge algebra and the scaling path.** The matrix identity $d(g^{-1})=-g^{-1}(dg)g^{-1}$ gives $F_{A^g}=g^{-1}F_Ag$ and $(A^g)^h=A^{gh}$ by expansion and cancellation. It applies to smooth gauges first; [F4]–[F5] pass it to $W^{2,3}$ gauges and their $W^{1,3}$ connection forms. Unitarity preserves pointwise curvature norms. Define $A_t(x)=tC(tx)$ for $0\le t\le1$. It is a smooth path of smooth zero-normal forms, starts at zero, and ends at $C$. Its curvature is $F_{A_t}(x)=t^2F_C(tx)$, hence $\|F_{A_t}\|_2=\|F_C\|_{L^2(B_t)}\le\|F_A\|_2$ for $t>0$, and $\|F_{A_t}\|_3=t^{2/3}\|F_C\|_{L^3(B_t)}\le\|F_C\|_3$. The same inequalities at $t=0$ are immediate. There are finite constants $L,X$ for which $\|A_t-A_s\|_{W^{1,3}}\le L|t-s|$ and $1+\sup_t(\|A_t\|_{W^{1,3}}+\|F_{A_t}\|_3)\le X$: differentiate $tC(tx)$ and $t^2DC(tx)$ in $t$, using bounded derivatives of the fixed smooth $C$ through order two.

**Uniform critical improvement in any admissible gauge.** Choose $\rho>0$ no larger than $\rho_c,\rho_2,\rho_3$ in [F1]–[F2]. Call $t$ admissible if some $g\in\mathcal G_N$ has $a=A_t^g\in Y_3$, $d^*a=0$ and $\|a\|_4\le\rho$. All such forms belong to $Y_2$ by finite-volume norm comparison of their smooth normal approximants. By [F1], curvature covariance and [F4], there is a fixed $K_0$ such that $\|a\|_{W^{1,2}}\le C_2\|F_A\|_2$ and $\|a\|_4\le K_0\|F_A\|_2$. Also $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_3\|F_{A_t}\|_3\le C_3X$. Choose the theorem's fixed $\varepsilon>0$ so that $K_0\varepsilon\le\rho/4$. Consequently every admissible gauge has the improved margin $\|a\|_4\le\rho/4$, and its higher connection norm is bounded by a constant depending only on $X$. These estimates require only the given curvature bound, once admissibility holds.

**A uniform bound on the transported perturbation.** In an admissible gauge, $dg=g a-A_tg$ holds as a weak matrix identity. Unitarity and [F4] give $\|dg\|_{12}\le C(\|a\|_{12}+\|A_t\|_{12})\le C_X$, with $C_X$ independent of $t$ and of the chosen admissible gauge. For another parameter $s$, set $\lambda=g^{-1}(A_s-A_t)g$. Product differentiation, $g^{-1}=g^*$, Holder and $W^{1,3}\hookrightarrow L^4$ give $\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C(1+\|dg\|_{12})\|A_s-A_t\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_XL|s-t|$. Moreover $\lambda\in Y_3$: approximate $g$ by the defining smooth Neumann gauges of $\mathcal G_N$; conjugating the smooth zero-normal form $A_s-A_t$ by these gauges preserves zero normal component, and [F5] gives convergence in $W^{1,3}$.

**A uniform admissibility step.** Let $K_4$ be the fixed embedding norm from $W^{1,3}$ to $L^4$. Using the uniform bound for $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}$ in step 3.1, choose $\delta_X>0$ below the perturbation threshold of [F2] and so small that $K_4C_c(1+C_3X)\delta_X\le\rho/4$. Choose $\kappa>0$ so that $C_XL\kappa<\delta_X$, replacing $L$ by $1+L$ in this choice if necessary. Whenever $t$ is admissible and $|s-t|<\kappa$, step 4.1 allows [F2] to correct $a+\lambda$ by $h\in\mathcal G_N$. The result is $b=(a+\lambda)^h=A_s^{gh}\in Y_3$, Coulomb, and $\|b-a\|_4\le\rho/4$. The group $\mathcal G_N$ is closed under multiplication by the Sobolev product and approximation argument in [F2], so $gh\in\mathcal G_N$. Step 3.1 gives $\|b\|_4\le\rho/2<\rho$. Thus $s$ is admissible, with the same step length $\kappa$ for every admissible $t$.

**Finite construction reaches the original connection.** At $t=0$, take $g=I$ and $a=0$, so admissibility holds. Choose a positive integer $N$ with $1/N<\kappa$ and successively apply step 5.1 to $t_j=j/N$, $j=0,\ldots,N$. This finite induction constructs an admissible $G\in\mathcal G_N$ at $t=1$, with $a=C^G$ Coulomb and in $Y_3$. Take the total gauge $g=UG$. Step 2.1 gives $a=A^g$, and step 3.1 gives $\|a\|_{W^{1,2}}+\|a\|_4\le(C_2+K_0)\|F_A\|_2$ and $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_3\|F_A\|_3$. In particular the construction obtains a gauge from small curvature alone. It used no assumed small potential norm of the original connection: the admissible small potentials were constructed from the zero starting connection by finitely many proved correction steps.

**Higher regularity from the constructed Neumann inverse.** The family gauge $G$ is in $W^{2,3}$ and obeys $\partial_iG=G a_i-(A_1)_iG$. Contracting its derivative and using $\sum_i\partial_i a_i=0$ gives $\Delta G=\sum_i((\partial_iG)a_i-(A_1)_i\partial_iG)-(\operatorname{div}A_1)G$. Initially $\nabla G,a\in L^{12}$ by [F4], while $A_1$ is smooth and $G$ is bounded; hence the right side belongs to $L^6$. The form $dG$ belongs to $Y_3$ with target the real eight-dimensional matrix space, by the defining smooth Neumann approximation of $G$. The integration identity of [F1] applied to $dG$ therefore gives the zero-normal weak identity for each component of $G$. In particular $-\Delta G$ has zero mean. Apply [F3] at $p=6$ to each component, after subtracting its mean, and use weak-solution uniqueness to conclude $G\in W^{2,6}$. By [F4] its first derivatives are now bounded; the displayed equation then has bounded right side, because $a=G^{-1}dG+G^{-1}A_1G$ is bounded as well. For every finite $p\ge2$, apply [F3] again to this same zero-mean source and uniqueness to obtain $G\in W^{2,p}$. The smooth factor $U$ preserves this regularity for the total gauge $g$, and the gauge formula gives $a\in W^{1,p}$ by ordinary weak product differentiation. This proves exactly the claimed Sobolev regularity, without asserting unproved smooth boundary bootstrapping.

**Given finite equivariance.** Suppose the stated $\Gamma,\tau$ data are present. The equality $M(s,\gamma x)=d\tau_\gamma(M(s,x))$ follows from the equivariance of $A$ evaluated on the radial vector. Constant conjugation commutes with all products and integrals in step 1.1, so $U(\gamma x)=\tau_\gamma(U(x))$. Hence $C$ and every $A_t$ have the same equivariance. The initial gauge $I$ is equivariant. If an admissible family gauge is equivariant, its transported perturbation in step 4.1 is equivariant, and [F2] supplies an equivariant correction. The finite induction of step 6.1 therefore produces equivariant $G$ and total $g=UG$. Only the conjugation action is used; scalar representatives of a projective unitary element act trivially, so a lift to an $SU(2)$ representation is unnecessary.

**Scaling and overlap compatibility.** For $B_r$, pull back the connection as $A_r(y)=rA(ry)$. Its critical curvature norm equals $\|F_A\|_2$. Apply the unit-ball construction and define the physical gauge by $g(x)=g_r(x/r)$. The transformed one-form obeys $a_r(y)=r a(ry)$, so $\|a_r\|_2=r^{-1}\|a\|_2$, $\|\nabla a_r\|_2=\|\nabla a\|_2$, $\|a_r\|_4=\|a\|_4$, and the derivative/curvature $L^3$ norms have common factor $r^{2/3}$. This gives both stated estimates and preserves the approximation class, regularity and equivariance. Finally, on the given overlaps the continuous representatives of $g_i$ supplied by [F4] make $h_{ij}=g_i^{-1}t_{ij}g_j$ continuous and $W^{2,3}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by [F5]. Direct multiplication gives $h_{ij}h_{jk}=h_{ik}$ pointwise, and the gauge composition identity of step 2.1 gives $a_j=a_i^{h_{ij}}$; smooth approximation justifies the equality for the Sobolev forms. Full AC is used only through the actual analytic suppliers [F1]–[F6].

boundaries.evidence: Small critical curvature on positive-radius balls gives Coulomb gauges and compatible finite overlap transitions. Assume full AC. Use the actual based earring $K\cup L\subset S^3$, its normal radius arc $\omega$, the compact exterior $X$ and a supplied $SO(3)$ bundle $P\to X$ with $w_2(P)=PD_{\mathbb F_2}[\omega]$ in the singular-data definition. Both boundary-torus restrictions of $P$ have nonzero $w_2$. The bundle admits a compatible extension to an order-two orbifold bundle over $(S^3,K\cup L)$ whose local isotropy is rotation by $\pi$, whose axis-orientation cover on each link component is nontrivial, and whose ordinary local singular residue is $\frac14\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)d\theta$ up to conjugation. It therefore supplies the compatible finite local data required by the order-two gauge-completion lemma.

For this completed data every connection has determinant-one stabilizer exactly $\{\pm1\}$. The bundle on the exterior also has an actual $U(2)$ lift with a chosen determinant line and determinant connection, as needed for cylinder holonomy functions. These statements concern the topology and analytic input data, not independence of the resulting choices or construction of Floer homology. The supplied-bundle existence clause of the original definition is retained; this result does not classify all singular extensions up to canonical isomorphism.

Assume full AC. Let a compact smooth pair $(M,S)$ without boundary of dimension three or four have $S$ of codimension two, and supply finite branched charts $(y,w)\mapsto(y,w^2)$ with group $\mathbb Z/2$ acting by $w\mapsto-w$, together with their compatible coordinate lifts. Supply a smooth orbifold metric and an $SO(3)$ bundle in these charts with nontrivial isotropy a rotation by $\pi$ about a line. Use its determinant-one gauge transformations: in each local quaternionic lift they obey $u(y,-w)=\rho u(y,w)\rho^{-1}$, where $\rho=\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)$ and $\rho^2=-1$. These conjugation conditions are independent of the sign of the lift.

Finite-chart invariant Sobolev spaces $H^k$ are Hilbert spaces with smooth invariant density, compact $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^k$ inclusion, and the usual dimension-three or dimension-four Sobolev product and embedding estimates. For $k\ge3$, the $H^{k+1}$ determinant-one gauge group is a Banach Lie group acting smoothly on the affine $H^k$ connection space. At an irreducible connection, Coulomb slices give a smooth unbased quotient and equation bundle; arbitrary connecting gauges between converging slice representatives have converging $H^{k+1}$ subsequences, up to their central ambiguity.

Every smooth first-order operator with scalar Clifford square, acting on these bundles and respecting the invariant local conditions, is Fredholm $H^k\to H^{k-1}$ on compact $M$. Its kernel and cokernel are smooth. A formally selfadjoint such operator $H$ has domain $H^1$ in $L^2$, compact resolvent and a complete real discrete spectrum of finite multiplicity. In particular this applies to the extended three-dimensional Hessian $H_B(\phi,b)=(d_B^*b,d_B\phi+*d_Bb)$, and in dimension four to $d_A^*\oplus\sqrt2d_A^+$.

On an infinite cylinder over the compact three-dimensional pair, suppose $H(t)$ has one fixed first-order principal part, shared by $H_\pm$, throughout the cylinder and differs from $H_\pm$ by smooth zero-order coefficients tending to zero with their first $k$ derivatives, while the selfadjoint limiting $H_\pm$ are invertible. The same assertion allows additional possibly nonlocal zero-order operators $R(t)$: every $\partial_t^aR(t)$ is bounded $H^j(Y)\to H^j(Y)$ for the needed integer orders, these bounds are uniform, and they converge on the ends in those operator norms; the two limiting full Hessians are selfadjoint and invertible on their $H^1$ domains. Then $\partial_t+H(t):H^k\to H^{k-1}$, including these additional terms, is Fredholm. The conclusion remains true on spaces weighted by $e^{\delta|t|}$ if $0\le\delta<\min\operatorname{dist}(0,\operatorname{spec}H_\pm)$. No index formula, nonlinear asymptotic convergence, transversality, trajectory compactification or Floer differential is asserted here.

Assume full AC. Supply a compact oriented three-dimensional order-two singular pair $(Y,K)$, compatible orbifold bundle data and determinant-one gauges as in the preceding completion lemma, and a fixed $U(2)$ lift on $Y\setminus K$ with fixed determinant connection. Suppose every connection in this singular configuration space has stabilizer $\{\pm1\}$. Use $H^k/H^{k+1}$, $k\ge3$.

There is a separable Banach space $\mathcal P$ of countable weighted sums of smooth cylinder functions supported away from $K$. For $\pi\in\mathcal P$ its function $f_\pi$ is bounded, smooth and gauge invariant, and its $L^2$ gradient $V_\pi$ is a smooth gauge-equivariant $H^k$ vector field. It is uniformly pointwise bounded by $C\|\pi\|_{\mathcal P}$, independently of the connection; its derivative is bounded on $L^2$ with the same type of uniform bound. Its spatial covariant derivatives have polynomial bounds in lower spatial covariant derivatives of curvature, with constants uniform on bounded perturbation sets.

The critical-point projection for $*F_B+V_\pi(B)=0$ is proper over compact subsets of $\mathcal P$ in the actual $H^k$ quotient. An open dense subset of $\mathcal P$ has only nondegenerate critical points; their set is finite. All critical connections are smooth in orbifold gauges. This result proves the critical set and not transversality, compactness or gluing for nonconstant trajectories. The existence of the stipulated global singular data and $U(2)$ lift is not asserted here.

Assume full AC. Fix the constructed earring data and a holonomy perturbation with finitely many nondegenerate critical points. There is a separable Banach space of further cylinder perturbations whose functions and all connection derivatives vanish at those critical points. Sufficiently small such perturbations retain exactly the same critical points and Hessians. A residual dense set of these perturbations makes every nonconstant finite-energy trajectory in every relative class regular, at every integer Fredholm index. The corresponding translation quotient is a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold of dimension $I-1$. In particular there are no nonconstant trajectories with $I\le0$.

Trajectories here are solutions in the actual unweighted cylindrical configuration spaces with critical asymptotics, and finite energy is the flow energy defined above. Establishing that arbitrary finite-flow-energy solutions have those asymptotics, and proving compactifications or gluing collars, remain separate claims. No orientability assertion is made here.

Assume full AC. Use the earring singular data, completed determinant-one gauge group $\mathcal G$, and fixed determinant lift constructed above. The restriction to the two core circles gives an exact sequence of component groups
$$0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\longrightarrow\pi_0\mathcal G\longrightarrow(\mathbb Z/2)^2\longrightarrow0,$$
where the kernel generator is a degree-one gauge transformation supported in a ball disjoint from the singular link. For a loop in the unbased configuration quotient define $I$ as the index of its cylindrical ASD deformation operator with fixed invertible asymptotic Hessian, and define its topological energy period by twice the Chern–Simons drop, using inner product $-\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb C^2}$. Then
$$\mathcal E=\pi^2 I,\qquad I\in4\mathbb Z.$$
Both quantities vanish on the central stabilizer and descend to actual quotient loops.

Fix any perturbation in the nondegenerate critical class of the preceding critical-set lemma. For critical endpoints $\alpha,\beta$ and a relative path class $z$, let $I_z$ be the corresponding cylindrical index and $\mathcal E_z$ twice the drop of the perturbed functional. There is a constant $C$ depending on this fixed data, but not on $z,\alpha,\beta$, such that $|\mathcal E_z-\pi^2I_z|\le C$. For every finite upper index bound $D$, only finitely many endpoint pairs and relative classes of nonconstant gradient trajectories with $I_z\le D$ can occur, and their flow energies satisfy $0<\mathcal E_z\le\pi^2D+C$.

Here finite flow energy means $2\int_{\mathbb R}\|\partial_tB\|_2^2dt$ in temporal gauge, equivalently the perturbed topological energy. It does not mean the unrenormalized integral of curvature squared over the whole cylinder when its perturbed critical endpoints are nonflat. No trajectory compactness, regularity or gluing conclusion is part of this result.

Assume full AC. Let $\Gamma=\mathbb Z/2$ act on $S^4=\mathbb R^4\cup\{\infty\}$ by rotation by $\pi$ in one normal two-plane, with fixed two-sphere. Supply a smooth equivariant $SO(3)$ bundle whose isotropy on that fixed sphere is a rotation by $\pi$. If $A$ is any nonflat equivariant anti-self-dual connection, its unbased invariant ASD complex has zero obstruction space and kernel dimension at least three. The corresponding flat reference bundle with constant fiber action has unbased index $-1$. Consequently the relative ASD index of this bubble against that flat reference is at least four.

At an ordinary point the analogous relative index loss is at least eight. These conclusions include every nonflat charge, not just BPST charge one.

More precisely, suppose two Fredholm ASD deformation operators on a compact four-orbifold, or on a cylinder with identical invertible limiting Hessians, have bundles identified away from one standard ball or one such order-two quotient ball. Form the comparison bundle $Q$ on $S^4$ (respectively $S^4/\Gamma$) by gluing their local ball bundles with that boundary identification, and let $Q_0$ be the constant reference. Then their index difference is exactly $\operatorname{ind}D_Q-\operatorname{ind}D_{Q_0}$. Thus when $Q$ is an actual nonflat ASD bubble the preceding lower bounds apply. The result does not assume that every degeneration has such a comparison until point-removal and topological identification have been proved for that degeneration.

Assume full AC. Use the fixed earring orbifold data, metric and an allowed holonomy perturbation in a bounded set of the constructed perturbation space. On every compact subcylinder, a sequence of smooth perturbed ASD trajectories with a common upper bound on flow energy has, after gauges and a subsequence, a limit away from finitely many points. On that punctured subcylinder the convergence is strong $W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $p$ in local gauges. The limiting connection extends across those points as a smooth perturbed ASD connection on an actual smooth orbifold bundle. The lost energy at each point is a positive multiple of $8\pi^2$ at an ordinary point and a positive multiple of $4\pi^2$ on the singular surface, in the fundamental trace convention.

All concentrated bundles are accounted for by finitely many nonflat ordinary or order-two invariant ASD sphere bubbles with flat matching collars and no additional clutching contribution on the intervening necks. Thus the cylindrical index difference is the sum of their actual relative indices, at least eight per ordinary bubble and at least four per invariant bubble. In particular every concentration point has index loss at least four. If there are no concentration points, convergence on smaller closed subcylinders is smooth in orbifold gauges. The statement is local in the cylinder direction and does not assert convergence at its infinite ends or any nonlinear gluing collar.

Assume full AC. For the constructed earring data choose one of the all-index regular holonomy perturbations with its finite nondegenerate critical set. Every smooth trajectory of finite flow energy has a single critical orbit at each infinite end and, in actual determinant-one orbifold gauges, converges to representatives exponentially in every Sobolev order. For every fixed integer index bound there are only finitely many possible endpoint pairs and relative classes of nonconstant trajectories.

Sequences of trajectories of index one or two have, modulo translations, subsequences converging to finite broken trajectories without bubbles. The total index is the sum of the positive indices of the nonconstant levels. Thus the index-one translation quotient is a compact finite set; an index-two sequence has either a smooth unbroken limit or precisely two index-one levels. This statement identifies sequential limits and does not yet assert gluing collars or orientations.

Assume full AC and the actual all-index regular earring perturbation. Every ordered broken pair of index-one trajectories has a gluing collar of index-two unparametrized trajectories. Each sufficiently broken index-two trajectory belongs to precisely the collar of its broken limit. The glued relative class is the actual concatenation class. Together with the unbroken moduli, these collars make the index-two compactification a compact one-dimensional manifold with boundary the ordered broken pairs. The smooth structure is its ordinary smooth structure in the interior and the collar smooth structure at its boundary. No assertion of analyticity in an arbitrarily preassigned exponential neck coordinate is made.

Assume full AC and the constructed earring data. The real determinant line of the cylindrical ASD operator is orientable on every fixed-endpoint trajectory configuration component. One can choose rank-one integral orientation modules for the critical points and compatible determinant identifications for every relative trajectory class. They are compatible with concatenation, gauge equivalence and the nonlinear broken-trajectory collars. With the translation orientation removed, the signed boundary of an index-two compactification is the signed sum of its ordered index-one broken pairs. Consequently the integral signed differential defined by those pairs has square zero. Choices of bases in the critical orientation modules change the resulting complex by the corresponding diagonal signs.

Assume full AC. Integral earring instanton complexes formed from any two regular orbifold metrics and allowed regular holonomy perturbations of the fixed based earring data are related by continuation chain maps. A map depends only on its endpoints up to chain homotopy and the declared determinant-orientation sign choices. Continuation maps compose up to chain homotopy, and the maps in reverse directions are inverse chain homotopy equivalences. Transport under an isotopy of the based knot and its earring data gives the corresponding homology isomorphism. This statement concerns the singular instanton complex; it makes no assertion about sutured-closure independence, a knot-detection theorem or an instanton surgery formula.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Let $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ be oriented by $dx\wedge dy$, and identify $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^2$ in the standard basis, so the algebraic intersection of classes $v,w$ is $\det(v,w)$. Let $\gamma_0,\gamma_1\subset T$ be smooth embedded circles that are not null-homotopic. Orient them so that their homology classes agree, and suppose their common class $v\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ is primitive, meaning it is not an integer multiple $m u$ with $|m|>1$. Then $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ are isotopic through embedded circles in $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, its Seifert genus is zero if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

Since $c$ is essential on the torus, it is nonseparating: a separating simple curve on a genus-one surface cuts off a disk on one side and is null-homotopic. Cutting the torus along $c$ therefore gives a connected orientable surface with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero, hence an annulus. An embedded arc joining its two boundary circles closes after regluing to a loop meeting $c$ transversely once. The algebraic intersection is therefore $\pm1$, so $[c]$ is primitive in $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Because $c=\partial D$, its image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero. By [F2], write $[c]=q[\lambda]$ for an integer $q$. Since both $[c]$ and $[\lambda]$ are primitive, $q=\pm1$. Orient $c$ to make $[c]=[\lambda]$. By [F3], $c$ is isotopic on $T_K$ to a chosen simple representative of the preferred longitude.

In product coordinates $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, the curve $c$ has core degree one by [F2], so its torus class is $(1,k)$ for an integer $k$. The graph $\gamma_k(t)=(e^{it},e^{ikt})$ has that class. By [F3], choose a smooth isotopy $c_s(t)=(u_s(t),z_s(t))$ on the boundary torus from $c$ to $\gamma_k$, stationary near its final time after smooth reparametrization. This isotopy need not trace an embedded annulus on the torus itself. Instead choose a smooth strictly decreasing radius $r(s)$ from $1$ to $1/2$ with nonzero derivative, and use $(s,t)\mapsto(u_s(t),r(s)z_s(t))$ in the tube. Distinct $s$ have distinct radii, while each fixed-$s$ curve is embedded; moreover the time derivative has nonzero radial component and is independent of its circle tangent. This gives a smooth embedded annulus with outer boundary exactly $c$ and inner boundary the radius-$1/2$ copy of $\gamma_k$. Continue it inward by $(r,t)\mapsto(e^{it},r e^{ikt})$ for $0\le r\le1/2$. The stationary final curve makes the collars agree; the inward annulus is smooth and regular even at $r=0$ and has core boundary $K$. The resulting annulus lies otherwise in the interior of $N(K)$.

If the given disk is only boundary-preimage embedded, first replace it using [F5] by a neat smooth disk in $E_K$ with the same boundary $c$. The annulus of step 3.1 has nonzero inward radial derivative at $c$ on the tube side. The resulting proper disk $D$ on the exterior side and this annulus on the tube side meet only along $c$. citations.quote:
Assume full AC. For any smooth based link $L\subset S^3$ with a chosen nonzero normal vector at its marked point, add the small meridional earring on that marked component and its joining arc. With the corresponding determinant-one singular bundle data, finite nondegenerate critical points and all-index regular holonomy perturbations give a finite free integral cochain complex. Its differential counts all index-one classes and has square zero; its homology, denoted $I^\natural(L;\mathbb Z)$, is independent of regular metric and perturbation and invariant under isotopy of the based link data, with the same orientation sign convention as for knots. For a knot it agrees with the singular knot complex already constructed.

For the standard $n$-component unlink with a marked component, $n\ge1$, this group is free of rank $2^{n-1}$. It has a chosen representative complex with zero differential and sphere-pole generators, in the even relative degrees of the unlink model. This theorem does not supply a canonical tensor-product identification under arbitrary cobordisms, saddle maps, an exact triangle or a KHI identification.

Assume full AC. In $[0,m]\times S^3$ take a finite composite of the specified local skein saddles and standard disk births or deaths, with every surface component meeting a temporal boundary and every local ball disjoint from the fixed basepoint earring and its radius arc. Include the vertical earring annulus in the surface $\Sigma$, and put $\Omega=[0,m]\times\omega$. There are actual marked order-two orbifold $SO(3)$ data on this four-dimensional pair, product in the temporal end collars, with surface isotropy rotation by $\pi$ and ordinary residue $\frac14\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)d\theta$. Their sheet cover on $\Sigma$ is dual modulo two to $\partial\Omega\cap\Sigma$. The exterior bundle has $w_2=PD_{\mathbb F_2}[\Omega]$ and an actual $U(2)$ lift with determinant class $PD_{\mathbb Z}[\Omega]$. Every determinant-one connection has central stabilizer only. The endpoint restrictions are admissible based-link earring data, with nontrivial axis cover on the two marked components and trivial axis covers on the other oriented end components.

The assertion is existence of compatible backgrounds for these actual surfaces. It asserts no four-dimensional count, cobordism-map invariance or sutured nonvanishing theorem. Whole end collars may be fixed for a chosen background. Cut pieces of that background retain their actual restriction identifications.

Assume full AC. Fix a marked earring cobordism made from the specified saddles and standard disk births or deaths, initially with every surface component meeting a temporal boundary, or any finite composite of such cobordisms with its actual glued background. Fix the actual orbifold and exterior determinant background, fixed regular nondegenerate critical data on its based-link ends, and a compact finite-dimensional parameter manifold with corners $P$. Boundary faces may prescribe broken metrics only along admissible based-link cuts carrying the same product data. Assume the prescribed face data already have regular counts and collars and agree on their corners. Then one can choose gauge-covariant bulk holonomy perturbations, product with the fixed gradient perturbations on the ends and relative to those face data, so all finite-energy fixed-endpoint cobordism moduli spaces are regular, for every marked relative class. In total expected dimensions zero and one, their unions over ALL relative classes are finite oriented sets and compact oriented one-manifolds with the expected broken ends and metric-face ends. Every such end has an exhaustive nonlinear collar and the determinant boundary sign is the ordered composition sign. Thus these counts give integral chain maps and relative chain homotopies; compositions are represented by the admissible stretching families with their actual orientation identifications.

No cut with a reducible critical point is included in this theorem. It does not prove the reducible unknot-cut vanishing, the triple-saddle degree-one cap count, or the identification of saddle maps with the Khovanov Frobenius operations.

Assume full AC. Let three based smooth links in the oriented three-sphere agree outside a ball disjoint from the earring and its marking arc, and differ there by the three cyclic skein tangles. Give their based-link instanton complexes compatible admissible marked backgrounds. The oriented saddle cobordism counts define an integral exact triangle on their instanton homology. With the actual relative grading shifts, the triangle is represented by a quasi-isomorphism of a mapping cone with the third instanton complex. These maps, null homotopies and mapping-cone comparisons can be chosen relative to any finite collection of already compatible disjoint saddle and continuation families.

Assume full AC and the actual based-link earring count, composition and integral skein operations of the named suppliers. Fix ONE finite planar resolution diagram, its marked base component and its finite collection of planar saddle cobordisms. Use the actual compatible backgrounds and determinant orientations relative to their common marked collars. Then the free integral unlink groups and these ACTUAL saddle maps admit simultaneous identifications with the reduced Frobenius module of
$$A=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^2),\qquad 1=v_+,\quad x=v_-,\quad |v_+|=0,\quad |v_-|=2\pmod4.$$
An unlink with one marked component and m other ordered components has group A tensor ... tensor A, with m factors; the marked factor is the quotient A/(x)=Z. A disk birth inserts v_+, and a disk death has epsilon(v_+)=0, epsilon(v_-)=1. On two unmarked components the merge and split are
$$\mu(1\otimes1)=1,\quad\mu(1\otimes x)=\mu(x\otimes1)=x,\quad\mu(x\otimes x)=0,$$
$$\Delta(1)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x,\qquad\Delta(x)=x\otimes x.$$
A merge with the marked component is the quotient action 1 tensor 1 to 1, 1 tensor x to zero; a split of the marked component sends 1 to 1 tensor x. The bases are primitive integral bases, not rational bases recovered after a rank computation. Reordering the unmarked components permutes their even factors.

These identifications are compatible with the actual finite planar vertex and saddle identifications used for that diagram, including the common marked collar. They do not assert a split-link excision theorem, invariance under arbitrary unlink concordances or arbitrary unlink-motion loops, or a new analytic construction beyond the named actual count suppliers. The cube's ordered orientation-line edge signs are retained; they are not replaced by independently chosen signs for each occurrence of a saddle.

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Edges not meeting the interval use $m$ or $\Delta$. This based tangle cube is the quotient complex above, with the stated quantum shift.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram, order its crossings as $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and form the direct sum of state modules $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$ over all functions $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$. Here $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, each crossing is changed from its A-smoothing at $0$ to its B-smoothing at $1$, and the edge map is the multiplication $m$ for a merge or comultiplication $\Delta$ for a split, multiplied by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$ on the edge at $c_j$. Then the sum $d$ of all edge maps satisfies $d^2=0$.

If the filtration on every $C_n$ is finite, the spectral sequence of the filtered chain complex stabilizes pointwise and naturally abuts to $H_n(C)$ with its image filtration. This homology filtration is finite, exhaustive and separated. No uniform filtration bound in n is required.

derivations.claim: **The multi-saddle parameter spaces and their entire boundary.** Use the resolution labels of the reflected diagram, with an edge increasing one coordinate. Write $C_v$ for the actual based-link complex of that planar resolution. For $v<w$, let $S$ be its set of changed crossings, $k=|S|$. Put one standard saddle at time $\tau_j$ in each of its disjoint crossing balls; collisions of times are allowed, since the spatial balls are disjoint. Divide simultaneous translation out of $\mathbb R^S$, giving a parameter space of dimension $k-1$. Its broken compactification is constructed as follows. A boundary chart is indexed by an ordered partition $S=B_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup B_l$: retain the centered finite times within each block, and give successive block centers gaps $T_r$, with boundary coordinate $q_r=e^{-T_r}\ge0$. At $q_r=0$ the corresponding cylinder is broken. Refining a block gives the corner charts. On chart overlaps centering changes a gap by a smooth bounded function of the retained block times, so $q_r$ changes by a smooth positive factor; two successive subdivisions give the same ordered gaps. These are manifold-with-corners charts. They cover a compact space: in any sequence normalize one time, pass to a fixed order of the finitely many labels, and select successive gaps which are bounded or diverge to positive infinity. The bounded clusters give finite centered limits after subdivision into their own bounded/divergent clusters, and there are at most $k$ labels. This proves sequential compactness in these finite partition charts; their countable coordinate basis and Hausdorff gap coordinates give compactness. Its facets are exactly the two nonempty ordered blocks. Such a facet is the product of the two smaller saddle parameter spaces, with the intermediate resolution as its cut; higher corners are their ordered iterates. Actual metrics are the fixed saddle metrics translated to these times, with product critical collars between separated blocks. Use their existing product metrics on every boundary chart and extend over the remaining compact interior by a finite partition in the convex cone of positive metrics. Here the background compatibility can be made literal. Put the planar resolution curves and the saddle surfaces in projection-plane times time; a local saddle has graph $t=x^2-y^2$ and normal coordinate $z=0$. The constant viewing-normal vector $\partial_z$ is a nonzero normal section on every such panel and every unchanged planar strand strip. Fix the product normal model on the separate earring annulus. Thus the normal splitting in [F2] uses the SAME section on every cube face, rather than separately chosen graph-spine sections. The sheet cover is cut along the SAME vertical marking arcs, outside all crossing balls. Construct the exterior determinant line by the degree-one angular Thom clutch around the fixed marking rectangle; it is the fixed product line outside the crossing balls and the fixed trivial line inside each ball, since the rectangle misses them. On the normal tube use the explicit common sheet gluing $\rho(v)w=v\bar w$ of [F2], with these normal coordinates. Restriction at an intermediate resolution, and commuting two disjoint saddles, now preserve these very transition functions and their determinant trivializations. Hence all backgrounds and all corner identifications agree as actual gluing data. Relative perturbations from [F2], by induction on $k$, therefore agree on all corners.

**The total differential and the exact edge signs.** Orient $\mathbb R^S/\mathbb R$ by the ordered crossing coordinates together with the positive simultaneous-translation direction. Retain the parameter orientation line instead of making separate arbitrary signs on its faces. At vertex $v$ tensor $C_v$ with the top exterior line $E_v=\bigwedge^{|v|}\mathbb Z^{\{j:v_j=1\}}$, of parity $|v|$. For an edge increasing $j$, identify the line map with insertion of $e_j$ and reorder into increasing crossing order. Its sign is exactly $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v_i}$. For a larger $S$, use the analogous ordered exterior insertion and the parameter orientation line to define the signed zero-dimensional count $D_{wv}$. Include the vertex differential as $D_{vv}$. The relative grading shift makes each total map odd: its unshifted parity is $1-k$, from its $k-1$ parameters and the even local saddle degree, whereas exterior insertion changes parity by $k$. A one-dimensional parameter moduli space has only end-trajectory breaks and the two-block facets of step 1.1; it has no unlisted bubbles or extra class ends by [F2]. Ordered determinant excision identifies each boundary count with its corresponding composition $D_{wu}D_{uv}$. Its sign is precisely the exterior shuffle sign: move the ordered first block past the second in the exact sequence of their time-coordinate spaces, separating the positive gap and translation factors. For one element in each block this is the anticommutation $e_ie_j=-e_je_i$; for general blocks it is its repeated shuffle. Thus the algebraic boundary-zero identity is the coefficient of $D^2$ at every vertex pair. The finite direct sum $T=\bigoplus_v C_v\otimes E_v$ with $D=\sum_{v\le w}D_{wv}$ is an integral complex. Checkerboard boundary orientations of the planar regions orient all the surfaces consistently; their product determinant orientations are those of [F4]. If the skein labels are initially decreasing, reversing all labels contributes the fixed edge factor $(-1)^{j-1}$, removed by the vertex sign $(-1)^{\sum_j(j-1)v_j}$. The displayed increasing edge sign is therefore literal in [F5]'s convention.

**Why this total complex is the original instanton complex.** Leave one crossing unresolved and keep the other resolution parameters. The total complex obtained by resolving that crossing decomposes into its two face totals and their off-diagonal saddle-family map; by step 2.1 this is its actual mapping cone, with the indicated shifts. Use [F3]'s cone comparison on that crossing relative to every already fixed disjoint saddle family. Its components with other crossings changed are the counts over the same disjoint time families, with the local two-saddle homotopy and three-saddle pentagon inserted. Their boundary strata are exactly those already specified in [F3] and step 1.1. The relative perturbations agree on their common faces, and their boundary formulas are exactly the assertion that these components give a filtered chain map from the partially unresolved total to this cone. Filter both by the other crossings. On its associated graded this map is the vertexwise cone quasi-isomorphism of [F3]. A finite filtered comparison with quasi-isomorphic associated graded is itself a quasi-isomorphism: induct on the filtration length, use the short exact sequence of a final filtration piece and its quotient, and chase the long exact sequences in cohomology. No convergence of an infinite filtration is used. Resolve the crossings one at a time. This gives a composite quasi-isomorphism between $T$ and the original complex $C(K)$, including the zero-crossing case, which is the identity. Hence $H(T,D)\cong I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$. This is an actual filtered-cone construction, not an inference that matching vertex ranks determines the abutment.

**The first two pages.** Filter $T$ by $F^pT=\bigoplus_{|v|\ge p}C_v\otimes E_v$. Every count increases the number of resolved coordinates, so this is a bounded filtration by subcomplexes. On the associated graded the differential is just the vertex differential, hence $E_1=\bigoplus_v I^\natural(D_v;\mathbb Z)\otimes E_v$. Its first differential is exactly the one-crossing saddle map, with the insertion sign computed in step 2.1; all larger saddle sets increase filtration by at least two. By [F4], the ordered planar unlink groups have the primitive reduced Frobenius bases and every one of these actual saddle maps is multiplication on a merge or comultiplication on a split, with the identity on the remaining factors. The marked circle uses the one-dimensional reduced factor. The local tetrahedral smoothing chart interchanges its two planar pairings when the over- and under-strands are reflected; these are precisely the A- and B-resolutions of the reflected diagram in [F5]. Thus the identified signed first-page complex is the reduced integral Khovanov cube of $\overline D$, not merely a vector space with the same rank. Its cohomology is the stated reduced integral $E_2$ page.

**Convergence and exact scope.** The filtration has only $n+1$ nonzero levels and the even and odd total chain groups are finite free abelian. Forget any finer instanton grading. To apply the ordinary integer-graded finite-filtration theorem literally, unroll this parity complex by $\widehat T^{2q+r}=T^r$, $r=0,1$, with the repeated differential, and reverse cohomological indices if using [F5] in its chain convention. Every integer degree has the same finite filtration bounds. The cycles, boundaries and pages are two-periodic, so [F5] applies degreewise and the result folds back to the two parity degrees. The uniform finite filtration length makes every differential with filtration change greater than $n$ vanish. Thus it gives a finite spectral sequence with finite total pages and abutment the associated graded of the induced finite filtration on $H(T,D)$. Step 3.1 identifies this abutment with $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$ in the usual filtered-homology sense. All counts used their actual integral determinant orientations, exhaustive collars and all-class finiteness. Full AC is inherited from their analytic and bundle constructions; once these finite chain groups and maps exist, the filtration, exterior signs and finite exact-sequence arguments introduce no additional choice. The construction is for the fixed finite based diagram; neither an invariance theorem for its intermediate pages nor a sutured/KHI nonvanishing statement has been used or asserted. This proves every claim of the original Statement.

citations.quote: Assume full AC and fix a smooth based knot $K\subset S^3$ with the earring and admissible singular bundle data of the preceding definitions. For regular perturbation data, the perturbed Chern–Simons critical points and finite-energy singular anti-self-dual trajectories define a finite free cochain complex $C^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$ with differential $d$ satisfying $d^2=0$. Its homology is independent of the chosen regular metric and perturbation up to the declared overall sign and is invariant under isotopy of the based knot data.

derivations.claim: In the chosen closure, the standard marked circle meets $\bar R$ once, so $c_1(w)$ evaluates oddly on $\bar R$. The ordinary admissible theory in [F3] therefore applies. The torus has genus one, so the extreme-surface identity in [F3] gives $\ker(\mu(y)-2)\cap\ker\mu(\bar R)^N=\ker(\mu(y)-2)\cap\ker\mu(\bar R)$ for every $N\ge1$. Taking the union over $N$ therefore identifies the Definition's generalized surface-$0$/ordinary point-$+2$ subspace with the source's ordinary simultaneous $(0,2)$ eigenspace $I_*(\bar Y\mid\bar R)_w$. This is the exact torus convention in [F4], rather than an assumption of semisimplicity. It is finite-dimensional, and [F4] identifies the allowed closures up to isomorphism. This proves well-definedness of the rational group used here, without choosing a canonical basis or confusing it with the doubled full ordinary group.

Apply [F6] with the same based earring, connecting arc and determinant normalization. It gives the required rational isomorphism $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Q)\cong KHI(K;\mathbb Q)$. The local complex in [F1] is exactly its source.

For a nontrivial smooth classical knot, the published genus/rank consequence in [F5] gives $\dim_{\mathbb Q}KHI(K;\mathbb Q)>1$. This is the established nonvanishing/decomposition input, explicitly imported rather than deduced from the already resolved singular complex or integral cube.

For the unknot $U$, combine [F2] with step 2.1 to obtain $\dim_{\mathbb Q}KHI(U;\mathbb Q)=1$. This retains the local integral unknot calculation; the external input is the excision bridge, not a replacement for that calculation.

The unknot and nontrivial cases exhaust the knots in the statement. Steps 3.1, 2.2 show that the finite-dimensional group always has dimension at least one and has dimension one exactly for the unknot. Step 2.1 supplies the additional isomorphism claimed in the statement.
